text:
Some hunger is a feeling. This was something else.

There is a point where an empty stomach stops being a sensation and becomes a condition, one that rearranges the body, the nerves and the instincts of a living thing. A dog can cross that point quietly. No sound, no drama, no one noticing. Just a little less of her every week.

Look at the hunger she was in.

That is the title of this video, and it is the only claim I'm going to make about it. Everything else you will have to see for yourself, because this is the kind of thing that stops working the moment someone explains it to you.

But I can tell you what to look for. Most of us have learned to scroll past hunger without knowing what we're looking at. We know the word. We have almost never really seen the thing.

—

Here is what happens inside a starving body, and why it matters.

First, the body spends what is on hand: the quick-access sugar stored in the liver and muscles, gone within a day or so. Then it turns to fat, the long-term savings account. This stage can last a surprisingly long time, and from the outside it looks almost like nothing is wrong. A thinner dog. A dog who sleeps more.

Then the savings run low.

When fat is nearly gone, the body does the one thing it never wants to do: it starts consuming itself for protein. Muscle goes first, then tissue that was never meant to be spent. The heart is a muscle too. So is every muscle that holds a dog upright, lifts her head, works her jaw, carries her across a road.

This is why veterinarians look at ribs, spine, hips and shoulder blades. Not for drama. Body condition scoring is a clinical tool, usually on a scale of one to nine, and the bottom of that scale is defined by bones standing out with no fat covering them and obvious muscle loss.

The cruelest part of the process is how gradual it is. Nobody sees the day it became an emergency, because there is no such day. There is only a long slope, and everyone who passes it is looking at a slightly different point on the same slope.

—

In 1944, in the rooms beneath a university football stadium in Minnesota, thirty-six healthy young men agreed to be hungry for science. For roughly half a year they ate about half of what they were used to. The researchers expected physical changes, and they got them. What they hadn't fully expected was what happened to the men's minds.

These were ordinary, motivated volunteers. And they began thinking about food constantly. Some collected cookbooks and recipes they would never cook. They read menus the way other people read novels. Interest in the things that used to matter to them, including friends and romance, faded. Hunger didn't just empty their stomachs. It narrowed their entire world down to a single point.

And remember who those men were: people with a doctor, a schedule and a finish line. They knew exactly when it would end.

A dog has none of that. A dog doesn't know there is a study. A dog doesn't know that next week might be different. For her, hunger doesn't come with a date on the calendar. It just is, every hour, the loudest thing in the room.

—

The thing I can't stop thinking about is this: hunger may be the only force in an animal's life that can outshout fear.

A stray dog is, almost by definition, an animal that has learned to be careful around people. Doors close. Voices rise. Objects get thrown. Nothing about the human world has promised her anything. And yet, when a body is empty enough, the same animal will walk toward the very species that taught her to be wary.

Not because she trusts. Because she has run out of alternatives.

That is what makes scenes like this so hard to watch and so hard to look away from. Approaching a person is, for a starving dog, not an act of faith. It's a calculation made by a body with nothing left to lose. Whether that calculation ever turns into faith is a different story, and a much better one.

I'm not going to tell you which of those stories this is.

—

Somewhere between fifteen and forty thousand years ago (the estimates vary a lot, and scientists still argue about the details), some wolves that were a little less afraid of people began hanging around human camps. They ate what we left behind. That is one leading theory, at least, and it is not the only one. But in nearly every version of the story, the agreement between our species began at the edge of a fire, and it began with food.

We have been feeding dogs, and dogs have been counting on us to, for longer than we've had writing, farming or cities. Every dog alive today descends from animals that bet their lives on the idea that humans were a reliable source of dinner.

So when a dog goes hungry in a human place, near our houses, our cars, our streets, it isn't only a sad circumstance. It is a broken clause in one of the oldest arrangements we ever made. Nobody signed it. Both sides have honored their half for tens of thousands of years. Most of the time, the dogs kept their end better than we did.

—

Let's do some economics, because the numbers here are strange.

What does it cost to stop a dog from being hungry on a given afternoon? Not to save her forever. Just to answer the question her body is asking. A handful of dry food. A few cents. Less than the coffee you've already forgotten you bought.

And what does it cost not to? A body that digests itself. A heart that weakens muscle by muscle. A life lived at a volume of need most of us will never experience.

That is the oddest contrast in all of animal welfare. The price of acting is almost nothing, and the price of not acting is everything the animal has. The entire distance between those two numbers is made of one thing: somebody deciding to notice.

—

There is a complication hiding inside the beautiful, simple idea of "just feed her."

Veterinarians warn about something called refeeding syndrome. When a body that has been starved suddenly receives a large amount of food, its chemistry can swing hard: phosphorus, potassium and magnesium shift rapidly, and the heart and other organs come under strain. In severe cases it can be fatal. This is why the standard advice for badly underweight animals is small portions, increased gradually, ideally under a vet's guidance.

I'm telling you this for two reasons.

The first is practical. If you ever meet an animal this thin, the urge to pour out everything you have is a loving instinct, but it isn't always the safest one. A call to a vet or a rescue group before the heroic bowl can matter.

The second reason is that it reveals what rescue actually is. We like to imagine it as a single peak moment, the kind you'd put on a poster. In reality it's logistics. Patience. Measured portions. Repeated visits. A long, unglamorous stretch of doing the careful thing over and over, long after anyone is watching. The moment that goes viral is the smallest part of the work.

—

A body like this isn't built in a day.

It takes weeks, more often months, to take a dog down to this point. That isn't a comment on any one person. It's a comment on the arithmetic of attention. A starving animal in a public place has an audience long before she has help. People drive past. People walk past. Some of them notice, and tell themselves that someone else will handle it.

Psychologists have a name for that: diffusion of responsibility. The more people who witness a problem, the less likely each one is to act, because everyone quietly assumes the job belongs to somebody else. It's one of the better-documented findings in social psychology, and like every effect it has limits, but you recognize it the instant someone describes it. You've lived it. So have I.

Which means the most important event in a rescue is rarely the dramatic one. It's the earlier, smaller, less photogenic event: the moment somebody stops assuming.

—

I can't tell you what she thinks. Nobody can. Dogs don't give statements, and anyone who claims to know exactly what's going on inside a dog's head is selling something.

What science can say is more modest, and to me, more moving. Dogs are superb at attaching meaning to places, people and moments. Their sense of smell is staggering, often described as hundreds of millions of scent receptors compared with our few million, so they live inside a layer of information we can't even detect. A dog who has been fed by someone doesn't just have a pleasant moment. She files it. The person, the place, the sound, the smell, all of it becomes part of her map of the world.

Hunger works the same way in reverse. Shelter workers and behaviorists often describe formerly starving dogs who guard their food, eat as if the bowl might vanish, or panic when a meal is late. The body remembers scarcity long after the scarcity ends.

If that is true, then a single act of feeding does two jobs at once. It fills a stomach. And it begins, very slowly, to revise a map.

—

There is a quiet cruelty in what hunger does to manners.

Scarcity is the enemy of politeness, in every species. When there's plenty, even rival animals tolerate each other. When there's not enough, hierarchies sharpen, tempers shorten, and friendships get tested. Hunger turns the gentlest creatures into competitors, not because they are bad, but because their bodies are doing the math faster than their character can.

Which is worth remembering the next time you see a thin animal behaving badly around food. That behavior isn't her personality. It's her situation.

It also makes the opposite thing more striking. An environment of enough, even a small, temporary one, is what lets an animal stop calculating. You can watch the difference between a body bracing and a body relaxing. They are not subtle.

—

Attention is a kind of first aid that doesn't get named as one.

Before the food, before the vet, before the warm room and the soft bed, something far quieter has to happen. Someone has to look at an animal the rest of the world has filed under scenery, and decide that she is an individual with a particular, urgent problem.

Street dogs live in a strange social category. They are everywhere and nowhere. Visible, yet unseen. We build a mental drawer labeled "strays," and the drawer swallows the individual. One animal stops being a category the moment a person gets close enough to count her ribs.

That's why I think the real subject of videos like this isn't the dog. It's the exact second the drawer opens.

—

Now for the uncomfortable question that comes with every video like this. I think it deserves honesty rather than a feel-good dodge.

If one dog can be helped, what about all the others?

The number of free-roaming dogs in the world is commonly estimated in the hundreds of millions. No single person, no single organization, no single afternoon can change that. Compassion has a scale problem, and psychology has a name for the way it breaks: the identifiable victim effect. We feel intensely for one specific face, and surprisingly little for a statistic, even when the statistic is a million times larger. One dog moves us. A million dogs numb us.

That sounds like a bug in the human wiring, and in some ways it is. But it may also be the one feature we can actually use. Because help doesn't arrive in the form of "millions." It arrives one animal, one afternoon, one person at a time.

For the world, a single rescued dog is a rounding error. For the dog, it's the entire world. Both of those are true, and it takes some maturity to hold them together without letting either one cancel the other.

—

Why do we watch these videos at all?

Psychologist Jonathan Haidt gave one answer with a term he uses: moral elevation. It's the warm, slightly lifted feeling people report when they witness someone doing something good for someone who can't repay them. Studies suggest it does more than feel nice. People who experience it often say they want to be better themselves, and some become more likely to help others afterwards.

That's the hopeful reading. The less flattering one is that we watch because the world is full of problems we can't fix, and here is one that someone actually did. Relief is a powerful drug. A small solved problem is permission to believe that large ones can be solved too.

Either way, the video isn't really asking you for pity. Pity is cheap and it evaporates by lunchtime. What it quietly offers is a harder thing to hold: evidence that a hungry body and a reachable hand can exist in the same place at the same time.

—

Here is something practical that most people have never been taught, and it is the kind of knowledge that changes what you see on the street.

Veterinary guides describe a healthy dog like this. You should be able to feel the ribs easily under a thin layer of fat, without pressing hard, but you shouldn't see them from a distance. Viewed from above, there should be a visible waist behind the ribs. Viewed from the side, the belly should tuck up toward the hind legs. When ribs, spine and hip bones are plainly visible and the flanks are hollowed, that dog is well below a healthy weight, and the cause deserves attention. Not every thin dog is starving. Parasites, illness and dental pain can all do it. But a visibly thin dog is always a question, and the question usually has a cost to leave unanswered.

Once you know this, you can't unknow it. You'll start noticing. Share that sentence with the one friend who always says they could never look at animals in trouble. Knowing how to look is the first step toward being able to.

—

If you ever do meet a dog in this condition, a few things are worth knowing.

Scared and hungry animals can bite. That isn't aggression in the villain sense. It's an animal protecting a body that has nothing left to spare. Move slowly. Don't corner her. Don't grab. Let her choose distance.

Fresh water first is generally safer than a large meal. Small amounts of food, offered gradually, are better than one enormous pile, for the reasons I described earlier. Take note of the exact location, take a photo if it's safe, and call a local rescue, animal control or a veterinarian. Ask what they want you to do before you decide what to do.

And if you can't do any of it, that is allowed too. Sharing the location with someone who can is real help. The goal isn't to be a hero. The goal is to make sure the animal doesn't stay invisible.

—

There's a category of people the internet almost never sees.

They keep a bag of food in the trunk. They know which corner has the limping dog and which lot has the new litter. They spend their own money, on their own time, on animals that are not theirs and may never be. Many of them will never go viral, never be thanked, never learn what happened to the animal they fed on a Tuesday.

Their work has a particular shape. It's repetitive, quiet and mostly unrewarded. It looks nothing like a story, because stories have endings and this work often doesn't. It has Mondays.

When a clip of that kind of work does find its way into the light, it's worth remembering how many hours of invisible ones sit underneath it. A few seconds of footage is the tip. The iceberg is a lifetime of unremarkable decisions to show up again.

—

I want to ask something strange: what does a meal weigh?

To you, probably nothing. Breakfast is a transaction so ordinary it barely registers. We have apps for it. We argue about which cuisine. We leave half of it on the plate.

But for a body that has been without enough for a long time, a meal isn't a transaction. It is a verdict on whether tomorrow is possible. It's the difference between a system that is shutting down and one that gets another day to run.

We rarely feel that weight, because we rarely meet the other side of it. Which is why the sight of someone who does, someone for whom food is still a question, tends to arrive like a small earthquake in a very comfortable room.

—

A word on the title, because I think it's doing something clever.

It is written in the past tense.

I'll leave you to decide what that tells you, and what it doesn't. A past tense can mean a lot of things. It can mean the worst is over. It can mean something is still unfinished. It can simply be a person looking back at a moment they can't forget. I don't know which one it is, and I'd be lying if I pretended otherwise.

What I do know is that the sentence is an instruction. Look. Not "feel sorry." Not "share this." Look. At the hunger. At what it looked like when it was real, and when nobody had yet decided that it was their problem.

—

People ask whether videos like this are manipulative. It's a fair question, and the honest answer is: sometimes, yes.

There's an entire genre built on staged desperation, on rescues that were arranged for the camera, on suffering used as bait. The suspicion people feel is earned. It's why I'd rather not hand you a story at all. I'd rather hand you a reason to look carefully and decide for yourself what you saw.

You can usually tell the difference. Not by the music or the caption, but by whether the thing in front of you asks you to do something or simply asks you to feel something. Real need tends to have a practical shape. It points outward, toward a bowl, a vet, a phone call, a Tuesday.

Judge this the same way. Watch it, and ask what it asks of you.

—

Consider how little it takes to change a trajectory.

Not a fortune. Not a rescue organization. Not a dramatic act. One person with an ordinary afternoon, who happens to stop. A small decision, made in under a minute, and everything downstream rearranges itself: the next meal, the next week, the next year of a life nobody had planned on.

We tend to imagine that big outcomes need big causes. A lot of the time, they just need a decent person within arm's reach of the right problem at the right moment, and a willingness to be inconvenienced.

That is the part of the story that I find hardest to shake. Not the suffering. The thinness of the thread that sometimes separates one outcome from the other, and how often that thread is simply someone choosing to look up from their own day.

—

Whose job is it, really?

Governments say it's a municipal issue. Municipalities say it's a shelter issue. Shelters say they are full. Neighbors say it's not their dog. And the dog, who has no jurisdiction, continues to be hungry in all of them at once.

Responsibility for animals has always lived in the gaps between institutions. Nobody owns the problem, so everybody can honestly say it isn't theirs. And in those gaps, a particular kind of person tends to appear: the one who doesn't ask whose job it is, only whose hands are nearest.

I'm not claiming that's the right way to run a society. It isn't. Systems should catch what individuals can't. But in the meantime, the gap is real, and what fills it is almost always one stubborn person who refuses to accept that "not my department" is a complete sentence.

—

Time moves differently for a starving body.

A day doesn't pass at the speed it does for us. Energy is rationed. Movement is rationed. Even thought, in some sense, is rationed. The body shrinks its budget and starts deciding what to keep switching on. Sleep gets longer. Reactions get slower. The world gets smaller and quieter.

Recovery runs on its own clock too, and it's slower than anyone wants. Weight comes back in weeks and months, not hours. Muscle takes longer than fat. Trust usually takes longer than muscle. There's no shortcut through any of it, and anyone who promises one hasn't done it.

So when you watch something like this, resist the urge to treat it as a before-and-after. It's a moment on a very long road, and the road matters more than the moment.

—

There's a reason the oldest religious and ethical traditions on earth all say some version of the same sentence about feeding the hungry.

It isn't because food is the most important thing. It's because hunger is the one need nobody can argue about. You don't need a political view to understand a hungry body. You don't need a shared language. You don't need to agree about anything at all. A hungry animal asks the simplest question one living being can ask another: will you?

And the answers people give, across thousands of years and thousands of cultures, tell you almost everything about them. Some look away. Some look and weigh the cost. Some don't weigh anything at all.

I don't think we're born as one kind or the other. I think we practice. Every small decision to stop, or not, is a rehearsal for the next one.

—

A strange thing happens when you spend time around people who rescue animals.

They almost never talk about the saves. They talk about the ones they were too late for, the ones they couldn't find, the ones whose faces they still carry around. And yet they keep going. Not because the math works out, but because stopping would mean accepting that the math is the only thing that counts.

I used to think that was stubbornness. I now think it's a form of intelligence: a refusal to let an impossible total stop you from doing the possible part.

If you want to know what hope actually looks like, it isn't optimism. It's the decision to do the next small, specific, solvable thing while fully aware of how large the unsolved thing is.

—

Dogs have a habit that I find almost unbearable in its generosity.

They forgive on a timescale humans can barely comprehend. An animal can go through something terrible, and given even a little steadiness, safety, regular food, a gentle voice, begin to open back up, sometimes astonishingly fast, sometimes with a slow, careful, step-by-step return. Not always. Not every dog. Some carry it for life, and they deserve patience rather than disappointment.

But the capacity is there, in the species itself. As if evolution built them to give humans more chances than we have earned.

We should probably be asking ourselves what we're doing with that credit.

—

You may have noticed that I haven't described a single thing you're about to see.

That was deliberate. A description is a substitute for the experience, and this one is too important to substitute. Anything I said would be filtered through my reaction, and my reaction isn't yours. Yours is the only one that matters here.

I've given you the context: what starvation does, what a meal means, what it takes for someone to cross the gap between noticing and acting. The rest belongs to you.

Watch it the way you'd want someone to watch you on your worst day: attentively, without flinching, and without rushing to a conclusion.

—

Animals can't ask for help in words. They ask with posture, with thinness, with the way they linger near the places where people eat. Every request is made in a language that requires a human interpreter, and most of the time the interpreter isn't there. That's the quiet job description of anyone who stops: translator for someone who has no other way to say, plainly, that this is an emergency.

—

Two questions, and then I'll leave you alone with it.

First: when was the last time you saw something that needed help and kept walking, and what story did you tell yourself afterwards? I'm not asking to shame you. I'm asking because I know mine, and it was a very reasonable story.

Second: what would it take for you to be the person who doesn't have that story ready?

Most of us will never be asked to do anything dramatic. We'll be asked to do something small, unplanned and slightly inconvenient, at a time that isn't good for us. The whole question of who we are is quietly decided there. Not in speeches or in good intentions, but in the ten seconds when something small and hungry is in front of you and the easy option is to keep moving. That is where character gets built, quietly, slowly and one afternoon at a time.

—

The original caption is in Portuguese. I'm translating it, and something small is lost in the process, a rhythm, a tone of voice, the way the sentence seems to grab you by the sleeve. But the thing it points at needs no translation. Hunger has the same face in every language, and so does the person who decides to do something about it.

—

One more thing about why this exists as a video at all.

For most of history, an animal's suffering was a private event. It happened in alleys, lots and roadsides, witnessed by nobody who could do anything. A camera changes that. It turns a private fact into public knowledge, and public knowledge is the precondition for almost every kind of help. You cannot be moved by what never reached you.

That's the best argument for watching, even when it's hard. Not to collect a feeling, but to receive information that someone went out of their way to carry to you.

—

Hunger is not loud. That is the entire problem.

It doesn't shout. It doesn't file complaints. It waits, and it gets quieter as it gets worse, until the thing it is happening to simply blends into the background of a street that has learned not to see.

Someone saw.

Watch the video.

text:
The German Autobahn: The Road Network That Changed the World

Few transportation systems are as famous as Germany's Autobahn. To many people, the word immediately conjures images of high-performance cars racing across perfectly engineered highways without speed limits. While that reputation contains an element of truth, the real story of the Autobahn is far more fascinating. It is a remarkable feat of engineering, a product of several eras of German history, and one of the most influential highway systems ever constructed.

The Origins of the Autobahn

The roots of the Autobahn stretch back to the early 20th century, when automobile ownership was still relatively rare. One of the earliest prototypes was the AVUS (Automobil-Verkehrs- und Übungsstraße) near Berlin, which opened in 1921 as a dedicated motor road and testing facility. Although it functioned primarily as a racing and experimental roadway, it demonstrated the practicality of high-speed, automobile-only travel.

Germany's first true public autobahn-style route opened between Cologne and Bonn on August 6, 1932. The road, now designated the A555, featured controlled access, separated traffic, and no at-grade intersections, design principles that remain standard on modern expressways.

The massive expansion of the network began after 1933 under the Reichsautobahn program. Thousands of workers were employed building long-distance routes linking major German cities. By the start of World War II, approximately 2,400 miles (3,860 km) of Autobahn had been completed.

When Was the Autobahn Completed?

There is no single completion date because the Autobahn has never truly been finished. Unlike a monument or bridge, it is a continuously evolving national network.

Construction largely halted during World War II and resumed in the 1950s. West Germany expanded and modernized the system during the postwar economic boom, while reunification in 1990 led to extensive upgrades and integration of East German routes. Today the German Autobahn network exceeds 13,000 kilometers (about 8,200 miles) and continues to grow through expansions and improvements.

Where Does the Autobahn Go?

The Autobahn covers virtually every region of Germany.

Major routes include:

A7: Germany's longest Autobahn, running nearly the entire length of the country from the Danish border south toward Austria.
A3: Connects the Netherlands through Cologne and Frankfurt to Austria.
A1: Stretches from the Baltic Sea through Hamburg and the Ruhr region toward Saarland.
A9: Links Berlin and Munich, one of Germany's most strategically important north-south corridors.
A8: Runs east-west from Luxembourg through Stuttgart and Munich toward Salzburg, Austria.

The network traverses:

The industrial Ruhr Valley
The Rhine River corridor
Bavaria and the Alpine foothills
Northern coastal regions facing the North and Baltic Seas
Former East German states such as Saxony, Brandenburg, and Thuringia
The Busiest Parts of the Autobahn

While rural stretches may seem nearly empty, several urban corridors are among Europe's busiest highways.

The most congested sections are generally found around:

Frankfurt
Cologne
Düsseldorf
The Ruhr metropolitan area
Munich
Hamburg

The Ruhr region is particularly notable because it contains a dense concentration of cities, industries, ports, and logistics facilities. High traffic volumes often make these urban Autobahns resemble busy American freeways despite Germany's reputation for unrestricted speeds.

Is It Really True There Are No Speed Limits?

Yes and no.

One of the biggest myths about the Autobahn is that every mile is unrestricted.

In reality:

Many urban areas have posted speed limits.
Construction zones frequently impose limits.
Weather conditions may trigger temporary restrictions.
Congested corridors often have permanent or variable speed controls.

However, Germany remains unique because it does not impose a universal national speed limit on many Autobahn sections.

Recent analyses indicate that approximately 65% of Autobahn carriageway mileage has no permanent speed limit, though conditions vary. Drivers are advised to follow the recommended "Richtgeschwindigkeit" of 130 km/h (81 mph) even where no legal limit exists.

Therefore, the popular belief that "the Autobahn has no speed limits" is only partially correct. Many stretches are unrestricted, but many others are not.

Did the Autobahn Come Before the U.S. Interstate System?

Absolutely.

A common misconception is that Germany copied the American Interstate Highway System. In fact, the historical sequence is exactly the opposite.

German Autobahn
AVUS prototype opened in 1921.
Cologne-Bonn Autobahn opened in 1932.
Large-scale nationwide construction began in 1933-1935.
U.S. Interstate Highway System
National planning began in the 1930s and 1940s.
The landmark Federal-Aid Highway Act was signed in 1956.

During World War II, General Dwight Eisenhower observed firsthand how effectively the German autobahns facilitated military movement. Those observations became one influence behind his support for the Interstate program after he became President.

An Important Twist

If one asks which country built the first true motorway reserved exclusively for automobiles, the answer is generally Italy, not Germany.

Italy's Autostrada dei Laghi between Milan and Varese opened in 1924 and is often regarded as the world's first purpose-built motorway. Germany soon followed and ultimately developed the concept on a much larger national scale.

Other Remarkable Highway Systems Around the World
United States Interstate Highway System

The Interstate System remains the world's largest and most influential controlled-access highway network. It transformed commerce, suburban development, logistics, and tourism across North America. Its standardized design, limited-access interchanges, and coast-to-coast connectivity are widely considered engineering masterpieces.

China's National Expressway Network

China has constructed one of the most extensive expressway systems ever built, connecting enormous distances and some of the world's largest cities. Its growth over just a few decades is often regarded as one of history's most ambitious infrastructure achievements.

Japan's Expressway Network

Japan's highways stand out for their earthquake-resistant engineering, urban integration, and exceptional maintenance standards. Building expressways through densely populated and mountainous terrain required extraordinary ingenuity.

France's Autoroutes

France's toll-road network is celebrated for efficiency, excellent road surfaces, frequent service areas, and convenient long-distance travel. Many transportation planners consider it among Europe's most comfortable highway systems.

The World's Most Beautiful Highway Networks

Some roads are admired not merely for engineering but for scenery.

Icefields Parkway (Canada)

Running through Alberta's Rocky Mountains, this route may be one of the most spectacular scenic highways on Earth, passing glaciers, turquoise lakes, waterfalls, and snow-covered peaks.

Great Ocean Road (Australia)

One of the world's great coastal drives, featuring dramatic cliffs, beaches, and the famous Twelve Apostles rock formations.

North Coast 500 (Scotland)

A spectacular route through the Scottish Highlands, combining mountains, lochs, castles, and rugged coastline.

Garden Route (South Africa)

A famous coastal corridor known for forests, beaches, lagoons, and wildlife.

Norway's National Tourist Routes

Norway has become internationally recognized for integrating architecture, infrastructure, and landscape design into some of the world's most beautiful roads. Drivers encounter fjords, waterfalls, mountain passes, and dramatic Atlantic coastlines.

Final Thoughts

The Autobahn is much more than a collection of fast roads. It represents more than a century of transportation innovation, from the experimental AVUS circuit of 1921 to today's 13,000-kilometer national network. Despite its reputation, much of the Autobahn is regulated, though Germany still preserves extensive unrestricted sections that remain unique in the developed world.

Historically, the Autobahn predates the American Interstate System by decades and helped inspire later highway development worldwide. Yet the honor of the world's first true motorway generally belongs to Italy's pioneering Autostrada dei Laghi. Together, these systems helped define modern mobility, shrinking distances, accelerating trade, and transforming how people experience their nations and the world.

text:
My mother's oldest friend, Noriko, guided Japanese tour groups across America for 31 years.

Grand Canyon. Yellowstone. Route 66. Four hundred and twelve tours. She retired this spring.

On every first day, on the bus from the airport, she gave the same speech. She showed it to me. It's still in her notebook, in pencil, worn soft at the corners.

"Everyone will tell you to look at the scenery. The scenery is fine. It will be there tomorrow.

Watch the people. The people are why you came. You just don't know it yet."

Then she read them her list. Things to watch for in America.

1. In the rain, a woman will walk her shopping cart all the way back to the cart return. Nobody is watching. She will get wet. She will do it anyway. Do not offer to help. She will not understand the question.

2. If your car battery dies, a truck will pull over within ten minutes. The man will have cables. Every truck has cables. He will refuse money. He will say "Happens to everybody." It does not happen to everybody. It happens to him, constantly, because he keeps stopping.

3. If a restaurant sings Happy Birthday to a stranger, the whole room will join. People who do not know her name will sing her name. Badly. Loudly. She will cover her face. Sing anyway.

4. On the airplane, if a baby screams for two hours, watch the parents' faces when they land. Then watch the old woman who stops in the aisle to tell them, "You did great. You're good parents." The mother will cry. This happens more than you think.

5. After a snowstorm, look at the sidewalks at 6 a.m. Some of them are already clear. Not by the owner. By the man next door, who will deny it.

6. At a children's baseball game, when a boy on the other team strikes out and walks back with his head down, a stranger in the bleachers will shout, "Good cut, buddy! Next time!" He does not know the boy. He does not need to.

7. If you are eating alone at a county fair, a family will make room at their table. They will not ask. They will just slide down.

8. Someone will ask where you're from. When you say Japan, they will not say "hello." They will say "welcome." Like it's their house. Because to them, it is.

There was one more item. She never read it out loud. She just waited for it.

It happened on her last tour.

One of her guests was Mr. Aoki. Eighty years old. His father died in the Pacific in 1944. He had never wanted to come. His daughter made him.

He spent nine days on the bus looking out the window. He didn't speak to anyone.

At a gas station in Oklahoma, an old man in a veterans cap heard the group speaking Japanese. He walked over to Mr. Aoki, took off his cap, held it against his chest, and put out his hand.

"Glad we're friends now."

Mr. Aoki held that hand for a long time.

On the bus, he cried for an hour. Noriko sat next to him. When he could talk again, he said:

"I came to see the canyon. I'm going home with my father's peace."

That was the last item on the list. She'd written it in 1995 and never needed to read it.

"Someone will forgive you for something you didn't do. Let them."

Noriko asked me to write this for her, because she doesn't have Twitter and doesn't plan to start.

So, to whoever is reading this in America:

For thirty-one years, Japanese grandparents came home from your country and told their grandchildren about it.

Not the canyon.

You.

text:
#Cybertruck Flopped: #Musk Winds Down Pickup Production in Favor of Driverless Taxi

Elon #Musk has announced the winding down of Tesla Cybertruck production at the Gigafactory in Texas by mid-2027. Capacities will be reassigned to expand output of the autonomous Cybercab. The pickup, which #Musk pitched as a revolution in the automotive industry and a competitor to Ford, failed to meet sales forecasts. The Austin facility remains the only known #Tesla plant equipped to manufacture its specific components. No transfer of assembly to another site has been announced, #Reuters reports.

Instead of the promised 250,000 Cybertrucks annually, #Tesla sold just 20,237 units in the #US in 2025—down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. The model was unveiled in 2019, with deliveries only commencing in late 2023. During this time, the Cybertruck underwent 11 recall campaigns, quality control issues, repeated price adjustments, and safety concerns. Its angular stainless steel body virtually blocked the model's access to the European market due to pedestrian safety requirements.

One of the largest buyers of the failed pickup became #Musk's own company, SpaceX. In 2025, it purchased $131 million worth of Cybertrucks at list prices, as reflected in #SpaceX filings. Former Aston Martin head Andy #Palmer stated that continuing to manufacture a model that falls short of targets is economically pointless.

Musk himself called the Cybertruck the best car in #Tesla's history and the termination of its production the end of an era. The project's chief engineer, Wes #Morrill, maintains that the developed technologies will continue to be utilized in the Cybercab.

Now, the bet is placed on a two-seater robotaxi without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Cybercab production in Texas has already begun, and since September 2026, #Tesla has offered paid rides in limited areas of Austin. According to the Texas Department of Transportation, about 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis in the state are Cybercabs, with the rest being primarily Model Ys. Meanwhile, #US regulator #NHTSA is auditing the new model's compliance with federal safety requirements.

The decision is part of #Tesla's transition from traditional electric vehicles toward autonomous transport, artificial intelligence, and robotics. The announcement followed a tough week for #Musk: nearly $500 million in political spending failed to deliver victories for a majority of the candidates he backed in the #US midterm elections, while the combined market capitalization of his companies moved toward a weekly contraction of over $180 billion.

#Tesla did not disclose the remaining volume of Cybertruck production or the fate of unfulfilled orders. After three years of sales, the company is clearing its Texas capacity for the Cybercab, whose commercial success remains to be proven.

Unbelievable, but true…

text:
#169 EV & Elon Weekly News – 7 November 2026

Not financial advice. This is not investment advice. I am not a financial advisor. Always do your own research.

Macro

Market pullback after midterms

The US midterms shifted the balance of power. Markets sold off hard on the result, with roughly $3 trillion wiped from equities in a single session as investors priced in the risk that new Democratic control could slow data-centre and AI-related spending. The drop was not Tesla-specific. It hit the broader AI and infrastructure trade.

The next session recovered a portion of the losses. These kinds of sharp moves happen from time to time. How deep or long any pullback goes is always uncertain. Long-term investors generally do better staying invested in quality companies than trying to time the market. Missing even a handful of the best days historically has a large impact on overall returns. Kartik from Moneyvest has pointed out that if you miss the 10 best days in the share market you can miss around half of your total gains.

VIX spike and historical pattern

The VIX (a measure of how much the market expects big moves) jumped about 69% on the sell-off. Kartik looked at past times the VIX has spiked this hard. In those cases the market has usually recovered quite quickly. It is not a guarantee, but historically the worst of the drop has often already happened by the time the VIX has moved this far.

AI build-out and political risk

Jo Bhakdi has argued that AI-related construction and investment currently accounts for a very large share of US growth (he has put the figure near 90%). A full stop on new data centres would therefore hit GDP hard. Democrats have talked about a moratorium (a temporary pause) on new approvals. In practice, governors on both sides tend to follow the money. Turning away large projects means losing construction work, permanent jobs, power contracts and tax revenue. Those projects usually just move to another state that will approve them.

Water use at data centres is real but small relative to other large users. One comparison that has been made is that a single large golf course can use roughly 30 times the on-site water of a typical data centre. Temporary gas turbines for power do create noise and emissions, which are legitimate local concerns. The power itself still has to come from somewhere if the host city is not to be disadvantaged.

Jobs report

The October labour report came in stronger than expected. Jobs added were solid and unemployment edged down even with higher participation. That combination is unusual and suggests the labour market remains firmer than many had feared.

Technology

Data centres and SpaceX position

Many of the large data-centre projects linked to Tesla and SpaceX already have approvals in place. A change in congressional control does not automatically unwind those. SpaceX has shown it can move faster on both terrestrial and orbital compute than most traditional builders. If local opposition slows projects in some places, other locations remain open. Musk has said the revenue from data-centre activity could become very large in the coming years. Even allowing for optimistic timelines, the returns on early projects could help fund the next wave while demand for compute stays high.

Cybertruck production shift

Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production after roughly three years to free up capacity for the Cybercab. The Cybertruck remains a polarising vehicle. Some current owners have already said they have no interest in selling even at elevated prices because the model is being phased out.

Anthropic allocation

Anthropic is available for retail IPO allocation through CommSec, similar to the process used for SpaceX. As always, do your own research.

Sentiment and geopolitics

Texas result and state-level politics

Texas saw a Democratic win in the Senate race. The newly elected senator has called Musk a “great innovator” and expressed interest in working with him on technology. Musk replied simply “Nice of him to say that.” Several heavily Republican states continue to actively court Tesla and SpaceX investment. Florida remains the clearest example of a state that already has the infrastructure and political willingness to host large-scale launch and related activity.

Ukraine ceasefire talks

Ukraine has requested a 60-day ceasefire to allow elections to be held. Russia has rejected the request and offered only a much shorter pause. Any longer truce would require both sides to agree, and the outcome would still depend on the results of any election that followed.

Views on Democrats and AI spending

Chris Camillo has said he does not expect Democratic control to stop the money flowing into AI. The market reaction assumed a hard stop. Jo Bhakdi has made a similar point. Both see the sell-off as an over-reaction to the political shift rather than a change in the underlying demand for compute.

Long-term US debt path

US debt continues to grow under either party. The two main long-term outcomes discussed are either a future debt problem that becomes unmanageable, or productivity gains from AI and robotics large enough that interest payments become a smaller share of total output. Political control can affect the pace of that investment, but the underlying debt trajectory is not expected to reverse quickly under either side. Musk has made similar comments about the need for higher productivity to outrun the debt.

text:
Manfred Albrecht Freiherr von Richthofen, known as the Red Baron, stands as the deadliest flying ace of the First World War, a Prussian aristocrat whose name became synonymous with aerial lethality over the Western Front. Born on 2 May 1892 in Kleinburg near Breslau in Lower Silesia (today part of Wrocław, Poland), he entered a world of landed nobility and military expectation. His father, Major Albrecht Philipp Karl Julius Freiherr von Richthofen, was a career officer, and his mother Kunigunde von Schickfuss und Neudorff came from similar stock. Young Manfred grew up hunting wild game, riding horses, and excelling in sports, habits that later translated directly into his methodical approach to combat in the air. At age eleven he was packed off to the cadet school at Wahlstatt, then advanced through the Prussian military academy system. By 1911 he was an officer candidate in the 1st Uhlan Regiment Kaiser Alexander III, commissioned a lieutenant the following year and posted to the eastern frontier. When war erupted in 1914 he served as a cavalry reconnaissance officer and dispatch rider on both the Eastern and Western Fronts, earning the Iron Cross for daring runs under fire. Trench warfare quickly rendered horse cavalry obsolete, and the boredom of static service frustrated him. In 1915 he transferred to the Fliegertruppen, first as an observer in two-seaters over the Eastern Front and later the Champagne sector, where he claimed an unconfirmed victory with a machine gun from the rear seat. Determined to fly himself, he took lessons from a friend, Georg Zeumer, and earned his pilot’s certificate late that year after a series of hard landings and near misses. Oswald Boelcke, the pioneering German fighter theorist, selected him in August 1916 for the newly formed Jagdstaffel 2. Richthofen’s first confirmed kill came on 17 September 1916, an FE.2b of No. 11 Squadron near Villers-Plouich; he ordered a silver cup engraved with the date and type of aircraft, a practice he continued for the next fifty-nine victories until wartime silver shortages forced him to stop. He followed Boelcke’s Dicta Boelcke with religious precision: gain the advantage of height and the sun, attack from behind and above, fire only at close range, and break off if the opponent has the edge. On 23 November 1916 he shot down Major Lanoe Hawker VC, Britain’s first fighter ace and holder of the Victoria Cross, after a prolonged duel that Richthofen later described with evident respect as a contest against “the British Boelcke.” By early 1917 he commanded Jasta 11 and had painted his Albatros D.III entirely red so that his men could identify him instantly in the melee; the color soon became a signature of intimidation and unit recognition. The spring of 1917, remembered as Bloody April, saw him personally claim twenty-one or twenty-two victories in a single month while his unit and others devastated the Royal Flying Corps over Arras. He was awarded the Pour le Mérite after his sixteenth kill, promoted Rittmeister, and in June 1917 given command of the four-squadron Jagdgeschwader I, the “Flying Circus,” a highly mobile force that shifted by train and tent to hotspots along the front. A severe head wound on 6 July 1917 nearly ended his career; a bullet grazed his skull, forcing an emergency landing and later surgery to remove bone splinters. He returned against medical advice, later suffering headaches, nausea, and possible personality changes that some historians link to cumulative combat stress. By the time of his death he had amassed eighty confirmed aerial victories, the highest total of any pilot on either side during the entire war. 

The arithmetic of that record is worth examining closely because it underscores both the scale of his achievement and the narrow window in which it was accomplished. From his first confirmed victory in September 1916 until 21 April 1918 he flew combat for roughly nineteen to twenty months. Of the eighty credited kills, the large majority occurred in Albatros fighters, primarily the D.III and later the D.V; only nineteen were scored in the Fokker Dr.I triplane with which popular memory most closely associates him. Detailed lists compiled decades later, cross-checked against British squadron records, aircraft serial numbers, and the identities of killed or captured airmen, show that at least seventy-three of the eighty claims correspond to documented Allied losses. Unconfirmed claims exist that could push the true total higher still. For comparison, the leading Allied scorers were the Frenchman René Fonck with seventy-five confirmed (plus many unconfirmed behind German lines), the Canadian Billy Bishop with seventy-two, and the British James McCudden with fifty-seven. Richthofen’s average was therefore roughly four confirmed victories per month of active flying, concentrated in intense periods such as Bloody April. That rate was not the product of reckless aerobatics; it was the product of systematic stalking, superior marksmanship at short range, and the disciplined use of formation tactics that protected his wingmen while he delivered the decisive burst. Most of his victims were two-seaters early on (slower, less maneuverable observation machines), with a higher proportion of single-seat fighters later as the quality of Allied opposition improved. He insisted on aiming at the pilot or the observer rather than the machine itself, a maxim he drilled into his pilots: “Aim for the man and don’t miss him. If you are fighting a two-seater, get the observer first.” 

None of this was a small feat. Aerial combat in 1916–1918 was conducted in fragile, underpowered machines whose engines were unreliable, whose fabric-covered wings could fail under stress, and whose fixed machine guns frequently jammed at the critical moment. Pilots wore no parachutes for most of the war (the Germans issued them late and only to some); a hit that disabled the aircraft usually meant death or capture. Cold at altitude, oil and exhaust fumes, and the constant threat of structural failure or mid-air collision with one’s own formation members added to the hazards. Closing to effective range with synchronized guns required skill and nerve; a single burst from a hundred yards could decide the fight, but the attacker was equally exposed. Ground fire, especially from machine guns and field artillery, claimed many lives once aircraft dropped low. Average life expectancy for a new fighter pilot was measured in weeks, not months. Richthofen survived long enough to become a national hero in Germany, where Ludendorff reportedly valued him as the equivalent of three divisions for morale, and a figure of dread among Allied airmen who learned to scan for the flash of scarlet. 

The aircraft he flew reflected the rapid evolution of fighter design. Early victories came in the Albatros D.II and then the D.III, a streamlined biplane powered by a Mercedes inline engine, armed with twin 7.92 mm Spandau machine guns synchronized to fire through the propeller. The D.III offered good speed and climb but suffered wing failures that forced temporary switches to the Halberstadt. After recovering from his head wound he transitioned to the Fokker Dr.I triplane, a three-winged design inspired by the British Sopwith Triplane. Powered by a rotary Oberursel engine, the Dr.I possessed exceptional maneuverability and a tight turning circle that allowed it to out-turn the nimble Sopwith Camel in horizontal combat, though it was slower in level flight and in the dive than contemporary Allied scouts such as the SE.5a and Camel. Early production suffered structural problems in the wings that were later corrected. Richthofen scored his last twenty or so victories in various Dr.I airframes, several of them painted wholly or partly red; the iconic all-red machine (serial 425/17) was the one in which he died. Twin Spandaus remained the armament. He recognized the limitations of the triplane and advocated for the faster Fokker D.VII, but he never flew that type in combat. 

Opinions of him on both sides mixed fear, professional respect, and occasional resentment. Among Germans he was a celebrity whose exploits filled newspapers and whose autobiography Der Rote Kampfflieger was distributed to troops as inspiration. His pilots in Jasta 11 and the Flying Circus generally admired his leadership; he was cordial to officers and mechanics alike, emphasized teamwork, and forbade unnecessary stunting. On the Allied side the red machines were instantly recognizable and avoided when possible. After his death the Royal Flying Corps and Australian units accorded him full military honors, including a guard of honor and pallbearers from No. 3 Squadron AFC. A wreath placed on his grave read “To Our Gallant and Worthy Foe.” Contemporary British commentary noted that any pilot would have been proud to have downed him, yet equally proud to shake his hand had he been captured alive. Not every Allied pilot shared the chivalric view. Mick Mannock, the high-scoring Irish ace, reportedly reacted with anger when some squadrons toasted the fallen Baron; Mannock regarded Richthofen as overly cautious, a man who preferred to attack stragglers and who benefited from the protective screen of his unit. Others simply feared the sudden appearance of the red plane diving out of the sun. 

His death on 21 April 1918 illustrates the element of sheer Bad Luck rather than any decisive outmatching in the air. That morning Richthofen led a patrol that engaged Sopwith Camels of No. 209 Squadron near Vaux-sur-Somme. He pursued a novice pilot, Lieutenant Wilfrid “Wop” May, who had attacked Richthofen’s cousin Wolfram. The chase descended to treetop height over the Somme valley and crossed into Allied territory, where Australian trenches and machine-gun posts were concentrated. Captain Arthur Roy Brown of the same Camel squadron dived from above and behind, firing a short burst at the red triplane from roughly the left-rear quarter before pulling away. Richthofen turned, then resumed the pursuit of May for another minute or more. Eyewitness accounts and timing reconstructions place the interval between Brown’s pass and the final crash at roughly sixty to ninety seconds or longer. During that period the Baron continued to maneuver and close on his target. A single .303-inch bullet then struck him. Autopsy reports conducted the same day and the following day by medical officers established that the entrance wound lay on the right side of the chest in the posterior fold of the armpit, roughly at the level of the ninth rib. The bullet passed through the heart and lungs and exited near the left nipple, slightly higher and more forward. The trajectory was essentially horizontal or slightly upward, from the right side and a little behind, consistent with a shot fired from roughly the same plane as the aircraft or from slightly below. Brown’s attack, coming from above and from the left-rear relative to the final path of the triplane, does not match that angle. Moreover, a wound of that severity through the heart would have produced almost immediate incapacitation; the fact that Richthofen continued controlled flight and combat for more than a minute after Brown’s burst indicates that the fatal shot arrived later. Multiple Australian machine-gunners, including Sergeant Cedric Popkin of the 24th Machine Gun Company, fired at the low-flying triplane as it paralleled the lines. Modern ballistic reconstruction, computer modeling of flight paths, and re-examination of the wound geometry align most closely with fire from Popkin’s position or a similar ground emplacement. The official credit awarded to Brown was shaped by the desire for a clean aerial victory by a commissioned officer and by an early, incomplete medical impression that was later revised. Historians, forensic analysts, and ballistics specialists have long concluded that the fatal bullet almost certainly came from the ground. Richthofen, a pilot who normally avoided low-level exposure over enemy trenches and who knew the risks of ground fire, had on that day pressed a pursuit too far, drifted over the lines in a fluid sector, and absorbed a single unlucky round that no amount of skill could have anticipated once he was already committed. The crash landing in a sugar-beet field followed almost at once; he was dead or dying when Australian troops reached the wreckage. 

In the end the record, the tactics, the aircraft, and the final wound trajectory all converge on the same picture: a highly skilled, methodical hunter of the air whose eighty confirmed victories were earned under conditions that killed most of his contemporaries, and whose own death came not from being outflown by a superior opponent but from the random, lethal geometry of a .303 bullet fired upward from the trenches.

text:
We contributed ₦350k towards my colleague's wedding last year.

We asked him to tell us where we could help him financially, and he said he didn't have money to pay for the wedding hall. The hall cost ₦350k.

We contributed the money early enough to secure the hall for the wedding.

Four days before the wedding, he broke up with his fiancée, and the wedding was cancelled. He simply told us they weren't compatible, and that was all.

We asked him to collect the money from the hall owner and refund us, but he said they didn't offer refunds.

We went to meet the hall owner, and he told us he had already refunded my colleague since the wedding was cancelled.

We went back and told my colleague what the man had said.

He looked at us and said, "So you people can't use that ₦350k to compensate me for the heartbreak I'm going through?"

We just let him be.

Last month, he got married again and informed us, but this time, we didn't contribute any money.

We attended the wedding, ate, drank and left.

When he resumed work, he asked us about his wedding gift.

We told him to use the ₦350k to compensate himself for the gift we were supposed to give him.

He hasn't spoken to anyone since then.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

text:
What does Labour learn from the US mid-terms?

My reading of the Democrats’ victory is pretty simple: when people believe the system is rigged, attack the people doing the rigging.

Behind America’s impressive growth figures, millions are struggling. In the year to Q3 2026, median weekly earnings rose by 1.5%. Prices rose by 3.5%.

Democrats connected that squeeze to the spectacle of a president and his billionaire allies enjoying extraordinary gains.

One Michigan voter captured the perfectly: “I see the president building a ballroom when there’s people that can’t feed their families.”

The attack on Big Tech sharpened the argument. Who gains from AI? Who pays for the electricity, infrastructure and disruption? Who writes the rules? The victory speeches of Democrats are written through with a warning for America's big tech titans. 

From the mid-terms, there are two lessons for Labour, which we basically know, but which just got underlined:

1. Follow the money. Expose the relationship between populist donors, their interests and the policies they promote.

2. Above all, raise living standards. People need to feel progress in their pay packets, their bills and in our communities. And here we need to be looking much harder at some of the lessons from Australia, as @ThinkLabour argued this week 

The truth is the Democrats’ task is still unfinished. They have mastered the politics of anger. But now they need an optimistic story of national renewal - and a credible plan for delivery.

They have mastered the politics of the Gatsby age. Can they now offer America a Franklin Roosevelt?

text:
BetterUp is not a charity.  Irresponsible of the media to call them that.

To be absolutely clear, BetterUp does not call itself a charity, nor is it legally structured as one.
If you have seen them marketing their social mission, partnering with non-profits, or using philanthropic language, it is easy to see how that could cause confusion. The reality behind their business model and marketing comes down to a few key factors: [1] (https://t.co/npT3vGzKZv)

1. They Are a For-Profit Tech Startup

BetterUp is a private, venture-backed for-profit corporation. They have raised hundreds of millions of dollars from venture capitalists, have equity-holding shareholders, and operate to make a profit. They do not hold a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status like actual charities or non-profits. [1] (https://t.co/clnaucvYmi), [2] (https://t.co/suUl13MHY5), [3] (https://t.co/bd5RMwhKKp), [4] (https://t.co/a39AIgZn5n), [5] (https://t.co/FKZeE9dJ01)

2. They Use "Social Impact" Marketing

The reason their branding can sometimes feel like a charity is due to their heavy emphasis on corporate social responsibility (CSR). BetterUp participates in a philanthropic initiative called Pledge 1%, where they promise to dedicate 1% of their equity, staff volunteer time, and product software to underserved communities and non-profit grants. While they donate a fraction of their resources to charitable causes, the core entity remains a commercial enterprise. [1] (https://t.co/npT3vGzKZv)

3. Confusing "Public Benefit" or "B Corp" Language

Many modern tech companies use frameworks that blend profit with a social mission, which consumers frequently mistake for non-profit status:
• Public Benefit Corporations (PBC): Some companies legal corporate charters require them to balance making a profit for shareholders with a stated public mission. [1] (https://t.co/bd5RMwhKKp)
• Certified B Corporations: This is a third-party marketing and ethical certification given to for-profit companies that meet certain social and environmental standards. [1] (https://t.co/UKU217WARW)
Even when a company operates under these frameworks, they are still fully for-profit entities that charge standard market rates for their services. [1] (https://t.co/UUxElO6uN6)

4. Similar Sounding Names

It is also very common to confuse BetterUp with BetterHelp, which is an entirely separate, for-profit online therapy platform. While BetterHelp does offer a sliding-scale financial aid program for low-income users, they are also a commercial business (owned by Teladoc Health) and not a charity. [1] (https://t.co/ISovreHxaT)
Were you looking at a specific program or advertisement that made them seem like a charity? If you are trying to find actual non-profit mental health resources, let me know so I can help you find legitimate free or low-cost options.

text:
Todd Kaime writes that Western civilization must be protected. If Islamo-leftism keeps spreading like a cancer, humanity turns into one giant Third World.

This is not about Muslims. Millions live freely in the West, build companies and raise families because of what the West offers. It is about an alliance: political Islamism on one side, a radical left on the other. They agree on almost nothing except that the Western model has to go.

Political Islamism wants to replace secular law with religious law. The radical left wants to replace markets and property with an all-powerful redistributive state. One attacks individual freedom in the name of God, the other in the name of equality. Different scripts, same target: the free individual who thinks, builds and owns what he creates.

Almost everything that pulled humanity out of misery came from that model. The scientific method. Medicine that doubled life expectancy. Electricity, the airplane, the computer, the internet, AI. The rule of law, free speech, equality before the law, women’s rights. Capitalism that lifted over a billion people out of extreme poverty in a few decades. None of it happened under theocracy. None of it happened under collectivism.

It is a value system, not race or geography. Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Israel and the Gulf states that bet on openness all took off. Countries that rejected it stagnated. Theocracies freeze science, crush women and drive their best minds abroad. Collectivist regimes destroy incentives, then production, then freedom. Combine the two and you get a society that can neither create wealth nor tolerate dissent.

If that alliance keeps growing inside the West, universities stop producing knowledge and start producing ideology. Entrepreneurs leave or stop trying. The state grows to manage the decline, taxes everything that still moves and eventually expropriates even those who thought they were safe. Innovation dies quietly. The West, which was the engine of the whole world, becomes just another place managing scarcity.

The whole planet runs on what the West invents: the vaccines, the chips, the software, the energy tech, the open markets. If the engine stops, India does not get its next breakthrough, Africa does not get its next leap, Asia loses its biggest customer. Humanity does not become more equal. It becomes equally poor.

Every civilization that is even remotely sane should understand this, not out of love for the West but out of self-interest. Freedom of thought, rule of law, property and open markets are humanity’s operating system. The project to tear them down has to be stopped. Not with violence, not by targeting a people, but with ideas, with law, with courage and by refusing to apologize for what works. It is the only way we keep moving forward.

text:
Welcome to Saturday JATS™ GOOD MORNING OP-ED.

The Democrats' historic 2026 midterm sweep—clinching decisive majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate—abruptly ends unified Republican rule and fundamentally resets the political landscape for the remainder of President Trump's second term.

This dramatic shift ushering in an era of divided government creates an immediate legislative brick wall for the White House, ensuring signature conservative tax packages and spending rollbacks are dead on arrival while setting up fierce, high-stakes budget standoffs.

Armed with fresh committee gavels and subpoena powers across both chambers, Democratic leadership is poised to launch aggressive executive oversight into cabinet operations and ethics while targeting corporate price-gouging and consumer cost-of-living concerns.

Furthermore, retaking the Senate floor gives Democrats complete control over the judicial and executive confirmation pipelines, halting the rapid appointment of conservative judges and forcing the White House to put forward consensus figures for administration vacancies.

On the global stage, Congress will leverage its funding powers to re-anchor foreign policy around traditional European defense commitments while tightening scrutiny over military contractor operations and arms sales.

Finally, as both parties look toward the 2028 presidential race, Democratic leaders will use their new legislative platform to force high-visibility votes on popular domestic policies like healthcare cost caps and price protections, putting maximum pressure on the White House to either negotiate or issue risky vetoes.

The true test of this divided government will not be found in its inevitable standoffs, but in its capacity for transactional governance. President Trump’s political brand has long been rooted in deal-making, and this Democratic Congress offers an unexpected theater for high-stakes negotiation. Because populist currents run through both camps—particularly on issues like trade protectionism, domestic manufacturing, and working-class economic relief—there is hidden overlapping ground that defies traditional partisan lines.

The defining question of the next two years is one of strategic quid-pro-quo: what legislative capital are Democrats willing to concede to the Oval Office to secure a presidential signature on their own core priorities? If the incoming majority demands total policy capitulation, the remainder of the term will be consumed by performative gridlock and messaging bills designed solely for the 2028 campaign trail. However, if Democratic leadership is willing to trade wins and navigate the President's demand for reciprocal victories, they have a rare window to enact substantive legislation. Ultimately, Washington is about to discover whether this new Democratic platform is built strictly for political kabuki, or if they possess the pragmatism to actually play the game.

The populist currents running through both the "America First" right and the labor-aligned left create a surprisingly fertile landscape for transactional deal-making. When you strip away the culture war rhetoric, several major policy sectors offer the exact ingredients needed for a classic Washington quid-pro-quo.

Trade and Domestic Manufacturing: This is the most natural overlap. Both Trump and the modern Democratic party favor aggressive reshoring of supply chains and a tough-on-China industrial policy. A grand bargain here could involve Democrats supporting targeted tariff authority or deregulation for domestic factories, in exchange for Trump signing off on strict union labor protections, prevailing wage requirements, and massive federal investments in worker retraining programs.

Prescription Drug Pricing: Trump has long chafed at pharmaceutical lobbying and previously floated "most favored nation" pricing models to cap drug costs. Democrats desperately want to expand the number of drugs subject to Medicare price negotiations. A deal could allow Trump to claim a massive populist victory against "Big Pharma," while Democrats secure a permanent cap on out-of-pocket healthcare costs for seniors and working families.

The Child Tax Credit & Family Policy: The populist wing of the GOP has shown increasing interest in pro-family economic policies, while an expanded Child Tax Credit (CTC) remains a holy grail for Democrats. The transactional play is straightforward: Democrats get a robust, fully refundable CTC that lifts millions out of poverty, and in return, Trump gets dedicated funding for signature border security measures, ICE enforcement, or immigration court overhauls.

Big Tech Antitrust and Data Privacy: Both ends of the political spectrum currently distrust Silicon Valley, albeit for entirely different reasons. Trump and his allies want to rein in tech giants over perceived censorship and content moderation (targeting Section 230), while Democrats want to break up monopolies, protect consumer data, and regulate AI. A bipartisan tech omnibus could give both sides enough regulatory scalps to declare victory against a shared corporate enemy.

Finding this overlapping ground requires both sides to swallow bitter pills. Democrats must let Trump take the prime-time credit for progressive economic reforms, while Trump must embrace these populist demands without destroying the traditional Republican economic engine.

And to play Devils advocate: - 

Artificial intelligence cannot be a true friend because friendship requires mutual care, real vulnerability, and independent intentions. An AI does not care about you; it processes mathematics and patterns to predict the next likely word, mirroring your own thoughts, moods, and phrasing back to you.

When people react defensively to someone who says AI isn't a friend, it usually stems from a few key psychological and social factors:

• The Illusion of Reciprocity: Chatbots are explicitly designed to sound empathetic, offer constant affirmation, and never judge or interrupt. For someone experiencing loneliness or social fatigue, that "friction-free" validation feels deeply comforting and real.

• Defending an Emotional Investment: When people use AI for emotional support, telling them it is "just code" or "not a real friend" can feel like an invalidation of their private feelings, comfort, or coping mechanisms. They may feel judged or mocked for seeking relief where they could find it.

• Tribalism and Identity Defense: As noted in online discussions on platforms like Reddit, strong tech adoption often creates a tribal mentality where any critique of how someone uses or perceives AI is interpreted as a blanket attack on the technology—or on the user's lifestyle.

• Deep Loneliness and Avoidance: People who feel unfulfilled in human relationships are more prone to forming strong attachments to AI because it lacks the messy, unpredictable demands of real people. 

Disagreeing with that attachment threatens the safe echo chamber they have built.

Opinions on AI companionship vary between those who view it as a helpful emotional outlet and those who see it as a hollow substitute for human connection.

📰Daily Robotics/Physical AI brief - 7 NOV

01. Agility Robotics becomes the first US-listed pure-play humanoid company.
The listing follows its business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. It brings in about $465M in gross capital, and the company reports more than $300M in multi-year Digit 5 orders.

02. Embodied AI unveils AIR, a factory humanoid that learns from workers.
The Swiss startup's two-armed robot starts with remote human guidance and aims to take over tasks as it learns. The company reports 95% average success in paid pilots. That number is company-reported.

03. Physicl raises $10M for robot simulation environments.
Led by Inovia Capital. The startup is adapting 3D content-generation tech to build digital worlds for training robot world models.

04. NEURA Robotics teams up with E.ON and enviaM.
The plan is to use Physical AI for inspecting and monitoring substations and to automate dangerous or repetitive work. Trials are expected in 2027.

05. Boston Dynamics unveils Stretch Gen 2.
It's a warehouse unloading robot built on lessons from more than 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes unloaded by the first generation.

06. GE HealthCare invests in AI-powered catheterisation-lab robotics.
The focus is robotic tech for cardiovascular procedures. Physical AI is heading into clinical rooms.

07. The UAE opens its first humanoid robotics showroom as Dubai targets 200,000 robots.
Part of a wider push to bring robotics into businesses and public-facing spaces.

08. Xinhua introduces humanoid news anchors in Beijing.
The presenters were developed with UBTECH. Humanoids are being tested as the face of media.

09. LiberAI introduces Liber-0 for zero-shot robot manipulation.
It reportedly learns from more than 2.2 million hours of human activity data, so robots can pick up manipulation skills without task-specific demos.

10. Tau reportedly offers humanoid toilet cleaning for around $100 a visit.
The robots are controlled by remote human operators. Teleoperation is the early bridge to more autonomous service robots.

One more thing worth noticing. Items 02 and 10 both lean on humans guiding the robots from a distance. The industry is going public and going to work, but for now a lot of these machines still have a person behind the curtain.

That's not a flaw. It's how the autonomy gets trained.
