text:
**Microsoft’s $25 Billion Question: Why Is Big Tech Borrowing Billions for AI While Reducing Its Workforce?**

A remarkable financial transformation is unfolding across the technology industry. Companies are committing unprecedented amounts of capital to artificial intelligence infrastructure while simultaneously restructuring the human workforce that helped build their success.

Microsoft is reportedly preparing to raise approximately $25 billion through debt financing, even as reports suggest the company has offered voluntary buyouts to a significant number of employees.

**The contrast is striking. Billions are being committed to expanding machine intelligence while companies reconsider the costs and composition of their human workforce.**

Microsoft's investment strategy reflects the enormous financial requirements of the AI revolution. Data centers, advanced processors, networking infrastructure, electricity, and cooling systems demand extraordinary capital expenditures.

Unlike traditional software businesses, where additional customers can often be served at relatively low incremental costs, frontier AI infrastructure requires substantial physical investment before future revenues are realized.

Borrowing through debt markets can provide financial flexibility, allowing Microsoft to accelerate infrastructure development while preserving cash for acquisitions, operations, and shareholder commitments.

However, debt also introduces financial obligations that must ultimately be supported by sustainable earnings and cash flow.

**The larger concern is whether the extraordinary capital being deployed into AI will generate returns sufficient to justify its growing financial and operational costs.**

At the same time, workforce restructuring raises another important question about the future of employment in technology.

Are companies simply adjusting staffing levels to changing business priorities, or are we witnessing the early stages of a structural shift where capital increasingly replaces human labor?

The answer is likely more complicated than either explanation alone. AI creates demand for specialized engineering, infrastructure, cybersecurity, and operational expertise while potentially reducing demand for certain traditional functions.

**The future technology workforce may not necessarily be smaller across every discipline, but its composition will be fundamentally different.**

For investors, the challenge is evaluating whether expanding AI revenues can support infrastructure spending without placing excessive pressure on margins and cash flow.

For employees, the challenge is adapting to an industry where technical capabilities and organizational priorities are changing rapidly.

The reported borrowing and buyout plans should be evaluated independently, since their timing alone does not establish a direct connection.

Nevertheless, they illustrate a defining tension in the AI economy.

**Technology companies are entering an era where investing in machines and investing in people must be treated as complementary strategic priorities, not competing obligations.**

Microsoft's long term success will depend not simply on how much computing capacity it builds, but on how effectively that capacity produces profitable growth and meaningful economic value.

**The winners of the AI revolution will be determined not by who spends the most billions, but by who converts those billions into sustainable business results without losing sight of the people behind the transformation.**

text:
Todd Kaime writes:

"Here's why Western civilization must be protected, and why, if Islamo-leftism keeps spreading like a cancer, humanity will turn into one giant Third World.

Let's be precise, because precision is what this debate lacks. This isn't about Muslims. Millions of Muslims live freely in the West, build companies, raise families, and came here precisely for what the West offers. It's about an alliance: political Islamism on one side, a radical left on the other. Two movements that agree on almost nothing except one thing: the Western model has to go.

Political Islamism wants to replace secular law with religious law. The radical left wants to replace markets and property with an all-powerful redistributive state. 

One attacks individual freedom in the name of God, the other in the name of equality. Different scripts, same target: the free individual who thinks, builds, and owns what he creates.

Why does that matter so much? Because almost everything that pulled humanity out of misery came out of that model. The scientific method. 

Medicine that doubled life expectancy. Electricity, the airplane, the computer, the internet, AI. The rule of law, free speech, equality before the law, women's rights. Capitalism, which took over a billion people out of extreme poverty in a few decades. None of this happened under theocracy. None of it happened under collectivism.

And none of it is about race or geography. It's a value system. Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Israel, the Gulf states that bet on openness: every country that adopted some version of it took off. Every country that rejected it stagnated.

Now look at the track record of the alternative. Theocracies freeze science, crush women, and drive their best minds abroad. Collectivist regimes destroy incentives, then production, then freedom itself. Combine the two and you get the worst of both: a society that can neither create wealth nor tolerate dissent.

If that alliance keeps growing inside the West, here's what happens. Universities stop producing knowledge and start producing ideology. Entrepreneurs leave or stop trying. The state grows to manage the decline, taxes everything that still moves, and eventually expropriates even those who thought they were safe. Innovation dies quietly. And the West, which was the engine of the whole world, becomes just another place managing scarcity.

That's the part people miss. This isn't a Western problem. The whole planet runs on what the West invents: the vaccines, the chips, the software, the energy tech, the open markets. If the engine stops, India doesn't get its next breakthrough, Africa doesn't get its next leap, Asia loses its biggest customer. Humanity doesn't become more equal. It becomes equally poor.

So every civilization that is even remotely sane should understand this. Not out of love for the West, but out of self-interest. Freedom of thought, rule of law, property, open markets: these are not Western privileges, they're humanity's operating system. 

And the project to tear them down, wherever it shows up, has to be stopped. Not with violence, not by targeting a people, but with ideas, with law, with courage, and by refusing to apologize for what works.
Because it's the only way we keep moving forward."

text:
In 1964 a textile boss promised Warren Buffett $11.50 a share, then mailed him an offer for $11.375. Buffett was so angry over 12.5 cents that he bought control of the company and fired him.
He calls it the dumbest stock he ever bought. He says it cost him $200 billion.

The whole story, on one page:

In 1962 Buffett was 32 and running a partnership of about $7 million.

He started buying shares of Berkshire Hathaway, a dying textile mill in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

Its boss, Seabury Stanton, asked if he'd sell back at $11.50. Buffett gave his word.

Then the letter came. $11.375.

"He chiseled me for an eighth."

So Buffett kept buying. In 1965 he took control and fired Stanton.

Now he owned a textile business that lost money for 20 years.

He says he should have bought insurance companies with a fresh company instead. Every deal after that got stuck with the mill.

His estimate: without it, Berkshire would be worth twice as much. Another $200 billion.

The mill closed in 1985. The name stayed.

Berkshire is now worth about $1.09 trillion. One Class A share costs about $765,000.

The worst decision of his life built the biggest fortune of his life.

Was it his biggest mistake, or the best revenge in business history?

text:
Alabama Supreme Court Upholds $900,000 Verdict Against Orange Beach Walmart

Along the sun-drenched and bustling South Alabama coast, establishments and retail stores licensed to sell alcohol face a critical, ongoing responsibility to remain vigilant against fake identification. Whether dealing with seasonal crowds, spring break visitors, or year-round patrons, rigorous ID verification is an essential safeguard for local businesses aiming to prevent underage sales and the catastrophic tragedies that can follow.

MORE DETALS:  https://t.co/L0IsnrxJ3t

The Incident

On March 15, 2022, a 20-year-old University of Alabama student named Walters purchased champagne and a 12-pack of hard seltzer at the Orange Beach Walmart. Using a self-checkout register, he presented a fake Georgia driver's license to an employee, Secret Harris, who examined the ID for less than five seconds.

The following afternoon, after drinking at least four hard seltzers at a beach house, an intoxicated Walters got behind the wheel to drive to dinner. Meanwhile, 80-year-old James E. Reed of Indiana was vacationing at Gulf State Park with his family. After an evening bike ride, as Reed crossed Highway 180 on a mobility scooter behind his wife and grandson, Walters struck and killed him. Investigators subsequently recorded Walters' blood-alcohol concentration at 0.11.

The Verdict and Court Ruling

Reed's wife filed a lawsuit against Walmart under Alabama's Dram Shop Act, which allows lawsuits against businesses that illegally provide alcohol when resulting intoxication causes injury or death. Following a three-day trial, a Baldwin County jury awarded Reed's estate $900,000 in compensatory damages.

Walmart appealed the decision, but the Alabama Supreme Court upheld the $900,000 verdict on November 6, 2026, based on three primary rulings:

Scope of the Dram Shop Act: The court formally overruled its 1934 Webb v. French decision, clarifying that the Act permits claims arising from fatal accidents rather than just injuries.
Standing: The court affirmed that the personal representative of Reed's estate had proper standing to bring the lawsuit.
Retailer Liability: The court ruled that an alcohol retailer is not automatically shielded from liability simply because a clerk asks for and examines an ID. Because the fake license had visible defects and was inspected for less than five seconds, the justices determined the trial court was correct in allowing a jury to decide whether Walmart complied with the law.

To help mitigate these risks, the state offers a Responsible Vendors Program through the Alabama Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) Board, providing structured training for retail staff. Ultimately, local employees who sell alcohol carry a tremendous responsibility, often holding the weight of a business's livelihood and community safety in their hands during every transaction.

text:
Mondelēz sues Joyride over Sour Smacks, alleging Sour Patch Kids trademark infringement

Mondelēz International has brought a trademark and trade-dress lawsuit against Joyride Sweets, saying the company’s Sour Smacks candy infringes rights associated with Sour Patch Kids. (The claim is Mondelēz’s allegation, not a finding by a court.) The complaint was filed on 2 November in the US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. Mondelēz seeks an order permanently ending sales, the destruction of packaging and promotional materials it considers infringing, and monetary compensation. The requested remedies show the dispute reaches beyond whether the candies resemble one another: the company is also challenging how the product is presented and sold. Food Dive’s reporting supports that narrower account of the complaint, which connects particular visual details and retail conditions with alleged shopper confusion.

The products at the center of the case developed under different names and forms over several years, according to the reporting on the complaint. Joyride began selling sour gummy bears in 2020 under a broad descriptive label rather than the later Sour Smacks name. The company rebranded in 2022, then brought the line back in 2025 as Sour Smacks, now featuring gummies shaped like people. Mondelēz says the newer candy uses a child-shaped mascot, while its yellow-and-green packaging resembles the presentation of Sour Patch Kids. Those details form part of the company’s infringement case; the available reporting describes them as allegations rather than established conclusions.

The complaint also puts the products’ position in shops at the center of the claimed risk, rather than treating package design in isolation. Mondelēz says Sour Smacks and Sour Patch Kids are often stocked beside one another by the same retailers. It argues that this setting matters because confectionery is commonly bought on impulse, which it says can make confusion possible before, during and after a purchase. The company further alleges that Joyride benefits from the combination of close placement and similar-looking packaging, leading shoppers to choose its product instead. The reported account therefore links a claimed resemblance to a specific shopping context, but does not establish that customers were in fact misled.

The complaint includes a separate strand about Joyride’s marketing, tied to YouTube creator Ryan Trahan’s role at the company. Joyride appointed Trahan as a co-owner and chief creative officer in 2024. According to Just Food, the filing refers to a video featuring Trahan that acknowledged copying a Sour Patch Kids meme format. The video described that imitation as part of an effort to surpass Sour Patch Kids in Instagram followers, as recounted in the complaint. Mondelēz says it had repeatedly asked Joyride to stop the alleged infringement, but that the company declined to do so.

The lawsuit also refers to Joyride’s financing and valuation, although those financial details are not themselves a ruling on the trademark dispute. In May 2025, Joyride completed a private-equity funding round worth $30m, with the company valued at roughly $100m. Mondelēz alleges that the valuation was substantially underpinned by a business strategy that drew on Sour Patch Kids’ reputation and recognisability. That contention is the plaintiff’s account of what contributed to Joyride’s value, not an independently established explanation of the valuation. The complaint thus places commercial growth alongside claims about product appearance, retail proximity and marketing, while asking the court to assess the alleged infringement.

The reporting does not include a response from Joyride in the complaint, and Just Food said it had requested comment from company representatives. Food Dive separately reported that Mondelēz had not received a reply from Joyride after filing the case. The same outlet said a Joyride spokesperson did not answer its request for comment. These accounts describe the status of requests for comment; they do not provide Joyride’s position on the allegations. No quotation from either company is included in the facts available for this account.

The Joyride case follows another legal dispute brought by Mondelēz, this time involving a British chocolate business and a different brand. Mondelēz has taken separate action against Catherine’s Originals over its O’bar chocolate, alleging infringement of Toblerone trademarks. Catherine’s Originals, founded by Catherine Dodd in 2021, makes its chocolate in Walberton in Sussex. In that UK dispute, the business denied Mondelēz’s allegations and said its chocolate had a distinctive design and identity of its own. That matter is distinct from the Joyride case: it concerns O’bar and Toblerone, not Sour Smacks and Sour Patch Kids.

A separate corporate filing record identifies Mondelez International, Inc. as the filer of a Form 8-K. The record gives the accession number as 0001628280-26-068233, but the available fact does not connect that filing to the Joyride complaint. In another separate disclosure, Mondelēz reported worldwide net revenue growth of 2.3% year over year, reaching $9.97 billion in its third quarter. Those corporate details offer context about the company, but the reported revenue figure is not presented as a measure of the Sour Smacks dispute. The central questions in the lawsuit remain the specific allegations about branding, packaging, store placement and marketing, and the remedies Mondelēz has requested.

text:
On the morning of November 7, 1811, American riflemen and militia under William Henry Harrison stood their ground on a wooded rise above the Tippecanoe and broke the power of the most dangerous Indian confederacy the young republic had yet faced. Tecumseh had spent years welding tribes from the Great Lakes to the Gulf into a single force whose purpose was simple: stop the advance of the American people into the Old Northwest. While he was away recruiting in the South, his brother Tenskwatawa—the Prophet—promised the warriors that American bullets would not touch them. Harrison, governor of the Indiana Territory, marched a thousand men north from Vincennes, offered talks, and camped in battle order a short distance from Prophetstown.

Just after four in the morning the warriors struck. They drove in the sentries and came howling out of the darkness in waves, fighting into the tents themselves. For two hard hours Harrison’s regulars and the raw Indiana and Kentucky militia held the line in the black woods. When the light came, a bayonet charge by the 4th Infantry and the dragoons finished it. The attackers broke. The next day Prophetstown was burned. Sixty-two Americans were dead or dying and more than a hundred wounded, but the field was held and the confederacy was shattered. Tenskwatawa’s magic had failed; many of his followers abandoned him. Tecumseh’s grand design never recovered.

That fight was not some regrettable misunderstanding. It was the necessary defense of the American frontier against a determined effort to halt the settlement of the continent by the people who had already won it from the wilderness and from the British. Harrison’s victory made him a national hero—“Tippecanoe”—and helped carry him to the White House nearly thirty years later. It also stripped away the illusion that the tribes were acting alone; British arms and encouragement were found in the village, and within months the United States was at war with the power that had long armed and stirred the tribes against American settlers. On the Tippecanoe the expanding nation met organized resistance and refused to yield. The land was held. The future of the American people in the Northwest was secured by men who understood that a country which will not fight for its frontier will not long keep its heartland.

text:
AMERICAN FILM AND TELEVISION PRODUCTION COMPETITIVENESS ACT OF 2027 (1/5)
PART I - EXECUTIVE POLICY PROPOSAL
1. Summary: A time-limited federal production tax incentive to strengthen U.S.-based film/TV production, encourage domestic employment, recognize collective bargaining, and support investment in underserved production jurisdictions. Production decisions are influenced by state and federal tax policy, international incentives, infrastructure, workforce, financing, and specialized services. State incentives can influence location but cannot establish a consistent national framework. The Act would complement state programs with a federal credit for qualifying production expenditures, subject to eligibility requirements, an annual nationwide ceiling, certification, audit, recapture, and public reporting.
Goals: (1) Competitiveness: predictable federal incentive for qualifying U.S. spending. (2) Employment/bargaining: added incentive when a production meets a CBA payroll threshold. (3) Geography: reward qualifying spending in underserved jurisdictions with no nationwide location quota. (4) Fiscal accountability: statutory annual ceiling; actual costs measured separately from projected economic effects. (5) Rights/transparency: preserve labor agreements and legal protections; require auditable eligibility evidence; protect confidential production information.
The proposal does not assume every supported production is incremental, that all foreign production spending would otherwise occur in the U.S., or that more production will make the program self-financing.
2. Incentive structure
Base rate: Tier 1 25%, Tier 2 30%. Maximum: Tier 1 40%, Tier 2 45%. Labor uplift +5 pts. Domestic-spend uplift +5 pts. Geographic uplift +5 pts (same for both tiers).
Tier 1: theatrical features with budgets of $20M+ and scripted TV with qualifying costs of $5M+ per episode. Tier 2: smaller features and TV, documentaries, qualifying short-form. The credit applies to statutorily defined qualified production expenditures (QPE), not automatically the entire budget. Uplifts are cumulative up to the maximum rates.
3. Fiscal controls
- Annual nationwide ceiling: $5.0B
- Direct-payment election: 90% of allowable credit value
- Transferability: up to 100%, subject to statute and Treasury rules
- Labor uplift: at least 90% of covered payroll is CBA-covered
- Domestic-spend uplift: at least 70% of applicable budget spent in the U.S.
- Geographic uplift: at least 25% of QPE in underserved jurisdictions (the 20 states ranked 31-50 under a Production Opportunity Index)
- Sunset: Dec 31, 2032, with mandatory evaluation before any extension
The $5B ceiling is a maximum, not a forecast of utilization, growth, or incremental production.
4. Outcomes and measurement
Intended to improve competitiveness, support domestic employment, increase CBA participation, broaden geographic access, and create a reliable performance record. Claims about new spending, jobs, runaway production, and tax revenue must be evaluated against defined baselines and transparent assumptions, not treated as established before independent analysis. GAO would evaluate credit utilization, domestic production, employment, geographic distribution, incremental activity, displacement, administration costs, and fiscal effects.
PART II - PROPOSED LEGISLATIVE TEXT
A BILL to establish a federal income tax credit for qualified film and television production expenditures, encourage domestic production employment and collective bargaining, support geographic production opportunity, and provide for certification, oversight, and evaluation.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled:
SEC. 1. SHORT TITLE. "American Film and Television Production Competitiveness Act of 2027."
SEC. 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSES
(a) Congress finds: (1) production supports employment, professional services, creative industries, and related activity; (2) location decisions are influenced by tax incentives, infrastructure, workforce, financing, and commercial considerations; (3) state/local incentives vary in eligibility, value, availability, and administration; (4) some foreign jurisdictions offer incentives that may affect comparative economics; (5) a federal incentive may complement state programs and improve competitiveness of qualifying U.S. spending; (6) collective bargaining and labor protections are important to the U.S. production workforce; (7) geographic incentives should be evaluated against actual capacity, workforce, and spending patterns; (8) federal incentives require clear eligibility standards, accurate reporting, oversight, and proportionate enforcement.
(b) Purposes: (1) establish a federal credit for QPE; (2) encourage qualifying U.S. production employment; (3) add an incentive for productions meeting CBA requirements; (4) encourage investment in underserved jurisdictions; (5) maintain access for independent and smaller productions; (6) establish a statutory annual ceiling; (7) prevent duplicate claims, abusive transactions, and fraudulent certification; (8) require evaluation of actual economic and fiscal performance.
SEC. 3. DEFINITIONS
(1) Qualified production: theatrical motion picture, scripted or unscripted TV program, streaming program, documentary, or qualifying short-form production meeting this Act. (2) QPE: expenditures satisfying section 6, including U.S. location, compensation, documentation, and anti-duplication requirements. (3) Tier 1: theatrical feature with budget of $20M+ or scripted TV with qualifying costs of $5M+ per episode. (4) Tier 2: qualifying production below Tier 1 thresholds, a documentary, or short-form, subject to rules preventing artificial division or restructuring. (5) Covered payroll: payroll categories specified by the Secretary under section 7 for the labor uplift, with a consistent denominator and payroll treatment. (6) CBA-covered payroll: covered payroll paid under an applicable CBA with a labor organization representing motion-picture or TV workers. (7) Underserved jurisdiction: a state designated under the Production Opportunity Index (section 7). (8) Secretary: Secretary of the Treasury, unless the Secretary of Commerce is expressly identified. (9) Administering office: federal office designated under section 7 to administer certification. (10) Taxpayer: a person or entity that incurs, claims, receives, or acquires a credit attributable to QPE.

text:
True mercy and grace do not affirm grave sin; they call the sinner to repentance so that the soul may be saved.
The reply—“Ask God rather for forgiveness of YOUR sins and trust for the same grace and mercy you would seek to deny others”–misunderstands both Catholic teaching and the Gospel. Pointing out that homosexual acts are intrinsically disordered and cannot be approved (CCC 2357) is not a denial of grace. It is an act of charity that refuses to leave someone in a state that Scripture and Tradition identify as incompatible with the Kingdom of God.
Sacred Scripture is unambiguous. Romans 1:26–27 describes same-sex relations as contrary to nature. 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 lists those who practice sexual immorality (including men who have sex with men) among those who will not inherit the kingdom–then immediately adds that some were such but were washed, sanctified, and justified (v. 11). The remedy is conversion, not affirmation. When the woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus, He does not say “your sin is fine”; He says, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11). Love and the call to repentance are inseparable.
The spiritual works of mercy include admonishing the sinner. Ezekiel 3:18–19 and 33:8–9 place a grave responsibility on those who see another headed toward death and fail to warn them. St. Augustine’s maxim cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum (“with love for persons and hatred for sins”) has long expressed the Catholic balance: every person is made in God’s image and must be treated with respect, compassion, and sensitivity (CCC 2358), yet the acts themselves remain objectively disordered and closed to the gift of life. Persons with deep-seated homosexual tendencies are called to chastity, not to the celebration of acts the Church has always rejected.
False mercy that affirms unrepentant mortal sin does not extend God’s grace; it obscures it. Grace is freely offered for the forgiveness of sins when we repent and believe (Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38). To treat grave sexual sin as a neutral or positive identity is to contradict the very Gospel that offers liberation from it. The prayer for prelates who will not affirm such sin is therefore a prayer that shepherds will fulfill their duty to lead souls to heaven rather than confirm them in a path that Scripture warns leads away from it.
We are all sinners in need of mercy. That truth does not erase the distinction between loving the person and approving the sin. The greatest mercy is to speak the truth that makes repentance–and therefore true forgiveness–possible.

text:
THE MEMOIRES of Dr. Theophilus Periwinkle Hulse
CHAPTER THE SEVENTH
Of my Service under Sir Francis Walsingham, which has been hitherto Secret; of a Cipher in three Tongues; of certain Persons in black Hats at Paris; of a Meeting by Torchlight among the Bones of the Innocents; of a Rapier, a Skull, and a Sloop; and how I emended the Spanish Armada

The Fellows of this College have long given out that I have never in my life been farther from St. Polyrots' than the Buttery, and that the most perilous journey I ever made was down the Great Staircase, and that not on my own feet. I have let them say it. A Secret, like a Fellow, keeps best when every Person concerned in it is dead. Sir Francis Walsingham has been dead two-and-twenty years, Her late Majesty nine, and the King of Spain fourteen; and I am now at liberty to reveal what I did in the Spring of the year 1588, when I was a young Master of Arts, newly qualified, with a sharp eye, a thin purse, and no Beard to speak of.
I. How I was taken into the Service
It began with a Letter, as all my misfortunes do. It came to me at Cambridge in the March of 1588, unsigned, sealed with plain wax, and bidding me present myself at a certain house in Seething Lane, London, upon a matter touching the Greek Tongue. I supposed it to be a Bishop wanting a Sermon corrected, and I went.
I was received in a small dark room by a small dark man, whose face was pitted with the smallpox and whose eyes were never still. He gave me no name, but I learned afterwards that he was Mr. Thomas Phelippes, who two years before had read the secret letters of the Queen of Scots and brought her to the block with his Alphabet. He set before me a sheet covered with signs, numbers, and little drawings of birds, and said: "Tell me what this says."
I looked at it for an hour. Then I said that it was manifestly corrupt in eleven places, and I emended it.
At this a door opened behind me, and a tall grave gentleman came in, all in black, with a face like a closed book. This was Sir Francis Walsingham, Principal Secretary to Her Majesty, whom the Papists called the Devil and the Protestants called Sir Francis. He took up my sheet, read my emendations, and said:
"Mr. Phelippes tells me that this letter says the Duke of Guise has bought six horses. You have made it say that the Duke of Guise has been bought by six Cardinals."
"Sir," said I, "it reads better."
"It is not true," said Sir Francis.
"It is not yet true," said I.
Sir Francis looked at me a long while. Then he said a thing I have never forgotten:
"Mr. Hulse, Her Majesty has many servants who see what is in a letter. She has none who see what is not there. In our trade that is called Intelligence."
I was sworn the same afternoon. I was given ten pounds, a cloak, a false name, and a Mission to Paris. The false name was Mr. Periwinkle, which I chose myself, upon the principle that no Spaniard would believe a spy could be called so.
II. Of my Cipher
Mr. Phelippes offered me his Ciphers, with their birds. I declined them. Any Cipher made of signs can be broken by any man who counts signs, and the Spaniards have men who do nothing else. I proposed instead a Cipher of my own devising, upon three principles.
First, that English be written in the Greek Letters. No Frenchman can read Greek, except Casaubon, and he was at Geneva.
Second, that the vowels be omitted and supplied, where needed, by Hebrew points beneath the line. No Spaniard can read Hebrew, because their King burned everyone who could.
Third, and this was my particular invention, that the whole message be concealed in the Apparatus Criticus of a little edition of Virgil, in the guise of Conjectural Emendations. For I had observed that, of all the pages ever printed, the Apparatus is the one that nobody reads. A Searcher at the Ports may open a Bible, a Psalter, or a Book of Hours, and shake it, and hold it to the light; but no man living has ever voluntarily read the foot of a page of Virgil.
I give a Specimen, as it stood in my little Virgil under Aeneid 2.49:
49 ferentes] ΘΕ ΓΥΙΣ ΙΣ ΑΤ ΘΕ ΙΝΝΟΣΕΝΤΣ ΑΤ ΜΙΔΝΙΓΘ Hulsius
That is: The Guise is at the Innocents at midnight. I gloss it:
ferentes]. The lemma, as the learned call it: the word of the Text that is being emended. It is the famous line timeo Danaos et dona ferentes, "I fear the Greeks even bearing gifts", which I thought fitting for a message about the French bearing anything.
ΘΕ ΓΥΙΣ. Θ for th, as is natural. The Υ in Guise is a refinement that I am still proud of.
ΜΙΔΝΙΓΘ. Mr. Phelippes objected that ΓΘ is no way to write ght. I replied that the English have no way to write ght either.
Hulsius. Every Emendation must bear the name of its Author, or it will look suspicious. I signed them all, so the safety of the Kingdom depended upon my Name.
There was one difficulty, which I did not foresee. I wrote my Greek with the Erasmian pronunciation, as we did at Cambridge since Sir John Cheke. Mr. Phelippes read it with the Reuchlinian pronunciation, as the modern Greeks do. To him every Η was an ee. The result, for the first fortnight, was that Sir Francis Walsingham received from Paris a number of reports that Mr. Phelippes deciphered as Welsh.
III. Of Paris, and certain Persons in black Hats
I came to Paris at the beginning of May, by Dieppe and Rouen, in the character of a poor English scholar seeking Manuscripts. This was a perfect disguise, being the truth.
Paris was then in a great ferment. The Duke of Guise and the Holy League governed the streets, the King governed the Louvre, and nobody governed anything else. I took a lodging over a bookseller's in the Rue Saint-Jacques and began at once to observe the Conspirators.
They were not hard to find. In Paris at that season every Conspirator wears a broad black Hat, pulled low, and a long black Cloak, thrown over the left shoulder, and they go about in companies of a dozen or twenty. The Reader would suppose this the worst possible way to conspire, and so it is. But the true peculiarity of the Paris Conspirator, which I have observed in no other nation, is that they whisper in unison. They came creeping through the streets at dusk, all together, upon the tips of their toes, going Zitt! zitt! and Chut! chut! and whispering Silence! Silence! to each other so loudly and in such excellent harmony that they could be heard on the far side of the River. I once followed a company of them for half an hour through the Marais, and they whispered in four Parts, the Bass taking the lowest notes very handsomely, and at a corner they all stopped, raised their Hats together, and sang a Cadence. It was the finest Musick I heard in France. I wrote to Dr. Pottinger about it afterwards, but he did not take it up, having then no Italian.
On the twelfth of May the Parisians rose against their King. They stretched great Chains across the streets and piled up barrels full of earth and paving-stones to make walls, so that the King's Swiss could not pass. I gloss the word, since it is new:
Barricade. From the French barrique, a Barrel. The Parisians made their Rebellion out of Barrels, which I note for the instruction of the Fellows of St. Polyrots', who have tried the same thing in their own Cellar with poorer results.
It was upon that same night, the night of the Barricades, that I received a message in my Virgil, at Aeneid 2.49, that I was to meet a friend at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents at midnight, and receive from him a Packet.
IV. Of a Meeting by Torchlight among the Bones of the Innocents
The Cemetery of the Holy Innocents is the greatest burying-ground in Paris. It is so full that the Parisians dig up the old dead to make room for the new, and pile their bones in the galleries round about, called the Charnel Houses, skull upon skull, under painted pictures of the Dance of Death. There is no more cheerful place in Paris to receive a Packet.
I went at midnight with a Torch. Among the bones a Figure came out to meet me, in a black hat, with a Torch of his own. We had a Password, agreed by Sir Francis, from my favourite line:
"Timeo Danaos," said I.
"Et dona ferentis," said he.
I almost drew upon him then and there. Sir Francis had given the countersign as ferentes. But I recollected that ferentis, with the old accusative plural in -is, is the reading of some of the better Manuscripts, and is defended by several Grammarians, and that a man who knew it was either a spy of the Spaniards or a scholar of the first rank. I asked him, to settle it, what College he was of.
"Corpus Christi, Cambridge," said he. "They call me Kit. I write plays."
He was a young man of about my own age, with a pale face, a little moustache, and an air of having been drinking with Atheists. He gave me the Packet, sealed in oilcloth, and then, as we stood together under the skulls, he looked up at the sky, which was beginning to lighten in the east, and said, as though he had been composing it on the way:
"O lente, lente currite, noctis equi!"
Run slowly, slowly, horses of the night! I corrected him on the spot, as was my duty.
O. Not in Ovid. Inserted for effect by a Player.
lente, lente. Ovid has lente only once. The second is a dittography, the commonest error of copyists and actors, who say everything twice in case the Audience was not listening.
noctis equi. Correct. The line is from Ovid's Amores, the first Book, where the poet wishes the night to last because he is in bed with his Mistress. Kit had applied it to a Cemetery at dawn, which shows either great wit or no taste. In a Cambridge man it is generally both.
Kit said that he would remember my correction and put it into a play. I told him that a correction is not improved by being put into a play. He said I should see. I have never seen it, and I believe him to have been killed shortly afterwards in a tavern at Deptford over the reckoning, which is a just end for a man who adds Syllables.
Then the black Hats came.
There were six of them, coming out from the Charnel Houses in a line, with drawn swords, whispering Zitt! zitt! in four Parts. Kit threw his Torch at the first, cried "I'll write you into a Tragedy!", and vanished over the wall, leaving me with the Packet, a Torch, and the Spanish Ambassador's Musicians.
V. Of a Rapier and a Skull
Now I had a Rapier, which Sir Francis had insisted upon, and I had a Book upon the use of it, which I had insisted upon myself: the Ragione di adoperar sicuramente l'Arme of Giacomo di Grassi, printed at Venice in 1570, with excellent Figures. I had studied it closely in the coach from Rouen, and I had found it corrupt in four places, which I had emended. Its Figures showed the right foot always advanced, which I perceived to be an error of the woodcutter, who had cut his blocks the wrong way about. In my copy I had corrected every Figure to the left foot.
I therefore stood upon the left foot, as emended, and received the first black Hat.
It is a fact well known to Fencers, and now well known to me, that di Grassi was right and I was wrong. Standing upon my left foot, every thrust I made came out sideways. But this proved to be my salvation. The black Hats, who had all learned their Fence from the uncorrected di Grassi, had never met a man who did everything the wrong way about. They could not tell where I was going, and nor could I. My first thrust took the Hat off the leader. My second took off the Hat of the man beside him. My third took the Hats of two men at once and pinned them to the Charnel House wall, where I left them. I have been told since that a man without his Hat is no longer a Conspirator in Paris, but only a Parisian. The four Bareheads retired to consult.
The last two came on together. I backed away among the graves, and set my foot upon a Skull, which rolled, and I fell flat. The first of them lunged at the place where I had been and, finding nothing there, went on past it into an open grave, which the gravediggers had left ready for the morning. The second lunged after him and fell in on top of him. I rose, picked up the Skull, and addressed it as I hope one day to be addressed myself by some young scholar:
Heu, quis es? Nescio. Sed bene me servasti.
Alas, who art thou? I know not. But thou hast served me well. I have since been told that a Player at the Globe put a scene like this into some Tragedy about a Dane. If so, he had it from Kit, who had it from me, and he has left out the Latin.
I put the Skull in my pocket, to show Sir Francis, and ran for Dieppe.
VI. Of the Sloop, and the Sea
At Dieppe I found the sloop that Sir Francis had promised me, the Swallow, of Rye, a little vessel built for speed and for carrying Brandy without the knowledge of the Queen's Customs. Her Master, a Rye man named Gilbert Flint, had one eye, three teeth, and no Latin. He said, "You're the scholar," in a tone that made it an accusation. We put out on the evening tide.
We were not two hours out of Dieppe when a Spanish pinnace came out after us from under the cliffs, with all sail set, and gained upon us steadily. Master Flint said that we were too heavy. He looked at my Box of Books.
The Reader will understand what I suffered then. In that Box were my little Virgil with the whole Cipher in its Apparatus; my Homer; my Hebrew Psalter; Stephanus' Greek Thesaurus in five volumes; and a number of French translations of Homer, which I had bought at Paris to laugh at. I considered for a long moment, as Aeneas considered whether to stay with Dido. Then I threw overboard the French translations of Homer.
The Swallow leapt forward like a horse let off the rein. In a quarter of an hour we had left the Spaniard far astern. I have often reflected that French translations of Homer are the heaviest books in the world, being full of nothing. I recommend them to any Captain in distress.
Then came on a storm, and I was sick. I was sick in Greek, from the Fifth Book of the Odyssey, where Odysseus on his raft cries out that he wishes he had died at Troy:
τρισμάκαρες Δαναοὶ καὶ τετράκις, οἳ τότ᾽ ὄλοντο
Thrice blessed the Danaans, and four times, who perished then (Odyssey 5.306). Master Flint asked what I was saying. I told him I was blessing the Greeks. He said that he would not bless them, nor the French, nor the Spaniards, nor scholars; and he steered for Rye.
VII. How I emended the Spanish Armada
I rode to Seething Lane with the Packet, the Skull, and the Virgil, and laid them before Sir Francis. Mr. Phelippes opened the Packet. It held a long letter in the Spanish Cipher, and he sat with it three days and nights, and at the end of the third night he came out pale and said that it was a List of the great Fleet then fitting out at Lisbon: the Ships, their Tonnage, their Guns, and their Men. I asked to see his decipherment, and he let me, which was his mistake.
I observed at once that the numbers were very low. A King of Spain, I reasoned, does not send against England an Armada of a mere hundred and thirty Ships. The thing is beneath him. Plainly a copyist had dropped a cipher-figure, which is the commonest of all errors in numbers. I restored it throughout. Where Phelippes had 130 Ships, I read 1300. Where he had 8,000 Sailors, I read 80,000. Where he had 19,000 Soldiers, I read, exempli gratia, 190,000, and wrote in the margin fortasse plures, perhaps more.
Sir Francis took my emended List to the Council. The Council took it to Her Majesty. Her Majesty, being informed that 1300 Spanish Ships were coming against her, sent for every Ship, every Gun, every Fireship, and every Man in her Kingdom, and put them all in the Channel at once. And when the Armada came in July, being in fact only one hundred and thirty Ships, it found waiting for it a Navy prepared for ten times as many, and was destroyed.
Sir Francis sent for me in August. He said: "Mr. Hulse, Mr. Phelippes's figures were correct. You have emended the Spanish Armada by a factor of ten."
"Sir," said I, "and we have won."
Sir Francis looked at me with his closed-book face, and then something opened in it a very little. He said that he would make a Report of my service to Her Majesty, but that, a spy's name being a thing that must never be written down, he would describe me only as a young man of Sheffield, a Grecian. I am told he did so. I am told Her Majesty said, "God bless the young man of Sheffield," and asked no more.
And this, as the attentive Reader will now perceive, is why, four years afterwards, when I sat down beside her at the High Table of St. Polyrots', Her Majesty looked at me and asked, "And who is this?" She had blessed me, but she had never been told my name. I never told her. When she asked how I came, I said, By emendation. It was the truest answer I have ever given, and the only Secret of State she never had out of me.

N.B. The Michaelmas Examinations are upon us, and I have set the Papers. I set them, from long habit, in my Paris Cipher, with the Questions in the Apparatus. Last night I discovered three Undergraduates in my study by candlelight trying to read them. They had the Greek letters right, and the Hebrew points right, and had deciphered the first Question: ΘΕ ΑΤΗΡΣ ΝΑΗΜ ΑΝΔ ΣΗΥΗΝ ΙΣ ΑΠΡΟΑΧΙΝΓ. But they read it with the Reuchlinian pronunciation, and have gone off to revise Welsh. I shall attend to the Examinations presently.

APPENDIX
The Michaelmas Examination of the Year 1612, as Set by the Master. Here transcribed out of the Paris Cipher, the Reuchlinian errors of the Undergraduates silently corrected.
COLLEGIUM SANCTI POLYROTI
EXAMEN MICHAELMASSIANUM, MDCXII
Time allowed: from the Chapel Bell at six of the clock until the Master is satisfied.
Instructions to Candidates. Candidates are to answer ALL the Questions, and such others as may occur to the Examiner during the Examination. Answers in English will be read with pain; in Latin, with patience; in Greek, with pleasure; in Hebrew, they will be believed.
Candidates may not bring into the Hall any Crib, Translation (French translations especially, which are heavy), Herring, or Powder.
Section A: Latin
1. Translate into English:
Nunc age, qui reges, Erato, quae tempora rerum,
quis Latio antiquo fuerit status, advena classem
cum primum Ausoniis exercitus appulit oris,
expediam, et primae revocabo exordia pugnae. (Aeneid 7.37–40)
Then emend Erato. Candidates who decline to emend Erato will be presumed to be in Love, and dealt with by the Dean.
2. Translate Aeneid 2.49, and decipher the Apparatus beneath it in the Master's edition. Candidates who arrive at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents will be deemed to have answered correctly, and need not return.
Section B: Greek
3. Decline γραῦς in all its Numbers. Then explain, in Greek, why γραῖε is not a word. Candidates are reminded that the Master has been called it, upon a Stair, in the dark.
4. Translate:
τρισμάκαρες Δαναοὶ καὶ τετράκις, οἳ τότ᾽ ὄλοντο (Odyssey 5.306)
Say whether you would rather have perished at Troy than sit this Paper. A candid answer will not be penalised; a long one will.
5. Construe Odyssey 6.149 and 16.187. Discuss what each implies about the relation of the Speaker to the Person addressed. Candidates who refer to Her late Majesty will be marked down for presumption, and up for loyalty, and the two marks will be added together.
Section C: Hebrew
6. Point the following:
שחורה אני ונאוה
Then state to what kind of Person it should never be addressed, and why.
Section D: Textual Criticism
7. The first line of the Aeneid is transmitted in three forms:
(a) Arma virumque cano (the Vulgate)
(b) Arma virumque CAVE (Hulsius)
(c) Arma virumque cane (Gudgeon, from Padua)
Draw the Stemma, identify the Archetype, and explain why (b) is right.
8. Correct the following sentence: Sentio quod Magister erret. Two of its errors are of Grammar. The third is of Fact.
9. A Fleet is reported in a Spanish cipher as 130 Ships. Supply the missing Figure, giving reasons. Show your working; the Admiralty will want to see it.
Section E: Composition
10. Render:
(a) into Latin Elegiacs: The Bursar has fainted again.
(b) into Greek Iambics: Who left the Herrings in the Cellar?
(c) into Sapphics: Mr. Hulse. I cannot read Latin. Pray stop.
11. An Essay, in Latin, of not less than forty pages: Is a Fellow a Person or a Thing? Candidates may consider the Ghost's Οὐεργίλιον.
Candidates who finish early are to sit quietly and emend the Paper.
N.B. The answer to Question 7 is (b).
The Examiner's Report
Thirty-one Candidates sat the Paper. Fourteen, having deciphered it with the Reuchlinian pronunciation, answered it in Welsh; I have sent their scripts to Jesus College, which is used to it.
Question 1. Every Candidate emended Erato. Nineteen restored Eri, after my Commentary. Eleven restored Bessa. These were dealt with by the Dean, and by Mistress Spigot, who was more severe.

Question 3. Answered well. I note with gratitude that the Undergraduates now know more about the vocative of γραῦς than any Fellow of the College, living or pretending to be dead.
Question 4. One Candidate translated the line correctly, wrote beneath it τρισμάκαρες indeed, and handed in. I passed him for candour.
Question 8. Every Candidate identified the error of Fact as lying in the word erret, on the ground that the Master is often wrong. This is the error. The error of Fact is that the Master never errs. All thirty-one were marked down, and the Welsh ones twice.
Question 9. Thirty Candidates supplied a nought and read 1300. One read 130, on the ground that this is how many Ships there were. He was right, and failed. A Critick is not examined on what happened, but on what ought to have happened.
Question 11. No Candidate reached forty pages. Mr. Bunce, who played my Ancestor in the Comedy of 1592 and has never left the College, wrote forty pages in English, all of them headed Is a Fellow a Person or a Thing? A Thing. He was given a Third, for brevity of argument.
The highest mark of all was obtained by a Candidate who left the Hall after ten minutes, having written on his sheet only:
Hulsius, Emendator optimus est.
I gave him a First. Flattery is not Scholarship, but it is the beginning of Taste.
T. P. H., Examiner.

I knew I could go to jail because of an old warrant.

He reached over and prayed for me and my family.

He even offered to drive me 100 miles closer to Detroit after my car was towed.

I usually don't like cops, but I am truly grateful for this man

text:
What will the future of AI offer for medicine? 

A radiologist in Jakarta flags a chest X-ray through an algorithm and catches what she nearly missed. A nurse in Ohio uses AI to triage 200 ER patients and cuts wait times by a third. A research lab screens 10,000 molecules in a week for a disease that took a decade to crack.

None of this replaces the doctor. That's the point.

The future of medicine isn't a machine that knows everything. It's a machine that helps us know more, sooner, with more room for the human part — holding a hand, explaining a scary diagnosis, making a judgment call when the data is ambiguous.

Three shifts I believe we'll see:

1️⃣ Diagnosis — from hunting rare diseases in weeks to catching what the human eye misses in seconds. 
2️⃣ Discovery — from 10 years and a billion dollars to months and a fraction of the cost. 3️⃣ Care — from reactive treatment to continuous, personal, proactive monitoring.

But the stakes are real. Bias, data privacy, unequal access, and trust aren't side problems — they're the problem. The biggest win isn't better diagnoses. It's extending high-quality care to the people who currently get none of it.

So what will the future bring? I think it brings more doctors, not fewer — with more time for the part that was never automatable.

Mr. Deutsch, if I may offer a riposte to your implication: my argument doesn't assume its conclusion. It's a chronology. I started out pro-Israel, and the conclusion came last, after the events I listed. You can only call that circular by ignoring the order in which I presented it.

Nor does it rest on any assumption that saving Israeli lives isn't legitimate. When the same two batteries went to Israel after October 7, I didn't object. I mentioned it because the timing matters: they had sat unused at a base in Washington state while Ukraine asked for them.

I grant that veto provisions are legitimate. My point is how they used this one. Netanyahu's reasons, in his own words to the Wall Street Journal, were that the technology might fall into Iranian hands and that Israeli pilots fly "right next to Russian pilots" over Syria. That was a choice to accommodate Moscow while Russia was firing Iranian-made drones at Ukrainian cities. A country is entitled to make that choice. I'm entitled to judge it.

If any of my factual claims are exaggerated, name the one, and I'll defend it or correct it.

WE HAVEN'T EVEN TALKED ABOUT THE BIGGEST ECONOMIC WINNER OF THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS: FLORIDA!

Florida just strengthened its position as one of the most business-friendly states in America. And the message to businesses, entrepreneurs, investors, and families couldn't be much clearer. Republicans swept the statewide races and retained control of the Legislature. That means continuity in Tallahassee and a continued commitment to Florida's low-tax, pro-business economic environment.

But that's not all.

Florida voters approved meaningful property-tax relief, including a substantially larger homestead exemption for homeowners and tighter limits on assessment increases for commercial and rental properties. And Florida still has something many other states cannot offer: ZERO state personal income tax.

Now look at what's happening elsewhere. California: Voters approved making higher income-tax rates on top earners permanent rather than allowing them to expire in 2031. Washington: A 9.9% income tax on annual income above $1 million is scheduled to take effect in 2028. Texas: Democrats swept statewide races and flipped the state House, changing the political landscape in what has traditionally been a Republican stronghold.

Now think about the message this sends to someone deciding where to start a business, build a company, invest millions, hire employees, raise a family, or eventually retire. Florida is making its economic proposition more attractive while other states are making theirs more expensive. Where do you think entrepreneurs, investors, and growing businesses are going to take a harder look? My bet is we'll see more founders, more investment, more businesses relocating, more jobs, and more customers for the small businesses already here.

Is Florida perfect? Absolutely not. Housing affordability and property insurance still need serious attention. But those are challenges to address, not reasons to overlook everything Florida has going for it.

And here's the bigger picture: Florida has no state personal income tax, just approved additional property-tax relief, and continues to offer an environment where businesses can grow without constantly wondering what new tax or fee is coming next. Florida's best economic development strategy might just be letting other states keep doing what they're doing! While some states are figuring out how to collect more of your money, Florida is making a case for why you should bring your business, your investment, and your future here.

WELCOME TO FLORIDA! Open for Business America!

Florida just strengthened its position as one of the most business-friendly states in America. And the message to businesses, entrepreneurs, investors, and families couldn't be much clearer. Republicans swept the statewide races and retained control of the Legislature. That means continuity in Tallahassee and a continued commitment to Florida's low-tax, pro-business economic environment.

But that's not all.

Florida voters approved meaningful property-tax relief, including a substantially larger homestead exemption for homeowners and tighter limits on assessment increases for commercial and rental properties. And Florida still has something many other states cannot offer: ZERO state personal income tax.

Now look at what's happening elsewhere. California: Voters approved making higher income-tax rates on top earners permanent rather than allowing them to expire in 2031. Washington: A 9.9% income tax on annual income above $1 million is scheduled to take effect in 2028. Texas: Democrats swept statewide races and flipped the state House, changing the political landscape in what has traditionally been a Republican stronghold.

Now think about the message this sends to someone deciding where to start a business, build a company, invest millions, hire employees, raise a family, or eventually retire. Florida is making its economic proposition more attractive while other states are making theirs more expensive. Where do you think entrepreneurs, investors, and growing businesses are going to take a harder look? My bet is we'll see more founders, more investment, more businesses relocating, more jobs, and more customers for the small businesses already here.

Is Florida perfect? Absolutely not. Housing affordability and property insurance still need serious attention. But those are challenges to address, not reasons to overlook everything Florida has going for it.

And here's the bigger picture: Florida has no state personal income tax, just approved additional property-tax relief, and continues to offer an environment where businesses can grow without constantly wondering what new tax or fee is coming next. Florida's best economic development strategy might just be letting other states keep doing what they're doing! While some states are figuring out how to collect more of your money, Florida is making a case for why you should bring your business, your investment, and your future here.

WELCOME TO FLORIDA! Open for Business America!

Stephen Kinzer, an award-winning journalist, author and former New York Times foreign correspondent, argues that the war in Ukraine is the culmination of a 75-year American effort to use Ukraine against Russia. Washington repeatedly rejected opportunities to prevent the conflict, prioritising geopolitical dominance over European security and ultimately turning Ukraine into the battleground of a confrontation between great powers.

A War 75 Years in the Making

Describing Russia’s 2022 invasion as “unprovoked” obscures the historical circumstances that produced it. The invasion was the final stage of a much longer process of American intervention in Ukraine.

That process began in 1947, when the newly established CIA sought to destabilise the Soviet Union by supporting armed Ukrainian resistance. American intelligence recruited anti-Soviet operatives through Reinhard Gehlen, the former Nazi intelligence chief responsible for Eastern Europe.

Many of these recruits had collaborated with Nazi Germany, and some had participated in massacres. The American project in Ukraine was therefore built partly upon networks previously employed by the Nazis, establishing connections that continued to influence Ukrainian nationalist movements.
The Origins of America’s Anti-Russian Foreign Policy

American hostility towards Russia did not originate with the Cold War. It inherited a tradition of anti-Russian thinking developed during Britain’s imperial competition with Russia in the nineteenth century.

This hostility subsequently became embedded in American foreign policy through influential officials with personal or family backgrounds in Eastern Europe.

Zbigniew Brzezinski, Madeleine Albright, Victoria Nuland and Antony Blinken exemplify the influence of this political tradition. Their historical experiences and inherited attitudes helped sustain policies directed towards weakening Moscow.

Rather than merely implementing presidential decisions, these officials exercised substantial influence over the formulation of American strategy.

Ukraine became particularly attractive because of its potential to undermine Russia from within its immediate neighbourhood.
NATO Expansion and the Lost Opportunity for Peace

The end of the Cold War offered an extraordinary opportunity to establish a European security architecture accommodating both Western and Russian interests.

Instead, the United States expanded NATO eastward.

Bill Clinton’s decision was heavily influenced by domestic electoral calculations. Polish-American and other Eastern European communities represented important voting constituencies, while the American defence industry anticipated enormous profits from supplying weapons to new NATO members.

Despite warnings from George Kennan and other experienced foreign policy specialists, Clinton proceeded.

Short-term electoral considerations and commercial interests prevailed over long-term European stability.

Washington’s unwillingness to construct an inclusive security system also reflected a deeper psychological obstacle: America’s inability to accept an international order it does not dominate.

The most consequential and potentially dangerous result of this election may be Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan.

His victory speech offered a glimpse of the posture he may bring to Washington: smug, self-congratulatory and eager to taunt his opponents. But personality is only part of the concern. We should judge him by his own words and policies, not by his faith.

In his 60 Minutes interview, he said he would accept a one-state outcome if Israelis and Palestinians chose it. But that answer leaves a fundamental question unresolved: would Israel continue to exist as the national home of the Jewish people?

That is not a minor distinction. A shared state could mean equal rights and security for both peoples or it could mean the end of Israel as a Jewish state. Voters deserve a clear answer about which future he would support.

El-Sayed also called for an arms embargo on Israel and accused the country of genocide. Those positions deserve serious scrutiny, especially as antisemitism rises and Israel faces threats to its security.

Some Jewish voters supported him. One early-voter survey put his Jewish support at about 57 percent, while also finding he underperformed other Democrats among the same voters. Their choices belong to them; no one should presume to tell Jewish Americans how to vote. But every voter should weigh carefully what a candidate says about Israel, Jewish self-determination and the security of Jewish communities.

The warning here is not about a candidate’s religion. It is about the consequences of his stated positions and the danger of dismissing those consequences until it is too late to debate them honestly.  AW

iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), the New York fund that holds South Korea's large and mid-size companies, at $137.01, +$5.36 / +4.07% on Friday.

Seoul halted trading for 20 minutes on Friday morning and still closed at its lowest since March, and New York's Korea fund rose anyway, because it had taken its fall on Thursday, before Seoul's Friday session began. Taipei had its fourth straight losing week, and Taiwan's regulator wrote emergency rules against short sellers that take effect at Monday's open. Tokyo had its worst week since March 2020, while Hong Kong, Shanghai and Europe lost a fraction of that. US stock futures stopped on Friday carrying the chip bounce. The weekend's open question is Iran, where President Donald Trump says a decision on resuming the war is coming soon and Qatar says the talks are alive. China's October prices land Sunday night and America's on Tuesday morning.

Seoul's main index fell more than 8% in the first three minutes of Friday's session and tripped a circuit breaker, the automatic 20-minute halt that stops all trading once the index has fallen 8%.
- Kospi (South Korea): 5,059.69, -324.11 points / -6.02% in Friday's session, now closed. Week: -11.7%.
Samsung Electronics (005930 in Seoul) and SK Hynix (000660 in Seoul), the index's two largest stocks, closed 6.35% and 10.44% lower. Neither is US-listed, and neither is on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es.

New York had already sold Korea on Thursday for what Seoul did on Friday.

- Friday: +4.07%, with Seoul's 6% fall already known.
- Week: -10.4%, against the Kospi's -11.7%.
Seoul gets to price the fund's Friday gain at 7pm ET Sunday.

Friday's fall in Taipei was the fourth-largest one-day point loss in its history.

- Daily short-sale limit: 3% of a stock's 30-day average volume, from 30%.
- Margin, the cash a short seller must post against the position: 130%, from 90%.
The Finance Ministry authorized its NT$500 billion stabilization fund, about $15 billion, to buy shares.
- iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF (EWT) at $89.24, +$3.36 / +3.91% on Friday. Thursday: -11.5%. Week: -11.7%, against the Taiex's -12.19%.

text:
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

Duty – Honor – Country

IN GOD WE TRUST

text:
Tweet 6
Pattern 5 — Forced continuity. The free trial that was always a subscription.

You give a card for a “free” trial. No reminder arrives. It converts silently. The first signal is a charge — and often the trial length is set just past the window your bank statement would make obvious.

Federal law already covers this. ROSCA requires clear disclosure of renewal terms before you hand over payment details, express consent to the recurring charge, and a simple way to cancel.

But know the current state honestly: the FTC’s “click-to-cancel” rule — which would have forced cancellation to be as easy as signing up — was vacated by the Eighth Circuit on July 8, 2025, on procedural grounds. It is not in force.

What still applies: ROSCA, FTC Act Section 5, and state auto-renewal laws in California, New York, Massachusetts and others, several strengthened in 2025.

What to do: the moment you start a trial, set a calendar reminder for two days before it ends. Use a virtual or single-merchant card number where your bank offers one. And screenshot the renewal terms at signup — that screenshot is your evidence under ROSCA.

text:
Good morning, friends. As the first light of November 7, 2026, gently touches the sky, we begin another day with the comforting words of Deuteronomy 20:3: "Be not weakhearted or afraid..." These ancient instructions were given to people facing real battles, and they speak directly to the quiet struggles we carry today.

Many of us wake up with concerns that feel heavy. Perhaps it's worry over job security in a shifting economy, the health of a family member, or the way global tensions seem to echo in our daily news feeds. Everyday life brings its own uncertainties—rising costs, divided communities, and the simple pressure to keep moving forward when rest feels far away. Yet this verse offers a steady invitation to release the grip of fear and trust that we are not facing these moments alone.

Think about the small battles that fill our hours. A difficult email at work, a conversation with a child about their future, or even the internal voice that questions whether we are enough. The words remind us that courage does not mean pretending everything is fine. It means choosing to stand with an open heart, knowing strength is available beyond our own resources. In a world that often highlights what could go wrong, this promise brings a quiet hope that steadies us for whatever lies ahead.

This morning, take a moment with your coffee or during the commute to let the verse settle. Be not weakhearted when anxiety rises about the unknown. Be not afraid when headlines feel overwhelming. Instead, lean into the presence that walks alongside us, turning ordinary routines into opportunities for grace and connection. Small acts of kindness, a few minutes of prayer, or simply breathing through a stressful moment can become powerful steps of faith.

As the day unfolds, carry this encouragement gently. We are all navigating real-life challenges, but we do so with the assurance that hope remains fresh each morning. Let today be marked by renewed courage and the warmth of knowing we move forward together.

text:
Atlantic Council: Putin wants peace talks. He doesn’t want peace. The upcoming round of US-Russia-Ukraine talks offers little reason for optimism, as the Kremlin has shown an unwillingness to make real concessions. For the Russian president, the goal of negotiations appears to be less to end the war and more to keep Washington distracted while it weakens Western support for Kyiv. Without more pressure on Moscow, Russia has little reason to change course, and the talks could become another tactic to prolong the war.               

WASHINGTON—Next week, Russian, Ukrainian, and US negotiators will meet in Abu Dhabi for the first time in months, and observers are asking whether this suggests the prospects are growing for a negotiated end to Moscow’s aggression in Ukraine. The question is understandable, but only for those who ignore Russian President Vladimir Putin’s objective in Ukraine—establishing effective political control over the country—and his principal method for achieving that goal—undermining Western and especially American support for Ukraine.

For Putin, this goal and the means to achieve it are complicated by US President Donald Trump’s stated objective since returning to the Oval Office, which is to establish a stable peace in which Ukraine is sovereign and secure. But Putin has one advantage in achieving his goal, at least with the United States. Trump shows uncharacteristic deference toward Putin that makes him reluctant to do what he has said he would do to achieve this peace settlement: put pressure on the side that rejects reasonable proposals to end the fighting. Since the spring of 2025, Trump has offered at least a half dozen proposals to end or limit the fighting. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has agreed to each one, and Putin has deflected or rejected them all. This includes the most recent proposal, which US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff brought to Putin in Saint Petersburg in October.

That brings us to Abu Dhabi. For unclear reasons, over the past few weeks Team Trump has taken several steps that make it easier for Moscow to continue its aggression in Ukraine and more difficult for Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks. The gifts to Putin include finalizing a deal to resume Russian diesel shipments to the US in violation of US sanctions policy, waiving the sanctions in the recently passed Lindsey Graham sanctions bill, turning off the intelligence provided to Ukraine by the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, and entertaining Putin’s proposal for a three-way summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Not surprisingly, the Kremlin has greeted all these concessions with great enthusiasm.

But Putin has not offered a single concession of his own that could lead to a stable peace, which is Trump’s stated goal. And the administration’s “peace offerings” to Russia sparked strenuous bipartisan criticism in Congress. So, in turning down Witkoff in Moscow, Putin needed to offer something. That something was a procedural accommodation: Russia agreed to a trilateral working-level meeting in Abu Dhabi. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov showed the limitations of this step when he announced that Moscow would offer no new concessions; its terms for “peace” would not change. The Kremlin underscored this when it named former Russian Minister of Culture Vladimir Medinsky as the head of the delegation. Medinsky has been involved in most of the talks with Ukraine dating back to the first sessions in March 2022; those negotiations were unsuccessful. That contrasts with last winter’s talks in Abu Dhabi, which involved intelligence and defense officials discussing important but technical aspects of troop dispositions as part of a ceasefire.

Any realistic expectations for the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks should therefore be very modest. They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine. This motivation also explains why the Kremlin chose to include First Lady Melania Trump as the intermediary in plans to evacuate beleaguered Ukrainians from Oleshky, a town near Kherson where Russian forces had created a humanitarian crisis months ago by preventing the supply of food, fuel, and medical supplies. Moscow knew it had to resolve the crisis it had created because global attention was starting to focus on this war crime. Why not give the first lady the leading role in this drama?

In the wake of Putin’s rejection of the peace proposal Witkoff offered last month, it seems that Team Trump chose to focus the Abu Dhabi talks on a new security architecture for Europe, a legitimate subject when considering a possible end to the war in Ukraine. The administration announced that it had put together an approach that all sides could accept. And to their credit, Witkoff and his fellow special envoy, Jared Kushner, stopped in Brussels on Thursday to go over the plan with Ukraine and the Europeans. Even more notable was that the administration’s plan includes a major role for NATO in providing security.

While these developments are positive, there is no indication that the underlying dynamics of the negotiations have changed. On this latest White House approach, the Kremlin has shown the same unwillingness to negotiate seriously. This time it was Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s foreign policy adviser, who delivered the message: Moscow believes that a new security system requires the former Warsaw Pact and Baltic states to withdraw from NATO. That is hardly a proposal that would serve US interests or provide stability in Europe.

None of this points to real progress in Abu Dhabi. As long as the White House is satisfied with small gestures rather than actual concessions, Putin will not reverse course. The war will not end. It might even get worse, as Putin’s hand would only be strengthened if the United States continued to reduce its pressure on the aggressor. Perhaps the only outcome of the talks, then, will be to agree to another round.

Stop paying someone to cut silences in CapCut by hand.

An agent can now do it inside your actual CapCut project, and every cut stays editable.

capcut-editing-skill by emirrcodes (https://t.co/BMcdWqb8gS) is a free MIT skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Antigravity. Created 2026-10-04, checked via GitHub API + README this run.

You type one line like:
"project name" cut the non-speech parts and add subtitles

The agent reads your CapCut Desktop timeline and writes the edits back into it:

1. Silence cut: volume based, -30 dBFS threshold, 80 ms minimum gap.
2. Non-speech cut: local Silero VAD finds speech, checks Whisper word timings, keeps a 30 ms edge so words don't get clipped. Built to tell fan and traffic noise apart from speech.
3. Subtitles: meaning-based lines, usually 4 to 6 words, added to the existing timeline.

No screen or mouse control. It edits the project files locally, so the project just needs to be saved and closed while it writes. If it finds zero speech, it stops instead of deleting your whole video.

Needs CapCut Desktop, Python 3.10+, FFmpeg. macOS and Windows install paths (README says Windows open-and-save check isn't fully verified yet). README is in Turkish, the commands work through your agent.

Money play: offer creators a "rough cut + subtitles inside your own CapCut file" service. They keep full control, you skip the boring hour.

Would you trust an agent to cut your raw talking-head take, or only the subtitles?
