Because the state schools are rated based on the Ofsted ratings which affects their funding, Ofsted ones tried to close down Summerhill in the 90's and they lost quite badly precisely because Summerhill works.

Remove Ofsted and all the strings attached to funding, and you will see Summerhill like settings becoming widespread.

Most colleges have to accommodate way more than 1500 and still they are able to do it without training the students like dogs.

So schools should run more like community learning centers than like one-size-fits-all institutions. Offer many things, let people choose.

Some people will always want standard, conventional education. Others want REAL alternatives. We can address this *within* each school.

You can run a 
completely standard ed program in each school, AND a self-directed program, AND a makerspace/experiential program.

That's only overwhelming if you imagine imposing it from above. If you imagine allowing communities to evolve/grow what they need, it's not.

Once you empower people to make decisions at local & individual level, things can begin to shift incrementally in an organic way.

It's only the structural obstacles of standards testing, compulsion that prevent that incremental growth/evolution from taking place.
 And most of all. the structural obstacle of one-size-fits-all" thinking: that keeps us eternally arguing instead of creating options.
 
Imposing one form of edu. on a whole community is like trying to impose one religion or political party. People need the right to disagree.

And I propose it's better to try to serve those needs *within* the neighborhood school community than force people out to get needs met.

Otherwise, what you get at the college level: different temperaments, beliefs, etc. completely segregated in different schools.
If we want the community school to be a place where diverse people mix, then we need diverse approaches to education within each school.

Full-time. conventional school for kids who thrive with that, part-time/alternative ed for active high-energy kids & quiet introverted kids.

Have the high-energy kids running a coffee shop, a garden, a wood shop, a music studio. Let the bookworm kids read for hours in the library.

Have a social makerspace for tech, video editing, robotics. Give kids access to art & lab & theater spaces for self-organized projects.

text:
🧵 WEB2 vs WEB3: PART 3.

Now that we’ve explored Web2 and Web3, let’s put everything together.

I’ll make this as simple as possible.

1. THE BIG DIFFERENCES

Imagine two playgrounds.

The first is owned and managed by a company.

The second uses blockchain technology to distribute certain responsibilities and give users more control over digital assets.

Here’s how they compare:

WEB2:

Companies largely control the platforms.
Your data is managed by centralized services.
You create content on platforms owned by others.
Your account can be suspended by the platform.
Monetization is often controlled by the platform.
You participate in digital communities.

WEB3:

Blockchain networks can distribute control.
Users can hold certain digital assets themselves.
Wallets can be used to connect to applications.
Smart contracts automate transactions.
Communities can participate in governance.
Digital assets can sometimes move between compatible applications.

2. DOES WEB3 MEAN WEB2 IS BAD?

Absolutely NOT!

Web2 has changed the world.

It gave us:

Social media.
Online education.
Digital businesses.
Global communication.
Content creation.
Online communities.

Web3 is introducing another approach to how the internet can work.

Both have strengths and weaknesses.

Web2 is generally easier to use.

Web3 can offer more ownership and decentralization, but it can also be more complicated and risky.

And remember, not every project calling itself Web3 is truly decentralized.

3. WHAT COULD THE FUTURE LOOK LIKE?

Imagine a world where:

A creator can experiment with new ways to own and monetize digital work.

A gamer can own certain digital items independently of a game company’s database.

A community can collectively govern a project.

People can access financial services through blockchain-based applications.

Digital assets can move across compatible platforms.

These are some of the possibilities Web3 is exploring.

Will Web3 replace Web2 completely?

Not necessarily.

The future could combine both technologies.

4. THE SIMPLEST WAY TO REMEMBER EVERYTHING.

WEB1 = READ.

WEB2 = READ + WRITE.

WEB3 = READ + WRITE + OWN.

Web1 made information accessible.

Web2 made the internet interactive and social.

Web3 is exploring greater ownership and decentralization.

That’s the difference!

You don’t need to be a programmer or crypto expert to understand the evolution of the internet.

You just need to understand that the conversation is moving beyond what we can do online to what we can actually own online.

NOW, LET ME ASK YOU SOMETHING.

If you had the choice, which internet would you prefer?

A. Web2, where companies control most of the platforms we use.

B. Web3, where users can have more control over their digital assets and activities.

C. A combination of both.

Drop your answer in the comments.

And if this thread taught you something new, repost Part 1 so more people can understand Web3 without feeling intimidated by all the technical language.

Let’s make Web3 easier for everyone to understand. 🚀

text:
☕ Two to three cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

A long-running study of U.S. adults has tied regular consumption of caffeinated coffee to a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age. With follow-up periods stretching as long as 43 years, the work offers an unusually long view of how an everyday drinking habit relates to brain health over time.

The difference the researchers measured was large. Among adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, they recorded 141 dementia cases per 100,000 people each year, compared with 330 cases per 100,000 among those who rarely or never drank it. The benefits extended beyond diagnosed dementia: 7.8% of higher-amount coffee drinkers reported subjective cognitive decline — the memory and thinking changes people notice in themselves even without formal testing — versus 9.5% of those who consumed little or none. Such complaints don't automatically indicate dementia, but they offer a window into how people perceive their own cognitive aging.

Dose appeared to matter, too. Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for both dementia risk and cognitive functioning, and the association held regardless of participants' genetic risk — it was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, though the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower. Decaffeinated coffee, notably, did not show the same benefits, raising the question of whether caffeine itself helps explain the connection.

Still, the findings show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia, and other differences between coffee drinkers and the people who avoid it could contribute to what was observed.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and everyday activities, with Alzheimer's disease its most common cause. Occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging; dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. As populations grow older, identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower risk has become an important area of research — and the new findings suggest regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit.

📎 Paper: ScienceDaily

10 million users. Millions of downloads. Still losing money.

Sounds impossible? Here's why free apps can grow fast and still struggle to make a profit.

Every user costs money. Servers, storage, development, and support don't become free just because the app is.

That's why many apps use a freemium model. They offer useful features for free, hoping a small percentage of users will pay for upgrades.

Others make money through ads, subscriptions, or transaction fees. Free users can still help the business grow by attracting more people, but growth alone doesn't guarantee profit.

If an app spends more serving users than it earns from them, getting bigger can actually make the problem worse.

Millions of users look impressive. A sustainable business model matters more.

text:
US LESSON-INNOVATION IS NO LONGER OPTIONAL.

By Kumar Shankar Roy
businessline

In America, established businesses have paid a price for losing their innovative edge. 
Nike, 
Netflix, 
Lululemon, 
Intel, 
Kraft Heinz, 
Dow Inc, 
Ford Motor,
Grappling with past valuation excesses, or stale product offerings or competition from nimbler rivals, individually trade more than 50 per cent below their respective all-time highs. Put simply, innovation is no longer optional, even for celebrated brands.

Tech companies have not been spared either. Adobe, for instance, is down 64 per cent from its all-time high and 31 per cent from its 52-week high, as concerns over AI disruption weigh on its prospects. Companies unable to adapt risk losing relevance.

Amid the global race for technological breakthroughs, the silence from India’s corporate giants is almost deafening.

Technological leadership demands more than just intent or ambition.

This is reflected in a more direct way in mutual funds marketed around innovation theme in India. 

Depending on the fund, top holdings included ICICI Bank, Eternal (Zomato), Axis Bank, HDFC Bank, Adani Ports, Reliance Industries, Info Edge, Trent and Varun Beverages among their largest investments. 

Compare these with Innovation ETFs in the US, whose holdings include Micron, Tesla, Tempus AI and Marvell Technology, businesses associated with autonomous technology, AI-driven healthcare and gene editing.

One can argue these funds have different mandates, and improvements in distribution, banking or consumer businesses certainly qualify as innovation. 

Yet the contrast highlights the relatively limited choice of frontier-technology companies available to domestic equity investors.

No breakthroughs
Money, meanwhile, has hardly been India’s principal constraint. For calendar 2025 (a year not impacted by war-related raw material spikes) the Nifty 500’s pre-tax profit margin of 12.8 per cent compared with 12.2 per cent for the S&P 500 excluding America’s Magnificent Seven stocks. 

Indian companies also enjoyed considerably higher margins than their counterparts in Germany (7.7 per cent), Japan (9.9 per cent) and the UK (11.2 per cent). 

Clearly, corporate India has hardly been starved of profitability cushion to back innovation.

Yet research spending tells another story. Top listed Indian IT services companies spent about ₹1,000 crore to ₹3,000 crore in R&D, or 1-2 per cent of total expenses, in FY26. Clearly, profitable businesses and a technology services workforce do not automatically produce globally dominant intellectual property without higher investments.

The government has hardly been inactive. Corporate tax cuts in 2019, manufacturing incentives and infrastructure investment sought to encourage businesses to invest. The results in breakthrough commercial innovation remain less impressive.

That is not to suggest India has never produced genuine innovators. The country has made significant strides in pharmaceuticals, automobiles, emerging technologies and digital payments, particularly UPI. 
Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI raised $234 million in June. Yet such companies are still largely missing from the listed universe and, consequently, have little bearing on overall stock market performance.

India cannot summon global capital merely by making its stock market friendlier. Taiwan’s semiconductors, South Korea’s memory chips and America’s AI ecosystem offer exposure to technologies the world increasingly needs. 

Indian companies must build more such globally indispensable businesses. Fund managers lobbying for LTCG tax cuts should also push for more innovation from their portfolio stocks. 
Otherwise, investors may continue debating the cost of owning Indian stocks while overlooking the more consequential question: what do these companies actually own?

text:
Donald Trump is considering an executive order that would hand him the power to brand American nonprofits as supporters of terrorism, a designation that would instantly strip their tax exemptions, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The news landed the same day he elevated Stephen Miller, the aide who insists the Democratic Party is "not a political party," to chief of staff.

The mechanism is an obscure corner of the tax code known as Section 501(p). Lawmakers buried it inside a 2003 tax relief package for military families. Its intended targets were charities serving as fronts for foreign terror networks.

Under the provision, a president can tag a group in an executive order as backing terrorism. The exemption vanishes immediately, and the organization is barred from challenging it in any tax proceeding. Contributions lose their deductibility. The funding pipeline collapses.

Nine groups have already been stripped of their status through this route, per the Journal. None of those designations came directly from the White House.

Officials have spent months combing through nonprofits' financial records to assemble a target list. No names have surfaced yet. But Trump's allies have already floated George Soros's Open Society Foundations, the Southern Poverty Law Center and the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

Florida offers a preview of what follows. CAIR closed its operations there Thursday after Ron DeSantis's state "terrorism" label took effect. CAIR has never been hit with a single terrorism charge in this country, and the federal government doesn't list it as a terrorist organization.

You can fight a parking ticket. An organization that monitors hate crimes or defends Muslim Americans' civil rights could be destroyed on one man's word, and some of the evidence against it might be classified.

Miller would be holding the pen. He's credited with drafting the September 2025 memo that counts "anti-capitalism" and "anti-Christianity" among markers of domestic terrorism. 

He has argued that calling Trump's immigration policies "fascist" amounts to incitement. In July he told a State Department audience the government could "disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute" the groups it labels.

On Tuesday voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress, a blunt repudiation of this agenda. Three days later Trump turned the White House over to the man who authored much of it. Bloomberg interpreted the promotion as evidence he has no intention of moderating.

Miller starts Monday.

Nine fingerprints recovered from the scene where Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman were murdered in 1994 have never been matched to O.J. Simpson, the victims, or 58 friends and relatives who were tested. 

Now, more than 30 years later, the co-director of the docuseries "OJ's Accomplice" is pushing for those prints to be run through modern forensic databases that are vastly more advanced than what existed during the original investigation.

Ari Mark told Fox News Digital that today's fingerprint systems collect far more data and cover far more people, meaning a match that was impossible in 1994 could surface now. The original fingerprint specialist from the case, Gilbert Aguilar, agrees, noting that in 1994, prints were only checked against LAPD arrests, then Sacramento, then Western states. 

"If somebody is arrested outside your database, like in New York or the state of Florida, you're not going to get anything," Aguilar said.

The LAPD told Fox News Digital the case remains "an open and ongoing investigation" but offered no details on whether the prints have been retested.

text:
The Alternate ending of The Town is reminiscent of American History X and, overall, makes for a better ending. Should redemption give someone a reprieve?

Lately, I've been on a crime movie kick, particularly films in which the protagonist is a criminal.

For those who haven't seen it, I wholeheartedly recommend Ben Affleck's The Town. In my estimation, this movie has the right combination of suspense, character development, plot pacing, and interpersonal drama to earn a place on my list of memorable films.

What I'd like to discuss is the ending, or more specifically, the alternate ending.

In the original ending, just to refresh your memory, Affleck's character, Doug MacRay, escapes to Florida and overlooks the ocean. In a separate scene, Claire Keesey finds the money MacRay had buried in the garden, along with a tangerine, hinting that he escaped to Tangerine, Florida.

While this ending is certainly pleasant, and I'm sure it played well with the average moviegoer, who by that point had developed an emotional investment in MacRay, I found that the alternate ending fit much better with the overall tone of the movie, which was rather dark and violent.

In the alternate ending, MacRay, in the midst of his escape, is confronted and killed by the Hispanic men he had assaulted earlier in the film. The assault scene is a relatively minor part of the movie and feels almost completely out of place without the alternate ending to tie it together. In the theatrical cut, we never hear from those men again. They are simply assaulted and told to leave the neighborhood for having thrown bottles at Keesey as she walks through the projects on her way to work.

Knowing about the alternate ending, I'm immediately struck by the resemblance to Daniel Vinyard's story in American History X. Early in the film, Vinyard has a minor confrontation with a Black student in his school's bathroom before his character begins his journey toward redemption. And although redemption eventually comes for both Daniel and Derek, it isn't enough to shield them from the consequences of their actions. Their respective fates are both realistic and fitting, though that shouldn't necessarily imply they were just.

I'm left with the same feeling when watching The Town. That relatively minor confrontation, in terms of screen time, fits perfectly with the alternate ending, in which MacRay is unable to escape the consequences of the choices he made and the lifestyle he lived. One of the film's major themes is the stagnation of life in Charlestown, where criminal methods and traditions are passed down from parent to child, and escaping that lifestyle seems almost impossible.

Is it fitting, then, that the film's dark tone should be replaced with a happy ending? Did MacRay find redemption? Perhaps. But not even to the same extent as Vinyard's character in American History X, and Vinyard himself ultimately had to die.

So, the question I'd like to pose for discussion is this: Should redemption lead to a happy ending, or is redemption something that should be portrayed more personally? In other words, should it offer a sense of self-forgiveness without absolving someone of the consequences of their choices?

In my estimation, although I did feel good about MacRay and Keesey making it out alive, I believe the movie would have been better if MacRay, at the very least, hadn't.🤺

text:
Arizona NIMBYs Heckle SpaceX Over Jobs, Tax Cuts, and Cheaper Power

A packed elementary school gym in rural Cochise County turned into a shouting match this week when SpaceX showed up with a straightforward offer: a massive AI supercomputing campus, a thousand permanent jobs, thousands more in construction work, a 20 percent cut in property taxes, lower electric bills for locals, hundreds of millions in county revenue, and $3.6 billion in grid upgrades paid for by the company.

The site is 747 acres near the Apache Generating Station, about 13 miles from Willcox. SpaceX says the facility will use dry cooling, pull no groundwater for industrial use, and consume roughly as much water as a few dozen houses. The full build-out would demand up to 6 gigawatts of power, phased in over years, with battery storage to keep the load stable.

Residents answered with interruptions, heckling from the first minutes of the presentation, and “No Data Center” signs. Concerns centered on water, rural character, noise, and the usual fear that growth will change the place. A petition against the project gathered thousands of signatures in days. County planning officials have a formal hearing set for December 9.

The reaction fits a pattern. Rural areas already irrigate thousands of acres of crops, dairies, and orchards that use far more water than this project proposes. Those uses draw less organized outrage. A private company offering local jobs, tax relief, and infrastructure investment gets the full treatment. Some attendees came from outside the immediate area to join the opposition. Others in the room, including contractors and longtime residents, saw the jobs and revenue as a net positive for a county that needs both.

SpaceX has built rockets, satellites, and energy projects under heavier scrutiny than this. The company stayed after the formal presentation to take questions one-on-one. The louder voices in the room treated the numbers as secondary to the desire that nothing large happen nearby.

Rural Arizona has the land, the existing power plant, and a chance at real private investment. Whether the county takes it will be settled in the zoning process, not in the volume of the shouting.

text:
3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says | Rebecca Cohen, NBC News

Three foreign nationals have been charged in connection with an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI technology to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million.

According to an indictment filed in the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, who went by “Rocky Balboa” and “Seba Clarke,” was arrested in Spain in June; Sharon Hazan, who used the nicknames “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission,” “Fat Boy” and “Ron,” was arrested in Spain in August; and Guy Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September.

All three are accused of participating in a scheme that ran from July 2024 to February 2026 involving the use of artificial intelligence to impersonate the voices and images of corporate executives and attorneys at major law firms to trick employees of several companies into transferring large sums of money to bank accounts controlled by the group, according to a press release from the U.S. attorney’s office.

The trio and their co-conspirators would tell these employees — typically in accounting departments — they needed help with a confidential financial transaction and would use AI technology to mimic the company CEO’s voice, according to the press release.

Then, while pretending to be the CEO, they would tell employees to contact attorneys at large international law firms who they said were also working on the transactions, but in reality, those “attorneys” were also part of the scheme, prosecutors said.

Finally, one of the people involved in the scheme would instruct the employee to wire large amounts of money to bank accounts set up worldwide, according to the press release.

Once the employee wired the money, the group would convert the cash into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distribute it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators,” prosecutors said.

The U.S. attorney’s office alleges the scheme stole more than $129 million from companies worldwide, including an investment bank in New York, a hospital system in Missouri, a bank in Rhode Island, a hospital system in California, a financial technology company in the U.K., a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida.

Soall, from Spain and the U.K., impersonated U.K. attorneys and used a script titled “Lawyer Call” to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with victims, the release said.

Hazan, from Israel, laundered the money from the scheme, according to the press release. Prosecutors allege that Hazan “boasted that he had been laundering money since 1994; that he had laundered over $400 million in just the past three years; and that, among professional money launderers, he was ‘number one all over the world.’”

Hazan was also convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008.

Sheetrit, from Israel and the United Arab Emirates, is also accused of laundering funds, the press release said.

All three have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy and two counts of money laundering. Each of the seven charges carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.

“SI technology offers tremendous potential. But the public should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release, using an abbreviation for super intelligence, the White House’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. “I encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime.”

Stephen Kinzer, an award-winning journalist, author and former New York Times foreign correspondent, argues that the war in Ukraine is the culmination of a 75-year American effort to use Ukraine against Russia. Washington repeatedly rejected opportunities to prevent the conflict, prioritising geopolitical dominance over European security and ultimately turning Ukraine into the battleground of a confrontation between great powers.

A War 75 Years in the Making

Describing Russia’s 2022 invasion as “unprovoked” obscures the historical circumstances that produced it. The invasion was the final stage of a much longer process of American intervention in Ukraine.

That process began in 1947, when the newly established CIA sought to destabilise the Soviet Union by supporting armed Ukrainian resistance. American intelligence recruited anti-Soviet operatives through Reinhard Gehlen, the former Nazi intelligence chief responsible for Eastern Europe.

Many of these recruits had collaborated with Nazi Germany, and some had participated in massacres. The American project in Ukraine was therefore built partly upon networks previously employed by the Nazis, establishing connections that continued to influence Ukrainian nationalist movements.
The Origins of America’s Anti-Russian Foreign Policy

American hostility towards Russia did not originate with the Cold War. It inherited a tradition of anti-Russian thinking developed during Britain’s imperial competition with Russia in the nineteenth century.

This hostility subsequently became embedded in American foreign policy through influential officials with personal or family backgrounds in Eastern Europe.

Zbigniew Brzezinski, Madeleine Albright, Victoria Nuland and Antony Blinken exemplify the influence of this political tradition. Their historical experiences and inherited attitudes helped sustain policies directed towards weakening Moscow.

Rather than merely implementing presidential decisions, these officials exercised substantial influence over the formulation of American strategy.

Ukraine became particularly attractive because of its potential to undermine Russia from within its immediate neighbourhood.
NATO Expansion and the Lost Opportunity for Peace

The end of the Cold War offered an extraordinary opportunity to establish a European security architecture accommodating both Western and Russian interests.

Instead, the United States expanded NATO eastward.

Bill Clinton’s decision was heavily influenced by domestic electoral calculations. Polish-American and other Eastern European communities represented important voting constituencies, while the American defence industry anticipated enormous profits from supplying weapons to new NATO members.

Despite warnings from George Kennan and other experienced foreign policy specialists, Clinton proceeded.

Short-term electoral considerations and commercial interests prevailed over long-term European stability.

Washington’s unwillingness to construct an inclusive security system also reflected a deeper psychological obstacle: America’s inability to accept an international order it does not dominate.

📍 IRAN — MIDDLE EAST

🚨 THE MILITARY CONFRONTATION BETWEEN THE UNITED STATES AND IRAN HAS ENTERED ANOTHER DANGEROUS PHASE AS AN IRANIAN MILITARY SPOKESPERSON WARNS THAT AMERICAN BASES AND INTERESTS BEYOND THE MIDDLE EAST COULD BECOME TARGETS IF U.S. ATTACKS CONTINUE!
According to November 7 reporting attributed to Agence France-Presse (AFP), Iranian Army spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia warned that American military facilities and interests outside the Middle East could be targeted in response to renewed U.S. military action.

The statement follows President Donald Trump's acknowledgment of a limited American strike against an Iranian air-defense installation near Qeshm Island, close to the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

The warning raises a troubling possibility:

COULD THE U.S.–IRAN CONFRONTATION EXPAND BEYOND THE PERSIAN GULF?

For now, this remains a military threat — not confirmation that Iranian forces have attacked American bases outside the region.

But the warning deserves serious attention.

🔥 1. IRAN EXPANDS ITS MILITARY WARNING

Iran's latest statement suggests that Tehran does not necessarily consider American military installations outside the Middle East beyond the reach of possible retaliation.

The warning is significant because the United States maintains an extensive international military presence.

American forces operate from installations in Europe, the Middle East, Asia and other locations.

Any expansion of the conflict beyond the Persian Gulf could introduce additional countries, military commands and security arrangements into an already volatile situation.

However, Iranian officials have not established that a new attack on American facilities outside the region has taken place.

THE WARNING IS REAL. THE THREATENED ATTACKS ARE NOT CONFIRMED EVENTS.

It is also important to recognize that similar Iranian threats were reported earlier in November.

The November 7 statement therefore represents a renewed and more prominent warning rather than an entirely unprecedented declaration.

💥 2. U.S. STRIKE AGAINST IRANIAN AIR DEFENSES

The latest tensions follow President Trump's confirmation of a limited American strike against an Iranian air-defense installation.

The reported operation involved the area around Qeshm Island, a strategically important location near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian media also reported explosions in the region.

Air-defense installations are important military assets because they help protect airspace, military facilities and other strategic targets from hostile aircraft and incoming weapons.

Such systems may include radar equipment, communications infrastructure and surface-to-air missile components.

Disabling air defenses can potentially reduce a military's ability to protect nearby installations.

But the full damage assessment from the reported strike has not been independently established.

Some social-media accounts have described the operation as an attack on an Iranian missile-launch site.

THE AVAILABLE CONFIRMATION IDENTIFIES AN AIR-DEFENSE TARGET, NOT A VERIFIED MISSILE-LAUNCH FACILITY.

That distinction matters.

🚢 3. THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ REMAINS A GLOBAL FLASHPOINT

Qeshm Island sits near one of the most strategically important waterways on Earth.

The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and international shipping routes.

Commercial vessels transporting oil, liquefied natural gas and other goods travel through this region.

Any serious disruption could affect global energy supplies and international commerce.

Potential consequences include:

🔴 Increased oil and natural gas prices.

🔴 Higher maritime insurance costs.

🔴 Disruptions to commercial shipping.

🔴 Increased military deployments.

🔴 Additional pressure on financial markets.

🔴 Greater instability throughout the Middle East.

Reports of maritime incidents and explosions in the wider region have already heightened concerns.

But each incident must be investigated independently before responsibility can be assigned.

THE WORLD'S ENERGY MARKETS ARE VULNERABLE TO ESCALATION IN THIS NARROW WATERWAY.

🌍 4. COULD AMERICAN BASES IN EUROPE BECOME TARGETS?

Iran's warning about military installations beyond the Middle East has raised questions about the potential geographic reach of the confrontation.

The United States maintains significant military facilities throughout Europe.

However, the existence of those facilities does not establish that Iran has selected specific bases for attack.

No independently confirmed new Iranian strike against a U.S. base in Europe has been established in the reporting reviewed for this update.

A threat against American interests is not the same as an operational attack order.

And an attack order is not the same as a completed strike.

THE DANGER IS POTENTIAL ESCALATION — NOT A VERIFIED EXPANSION OF THE WAR INTO EUROPE.

Nevertheless, military planners must consider such warnings seriously because the consequences of miscalculation could be severe.

⚠️ 5. THE DANGER OF RETALIATION AND COUNTER-RETALIATION

One of the greatest risks in a military confrontation is the possibility that each side responds to the other's actions with increasingly forceful measures.

A limited strike can produce threats.

Threats can produce military deployments.

Deployments can increase the risk of accidental confrontation.

And an actual retaliatory attack could trigger another round of military action.

The resulting cycle can become difficult to control.

That is why diplomatic communication remains important even when governments are exchanging hostile warnings.

The present situation does not establish that a full-scale regional or global war is inevitable.

But it demonstrates how quickly military tensions can spread beyond their original geographic boundaries.

🤝 6. QATAR CONTINUES DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS

Despite the increasingly confrontational statements, diplomatic efforts have not entirely ended.

Qatar has reportedly continued mediation aimed at reducing tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Diplomatic discussions may provide an opportunity to prevent further escalation.

However, no comprehensive peace agreement has been confirmed.

The military situation remains uncertain.

THE UNITED STATES AND IRAN ARE STILL FACING A DANGEROUS CONFRONTATION — BUT DIPLOMACY HAS NOT BEEN ABANDONED.

🚨 7. WHAT IS VERIFIED — AND WHAT REMAINS UNCONFIRMED?

VERIFIED OR REPORTED BY ESTABLISHED NEWS ORGANIZATIONS:

✅ Iranian military spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia issued a warning concerning American military interests beyond the Middle East.

✅ The statement was reported on November 7, 2026.

✅ President Trump acknowledged a limited U.S. strike against Iranian air defenses.

✅ Qeshm Island and the Strait of Hormuz remain central to the military confrontation.

✅ Qatar has continued efforts to reduce tensions.

NOT INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED:

❌ A new Iranian attack on an American base in Europe.

❌ A completed Iranian military offensive against U.S. facilities worldwide.

❌ A newly declared global war.

❌ A confirmed decision by either government to launch an unrestricted military campaign.

THE THREAT IS SERIOUS — BUT WE MUST NOT PRESENT POSSIBLE FUTURE ATTACKS AS EVENTS THAT HAVE ALREADY OCCURRED.

MATTHEW 24:6 (KJV)

"And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet."

Scripture does not identify this November 7 statement as the fulfillment of a specific end-times prophecy.

The proper response is biblical discernment, not speculation.

"Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober."

WATCH — BUT BE SOBER.

Pay attention to world events.

Examine the evidence.

Distinguish confirmed developments from rumors.

And remain spiritually prepared.

MATTHEW 24:44 (KJV)

"Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh."

Our readiness for the return of Jesus Christ must not depend upon the next headline.

But as Christians, our responsibility is not to sensationalize war.

A WATCHMAN MUST KNOW THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A WARNING AND AN ATTACK.

Between a threat and a declaration of war.

We should never manufacture certainty where the evidence does not provide it.

Jesus Christ remains our hope in an uncertain world.

JOHN 14:27 (KJV)

"Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."

The world may be filled with military threats.

OUR HOPE IS IN JESUS CHRIST — NOT IN THE WEAPONS OR STRATEGIES OF NATIONS.

Think about the bottom 100 million Americans on the economic ladder.

Four major American cities representing approximately 14 million residents.

After decades of Democratic promises, the answer apparently is MORE government, MORE spending, MORE redistribution, and MORE socialism.

I believe we are moving in precisely the wrong direction.

America’s poorest citizens do not need another generation of politicians promising to take care of them. They need excellent schools, safe neighborhoods, strong families, personal responsibility, employment opportunities, and a realistic pathway toward financial independence.

And Republicans must be held accountable for delivering those opportunities, too.

That is the American Dream.

Socialism promises to redistribute prosperity. Capitalism offers people the opportunity to create it.

And after the 2026 elections, I fear we are about to learn that distinction the hard way.

Ambushed by six leading geologists at a scientific assembly specifically arranged to dismantle his career, he stood entirely alone in defense of a radical truth. He would wait fifty-six years for the establishment to admit he was right, only to deliver one perfect, devastating sentence when vindication finally arrived at age ninety-six.

His name was J Harlen Bretz.

Born in Michigan in 1882, Bretz spent years conducting grueling fieldwork across the scarred, gouged landscape of eastern Washington’s Channeled Scablands. In 1923, he published a paper proposing a breathtaking theory: the massive canyons and giant dry waterfalls hadn't been carved over millions of years of gradual erosion, but by a sudden, catastrophic Ice Age megaflood.

His hypothesis directly challenged uniformitarianism, the foundational doctrine of geology that insisted all planetary changes occurred slowly over vast epochs. Mainstream scientists condemned his work as outdated fiction.

In 1927, the Washington Academy of Sciences invited Bretz to present his research, only to set a trap. They lined up six prominent scientists to deliver scathing rebuttals, attempting to publicly humiliate Bretz and bury his theory forever.

Dismissed as a outcast, Bretz refused to retreat. For decades, he quietly continued his fieldwork alone.

The tides finally began to turn in 1940 when fellow geologist Joseph Pardee discovered physical evidence of Glacial Lake Missoula, the massive ice-dammed lake that had ruptured to unleash the exact floodwaters Bretz had calculated. Decades later, in the 1970s, NASA satellite imagery taken from orbit revealed the scablands' full scale, confirming Bretz's fifty-year-old maps with undeniable visual proof.

In 1979, the Geological Society of America awarded ninety-six-year-old Bretz the Penrose Medal, geology's highest honor, fifty-six years after his original paper was first ridiculed. When his son gave him the news of his ultimate scientific vindication, Bretz offered no boastful victory lap, responding with a single legendary line: "All my enemies are dead, so I have no one to gloat over."

J Harlen Bretz proved that truth does not depend on majority vote or establishment consensus, and that standing firm in your convictions can outlast an entire generation of skeptics.

NATO EXPANSION: DID THE WEST BREAK A PROMISE TO RUSSIA?

In Britain during the 1980s, Ronald Reagan was probably as familiar as a rubber puppet on the satirical television show Spitting Image as he was as President of the United States. Frequently appearing alongside Margaret Thatcher, he wasn't exactly portrayed as the sort of man you'd entrust with the nuclear codes.

Yet while British television was busy taking the piss out of him, Reagan was doing something rather extraordinary. He was negotiating with Mikhail Gorbachev, leader of the Soviet Union, about how to reduce the possibility of their countries blowing each other, and quite possibly the rest of us, to pieces.

Not bad for a former Hollywood actor who had once starred alongside a chimpanzee in a film called Bedtime for Bonzo.

Reagan, of course, was considerably more politically experienced than his rubber counterpart suggested. He'd spent eight years governing California before becoming president, and although he'd once described the Soviet Union as an evil empire, by 1987 he and Gorbachev were signing an agreement to eliminate an entire category of nuclear missiles.

After decades of confrontation, two men representing the world's greatest nuclear powers were seriously discussing how to make the world a safer place.

And then, in November 1989, the Berlin Wall came down.

For anyone who remembers that period, it was extraordinary. Communist governments were collapsing across Eastern Europe, the Soviet Union was struggling to hold itself together, and the Cold War appeared to be approaching an end that few people would have imagined just a few years earlier. There was genuine optimism that Europe might finally put decades of confrontation behind it.

So how on earth did we get from there to where we are today?

Well, I'm afraid this first instalment involves a little history. Not because I've suddenly developed an enthusiasm for dusty diplomatic paperwork, but because some of the conversations taking place behind closed doors in 1990 are still being argued about more than thirty years later. And those arguments matter enormously if we're going to understand the war in Ukraine.

The central question is surprisingly simple.

Did Western leaders promise the Soviet Union that NATO would never expand eastwards?

Depending on whom you listen to, the answer is either an emphatic yes or an equally emphatic no. The actual history, however, is considerably more interesting.

To understand it, we need to remember what Europe looked like at the time.

Germany was still divided into two countries. West Germany belonged to NATO, the US-led military alliance, while East Germany belonged to the Soviet-controlled Warsaw Pact. And despite the celebrations surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall, hundreds of thousands of Soviet soldiers were still stationed in East Germany.

Reuniting the country therefore presented an enormous diplomatic problem. The Germans wanted their country back together, the Americans wanted a reunited Germany to remain within NATO, and the Soviet Union was being asked to accept the loss of its military position in East Germany while a Western military alliance extended into territory it had previously controlled.

From Moscow's perspective, this was hardly an insignificant concession.

The Soviet Union had suffered unimaginable losses fighting Nazi Germany, subsequently dominated Eastern Europe for decades, and now found itself watching that entire political and military arrangement collapse. Gorbachev was attempting to manage an extraordinary retreat from Soviet power without leaving his country feeling humiliated or strategically exposed.

Western leaders understood the sensitivity of what they were asking him to accept. But there had also been an important change of leadership in Washington.

Reagan had left office in January 1989, and George H. W. Bush had become president. Although they belonged to the same political party, they were rather different characters.

Reagan had come from Hollywood, built a political career largely outside Washington and developed an unlikely working relationship with Gorbachev. Bush, on the other hand, was about as close to the American political establishment as you could reasonably get. He'd served in Congress, represented America at the United Nations and in China, directed the CIA and spent eight years as Reagan's vice-president.

If Reagan was the former actor who had helped transform relations with Moscow, Bush was the seasoned Washington insider who would help decide what came next.

One of Bush's first decisions was to review America's policy towards the Soviet Union. His administration was more sceptical about Gorbachev's reforms and initially slowed the diplomatic momentum established during Reagan's final years. Cooperation subsequently resumed, and Bush would help negotiate some of the most important agreements of the period, but his administration brought a different approach to deciding what the new European order should look like.

The Cold War might have been ending, but the question of what America wanted Europe to look like afterwards was only beginning. And there were enormous strategic interests at stake.

In February 1990, Bush's Secretary of State, James Baker, travelled to Moscow to discuss German reunification. During his meeting with Gorbachev, Baker raised the possibility of NATO's military jurisdiction not moving "one inch eastward" as part of an arrangement allowing a reunited Germany to remain within the alliance.

Those words have become central to one of the most contentious arguments about the origins of today's European security crisis.

And contrary to what some people might assume, they aren't a Russian invention. They're recorded in declassified American diplomatic documents.

Nor was Baker the only Western politician discussing restrictions on NATO's future expansion.

Just days earlier, West German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher had discussed the issue with Britain's Foreign Secretary, Douglas Hurd. And this is where the documents become particularly interesting, because Genscher wasn't talking exclusively about East Germany.

The British diplomatic record shows him raising the possibility of Poland leaving the Warsaw Pact and subsequently seeking NATO membership. He argued that Moscow needed reassurance that Poland wouldn't leave one military alliance only to join the other immediately afterwards.

The precise scope and duration of these early proposals would become disputed, but the significance of the conversation is unmistakable. Senior Western politicians were discussing the future military position of countries beyond East Germany, and West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl subsequently discussed similar limitations with Gorbachev as negotiations over reunification continued.

Think about the significance of that.

At the very moment the Cold War was ending, Western leaders were considering restrictions on NATO's eastward reach because they understood how Moscow might react to the alternative.

This wasn't something Vladimir Putin dreamed up thirty years later. The evidence is sitting in Western diplomatic archives.

And the story didn't end in 1990.

In July 1991, a delegation of Russian parliamentarians visited NATO headquarters in Brussels. According to their written report, NATO Secretary General Manfred Wörner told them he opposed enlargement and that 13 of the alliance's 16 members shared that position.

That's the Russian delegation's account of the meeting rather than a recorded NATO vote, but it tells us something about the messages Russian officials reported receiving as the old European order was coming apart.

So surely that settles it? The West promised not to expand NATO and subsequently broke its word?

Not quite.

Because there's an important difference between what politicians discuss during negotiations, what their counterparts understand from those discussions, and what governments eventually commit themselves to in a signed agreement.

And the final agreement was narrower than some of the possibilities discussed earlier.

In September 1990, the two German states and the four Allied powers from the Second World War, the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union, signed the treaty governing German reunification. It allowed a united Germany to remain within NATO while establishing specific restrictions on foreign military forces and nuclear weapons in the former East Germany.

What it didn't do was permanently prohibit Poland, Hungary or other Eastern European countries from joining NATO in the future.

That's the crucial distinction.

The diplomatic reassurances were real. The expectations they helped create were politically important. But the signed agreement did not impose a permanent ban on NATO expanding across Eastern Europe.

And the difference between those things would become increasingly contentious.

Because while Moscow was worried about losing its influence over Eastern Europe, the countries emerging from Soviet domination had their own ideas about the future.

Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia had spent decades under communist governments backed by Soviet power. They weren't particularly enthusiastic about regaining their independence only to discover that Moscow still expected to decide which military alliances they could join. From their perspective, NATO membership offered protection against the possibility of Russia becoming a threat again, and given their history, it isn't difficult to understand why they wanted that protection.

But there was an obvious problem developing.

Eastern European countries wanted security against Russia. Russian leaders objected to NATO potentially moving closer to their borders. And Western governments wanted to establish a new European order while retaining the military alliance they had built during the Cold War.

Three sets of interests, all colliding at precisely the moment Europe was supposed to be leaving its old divisions behind.

The Soviet Union finally collapsed in December 1991. The Cold War was over, at least officially, but the disagreement about NATO's future hadn't disappeared with it.

In September 1993, Russia's President Boris Yeltsin wrote to US President Bill Clinton expressing concern about NATO's proposed expansion.

His letter is fascinating because it acknowledges something that is often missing from arguments about this period. Yeltsin accepted that Eastern European countries had the sovereign right to choose their own security arrangements, and recognised that their fears about Russia had historical foundations. But he also argued that expanding NATO risked isolating Russia and that Europe should instead develop a broader security system involving Moscow.

He invoked the spirit of the German reunification settlement, arguing that NATO's expansion eastwards was inconsistent with what Russia had understood from the earlier negotiations.

Notice whose name we're talking about.

Boris Yeltsin. Not Vladimir Putin.

These concerns were being expressed by Russia's leadership years before Putin came to power, and Yeltsin's letter captures the dilemma rather neatly.

The Eastern Europeans wanted independence from Moscow's military influence. Moscow wanted to avoid being excluded from the new European security arrangements. And Washington was increasingly considering how NATO might develop in a Europe no longer divided by the Iron Curtain.

The interests weren't necessarily impossible to reconcile, but they weren't automatically compatible either. What had begun as a conversation about the future of Germany was becoming an argument about the security of an entire continent.

And I think this is where the history becomes so important.

It's perfectly possible to recognise Russia's responsibility for its later military actions while also asking whether the expectations created at the end of the Cold War were subsequently disappointed, and whether different decisions might have reduced the danger of future confrontation.

These aren't questions that require accepting the Russian government's account of everything that followed. They're questions raised by the diplomatic record itself.

For me, one of the great ironies of this period is that the men who helped bring the Cold War to an end appeared to have opened the door to a more peaceful Europe. Yet the question of how to provide security for Russia, its neighbours and the rest of the continent remained unresolved.

And that brings us to what happened next.

During the following decade, NATO would begin expanding across Eastern Europe. The countries joining had their own reasons for wanting membership, while Russian opposition became increasingly pronounced. How that process unfolded, and why Ukraine eventually became such a contentious part of it, deserves an article of its own.

The Cold War ended. Unfortunately, the argument about what should replace it never really did.

Next week, Part 2: NATO, Russia and the competing struggle for European security.

In court, Joseph DeAngelo sat in a wheelchair and stared at nothing. In his jail cell, a camera watched him climb the furniture. He wasn't frail.

He was the Golden State Killer. Between 1974 and 1986 he murdered 13 people, committed at least 51 r*pes and broke into more than 120 homes across California. For the first five of those years, he was a police officer.

He was caught in April 2018, at 72, after investigators traced his relatives through a DNA genealogy site and pulled his DNA off a car door handle.

It took 44 years.

Prosecutors announced they would seek the death penalty. In March 2020 he made an offer: he would plead guilty to everything if death was off the table. They took it.

In the video below, it's summer 2020, Sacramento County jail. No cane, no wheelchair. He stretches, walks the cell, climbs up on the bench to cover the light with paper. The camera's own clock runs along the bottom. One minute of video covers more than five weeks, June 17 to July 24.

The judge wouldn't let it be played in court.

On August 21, 2020, he got life without parole, stacked consecutive for every murder. He stood up out of the wheelchair to say, "I'm truly sorry to everyone I've hurt."

Then the DA released the tapes: "The truth of who Joseph DeAngelo is, lies not just in what happened in the courthouse, but what has happened in his jail cell."

He will never leave a room like this one.

Thirteen people dead, and the deal lets him grow old in a cell. Is that worse than the death penalty, or the best deal he ever made?

text:
Scientists Make A Breakthrough In Physics. Your Laptop May Never Be The Same. | Hank Berrien, Daily Wire

Forget everything you learned in high school science class.

A team of researchers has confirmed a third kind of magnetism, and scientists say the find could one day lead to lightning-fast computers, gadgets that use less power, and internet server farms that use far less electricity.

For nearly nine decades, the rulebook said magnets came in only two kinds. The first is the everyday kind, ferromagnets. That’s the stuff holding your child’s report card to the refrigerator.  Inside them, electrons all “spin” the same way, teaming up to create a magnetic pull.

The discovery, led by the federal Department of Energy’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in California and published in the prestigious journal Science, provides the strongest evidence yet that a third category called “altermagnetism” is real.

The second, discovered back in 1933, is the antiferromagnet. Electrons close to each other spin in opposite directions and cancel each other out, so the material shows no outside pull at all.

But in recent years, scientists kept bumping into strange materials that didn’t fit the mold. They looked like the second type on paper but acted a lot like the first. In 2022, researchers started calling them “altermagnets.”

SLAC scientist Daniel Jost and his team focused on manganese telluride, considered an antiferromagnet, and took it to a giant X-ray facility in France.

The team blasted it with “circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction,” per Science Daily . A typical antiferromagnet would react the same way to both beams. But manganese telluride reacted differently, revealing a built-in “handedness,”  like the difference between a left and a right glove.

That signal was exactly the fingerprint experts expected from an altermagnet. Jost said it gave researchers grounds to declare the new magnetism a class of its own.

The team first ran the tests in 2024, then went back in early 2025 and got the same result.

In an editor’s note accompanying the study, Science editor Jelena Stajic pointed out that “two groups are now reporting evidence of these chiral magnons,” magnetic ripples with a built-in left- or right-handed twist. A second team, using beams of polarized neutrons instead of X-rays, found similar evidence in a different material: manganese fluoride.

Today’s phones and computers work by pushing electrons around and reading their electric charge. But electrons have a second property, spin, that can also carry information. A  field called spintronics wants to use both, which could make gadgets faster, sturdier, and far less power-hungry.

It’s similar to a road that suddenly gets a second lane. Using an electron’s spin as well as its charge gives data another way to travel.

But both old-school magnet types have drawbacks. Jost warned that devices built with regular magnets are so sensitive that simply walking past a device with a magnet in your pocket could scramble its stored data. Antiferromagnets are not bothered by interference, but they’re so magnetically “quiet” that reading information from them is a nightmare.

Altermagnets offer the best of both worlds. They’re stable like antiferromagnets yet can still send useful signals that carry information.

That could mean sturdier computer memory, better quantum tech, and data centers that use less power.

Researchers say lots of work lies ahead. Their next challenge is learning to control these magnets with light and electricity so they can be built into real-world devices.

Cavaliers Blow Out 76ers 119-95 in NBA Cup Opener; Mitchell Shines as LeBron's Return Spoiled

Donovan Mitchell delivered a stellar, near triple-double performance to power the Cleveland Cavaliers (5-4) to a dominant 119-95 blowout victory over the Philadelphia 76ers (8-2) in their Emirates NBA Cup opener on Saturday night.
Mitchell orchestrated the offense masterfully, racking up 23 points, 8 assists, and 7 rebounds. Cleveland's defense swarmed the Sixers from the opening tip, completely spoiling LeBron James' highly anticipated first return to Rocket Arena as a member of the 76ers.

The Cavaliers' swarming defensive game plan thoroughly frustrated James, holding him to just 8 points on 3-of-12 shooting from the field, including a 0-for-4 mark from beyond the arc. In his 32 minutes of action, James also logged 7 rebounds, 3 assists, and a game-high 6 turnovers while battling heavy boos from the hometown crowd. The suffocating effort limited the 24-year veteran to a rare single-digit scoring output—marking only the 10th time in his regular-season career he has failed to cross the 10-point threshold.

Cleveland controlled the tempo almost the entire night, expanding their lead to as much as 25 points in the fourth quarter. The definitive victory offered sweet revenge for the Cavaliers, comfortably avenging a 29-point blown lead against Philadelphia from earlier in the season.

Textron Systems and its subsidiary Howe & Howe have secured a contract to supply two RIPSAW M3 unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) to the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory in Quantico, Virginia.

The vehicles will serve as experimental platforms for integrating advanced sensors and mission-specific payloads, testing operational capabilities, and evaluating future military robotics requirements.

Built with a Modular Open Systems Architecture (MOSA), the RIPSAW M3 offers a payload capacity exceeding 5,000 pounds (2,268 kg), a configurable flat-deck design, and speeds above 30 mph (48 km/h), supporting operations across challenging terrain.

text:
True mercy and grace do not affirm grave sin; they call the sinner to repentance so that the soul may be saved.
The reply—“Ask God rather for forgiveness of YOUR sins and trust for the same grace and mercy you would seek to deny others”–misunderstands both Catholic teaching and the Gospel. Pointing out that homosexual acts are intrinsically disordered and cannot be approved (CCC 2357) is not a denial of grace. It is an act of charity that refuses to leave someone in a state that Scripture and Tradition identify as incompatible with the Kingdom of God.
Sacred Scripture is unambiguous. Romans 1:26–27 describes same-sex relations as contrary to nature. 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 lists those who practice sexual immorality (including men who have sex with men) among those who will not inherit the kingdom–then immediately adds that some were such but were washed, sanctified, and justified (v. 11). The remedy is conversion, not affirmation. When the woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus, He does not say “your sin is fine”; He says, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11). Love and the call to repentance are inseparable.
The spiritual works of mercy include admonishing the sinner. Ezekiel 3:18–19 and 33:8–9 place a grave responsibility on those who see another headed toward death and fail to warn them. St. Augustine’s maxim cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum (“with love for persons and hatred for sins”) has long expressed the Catholic balance: every person is made in God’s image and must be treated with respect, compassion, and sensitivity (CCC 2358), yet the acts themselves remain objectively disordered and closed to the gift of life. Persons with deep-seated homosexual tendencies are called to chastity, not to the celebration of acts the Church has always rejected.
False mercy that affirms unrepentant mortal sin does not extend God’s grace; it obscures it. Grace is freely offered for the forgiveness of sins when we repent and believe (Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38). To treat grave sexual sin as a neutral or positive identity is to contradict the very Gospel that offers liberation from it. The prayer for prelates who will not affirm such sin is therefore a prayer that shepherds will fulfill their duty to lead souls to heaven rather than confirm them in a path that Scripture warns leads away from it.
We are all sinners in need of mercy. That truth does not erase the distinction between loving the person and approving the sin. The greatest mercy is to speak the truth that makes repentance–and therefore true forgiveness–possible.

Ven. Lazarus, Wonderworker of Mt. Galesius near Ephesus (1053). Ven. Zosíma, Abbot of Vorbozómsk. Finding of the Relics of Ven. Cyril, Abbot of Novoezérsk (Vologdá—1649). Martyrs Melasippus, Carina, their son, Antoninus, and forty children converted by their martyrdom, at Ancyra (363). Martyrs Auctus, Taurion, and Thessalonica, at Amphipolis, in Macedonia.

33 Holy Martyrs of Melitene
Commemorated on November 7
The holy martyr Hieron was born in the city of Tiana in great Cappadocia. Raised by a pious mother, he was a kindly and good Christian.

The co-ruling emperors Diocletian (284-305) and Maximian (284-305) sent a large military detachment headed by Lysias to Cappadocia to eradicate Christianity there, and also to conscript healthy and strong men into the imperial army. Among those pressed into service, Lysias also ordered his men to draft Hieron, who was distinguished by his great physical strength and dexterity. But Hieron refused to serve emperors who persecuted Christians. When they attempted to seize him by force and bring him to Lysias, he took a stick and started beating the soldiers who had been sent to bring him. The soldiers scattered, ashamed of being defeated by a single man. Hieron then hid himself in a cave with eighteen other Christians. Lysias would not risk losing his soldiers by storming the cave.

Upon the advice of Cyriacus, one of Hieron’s friends, Lysias lifted the siege of the cave and withdrew his detachment. Then Cyriacus persuaded Hieron not to offer resistance to the authorities. He and the other new conscripts and accompanying soldiers were sent to the nearby city of Melitene.

Soon Hieron had a vision in his sleep, in which his impending martyrdom was foretold. Lysias told the soldiers gathered at Melitene to offer sacrifice to the pagan gods. Hieron and another thirty-two soldiers refused to do this, and openly confessed their faith in Christ. Then the persecutor gave orders to beat the martyrs, and to cut off Hieron’s arm at the elbow. After cruel tortures they threw the martyrs into prison barely alive, and they beheaded them four days later.

A certain rich and illustrious Christian by the name of Chrysanthus ransomed Hieron’s head from Lysias. When the persecutions finally ceased, he built a church on the place where they executed the holy martyrs, and he placed the venerable head in it. The bodies of all the executed saints were secretly buried by Christians. In reign of the emperor Justinian, during the construction of the church of Hagia Eirene (Holy Peace), the venerable relics were uncovered and found incorrupt.

The other martyrs are: Hesychius, Nicander, Athanasius, Mamas, Barachius, Callinicus, Theogenes, Nikon, Longinus, Theodore, Valerius, Xanthius, Theodoulus, Callimachus, Eugene, Theodochus, Ostrychius, Epiphanius, Maximian, Ducitius, Claudian, Theophilus, Gigantius, Dorotheus, Theodotus, Castrichius, Anicletus, Themelius, Eutychius, Hilarion, Diodotus and Amonitus.

text:
Back to the Library

Today is the anniversary of the Bolshevik October Revolution of 1917.  It is also a good day to go back to the library and read more on the Revolution that changed the world three quarters of a century.  Here are a few books that I would recommend to learn more of the Revolution and the Civil War that followed. 

The first, “The Russian Revolution” is from 1995 by Richard Pipes and offers a scholarly perspective. He emphasizes the Bolshevik seizure as a well-organized coup rather than a spontaneous mass uprising, and he is particularly strong on the political dynamics, ideology, and the path from the Provisional Government’s weakness to Bolshevik consolidation. 

“Five Days Which Transformed Russia” by Sergei Mstislavkii is a 1988 translation of a firsthand memoir by a Left Socialist-Revolutionary who was actively involved in 1917 (including in the arrest of Nicholas II). It focuses on several pivotal days, especially around the February Revolution and its immediate aftermath, giving a non-Bolshevik leftist view of the chaos, spontaneity, and lack of organization that the Bolsheviks later exploited.

The third book “The Russian Revolution” by Sheila Fitzpatrick in 1982 covers the events of 1917 and continues through the Civil War, NEP, collectivization, and into the Stalin era, giving a clear, relatively balanced synthesis of the revolution and its early aftermath. 

The fourth book, “The Ignorant Armies” by E. M. Halliday is from 1964 and details the nine month campaign against the Red Army in northern Russia.  The ultimately futile effort by the 339th Infantry Regiment, and gives a look into one of the many Fronts of the Civil War that followed the Bolshevik seizure of power.

If you are interested in the Bolshevik Revolution, its causes and effects, as well as the civil war that followed, these are good books to add to your library.  Most are available on eBay or in used book reseller shops.  Build your personal library, save these books from the data center shredders!

But we haven't been told what terrible punishment God gave the three main figures of this massacre.
Direct Action Day had three main figures.

The first was Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The second was Husain Shaheed Suhrawardy, then Chief Minister of undivided Bengal (today's Bangladesh and West Bengal), who belonged to Jinnah's Musl!m League. The third and most prominent was the head of the Muslim League's youth wing, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

These three carried out the massacre on a large scale. Jinnah was sitting in Delhi, but his two pawns, Husain Shaheed Suhrawardy and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, went around the streets of Kolkata and Noakhali and had Hindus slaughtered.

And because they were in power (in the 1940s the British held elections in several provinces of India; Congress won in some provinces and the Musl!m League in others; the Muslim League won in Bengal, and Suhrawardy was made Chief Minister), Hindus were selectively killed on a large scale by the police and administration. The massacre was so terrible that Nehru and Gandhi were frightened and accepted the demand to divide India without conditions.

Now to their fates...

Muhammad Ali Jinnah was liberal in his views. He often lived in London. He was never a freedom fighter; he was a barrister. He smoked cigarettes and ate pork, which is forbidden in Islam. In his entire life he never offered namaz. He never even went on Hajj, and he married a non-Muslim.

Jinnah did not want Pakistan to be a hardline Islamic country, but after Pakistan was formed, nothing he said carried weight, and gradually Pakistan fell into the hands of extremists.

His health became very bad, but he was deliberately kept at the airport for 5 hours. He died writhing in agony inside the ambulance.
Not only that, his sister Fatima Jinnah's grave was dug up from a Karachi cemetery and thrown out. On the day of Fatima Jinnah's funeral procession, extremist Musl!ms attacked it, terrible riots broke out, and 5,000 people were killed in Pakistan that day.

It was the first terrible riot in Pakistan after its creation, and it was Musl!m against Musl!m. You can search on Google.

He became Prime Minister of Pakistan, but he was Bengali, and so the Pakistani army did not like him.

text:
In 1908 Walter Chrysler spent seven times his savings on a car he couldn’t drive.

He was a railroad mechanic in Oelwein, Iowa, in charge of the locomotives for the Chicago Great Western Railway.

At the Chicago auto show he saw a Locomobile. It cost $5,000.

He had $700 in the bank and a wife and two kids at home. A bank lent him the rest.

The car came home by train. He hired a team of horses to pull it from the freight office.

Then he didn’t drive it.

For three months he took it apart and put it back together, again and again, until he knew how every part worked.

Two years later he was running a big locomotive plant in Pittsburgh. Charles Nash, the president of General Motors, heard how well he ran it and offered him a job at Buick, the brand at the heart of GM.

The job paid half what he was making. He took it anyway, because it meant working on cars.

Buick was still building cars mostly by hand. Chrysler went through the factory the way he went through the Locomobile, one part at a time. 

He brought in machines and assembly line methods and cut costs wherever he found waste. Buick more than tripled its output.

In 1916 he became president of Buick, at half a million dollars a year.

In 1919 he fell out with GM’s boss over how the company was run. He sold his stock for $10 million and planned to retire.

That didn’t last. Bankers paid him $1 million a year to rescue Willys-Overland, a car company in trouble. Then he took over another struggling one, Maxwell Motor.

At Maxwell he built the first car with his name on it. 

The 1924 Chrysler sold for about $1,500 and was made to compete with cars that cost $5,000 and up, the same price as his old Locomobile.

A year later Maxwell became the Chrysler Corporation. 

In 1928 he bought Dodge, which made Chrysler the second biggest car maker in America, and in 1930 his name went on the tallest building in the world.

text:
Michelin as a destination business

The origin of the Michelin Star goes back to the early days of the automobile. French brothers Ándre and Édouard Michelin founded their self-named tiremaking company in 1889 — a pioneering move, considering that there were fewer than 3,000 automobiles in France at the time.

Michelin wanted to increase profits made by their tyres. Which meant selling more. But they are not a commodity that one holds in stock like soup, or rice – you only need 5 tyres for a car. And they couldn’t sell ‘spares for your spares’. Also, they couldn’t sell more cars (and hence more tyres) because they weren’t a motor manufacturer.

All they could do was to get car drivers to wear their tyres out faster.

The solution? They made it chic to drive hundreds of miles by inventing the Michelin Guide. They started the Guide in 1900. It contained everything you needed to know about staying, driving, and eating in Europe. All this done in (what was by today’s standards) an uncomfortable car. The Michelins distributed their guide for free until 1920, when they initiated a fee of seven francs for the booklet. They introduced the concept of using a Michelin Star to rank restaurants in 1926

The Côte d’Azur had never seemed so sexy. Or close.

Now let’s reframe: Michelin isn’t just about selling rubber; they’re in the destination business. They rank experiences, which opens up a world of possibilities – Michelin could develop destination apps, offer chef training programs, support sustainable ingredient farming, or even move into the visa and accountancy business for digital nomads working from any country in the world.
