text:
Pure capitalism enjoys a divine privilege: it gets to claim every success in the real world while remaining exempt from its judgment. Whenever businesses create wealth, the free market can declare another victory; whenever they pollute, buy political protection, or demand that the public cover their losses, they are expelled from capitalism and transferred to a department called “cronyism.” You see how elegant this arrangement is: capitalism attends the awards ceremony, the mixed economy attends the hearings, and the government stands trial. A system supposedly never fully implemented gets to claim prosperity that has already occurred, then invokes its own absence as proof of its innocence. By this method, any system can achieve immortality: write success into its definition, classify failure as a betrayal of its principles, and keep demanding that reality preserve the purity of the theory. The hard work of explaining cause and effect disappears into a ritual of relabeling.

“Voluntary exchange” offers a similar reassurance, as though two signatures on a contract amounted to society’s consent. Imagine a factory happily making a deal with a buyer while discharging its wastewater into a river that supplies drinking water to communities downstream: both parties get what they want, while the residents were never invited to participate in this exercise of free choice. Declare the pollution a violation of property rights, and you still have to explain who determines the damage, who pays to prove it, who can force the factory to compensate its victims, and how those victims survive while the case drags on. Invoking property rights cannot magically produce a justice system everyone can afford. Here is the absurdity: a transaction can keep its benefits inside the contract and its costs outside it, then cite the satisfaction of its signatories as proof that the whole arrangement is legitimate. A contract can record the consent of those who sign it, yet it has no authority to sign on behalf of everyone who bears the consequences; erase those third parties from the ledger, and the profits will naturally look much cleaner.

The deeper contradiction emerges when the winners of competition start calculating how to avoid having to compete any longer. Suppose a company discovers that developing a better product takes ten years, while securing a rule that keeps competitors out requires cultivating a few well-placed officials: why should the much-celebrated profit motive suddenly switch itself off at the doors of government? A business can accumulate wealth by satisfying consumers, then use that wealth to buy the power to escape their discipline, with both decisions emerging from the same calculation of profitability. Calling the second step “cronyism” still leaves you to explain how the advantages accumulated in the first step became the means to purchase privilege, and what institutions could prevent that conversion. Declaring that government should remain limited also requires explaining who has the power to keep it that way, especially when the wealthiest market winners are demanding protection. The fundamental difficulty with free competition is that its winners may be able to afford to abolish it. A theory that celebrates capital’s pursuit of profit, then declares the subject has changed as soon as capital starts buying political power, gives capital unlimited room to pursue its interests—and gives itself an equally unlimited supply of escape routes from accountability.

text:
Raiders Vs 49ers tomorrow is the wake-up game the Raiders need to turn this season around. No excuses, beat the man in front of you because there is no reason he should be better than you unless you truly believe you’re not cut out to play in the NFL. 

Yes, I’m calling an upset. But there’s a path to it.

1️⃣ Brock Bowers is a matchup nightmare

Bowers gives the Raiders someone they can build the passing game around. Move him around the formation, find favorable coverage and make San Francisco adjust. The goal isn’t just getting him catches—it’s forcing the defense to devote attention to him and creating opportunities elsewhere. If the Raiders need a big third-down conversion, he’s the player I want involved.

2️⃣ Kirk Cousins gives this offense a chance to finish drives.

Cousins has been finding the end zone, and his ability to work through his reads matters against a defense that can punish rushed decisions. Vegas needs patience without becoming conservative: take the underneath completion when it’s there, then attack when the coverage opens up. Field goals probably won’t be enough. Cousins turning scoring opportunities into touchdowns is a big part of the upset formula.

3️⃣ Max Crosby can change a possession 

You don’t have to shut down San Francisco on every snap to change the game. A sack, a tackle for loss or pressure that forces an incompletion can turn a promising drive into a punt. Crosby gives the Raiders a player capable of producing those moments. Against an offense this dangerous, getting it behind schedule could be the difference between surviving a possession and surrendering seven points.

4️⃣ Ashton Jeanty can hurt them through the air

His rushing production has been frustrating, but that doesn’t erase what he offers as a receiver. Screens, checkdowns and routes out of the backfield give the Raiders another way to get him the ball in space. If San Francisco puts extra attention on Bowers, Jeanty needs to make that decision expensive. A short completion that becomes a big gain counts just the same.

5️⃣ The Jets game gives them something to build on 

Confidence alone won’t beat the 49ers. But coming off a win gives the Raiders evidence that they can execute when a game gets tight. The challenge is carrying that into Sunday without giving away possessions through penalties, turnovers or missed assignments. They don’t need to play like a favorite. They need to stay close enough for their playmakers to decide it.

That’s it that is the formula. The same playmakers that have been the reasons we have won games all have to show up together this game to get the win.

text:
La dolce vita (1960) offers a remarkable portrait of Rome, from its ancient monuments and Baroque architecture to the fashionable streets and modern neighborhoods of the Italian economic boom.
An interesting distinction: some locations were filmed in Rome, while others were reconstructed at Cinecittà. Fellini's Rome is both a real city and an imagined one.

Rome on Screen: La dolce vita (1960)

1. Historic Rome — monuments and landmarks
Trevi Fountain (Fontana di Trevi) — The famous nocturnal scene with Anita Ekberg and Marcello Mastroianni. One of the most recognizable images in cinema.
St. Peter's Basilica (Basilica di San Pietro) — Sylvia and Marcello climb toward the dome, with extraordinary views over Vatican City and Rome.
St. Peter's Square (Piazza San Pietro) — Bernini's monumental colonnades, visible in the sequence at the basilica.
Ancient Roman aqueducts — The opening helicopter sequence carries a statue of Christ above the outskirts of Rome, contrasting ancient ruins with modern technology.

2. Streets, squares, and fashionable Rome

Via Veneto (Via Vittorio Veneto) — The center of Rome's fashionable nightlife, luxury hotels, cafés, celebrities, journalists, and paparazzi.
Piazza Barberini — The square at the lower end of Via Veneto, part of the geography of fashionable central Rome.
Cinecittà Studios — Fellini reconstructed much of Via Veneto here, creating his own version of Rome's glamorous nightlife.

3. Ancient Rome and aristocratic spaces

Baths of Caracalla (Terme di Caracalla) — The ancient Roman baths associated with the nightclub sequence, where Sylvia dances.
Aristocratic palaces and castles — The nocturnal gathering with Maddalena and Marcello evokes the interiors, galleries, and inherited grandeur of Rome's old nobility.

4.Modern Rome — postwar architecture

EUR district (Esposizione Universale Roma) — Monumental modern architecture, broad avenues, and a striking contrast with historic Rome.
Palazzo dei Congressi — A major example of twentieth-century rationalist architecture, associated with the film's modern urban settings.
Piazza San Giovanni Bosco — The modern residential neighborhood associated with Steiner's world.
Church of Santi Martiri Canadesi — The church where Steiner plays the organ. 

5.Beyond central Rome — countryside and coast

Palazzo Giustiniani-Odescalchi, Bassano Romano — The historic palace north of Rome used for the aristocratic gathering.
Tivoli and its surroundings — The countryside outside Rome, associated with the film's religious apparition sequence.
Fregene — The coastal pinewoods and seaside environment of the film's final episodes.
Passoscuro Beach — The Tyrrhenian coast, where the film ends with Marcello and Paola separated by the sound of the 

The four most relevant landmarks and settings are St. Peter's Square, the Trevi Fountain, Via Veneto, and the streets surrounding its celebrity nightlife.

text:
Royalty was 17 when a stranger on a San Diego trolley offered her $100 to sleep with him. She wasn't a prostitute. She'd never done it before. But her boyfriend had just kicked her out - no family to call, no money, no phone, nowhere to go. She took the money. The next morning she spent it on food. By noon she needed more. By 18 she was on crystal meth, working Hollywood Boulevard at 3 AM, so thin her ribs showed through her shirt. She's been raped. She's almost been killed. She was born to a 15-year-old girl in foster care who couldn't keep her.

Her birth mother had her at 15 - while she was in foster care herself. Royalty was taken away at two. Bounced through foster homes. One foster mother had cats and a big dog. Royalty still says she was the best one. She wishes she'd been adopted by her instead.

She was adopted around five by a couple in Kansas City. The house was nice. The food was good. The love was not. Her adoptive father was a strict Christian who demanded perfection. When she failed math, he made her eat peanut butter and jelly sandwiches for a year. When she acted out at 12, he beat her in a way she says "wasn't understandable."

She started sneaking out. Smoking weed. Running away for longer and longer. She says she felt "really lost" - she didn't know who she was, didn't know where she came from, and had accepted the fact that nobody was out there for her.

At 15 she met a guy in San Diego - a skater in his early twenties. They were together for two years. He called it saving her. She calls it control. At 17, she broke something of his. He was done. She was on the street.

She rode the trolley downtown. A man approached. She said no. Then she thought about where she was going to sleep. She said yes.

A pregnant woman on the trolley the next day taught her how the track worked. Showed her National City. Explained the rules. Within weeks, Royalty was catching dates on the street.

At 17 she moved to Los Angeles with a man who said he was a pimp. She worked Hollywood Boulevard - open street, catching dates in traffic. Then Figueroa. She was once out there with nothing on.

On her 18th birthday she tried crystal meth for the first time. Made $1,800 that night. Stayed up all night. She says it made her feel happy. Made the work easier. Brought out her personality.

Within months she was skeletal. "I was getting skinny as fuck. I lost hella weight." She hid her addiction from her family, sneaking to a neighbor's house to get high before coming home like nothing happened.

Clients tried to remove condoms during sex. She held them in place herself. Some got violent about it. There's no vetting process. You get in a car with a stranger and hope.

She was arrested after a date - police pulled up, she jumped out. They searched the client's car and found an AK-47. They let him go. They took her to jail. Released her around 2 AM - back on the street, alone.

She met a 14-year-old girl working the track.

She got clean from meth in April 2021. Someone close to her told her she'd changed. She listened.

At the end of the interview she says: "I've been raped in this game. I've almost died in this game." Then she adds - she wouldn't trade any of it.

When a girl born to a teenage foster kid bounces through the system, gets adopted into a house with no love, and ends up on a trolley at 17 saying yes to the first stranger who offers cash - did she choose this life, or did every system that was supposed to protect her push her straight into it?

text:
IMO almost every move Tesla has made the last five years has been due to their dawning realization that 4680 specifically, but battery tech and manufacturing capacity in general, was not going to achieve their dreams anytime soon. 20M cars a year was a pipe dream. They saw the writing on the wall for a high volume EV world. So they pivoted to autonomy and robots, which offer high margin, continuous revenue while minimizing battery usage.

Cybercab uses only 48KWh of batteries, and more importantly, if the theory holds true, autonomy should effectively remove 5-10 cars from the road. So that's 5-10x fewer batteries Tesla needs to make or source. 5-10x fewer batteries the world needs to transition to sustainable personal transport.

It's also why they now consider the 4680 a success even though from a consumer facing viewpoint it's not all that great. Because they finally figured out how to make enough of them they need by solving DBE process (which in turn probably helped the unboxed process work efficiently), and cheaply enough to be useful/profitable for Cybercab and Semi, while not really making many significant improvements on charging rates, density or range. In an autonomous world, none of those factors really matter as much.

text:
Thank you Eric. 

You’re a fiercely loyal friend and a fiercely loyal  patriot. I can’t overstate how admirable that is to me.

Your words of never burning bridges have always been a reminder to myself of the ultimate mission we are on.

I don’t want to ever burn this bridge when I question some people’s loyalty to America First .

I never thought I would question Stephen.

My father was a staunch advocate of immigration for only the best and brightest.

He scolded my mother’s father and his son for trying to receive any social security benefits or any free benefit from the US government without earning it.

This was in the 70s, when I was a little kid. But I remember it clearly.

My father was proud to pay taxes to the US government.  He raised me to be proud to pay taxes and to give back to the US. He made me walk up and down the Statue of Liberty to acknowledge the greatness of the USA every year.

My father made a speech at the age of 7 in a village where no one spoke or could read English,

He recited one of Lincoln’s speeches to that village. He felt he was Lincoln reincarnated, as crazy as that sounds.

He was determined to come to the US even though he was orphaned by the separation of Pakistan from India by the British.

My grandfather was one of the architects of the Karachi airport when it was still part of India.

When my father was hit by a car when I was 11, it was a cover up.

The local newspaper, and the police wrote on the newspaper that he had been hit at 8pm.

But everyday, I would pour a glass of black label whisky on ice for him.

He would make me watch the local news which started at 5 pm, the national news which started at 6 pm, the international at 7 pm and usually McNeil Lehrer or The McLaughlin Group.  That’s where I got introduced to conservative ideas from the likes of Pat Buchanan, William Buckley, and many others.

So I knew he didn’t come home at 8pm. Luckily it was cold enough for my father’s brain to not hemorrhage and the blood that leaked from his Skull formed a circular pool but it coagulated so he could survive for those 3 hours.

Before he was hit by that car, he warned Pfizer that he would be filing a class action lawsuit(but he was offered a board position with IBM and CFO of international paper, so he never intended to sue anyone.)

Also the FBI came to visit my father before the accident.

And after 3 days in a coma, month of anterograde amnesia, and basics he finally left the hospital.  My mother was hit and run by a car before she made it home with him.

The man who ran my father over was best friends with a high level mason involved in the building of Sing-Sing prison.  The area was at the edge of Ossining and Scarborough. One of the Rockafellas had a house not too far from there.

My father’s proudest moment was being a delegate for Reagan two years before that.

My father criticized both Canada and the UK for letting any type of uneducated Indian immigrant into their countries.

He always told me what makes the US great is that the process of immigration is so cumbersome and based on qualifications and thats what sets it apart from those countries.

Even though, thanks to my birth in NYC, dozens of family members got a chance to become US citizens, lawyers, doctors, accountants, tech giants etc…after my father’s accident they disappeared from my life.

My 4 children never even met them.

The first time my oldest daughter and son met an aunt and uncle was after he graduated as a lab technician for the army in San Antonio. 

They all held a grudge because he called it straight and forcefully argued for them to all contribute to the country that gave them so much.

The reason I admired Vivek was because he was the first American of Indian heritage who reminded me of my father’s values.

I tell you all this to recognize your gift to judge a man’s character.

Probably why I went off on a rant on Stephen, because I really like him. I admire him and wish I could be half as brilliant.

text:
Stuart, absolute Irish tonnage does not disprove displacement. The largest incumbent supplier can lose market share to several smaller competitors.

In the first half of 2026:

• Ireland supplied 78,066 tonnes, over 10,000 tonnes less than in 2025.
• Ireland’s share of UK beef imports fell from 73% to 64%.
• Total UK imports nevertheless increased.
• The principal winners were Australia and New Zealand, operating with favourable tariff-free quotas secured through post-Brexit trade deals.

That is market displacement.

Teagasc explicitly says increased New Zealand beef exports had a “direct negative impact” on UK beef prices, followed by an impact on Irish prices. Take your argument up with Ireland’s agricultural research authority.

Your live-cattle explanation also mixes animals with tonnes of beef. Irish live exports were themselves down 15%, more than 80% were calves, and only comparatively small numbers went to Algeria and Tunisia. Exporting calves cannot explain 10,000 tonnes of Irish beef being displaced from the UK market now.

Finally, prices are set at the margin, not according to which country remains the largest supplier. A relatively small influx offered below British and Irish production costs can move the market price for everybody.

This is market economics, Stuart, not “% news”.

text:
**The Scottish Enlightenment** (roughly the 1730s–1820s, centered in Edinburgh and Glasgow) was a distinctive intellectual flowering within the broader European Enlightenment. It emphasized empiricism, the “science of man,” practical improvement, natural sociability, and the study of society, history, and the natural world over pure rationalism or abstract speculation. It was fueled by Scotland’s universities, debating clubs (such as the Select Society and Poker Club), a literate Presbyterian culture moderated by the Moderate party in the Kirk, post-Union economic growth, and networks of thinkers who often knew one another personally.[](<https://t.co/ZQ14feIY2q>)[](<https://t.co/q1OEoaCyQ8>)

The core “architects” were primarily moral philosophers and social theorists who developed a shared approach to human nature, ethics, and society. Here are the central figures and their main ideas:

### Francis Hutcheson (1694–1746)
Often called the “father” of the Scottish Enlightenment. An Irish-born Presbyterian who held the chair of moral philosophy at the University of Glasgow (where he taught Adam Smith).  

**Main ideas**: He developed the *moral sense theory*—an innate faculty that perceives virtue and vice and produces pleasure or pain in response to them, independent of self-interest. Virtue consists largely in *benevolence* (disinterested concern for others’ happiness). He rejected Hobbesian egoism and pure rationalism in ethics, arguing that affections and sentiment precede and guide reason. He formulated an early version of the utilitarian principle (“the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers”). He also wrote on aesthetics (a sense of beauty linked to “uniformity amidst variety”). His work grounded later Scottish thinking in sentimentalism and a naturalistic view of morals.[](<https://t.co/UKuX9LCSjQ>)[](<https://t.co/Afvl9j1fa0>)

### David Hume (1711–1776)
The most radical and influential philosopher of the movement. Essayist, historian (*History of England*), and author of *A Treatise of Human Nature* (1739–40) and the later *Enquiries*.

**Main ideas**: He aimed at a fully empirical “science of human nature.” All knowledge derives from experience (impressions and ideas); reason is the “slave of the passions.” He offered a devastating skeptical analysis of causation (it is a habit of the mind based on constant conjunction, not a necessary connection we can perceive), induction, personal identity, and the external world. In ethics, he developed a sophisticated sentimentalism: morality arises from feelings of approval/disapproval rooted in sympathy, not reason or divine command. He defended commerce and luxury as civilizing forces, analyzed the origins of government and justice as conventions arising from self-interest and limited benevolence, and wrote critically on religion (natural history of religion, critique of miracles and design arguments in the *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*). His work shaped Kant, later empiricists, and much of modern philosophy.[](<https://t.co/ZQ14feIY2q>)[](<https://t.co/Afvl9j1fa0>)

### Adam Smith (1723–1790)
Hume’s close friend; moral philosopher and the founder of modern political economy. Professor at Glasgow; author of *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759) and *An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations* (1776).

**Main ideas**: In moral philosophy, he refined Hutcheson’s sentimentalism with the concepts of *sympathy* (imaginative fellow-feeling) and the *impartial spectator*. Moral judgments arise when we imagine how an impartial observer would approve or disapprove of our actions; this corrects pure self-interest. In economics, he explained how the division of labor, specialization, free markets, and the pursuit of self-interest (guided by competition) produce social wealth via an “invisible hand.” He analyzed capital, trade, and the stages of society (hunting, pastoral, agricultural, commercial). He valued commercial society for its prosperity and civilizing effects while noting its risks (e.g., the stupefying effects of extreme division of labor). His work combined moral psychology with institutional analysis.[](<https://t.co/GqaFBWDRwH>)[](<https://t.co/Afvl9j1fa0>)

### Thomas Reid (1710–1796)
Founder of the Scottish “common sense” school. Succeeded Smith at Glasgow; author of *An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense* (1764).

**Main ideas**: He rejected Humean skepticism as absurd and self-refuting. Certain principles (e.g., the existence of the external world, other minds, basic moral distinctions, and the reliability of the senses and memory) are self-evident first principles of “common sense” shared by all humanity. Perception is direct (not mediated by ideas that could deceive us). He offered a more realist and providential account of human faculties, arguing they are trustworthy because of their design. His philosophy reassured many contemporaries that science and ordinary belief could coexist with religion and was highly influential in America.[](<https://t.co/ZQ14feIY2q>)[](<https://t.co/Afvl9j1fa0>)

### Adam Ferguson (1723–1816)
Highland-born professor of moral philosophy at Edinburgh and a pioneer of sociology. Author of *An Essay on the History of Civil Society* (1767).

**Main ideas**: He stressed that humans are naturally social; there is no evidence of a pre-social “state of nature.” Society and institutions arise spontaneously through unintended consequences of human action rather than deliberate design (a theme shared with Hume and Smith). He traced the progress of societies from “rude” to “polished” stages, analyzed civil society, the division of labor, and the tensions of commercial modernity (including risks of corruption or loss of civic virtue). He is often regarded as a founder of modern sociological thinking.[](<https://t.co/Afvl9j1fa0>)

### Other Significant Figures
- **Henry Home, Lord Kames** (1696–1782): Judge, legal theorist, and historian who developed the “four stages” theory of society and wrote on aesthetics, agriculture, and human history.  
- **William Robertson** (1721–1793): Historian, Principal of Edinburgh University, and Moderate leader in the Church of Scotland; wrote influential histories of Scotland, America, and Europe.  
- **Dugald Stewart** (1753–1828): Popularizer and systematizer of Scottish philosophy who refined the idea of “conjectural history.”  

In the sciences and practical arts: **James Hutton** (geology and deep time), **Joseph Black** (chemistry, latent heat, carbon dioxide), **James Watt** (improved steam engine), **Robert Adam** (neoclassical architecture), and figures in medicine such as **William Cullen**. Literature and the arts featured **Robert Burns**, **Allan Ramsay**, and others.[](<https://t.co/ZQ14feIY2q>)

**Shared characteristics** across these thinkers included: skepticism toward pure Cartesian rationalism; emphasis on experience, sentiment, and the empirical study of human nature and society; a belief in natural sociability (contra Hobbes); interest in “conjectural” or stadial history; and a practical orientation toward improvement, virtue, and useful knowledge. The movement was not monolithic—Hume’s skepticism and Reid’s common-sense realism stood in productive tension—but it produced a coherent, influential body of thought that shaped economics, sociology, philosophy, and liberal institutions far beyond Scotland.[](<https://t.co/eObecGLZ0f>)

The statues of Hume and Smith in Edinburgh still symbolize this legacy of intellectual achievement.

text:
He advised us to request the association's financial records through Arizona's statutory right-to-inspect process, which would put the board on formal notice without revealing everything we had.

I filed the request that same afternoon.

Two days later, Craig called me personally.

His voice was warm and false.

He said the fine had been "a misunderstanding" and offered to waive it entirely. He suggested we forget the whole matter.

I thanked him politely and told him I would still like to inspect the records.

There was a long pause.

Then he said, "Ruth, these things get complicated. I'd hate for a grieving widow to get dragged into something."

I recorded the call, legally, as Arizona is a one-party consent state, and sent it to my lawyer.

At the inspection, a nervous bookkeeper handed over a stack of files. My daughter and I spent six hours comparing them to Frank's spreadsheet.

Every figure matched.

My lawyer wrote to the board and to the state's regulatory office.

Within a week, three board members resigned. Craig refused. He told neighbours that I was an emotional widow attacking him for revenge.

Some believed him.

A few neighbours stopped waving to me at the mailbox.

One evening, an elderly man from the next street knocked on my door and said, quietly, "Frank once told me he was worried about the books. I never asked what he meant. I'm sorry."

Then he handed me a folder.

He had kept his own copies of three invoices that didn't add up.

text:
ON THE SHAMAN PATH

In the King County Courthouse, our client is being sentenced for the murder of forty-nine women. It is a week before Christmas and a man who works as a seasonal Santa is confronting the killer for the sadosexual murder of his daughter. The aggrieved father presents well as Santa with his white beard, ruddy cheeks, and ample belly. Wearing rainbow-colored suspenders, he offers his forgiveness and expresses his sadness that the killer will never know the joy of the Christmas season. At this, the killer is overcome with emotion and tears fill his eyes. At our Christmas party later that evening, I am unable to drink away the disturbing image of Santa making the serial murderer weep.

In the five-star Connecticut detox, the Anger Christ is pacing the hall outside my room, threatening out loud to do violence to the people in his head. He looks like the Catholic Jesus of my childhood, but he is a sick and angry meth-head whose demeanor warns of imminent violence. I am unable to enjoy my blackberry cobbler as I brace for a possible attack.

In the Seattle psych-ward, they let me order from the normal-person menu and I become attached to a companion dog named Star. I meet a woman who is hopeful that electroconvulsive therapy will restore her former happiness. After discharge, we conduct a brief affair that ends when she shoots herself a day after feeling “happier than ever.” 

In Carmel-by-the-Sea, I am on all fours trying to gather Ativan pills from the floor while the twenty-seventh love of my life is kicking me in the ribs. Between kicks, she’s frantically splashing water from a pitcher to dissolve the pills. When the violence subsides, I have recovered eight pills, and I hitch a ride to Big Sur where I eventually abandon a suicide plan in favor of vodka shots at Nepenthe. 

In Santa Cruz, I wake up on the sidewalk in front of State Farm Insurance. As I come to, I realize I am newly homeless and have no money and nowhere to go, but upon discovering a half-full pint of Gran Legacy in my waistband, I am overcome with desperate enthusiasm. I offer a prayer of thanks to the God of Small Things and begin looking for somewhere to steal cigarettes. 

In the Big Sur monastery, the monks are disappointed when I am arrested for DUI while driving their recently donated Chevy pickup to Monterey to rescue Brother Ezekiel, who is suffering a panic attack at the Comfort Inn. In the Salinas holding tank, I befriend Ricardo, a Mexican fellow charged with “terroristic acts” for kicking someone’s door in after they interrupted his effort to steal a bike from their yard. We find common ground in the way hard liquor informs our poor choices. 

In the Flushing park, a man is explaining that his family owns an “attack dog farm” upstate. He says they have African attack dogs, Canadian attack dogs and every other kind of attack dog you could imagine. I notice he has an axe attached to his belt, and behind him my sister is vomiting after accepting a challenge to “fire the red bottlecap” full of Bacardi 151. There is a sense of foreboding in the hot and humid air, and the party has hardly started. 

I am on the far night journey. Not the straight path. Not any path. I run from the police through suburban vegetable gardens. I am drunk and unruly in Seat 32F. I fire airline bottles in the 26th-floor men’s room of Seattle’s finest office tower. I see God in emergency room lights. I fall in love with table dancers. I climb through the doggy-door of the Jordanian Sex Witch. I hold counsel with bus-stop inebriates. I help Larry empty the piss buckets. In a hallucinogenic nightmare, I tour hell on a donkey. I sprout soul tumors. I almost die in Burien. I am a sex-addict, a failed poet, a convicted felon, and a disappointment to Uncle Desi. And it goes on and on and on. 

And then,
an epiphany:
I must extricate
my life
from my ass.

text:
I am the Deputy Program Manager for Rewards for Justice at the State Department’s Bureau of Diplomatic Security. As of Friday night, I am offering $20 million for something the President blew up.

We pay people to tell us things. Since 1984 the United States has paid “in excess of $250 million to more than 125 people,” about $2 million a secret. It is the only honest price list in Washington. I keep it laminated, on a lanyard, next to my badge.

Our office is in Rosslyn, across the Potomac from Foggy Bottom, in the kind of beige federal tower where hope goes to get its parking validated. Outside my door hang the old posters, framed like family photos. In the 90s we printed them on matchbooks, because a man lighting a cigarette has 4 seconds to reconsider his life. Ramzi Yousef, $2 million, paid. Then the 1 we don’t discuss. Osama bin Laden. $25 million. Offered for 10 years. Never collected. The Navy found him a mile from Pakistan’s national military academy. 1 mile. Nobody called. Not 1 cadet. We keep him up the way a family keeps a photo of the uncle who drove the boat into the dock.

Let me tell you how it actually works. The world imagines a war room. It is, I promise you, an inbox with a budget and a bowl of leftover Halloween candy nobody will admit to restocking. Tips arrive by Signal, Telegram, WhatsApp, and a Tor address so long it looks like a cat sat on a keyboard and achieved enlightenment. Our website promises “RFJ reads every tip we receive.” Every tip. I want you to remember that sentence. It is about to ruin my life.

In June 2025, B-2s flew 18 hours from Missouri and dropped 14 bombs of 30,000 pounds each on Fordow and Natanz. The President addressed the nation: “Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.” Completely. Totally. 2 adverbs guarding 1 verb like Secret Service agents around a man who has already left the building. He has said it, in some form, for 17 months. I believe him. I believe him with my whole chest and my TS/SCI.

So on Friday the poster went through clearance. In this town every document is “cleared” by every office that might be blamed for it. Mine was cleared by 11 offices, 2 bureaus, the 7th floor and a lawyer who only communicates in tracked changes. Nobody cleared it for meaning.

At 7:15 p.m. I published a reward of up to $20 million “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program, “including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel,” or “the movement of any of the above.”

The movement.

Of the obliterated facilities.

Somewhere in Iran, a pile of rubble has packed a carry-on and is trying to get a slot at Reagan National.

7:19 p.m. First tip. “It’s under the mountain. You bombed it. I watched it on TV.” Technically correct. Ineligible. Information must be new.

7:22 p.m. A man in Fairfax reports that the nuclear program is his neighbor’s satellite dish. He has reported this to us 46 times since 2019. Every time he has been wrong. Tonight, for the first time, I couldn’t prove it.

7:25 p.m. CENTCOM posts the reward.

Minutes later. Piers Morgan: “WTF????”

4 question marks. I printed it. I framed it next to bin Laden. It is the most rigorous review the reward ever received. 11 offices produced 0 question marks. The 7th floor produced 0 question marks. A man who was fired as a newspaper editor over fake photos from the Iraq war produced 4 in under a minute, for free, without a clearance. He knows a doctored picture when he sees one. I have nominated him for a TS/SCI. The background check will take 14 months. He will be faster than the program.

7:58 p.m. Someone else asks, “The one that’s destroyed?” I have no talking points for this. I draft a response. It goes to clearance. It is still in clearance. It will be in clearance when I retire.

8:15 p.m. 1,100 tips. A woman says she saw a centrifuge at the Costco in Pentagon City, spinning near the rotisserie chickens. A lobbyist on K Street says he knows exactly where the program is and will tell me over lunch at the Palm, if I’m buying. A Hill staffer says it’s in the SCIF in the Capitol Visitor Center basement and nobody can check because nobody’s allowed to bring their phone.

8:40 p.m. The rubble files a tip. Through Tor. It says it is “open to new opportunities” and has relocated to Dubai, where it now operates a smoothie bar called Fordow Fresh. It requests possible relocation to Arlington. I flag it as credible. It is the most self-aware tip we have received since 1984.

9:02 p.m. I reread our fine print. To justify the reward, we cite a 2025 report that Iran was enriching uranium to 60 percent. We published a missing-person poster with a photo from last year, which is what you do when the kid has grown a beard and you’d rather not ask how. The same paragraph says the IAEA has lost “continuity of knowledge” of Iran’s centrifuges. Philosophers spent 3,000 years on the problem of knowledge. The IAEA solved it with 1 verb. Lost. Officially, the centrifuges are obliterated and we have also lost them. In Washington we call that “pre-decisional.” Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays they are obliterated. Tuesdays and Thursdays they are missing. Weekends they are a smoothie bar.

10:30 p.m. 3,000 tips. 400 of them are just the word “obliterated” with a question mark. 1 is from an IP address in Moscow that says “lol.” I flag it as the most honest tip of the night.

11:58 p.m. Someone adds me to a Signal group called “Houthi PC small group 2.” I recognize 0 of the 14 members. Somebody posts a map. Somebody posts a fire emoji. Somebody posts “who added the State guy.” I leave. They add me back. Yes, that Signal. In 2025 the editor of The Atlantic was added to the original and got the strike plans before the Houthis did. It remains the fastest interagency process in American history. Every office was in the loop. So was a magazine.

12:40 a.m. A colonel calls from the Pentagon to ask whether bombing it again counts as a tip.

1:12 a.m. An anonymous message, in perfect English: “I am a centrifuge. I spin at 60 percent. I have been obliterated since June 2025 and I have never felt more alive. Is the relocation to Northern Virginia? Is there a Sweetgreen? Asking for 6,000 of my friends.” I put my head on the desk, directly on a fun-size Snickers.

And this is where it all comes apart. At 2:00 a.m., I reread our payout rules. To pay a reward, I have to certify the information is accurate. To certify it’s accurate, I have to certify the program exists. And to certify the program exists, I would have to certify, in writing, on State Department letterhead, that the 2 adverbs were wrong. That memo would need clearance. There is no office in this government that will clear it.

So the reward can never be paid. The only way to collect $20 million is to prove the President was mistaken, and nobody in this town is authorized to say that out loud. I have created the safest money in the federal budget. It is a $20 million bill locked inside a box, and the key is a Truth Social post.

3:15 a.m. The colonel calls back. If they bomb it again, can the Air Force claim the reward? I tell him the reward is for information. He says, “That’s what the bombs are.”

4:02 a.m. I submit a tip. To myself. Through Tor. “The program is wherever it was before you obliterated it.” I review it. I reject it. Information must be new. I appeal. I deny my own appeal. I send myself a “per my last email.”

6:30 a.m. The rubble replies to my rejection with a job offer. Shift manager, Fordow Fresh, Dubai. Dental. 401(k). Possible relocation. It’s the first offer of relocation anyone in this story has actually received, and it came from the rubble. It does not require a continuing resolution.

Every war produces 2 pieces of paper. A banner that says it’s over, and a poster that says we’re still looking. In 2003 the banner said “Mission Accomplished” over weapons we swore were there and never found. In 2025 we swore the weapons were gone, and now we’re paying to find them. History rhymes. This time it rhymes backward, and I’m the one holding the stapler.

The second war, this year’s, the one that sent tankers into mines in Hormuz and gas to the highest Election Day price ever recorded, the one the President now agrees cost his party Congress on Tuesday, has produced as its final deliverable a laminated flyer, which I stapled at dawn to a light pole on Wilson Boulevard. LOST: 1 nuclear program. Last seen obliterated. Answers to “60 percent.” Shy around inspectors. Do not approach. Do not feed. If found, do not tell the President.

It’s 9 a.m. Saturday. 9,400 tips. RFJ reads every tip we receive. I have read 9,400 tips. I have eaten 11 fun-size Snickers. My wife has asked if I’m being relocated. I said, “possibly.”

Up on Wilson Boulevard the ginkgoes have dropped their fruit and the whole city smells like a gym bag. I’m on the Orange Line now, standing on the right, lanyard still on, flyers under my arm. The train is holding at Foggy Bottom. Of course it is. Somewhere a very powerful man is telling a camera, again, that Iran’s program was obliterated. Good. Then the money is safe. Bin Laden’s $25 million sat on that wall for 10 years. This one will sit there forever.

Somewhere under a mountain, a centrifuge is reading this.

We just want to talk.

Tips welcome. Signal preferred. Please check who else is in the chat.

text:
On this day in 1775, a cornered British governor issued a proclamation that struck at the economic foundation of the entire South, and in doing so he did as much to push wavering Virginians toward independence as any battle of the war. It was one of the most explosive documents of the Revolution.

The man behind it was Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, and by November 1775 he was in deep trouble. He had lost control of the colony, been driven out of the capital at Williamsburg, and was reduced to governing from the deck of a British warship offshore, with only a small force at his command. He needed men, he needed leverage, and he needed to frighten the rebel planters who had risen against him. So he reached for the one thing he knew would terrify them most.

Dunmore's Proclamation declared martial law in Virginia, and then it did the truly incendiary thing: it offered freedom to the enslaved people and indentured servants of rebel masters, if they were willing and able to leave those masters and take up arms for the King. In one stroke, Dunmore had aimed a weapon straight at the heart of the Southern economy and the Southern social order, the system of enslaved labor on which the planters' entire world was built.

The effect was immediate and enormous, in two very different directions. On one side, enslaved people responded. Hundreds, by some counts approaching a thousand or more, risked everything to flee toward Dunmore and the promise of freedom, and he organized some of the men into a unit the British called the Ethiopian Regiment, whose members famously wore sashes reading "Liberty to Slaves." For those people, the Revolution's grand talk of liberty had come, ironically, from the British side, and many seized it at terrible risk.

On the other side, the proclamation enraged and terrified white Virginians across the political spectrum, and this is where its biggest strategic impact lay. Nothing could have united the Southern planters against Britain faster. Men who had been lukewarm about the rebellion, who might have stayed loyal or neutral, were pushed firmly into the Patriot camp by their fury and fear at a British governor threatening to overturn slavery and arm the enslaved. Dunmore had meant to intimidate the rebels. Instead he hardened them, and helped drive the wealthy, hesitant South toward the cause of independence.

The human cost for those who fled to Dunmore was often tragic. His crowded, unhealthy camps were swept by disease, especially smallpox, which killed many of the people who had risked everything for his promise. His own military position collapsed within months, and he was eventually driven from Virginia entirely.

But the proclamation's shadow was long. It was the first large-scale offer of freedom in the war, and it opened a painful, complicated chapter that would run through the whole Revolution: the tens of thousands of enslaved people who would seek their liberty amid a war fought, by white Americans, in the name of liberty. Remember November 7, 1775, as a day that exposed the deepest contradiction at the center of the American founding, a contradiction the new nation would not resolve, and that would take another, far bloodier war to confront.

We watched the mogul take the rally stage, 
A loud disruptor in a restless age. 
Though skeptics questioned how his circuit ran, 
Cold logic proved he beat the Clinton clan. 
She offered central control and state decay; 
He cut through fluff and blew their plans away.

Rogue agents wired the grid with covert lies, 
Spurious probes under deep-state disguise. 
They shorted out his term with constant noise, 
As media hacks deployed their partisan toys. 
False charges drained the power from his drive, 
While partisan machines kept fraud alive.

Though rough in speech, he kept the engine high, 
Till panic struck beneath a darkened sky. 
Deep lockdowns choked the economic flow, 
As midnight ballots dealt the fatal blow. 
Fraud flipped the switch and stole his rightful win;
Machine politics let the dark state in.

We backed his third run for a righteous fight, 
To crush the swamp and set the circuit right. 
To give the Democrats the hell they earned, 
And fix the grid that Biden's madness burned. 
Bad policy demanded fast redress; 
We sought a shock to clean the corrupt mess.

Yet victory brought a bitter, sudden twist, 
As broken promises filled out the list. 
He swore to pull our troops from foreign soil, 
Yet plunged our budget into foreign toil. 
He promised peace, yet funded Kyiv's fight, 
And let offensive strikes obscure the right. 
Heavy tariffs overload the buyer's class, 
While rising prices choke the working mass.

This economic short brings blue waves in, 
A total blowout where the left did win. 
Eight years of Democrats will take the wheel, 
And crush our liberty with iron steel. 
As conservative dinosaurs expire, 
Progressive zealots set the Court on fire. 
For thirty years the left will hold the bench, 
With radical decrees we cannot quench. 
This self-inflicted shock resets the clock, 
And locks the freedom movement in the dock. 
The blue tsunami surges on the shore, 
And sets the right back thirty years or more.

text:
World governance will usher in an age of peace. Not an eternal peace, for mankind has never learned to preserve what it has not first suffered to obtain. Nevertheless, it will bring forth an era of prosperity unlike anything recorded in human history.

Yet within that prosperity, an Ouroboric seed shall take root: a quiet inheritance of self-hatred, suspicion, and doubt. Having exhausted its external enemies, mankind will eventually turn inward, until even brother comes to regard brother as an adversary.

But before that hour, certain indignities must be brought to an end.

No longer shall infants starve in forgotten corners of the Earth while the privileged purchase seventeen-dollar smoothies without a second thought.

No longer shall fifty-million-dollar yachts race along the shores of Monaco merely to entertain those who have inherited more wealth than they could exhaust in a thousand lifetimes.

No longer shall religion serve as the convenient instrument through which men disguise their appetite for superiority as divine righteousness.

And no longer shall autolytic, nepotistic ruling dynasties consume the very civilizations upon which their privileges depend.

The ancient architecture of human class, fortified over thousands of years by bloodlines, inherited wealth, manufactured scarcity, and carefully cultivated ignorance, shall be brought to its knees.

Not over centuries.

Not over generations.

But within the coming year.

For the age of secrecy cannot survive the arrival of transparency. And those who have mistaken their temporary stewardship of the world for divine ownership of it shall discover that even the highest throne is merely borrowed furniture.

Yet I offer mankind no promise of paradise.

A world relieved of its ancient oppressors must eventually confront the possibility that oppression was never exclusively the invention of its rulers, but also a temptation concealed within the human heart.

And therein lies the final examination.

For centuries, humanity begged God to deliver it from the tyranny of men. Yet in its desperation, it also begged to be relieved of the terrible burden of choosing for itself.

It desired freedom without responsibility, abundance without restraint, and peace without the discipline required to preserve it.

Soon, mankind shall be presented with the very conditions it once believed would guarantee its salvation.

And when the old chains have fallen, we shall discover whether humanity desired liberty…

Or merely a kinder master.

Well, then. We shall see.

GE VERNOVA $GEV HAS 58 GIGAWATTS RESERVED, NOT ORDERED:

GE Vernova (GEV) at $774.11, +$3.60 / +0.47% on Friday.

GE Vernova is still on none of the Len5es we weigh, and since our post the question behind its fall has moved from Washington to its own order book. The shares lost another 7% in two sessions, and on Friday they gave back a morning gain while the broader market kept its bounce. Before dawn on Friday, Elon Musk wrote that SoftBank is defaulting on its turbine orders, and SoftBank's power developer had said in May that it reserved turbines from several makers, GE Vernova among them. That claim lands on the 58 gigawatts GE Vernova holds as reservations rather than orders. Those reservations come with down payments, and Scott Strazik, GE Vernova's chief executive, told analysts on October 28 that no customer had asked to leave one. SoftBank reports on Tuesday, and GE Vernova's January report shows whether the reservations kept turning into orders.

GE Vernova is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and it still passes the Quality Len5: a profit in each of the last four quarters, with debt about a quarter of the owners' equity. Momentum wants months of gains near the high, and Friday's close sits 35.3% under the July 6 high. The value Len5es want a discount to the cash a business earns, and most of GE Vernova's September-quarter cash was customers paying ahead for turbines it has not built yet. What would put it on the Quality-Value Len5: a far lower price with the 58 gigawatts of reservations still turning into orders.

The shares since our post:
- Thursday: closed at $770.51, -7.48%, on 7.6M shares, about twice the 30-day average. The lowest close since February 5.
- Friday: touched $821.50 in the first half hour, +6.6%, then $751.25 between 12:30 and 1pm ET, and closed at $774.11.
- Since our post: -$58.72 / -7.05% from the $832.83 we quoted, about $15.5 billion of market value. Since Tuesday's close, before the result: about $38 billion.
- Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, at $656.10, +$9.05 / +1.40% on Friday.
Thursday was the worst day for US chip stocks since March 2020, a rout most reports tied to the same election result, so our Washington call held. Friday's slide from the morning high came on no company news, and the Nasdaq-100 fund finished with three times GE Vernova's gain. Our read: Friday's sellers were weighing the turbine book, not Congress.

Elon Musk, who has questioned whether SoftBank has the money for its AI data-center plans since January 2025, wrote on X at 1:25am ET Friday: "SoftBank is defaulting on their turbine orders." He named no turbine maker, project or amount and offered no evidence. Neither SoftBank nor any turbine maker has confirmed a default, and GE Vernova has not commented. SB Energy, SoftBank's US power developer, said in May that it had reserved gas turbines "from multiple sources including GE Vernova" for a planned 9.2-gigawatt gas plant near Portsmouth, Ohio.

SoftBank Group (SFTBY) at $11.47, +$0.30 / +2.69% on Friday. Its US shares fell 14.4% on Thursday, before the post. Musk wrote five minutes before Tokyo's close. SoftBank's 10.83% fall there on Friday was nearly all in place when he posted. With the post out all day, the US shares rose. The cost of insuring SoftBank's debt against default reached its highest since October 2022 on Friday. SoftBank is on none of the Len5es we weigh, because its profit swings each quarter with the value of the companies it holds stakes in.

The reservations are the softer half of GE Vernova's book, and they come with cash. At September 30, the 122 gigawatts of gas turbines we cited split this way:
- Firm orders: 64 GW, from 53 at June 30.
- Slot reservations, a paid place in the factory line that becomes an order later: 58 GW, from 63.
- In the quarter: 13 GW of reservations became orders, 8 GW of new ones were signed, and 5 GW shipped.
Ken Parks, the finance chief, said customers' down payments on new orders and reservations were the main source of $5.3 billion of extra cash in the quarter. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment, was $5.4 billion, so most of it was customers' money paid ahead. On the October 28 call, David Arcaro, Morgan Stanley's analyst, asked whether financing trouble had brought any requests to exit reservations. Strazik answered, "No, David, we are not," and said the cash terms customers pay to secure equipment had not changed.

GE Vernova fell first on the election and now trades on whether its reserved customers stay. SoftBank reports its September quarter in Tokyo on Tuesday, November 10, its first scheduled chance to answer Musk on the record. GE Vernova's January report has to show more than 13 gigawatts signed in the fourth quarter, the pace Strazik said his year-end goal requires, with the reservations still becoming orders rather than leaving.

This masked letter was a form of secure communication used during the Revolutionary War by Sir Henry Clinton, a British Army General. The letter was sent to General John Burgoyne in July 1777.
 
This clever but simple encryption system uses the Cardan mask, named after Girolamo Cardano, a 16th Century Renaissance mathematician and philosopher who first envisioned this form of cryptography. In this case the Cardan mask overlay is in the shape of an hourglass. The intended message is written down with the overlay in place. The overlay was then removed and the page further filled out with innocuous information to throw off any examiners. The overlay and the letter were sent separately to the recipient, to reduce the likelihood they would both be intercepted. 
 
The full letter shows Henry Clinton’s high confidence in General Sir William Howe’s campaign in the Chesapeake Bay area, and that George Washington’s forces were marching back and forth ineffectively. Clinton offers 1,500 men in support of Burgoyne, saying that General Howe’s moves have been “capital”, and that Washington’s moves had been “the worst he could take”.
 
With the Cardan mask overlay however, the true message reveals a very different story:
 
“Sir. W. Howe / is gone to the / Chesapeak bay with / the greatest part of the / army. I hear he is / landed but am not / certain. I am / left to command / here with / too small a force / to make any effectual / diversion in your favour. / I shall try something / at any rate. It may be of use / to you. I own to you I think / Sr W’s move just at this time / the worst he could take. / Much joy on your success.”
 
General Burgoyne was defeated by Washington’s forces at the culmination of the Saratoga campaign, just two months after this letter was sent. Clinton replaced Sir William Howe as commander of all British forces in the American colonies the following year.
 
Despite Henry Clinton’s clever use of encryption seen here, neither he nor any other British officer were a match for General Washington, one of the greatest spymasters in history.

Democrats Need a Bold Governing Agenda

The Editorial Board
Democrats Need a Bold Governing Agenda
Nov. 7, 2026

By The Editorial Board
The editorial board is a group of opinion journalists whose views are informed by expertise, research, debate and certain longstanding values. It is separate from the newsroom.

The voters have spoken, and they have handed the Democratic Party something rarer than a victory: They have offered the party a chance to prove government’s worth again. The questions now are whether Democrats will seize it and whether they can show a doubting nation that its lawmakers can still lift burdens, open doors and make lives better.

The task ahead won’t be easy. Americans have watched institutions falter and promises fade, and many have stopped expecting much from Washington. Yet beneath that weariness is still hope. Families feel the squeeze of rising prices every time they shop for groceries, fill a prescription or a gas tank or dream of a home of their own. They are frustrated by failed wars, growing debt and flagrant corruption. They watch artificial intelligence advance and ask what it will mean for their jobs, their children, their communities and their future. They want change, and they want someone to deliver it.

Democrats should remember that they won this election mostly because of President Trump’s unpopularity and that their party’s approval rating is well below 50 percent. They also won this election without telling the country where they intended to lead it. Most voters — 57 percent in a CBS News/YouGov poll last month — said the party had no clear plan for governing. Voters chose Democrats anyway, recoiling from Mr. Trump’s shambolic Republican Party. But to keep their support, Democrats must give Americans something to believe in. They must show that they are relentlessly working to get results.

That vision need not become law in the next two years in order to matter. Mr. Trump may veto bills, and Senate Republicans may use the filibuster as a wall. Let them. Democrats can still declare what government should do for the people it serves. The party can champion ideas that Americans already embrace, like more affordable health care and housing, and invite Republicans to join them. If Republicans do not, it will set the stage for a 2028 campaign in which the choice before the nation is clear.

For half a century, Democrats offered American voters technocratic policies designed to improve their lives, like tax credits and regulations. Many did real good. Still, trust in government has remained low, and working Americans drifted away. Even in this year’s rout, Democrats only narrowly carried voters without a four-year college degree, according to New York Times estimates. But working-class Americans did move sharply toward Democrats, and their hopes are the party’s now to honor. Every lasting majority in American electoral history has stood on the shoulders of working people. The coming one must, too.

Here lies the hard lesson. Democrats have too often built quietly, crafting programs so subtle that the people they helped never saw the hand that helped them. The political scientist Suzanne Mettler calls this “the submerged state.” The expanded child tax credit lifted millions of families, yet it slipped away with hardly a protest. Clean-energy projects rose across the country, and the people living beside them rarely connected them to the federal government. Try to name a single project in your own state that the vast stimulus efforts of the Biden or Obama years made possible. Most Americans cannot, and that’s not their fault.

Complexity has often deepened the wound. Too many Americans have had to fight their way through confusing rules, jargon-filled forms and endless waits simply to claim help they were promised. They have wondered why the country finds it so hard to build new homes, bridges and factories. Nicholas Bagley, a legal scholar, warns against “the procedure fetish,” the conviction that bureaucratic rigor earns public trust. In truth, every confusing form erodes that trust a little more. Every hour on hold teaches a citizen to expect less.

Fortunately, history can light the way to a better society. Americans greeted the Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare, with skepticism, too. It took years to become popular. It still isn’t perfect. Over time, though, people came to rely on it, and then to defend it. When Republicans tried to repeal it, the public stopped them, just as Americans once rallied behind Medicare when small-government Republicans tried to quash it in the 1960s.

Today, health care stands as the Democrats’ strongest issue, in large part because Obamacare — and its nickname helps — touches people’s lives in ways they can feel. That includes people who already have health insurance, thanks to, among other things, its provision that lets adult children remain on a parent’s plan until age 26. They noticed when the program helped them, and they noticed when Mr. Trump cut its subsidies. In all seven states that have put an Obamacare expansion (through Medicaid) to a popular vote, the people said yes. Six of those seven states are deep red.

This tradition, of smart, bold and salient government, is one that Democrats must reclaim. Social Security brought dignity to old age. The G.I. Bill sent a generation to college and into homes of their own. Rural electrification carried light into farmhouses that previously had known only candlelight. Enshrining labor rights in federal law empowered workers to fight to better their lot. Public schools spread across the country because ordinary citizens demanded them in the 1800s and early 1900s. In our own time, voters in red states and blue have raised the minimum wage and protected reproductive rights with their ballots. And leaders as different as Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania have shown how to make concrete change and then tell its story with clarity and conviction.

Making democracy visibly responsive is not just good politics, but how a republic keeps the public’s faith. Democrats must now do that, not just for their party’s sake but for the country’s.

With the power they have won, Democrats will need to hold Mr. Trump to account. They can name his corruption as the capture of public power for private gain. They can expose the policies that make American life harder, like his scattershot tariffs, his cruel budget cuts and the mounting costs of his reckless war in Iran.

The greater work, though, lies far beyond Mr. Trump. Democrats need to sketch the outlines of a post-Trump America, a country where people can see and feel what their government does for them.

Where can a modern national agenda begin? Picture a parent who can afford a child’s medicine without dread. Picture families who can raise young children without drowning in costs. Picture a generation that can once again own a home. Picture an economy in which those who have prospered most, including the titans of artificial intelligence, help build a bountiful future for everyone else. Every idea Democrats advance should pass three simple tests: Will it work? Will it reach as many Americans as possible? Will people feel it?

The conversation has already begun. Writers and experts are offering ideas in Opinion’s pages, and a few Democratic officials — from Representative Ro Khanna of California on the left to the former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel in the center — have stepped forward with plans of their own. The rest of the party must join them, and quickly. Twenty years ago, after the 2006 midterms, Democrats carried a bolder and more developed agenda into the next presidential campaign than they carry today. That agenda gave the country Obamacare.

This week Democrats have earned the right to celebrate. Their victory surpassed many of their hopes, and they will soon govern Congress with comfortable margins. Let them also remember 2006 and 2018, triumphs that promised a lasting majority and then slipped away within a few short years.
Republican unpopularity will carry Democrats only so far. The party must prove that the immense power of government can ease the burdens of American families and help them imagine a brighter future. Let them build so boldly and visibly that Americans can feel the difference in their daily lives. If Democrats rise to this moment, they can turn a single night’s victory into a new American promise.

They also won this election without telling the country where they intended to lead it. Most voters — 57 percent in a CBS News/YouGov poll last month — said the party had no clear plan for governing. Voters chose Democrats anyway, recoiling from Mr. Trump’s shambolic Republican Party. But to keep their support, Democrats must give Americans something to believe in. They must show that they are relentlessly working to get results.

That vision need not become law in the next two years in order to matter. Mr. Trump may veto bills, and Senate Republicans may use the filibuster as a wall. Let them. Democrats can still declare what government should do for the people it serves. The party can champion ideas that Americans already embrace, like more affordable health care and housing, and invite Republicans to join them. If Republicans do not, it will set the stage for a 2028 campaign in which the choice before the nation is clear.

For half a century, Democrats offered American voters technocratic policies designed to improve their lives, like tax credits and regulations. Many did real good. Still, trust in government has remained low, and working Americans drifted away. Even in this year’s rout, Democrats only narrowly carried voters without a four-year college degree, according to New York Times estimates. But working-class Americans did move sharply toward Democrats, and their hopes are the party’s now to honor. Every lasting majority in American electoral history has stood on the shoulders of working people. The coming one must, too.

Here lies the hard lesson. Democrats have too often built quietly, crafting programs so subtle that the people they helped never saw the hand that helped them. The political scientist Suzanne Mettler calls this “the submerged state.” The expanded child tax credit lifted millions of families, yet it slipped away with hardly a protest. Clean-energy projects rose across the country, and the people living beside them rarely connected them to the federal government. Try to name a single project in your own state that the vast stimulus efforts of the Biden or Obama years made possible. Most Americans cannot, and that’s not their fault.

Complexity has often deepened the wound. Too many Americans have had to fight their way through confusing rules, jargon-filled forms and endless waits simply to claim help they were promised. They have wondered why the country finds it so hard to build new homes, bridges and factories. Nicholas Bagley, a legal scholar, warns against “the procedure fetish,” the conviction that bureaucratic rigor earns public trust. In truth, every confusing form erodes that trust a little more. Every hour on hold teaches a citizen to expect less.

Fortunately, history can light the way to a better society. Americans greeted the Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare, with skepticism, too. It took years to become popular. It still isn’t perfect. Over time, though, people came to rely on it, and then to defend it. When Republicans tried to repeal it, the public stopped them, just as Americans once rallied behind Medicare when small-government Republicans tried to quash it in the 1960s.

Today, health care stands as the Democrats’ strongest issue, in large part because Obamacare — and its nickname helps — touches people’s lives in ways they can feel. That includes people who already have health insurance, thanks to, among other things, its provision that lets adult children remain on a parent’s plan until age 26. They noticed when the program helped them, and they noticed when Mr. Trump cut its subsidies. In all seven states that have put an Obamacare expansion (through Medicaid) to a popular vote, the people said yes. Six of those seven states are deep red.

This tradition, of smart, bold and salient government, is one that Democrats must reclaim. Social Security brought dignity to old age. The G.I. Bill sent a generation to college and into homes of their own. Rural electrification carried light into farmhouses that previously had known only candlelight. Enshrining labor rights in federal law empowered workers to fight to better their lot. Public schools spread across the country because ordinary citizens demanded them in the 1800s and early 1900s. In our own time, voters in red states and blue have raised the minimum wage and protected reproductive rights with their ballots. And leaders as different as Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania have shown how to make concrete change and then tell its story with clarity and conviction.

Making democracy visibly responsive is not just good politics, but how a republic keeps the public’s faith. Democrats must now do that, not just for their party’s sake but for the country’s.

With the power they have won, Democrats will need to hold Mr. Trump to account. They can name his corruption as the capture of public power for private gain. They can expose the policies that make American life harder, like his scattershot tariffs, his cruel budget cuts and the mounting costs of his reckless war in Iran.

The greater work, though, lies far beyond Mr. Trump. Democrats need to sketch the outlines of a post-Trump America, a country where people can see and feel what their government does for them.

Where can a modern national agenda begin? Picture a parent who can afford a child’s medicine without dread. Picture families who can raise young children without drowning in costs. Picture a generation that can once again own a home. Picture an economy in which those who have prospered most, including the titans of artificial intelligence, help build a bountiful future for everyone else. Every idea Democrats advance should pass three simple tests: Will it work? Will it reach as many Americans as possible? Will people feel it?

The conversation has already begun. Writers and experts are offering ideas in Opinion’s pages, and a few Democratic officials — from Representative Ro Khanna of California on the left to the former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel in the center — have stepped forward with plans of their own. The rest of the party must join them, and quickly. Twenty years ago, after the 2006 midterms, Democrats carried a bolder and more developed agenda into the next presidential campaign than they carry today. That agenda gave the country Obamacare.

This week Democrats have earned the right to celebrate. Their victory surpassed many of their hopes, and they will soon govern Congress with comfortable margins. Let them also remember 2006 and 2018, triumphs that promised a lasting majority and then slipped away within a few short years.
Republican unpopularity will carry Democrats only so far. The party must prove that the immense power of government can ease the burdens of American families and help them imagine a brighter future. Let them build so boldly and visibly that Americans can feel the difference in their daily lives. If Democrats rise to this moment, they can turn a single night’s victory into a new American promise.

text:
Last spring, my wife spent two weeks in Wisconsin on a teacher exchange. Her host family had a nine-year-old son. On her last night, they took her to his school's spring concert.

My wife has watched Japanese school performances for twenty years. She knows exactly how they go. Polite applause. Silent filming. Parents bowing to other parents.

She came home with one page of notes. At the top she'd written: "What American parents do at a school concert."

It's my favorite thing she has ever written.

1. When the second-graders walked out, a father stood up and yelled, "THAT'S MY TREE!"
His son was Tree #3. He had no lines. He was a tree. His father filmed the entire song from the aisle, on one knee, like a war photographer.

2. A grandmother brought a sign. Poster board. Glitter. "GO MADISON."
Madison had one line. The line was "Look, it's spring!"
When Madison said it, the grandmother rose to her feet, and the people around her clapped like Madison had just hit a walk-off home run.

3. One boy sang every song half a second behind everyone else and twice as loud.
In Japan, a teacher would quietly ask him to sing a little softer.
In Wisconsin, he got the biggest cheer of the night.

4. Three fathers came straight from work, still in their reflective safety vests. They stood at the back. Watched one song. Waved at somebody. Left.
My wife wrote: "The waving was the important part."

5. About three hundred phones in the air. And one grandfather with a camcorder from the 1990s, roughly the size of a toaster, which he held steady above his head for forty-one minutes.
Nobody asked him to put it down. During the last song, the man next to him quietly offered to hold it for him.

6. A little brother, maybe four years old, waved at his big sister onstage with both arms. The entire concert. Nonstop.
In the middle of a song, she waved back. Once.
The whole gym said "awww" at the exact same moment, like they had rehearsed it.

7. A girl stepped forward to say her line and froze. Three seconds of silence. Then a man in the back called out, "YOU GOT THIS, SWEETHEART."
He was not her father. My wife is sure of it.
The gym started clapping. Slowly. Steadily. Until she remembered.

Then there was the one that made my wife stop writing for a while.

A girl in the fourth grade had a solo. My wife's host mother leaned over and whispered that the girl's dad hadn't been around in a long time. Nobody from her family had come.

When the girl stepped up to the microphone, three fathers in the front row stood up.

None of them were hers. They hadn't planned it. My wife watched them notice each other. They just stood. Big men in folding chairs, standing for a ten-year-old they barely knew.

She sang the whole song looking at them.

When she finished, they cheered for her like she was theirs.

For four minutes, she was.

At the bottom of the page, my wife wrote one more line.

"In Japan, we clap for the performance. In Wisconsin, they clap for the child."

Last month, at the culture festival at her school in Tokyo, the student band played. In the middle of the drum solo, a teacher in the back of the gym yelled the drummer's name and "YOU GOT THIS!"

The other teachers pretended not to know her.

It was my wife.

text:
In 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million.

Blockbuster said no. Ten years later, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy.

In the video below, Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph describes the meeting that decided it.

Netflix was two and a half years old. It had fewer than 100 employees and was on track to bring in about $3 million that year.

It was also on track to lose a cumulative $50 million.

Blockbuster was on track to do $6 billion. It had 60,000 employees and 9,000 stores.

Netflix called. Blockbuster wouldn't take the calls. It didn't answer the emails.

After a lot of pounding on the door, Blockbuster agreed to a meeting. Randolph and Reed Hastings flew to Dallas and went up to the 27th floor of the Renaissance Tower.

The Blockbuster executives came in wearing expensive suits. The Netflix founders wore T-shirts and jeans.

The pitch was simple. Netflix would run the online business. Blockbuster would run the stores.

Then Blockbuster asked how much it should pay.

Hastings said: "$50 million."

"The meeting went downhill very quickly after that," Randolph says.

In his book, he writes that Blockbuster's CEO, John Antioco, was struggling not to laugh.

It was a long, quiet flight back to California. Randolph remembers thinking one thing: "Oh, now we're gonna have to kick their ass."

The case for Blockbuster: in 2000, Netflix was a money-losing DVD-by-mail startup in the middle of the dot-com crash. Paying $50 million for it looked like the risky move.

Today, one Blockbuster store is left, in Bend, Oregon. Netflix is worth more than $150 billion.

In 2000, one company had 9,000 stores. The other had a website and $50 million in losses.

Was Blockbuster blind, or was passing on a money-losing startup the right call in 2000?

The Back Story was that I was celebrating my anniversery with Kim. Working at San Quentin prison was just a side bar and pillar to my life with Kim, it was a very good life and still is.

Memories are reconstructed, and on this anniversery of November 7, 2009 is the reconstruction is much different in positive tone.

Working in prisons, and state psychiatric facilities is a much darker tone on average, but on anniverseries, the tone is much lighter evern when working at Atascadero State Hospital, Pelian Bay Prison, San Quentin Prison or I-Max in Ionia, Michigan.

Every time I write about working in those places the story is reconstructed and placed into a different subjective universe...just saying.

California spent $5 million recruiting health care workers from across the country because of a federal court order to build a psychiatric hospital for about 700 hundred prisoners on Death Row....

I came from Michigan where I had a a friend, David Dawdy who was the Director of Mental Health Services for the Michigan Department of Corrections. 

I had a salaried position with a private company that contracted to provide mental health services for the Michigan Department of Corrections.

 I had a reputation at the Michigan Department of Corrections going back to 1987 and it was a good reputation and I had many friends at Bellamy Creek and I-Max in Ionia, Michigan.

I left the Michigan Department of Corrections knowing I could return at will.

Unfortunately for many who moved to Califonia and rented or bought homes near San Quentin, the Death Row prisoners were moved to general population throughout the state and many health care workers had expensive housing, and no job in January of 2015.

I had a townhouse in Albany that was paid for and I had a job in Ionia, Michigan and I did not miss a days work.
I have always been lucky.

It is best to make friends, you never know when you will need a helping hand. I have always had a helping hand when I needed it.

The environment in prisons and state hospitals are hostile working environments with health care burnout and moral injury and individuals always willing to be spiteful when it was not necessary.

The social worker who ran the mental health services was not shy  in displaying a spiteful attitude to the chief psychiatric resident as I recall.

I did not understand it because I was not privy to the details, but the public display was brutal, and not necessary from my point of view.

But I was a contract psychiatrist, a bottom feeder, just a pilgrim passing through and my opinion was not important.

On this day in 2014 I was celebrating an anniversary with Kim and it was a very happy anniversery then and it is a very happy anniversary today
...just saying...what say you?
