Thought for 22s
Lecture: Contingency, Memory, and the Total Institution — A Case Study in Carceral Psychiatry for Graduate Students in Law, Political Science, Psychiatry, and Social Anthropology

We begin 
with a single Facebook post 
from November 7, 2014: 
“Another beautiful day. 
This is how I end a day at work.” 

The image shows a sunset 
over water, 
a car parked near the shore. 

The author is a contract psychiatrist 
who has spent the day inside San Quentin State Prison. 

That same date 
is also an anniversary with his partner, Kim. 

Twelve years later 
the memory has been reconstructed 
in a markedly lighter key. 

The professional environments he inhabited
—San Quentin, Pelican Bay, Atascadero State Hospital, and I-Max in Ionia, Michigan
—are, on average, darker. 

Anniversaries recolor them.

This reconstruction is not merely private. 
It is a useful empirical window 
onto four interlocking professional domains. 

Law sees a federal court order 
that compelled California 
to create specialized psychiatric capacity 
for roughly 700 death-row prisoners
 and the subsequent redistribution 
of those prisoners into general population. 

Political science 
sees the gap 
between judicial mandate 
and bureaucratic implementation. 

Psychiatry sees 
moral injury, 
dual loyalty, 
and the phenomenology 
of working inside total institutions. 

Social anthropology 
sees the everyday production of 
spite, 
hierarchy, 
and narrative inside those institutions, 
and the way personal 
memory later reorganizes the same events.

I will examine the episode 
through five analytic lenses: 
self-organizing systems, 
plausible deniability, 
Murphy’s Law, 
Pandora’s box, 
and the butterfly effect. 

Each lens 
is offered 
as a portable instrument 
rather than a finished theory.

Self-organizing systems.
Prisons and state hospitals 
are classic total institutions (Goffman). 

They are also complex adaptive systems.
 Formal rules
—court orders, 
staffing ratios, 
clinical protocols
—do not fully determine behavior. 

Informal norms, 
status hierarchies, 
and emotional economies 
emerge and stabilize. 

Contract psychiatrists 
occupy a distinctive niche: 
“bottom feeders,” 
“pilgrims passing through.” 

They possess clinical authority 
but little institutional capital. 

Staff who hold permanent posts 
can therefore 
afford public displays 
of spite toward chief residents 
or temporary clinicians; 
the cost is low 
and the signal of rank is high. 

These patterns self-organize. 
They are not written 
into any contract 
or court decree, 
yet they reliably appear. 

For political scientists 
the implication 
is that implementation capacity 
is not merely a matter of resources 
or clear rules; 
it is shaped 
by the informal order 
that the formal order itself generates. 

For anthropologists 
the spite 
is a form of social control 
that polices 
the boundary 
between permanent and itinerant staff. 

For psychiatrists 
it is one of the everyday conditions 
that produce moral injury: 
the clinician is required 
to deliver care inside a system 
whose informal logic 
systematically devalues that care.

Plausible deniability.
California spent five million dollars 
recruiting clinicians from across the country. 

Many of those clinicians 
rented or purchased housing near San Quentin. 

When death-row prisoners 
were redistributed 
to general population facilities statewide, 
the specialized posts vanished. 

The state could plausibly claim 
that the court order had been satisfied 
by the creation of capacity; 
the subsequent administrative decision 
to disperse the population 
was a separate operational matter. 

Individual administrators 
could claim 
they were merely executing 
higher-level directives. 

The clinicians who had relocated 
bore the residual risk. 

In legal terms 
this is a classic allocation 
of residual risk 
onto the least organized party
—the temporary contractor. 

In political terms
 it is a textbook illustration 
of how judicial remedies 
can be satisfied 
at the level of formal compliance 
while the original problem 
(inadequate mental-health care under conditions of extreme custody) 
is displaced 
rather than solved. 

Plausible deniability 
is the lubricant 
that keeps the formal system 
and the lived system 
from colliding too visibly.

Murphy’s Law.
Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.

 Housing markets 
near high-security prisons are thin. 

Clinicians who uprooted families 
and acquired mortgages 
discovered that the demand for their services 
could be extinguished 
by a single classification decision. 

Burnout and moral injury are not anomalies; 
they are predictable 
under conditions of high clinical need, 
low institutional support, 
and status inequality. 

The hostile interpersonal climate 
is not an accidental failure of manners; 
it is the system operating under stress. 

For psychiatrists 
this is the familiar terrain 
f secondary trauma 
and dual loyalty. 

For lawyers 
it raises questions 
about the duty of care 
owed by the state 
to the very contractors
 it recruits under court compulsion. 

For political scientists 
it is a reminder 
that implementation failure 
is often over-determined 
rather than surprising.

Pandora’s box.
A federal court order 
that opens 
the question of death-row psychiatric care 
also opens a cascade 
of second-order effects: 
recruitment campaigns, 
geographic mobility, 
housing commitments, 
subsequent reclassification, 
job loss, 
and the continued existence 
of the same institutional pathologies 
under new administrative labels. 

Once the box is opened, 
the original actors 
cannot control what emerges. 

The hope was improved care; 
one durable outcome 
was a cohort of clinicians 
left with expensive housing 
and no specialized posts. 

Anthropologically, 
the box 
is the moment when 
an external legal force 
reorganizes an internal status system, 
producing new winners and losers 
inside the total institution. 

Legally, 
it is the difficulty 
of writing remedies 
that do not generate 
new classes of injury. 

Politically, 
it is the classic problem 
of judicial intervention 
in complex organizations: 
the court can compel a process
 but cannot fully specify 
the equilibrium that will result.

The butterfly effect.
Small, 
contingent personal facts 
produced large differences in outcome. 

A prior relationship with David Dawdy, 
then Director of Mental Health Services 
for the Michigan Department of Corrections, 
and a townhouse in Albany 
that was already paid for, 
meant that the clinician 
could return to Ionia 
without missing a day’s work. 

Most colleagues 
who had relocated to California 
could not. 

Friendship networks 
and prior capital 
functioned as attractors 
in a chaotic system. 

The same court order 
that produced widespread dislocation 
left this individual 
largely unharmed. 

In systems terms, 
sensitive dependence 
on initial conditions 
is not merely a meteorological metaphor; 
it is an empirical feature 
of careers 
that cross 
multiple jurisdictions and employment statuses. 

For all four disciplines 
the implication 
is that aggregate policy analysis 
must be paired 
with attention to 
the micro-conditions 
that sort individuals 
into protected and exposed positions.

Cross-disciplinary implications.
Law students 
should note that formal compliance 
with a court order 
can coexist 
with the externalization of risk 
onto temporary labor 
and the preservation 
of underlying institutional dysfunction. 

Political science students 
should treat judicial mandates 
as inputs 
into self-organizing bureaucratic systems 
rather than 
as self-executing commands. 

Psychiatry students 
should treat moral injury 
and memory reconstruction
 as clinically and ethically relevant: 
the same events 
are narrated differently 
on an anniversary 
than on an ordinary workday, 
and that difference 
is itself data 
about how clinicians survive 
total institutions. 

Anthropology students 
should see the spiteful public exchange 
between the social-work administrator 
and the chief resident 
as a ritual performance 
of hierarchy, 
and the later positive reconstruction 
of the anniversary 
as an instance of 
narrative agency 
exercised outside the institution’s control.

The clinician who posted 
“Another beautiful day” 
was, on that November evening, 
both inside the institution 
and outside it. 

The sunset was real. 
The anniversary was real. 
The system that made the day’s work possible 
was also real, 
and it continued to organize itself 
according to logics 
that no single court order, 
recruitment campaign, 
or individual career fully mastered.

If You Could Read My Mind
(after Gordon Lightfoot)

If you could read my mind, love,
what a tale my thoughts would tell.

Just like an old-time movie
’bout a prison by the bay,
where the sunset paints the water
and the gate still locks the day.

I’d say I took the contract,
a pilgrim passing through,
bottom feeder on the roster,
but the friends I kept were true.

A townhouse paid in Albany,
a hand held out in Ionia’s cold—
Murphy wrote the housing papers,
yet the butterfly stayed gold.

Pandora’s court-room order
spilled five million down the road;
death-row beds were built then emptied,
and the rent came still was owed.

Plausible the denials,
self-organizing spite,
yet on the anniversary evening
the darker tone went light.

If you could read my mind, love,
you’d see the water turning rose,
Kim beside me on the shoreline,
while the system re-composed.

Memories rearrange the pillars,
San Quentin, Pelican, I-Max stone—
but the helping hand still finds me,
and the beautiful day is my own.

text:
$UBER KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM UBER’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Uber’s results point to resilient consumer demand but increasingly binding constraints in labor availability, fulfillment capacity, and autonomous commercialization. The strongest cross-company implications are not a generalized consumer slowdown or an immediate robotaxi earnings inflection. They are geographically differentiated rideshare economics, stronger underlying delivery demand, rising competition for couriers, retailer resistance to concentrated distribution, and a widening distinction between autonomous technology commitments and revenue-producing deployments. The most actionable near-term signals concern Lyft’s November 5 results and Lucid’s November 9 update. For delivery platforms, an important distinction is that DoorDash and Instacart had already announced a definitive acquisition agreement on October 29; Uber’s discussion of a “potential” combination concerns completion and competitive consequences, not an unannounced transaction. Directional assessments below distinguish operating-business effects from consolidated earnings and share-price implications.

RIDESHARING

CALIFORNIA AFFORDABILITY PROVIDES A POSITIVE LYFT READ-THROUGH DESPITE UBER’S INTERNATIONAL MISS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Lyft, Inc. (LYFT: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive, with moderate near-term operating significance. The strongest implication is resilience in North American demand and insurance-related unit economics, not an automatic earnings beat.

Call evidence: Uber described U.S. Mobility growth as “relatively resilient” compared with international markets and stated that California trip growth continued to outperform the rest of the country as “insurance tailwinds continue to build.” The principal international supply problems were concentrated in Brazil, India, and Canada.

Transmission mechanism: Uber’s international Mobility miss should not be applied indiscriminately to Lyft. Brazil and India are not equivalent exposures for Lyft, while California insurance savings directly affect both platforms’ economics. Lower insurance expense per ride creates capacity to reduce consumer prices, stimulate additional trips, and improve utilization without requiring an equivalent deterioration in contribution profit. Lyft’s Q2 prepared remarks independently reported California rideshare growth above the national average and lower insurance costs per ride, making Uber’s Q3 commentary corroborating evidence that this mechanism continued.

The qualification is important: Lyft is not geographically insulated from every issue. Canada is an overlapping exposure, Uber acknowledged some U.S. supply pressure, and Lyft now has European operations through Freenow. Moreover, insurance savings passed to consumers cannot simultaneously be counted as fully retained margin expansion. The positive read-through is stronger for demand and cost flexibility than for a specific margin increase.

Timing: Lyft’s November 5 earnings release is the immediate catalyst. The relevant disclosures are California trip growth, North American driver availability, insurance cost per ride, and the proportion of savings reinvested in affordability. Over 2027, sustained lower insurance costs could support higher category penetration rather than merely a temporary promotional benefit.

LOCAL COMMERCE AND DELIVERY

MERCHANT DIVERSIFICATION CREATES A HEADWIND TO DOORDASH-INSTACART DEAL ECONOMICS (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected companies: DoorDash, Inc. (DASH: United States); Maplebear, Inc., operating as Instacart (CART: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Negative for acquisition underwriting and merchant bargaining power, with potentially material longer-duration implications. The immediate effect is more relevant to transaction risk and expectations than to 2026 earnings.

Call evidence: Khosrowshahi said merchants were concerned about the combination and were asking to work more closely with Uber “so that they are not overly dependent on a single platform.” He also emphasized merchants’ preference for direct channels and multiple distribution partners.

Transmission mechanism: Consolidating restaurant delivery, grocery ordering, fulfillment technology, and advertising creates benefits for DoorDash, but also increases retailers’ incentive to preserve an independent alternative. That can encourage merchants to improve their Uber assortment, allocate promotional budgets to Uber, or negotiate more aggressively over fees, data access, and customer relationships. Consequently, acquisition scale does not translate mechanically into higher pricing power. Part of the expected economic benefit may have to be shared with merchants to preserve participation.

The existing commercial relationships make this more complex than a straightforward consolidation of competitors. Instacart already supplies advertising technology to Uber Eats in the U.S. A change in ownership could therefore place an important Uber advertising partner under a larger direct competitor. Neither the call nor the published commercial announcement establishes that this relationship terminates on a change of control. Assuming an immediate contract cancellation, data transfer, or loss of revenue would be unsupported.

The October 29 agreement values Instacart at approximately $17 billion and provides for at least 75% aggregate cash consideration, with stock elections and proration mechanics. Expected completion is late 2027 or H1 2028, subject to approvals. This creates a lengthy period during which merchant relationships can evolve before operating synergies are realized. Uber’s merchant anecdotes are commercially relevant, but they are statements by an interested competitor, not regulatory findings or proof of deal failure.

Timing: Near-term catalysts are documented merchant responses, transaction filings, and regulatory developments. Longer-duration implications concern fee realization, retention of enterprise customers, and achievable synergies after closing. Instacart’s previously scheduled November 5 earnings call was cancelled following the transaction announcement, so it is not an upcoming standalone operating catalyst.

RESTAURANT DELIVERY STRENGTH IS CATEGORY-WIDE, NOT EVIDENCE OF DOORDASH SHARE LOSS (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: DoorDash, Inc. (DASH: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for underlying demand, with moderate fundamental significance. The evidence supports continued order growth more strongly than an additional near-term earnings upgrade.

Call evidence: Uber reported accelerating organic Delivery growth for the 2nd consecutive quarter and explicitly stated, “Our core restaurant business is also accelerating.” Management attributed the improvement to selection, membership, sparse-market expansion, and merchant-funded offers.

Transmission mechanism: Acceleration at Uber need not imply deterioration at DoorDash when the category itself is expanding through improved affordability, broader merchant coverage, and higher customer frequency. DoorDash’s October 29 results independently reported accelerating U.S. restaurant Marketplace GOV growth, stronger mature-cohort ordering, and growth in new consumers. These disclosures are mutually reinforcing evidence of category expansion rather than a clear zero-sum transfer of demand.

DoorDash’s reported 36% Marketplace GOV growth should not be directly compared with Uber’s 23% constant-currency Delivery growth to infer market-share movements. DoorDash disclosed 23% GOV growth excluding Deliveroo, and the companies have different geographic, product, acquisition, and metric definitions. The more reliable comparison is that both reported stronger underlying U.S. restaurant activity.

There is a margin qualification. Uber identified courier availability as its largest current Delivery challenge. Shared labor-market pressure can require higher fulfillment compensation even when demand remains strong. DoorDash’s own Q3 adjusted EBITDA increased 41%, however, so the call does not justify overriding demonstrated operating leverage with a generalized margin-collapse thesis.

Timing: DoorDash already reported Q3, making Uber’s call corroboration rather than a prediction of that release. The next operating catalysts are Q4 holiday fulfillment, courier incentives, and continued cohort-frequency growth. The longer-duration positive is that membership and improving service quality can expand transaction frequency without relying entirely on new customer acquisition.

BRAZIL’S COMPETITION IS BIDDING UP THE SAME LABOR POOL ACROSS MOBILITY AND DELIVERY (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies: Prosus N.V. (PRX: Netherlands), through iFood; Meituan (3690: China), through Keeta.

Direction and magnitude: Negative for Brazilian delivery unit costs and the pace of profit improvement. Potentially meaningful for iFood’s incremental margins and Keeta’s local investment requirements, but smaller and less directly measurable at the listed-parent level.

Call evidence: Uber attributed Brazil’s constraints partly to competition from delivery platforms for 2-wheel supply and said elevated fuel costs had become a more meaningful problem. Management is responding through driver acquisition, retention, engagement, and greater allocation of incentives to supply.

Transmission mechanism: Motorbike drivers and delivery couriers can switch between platforms and, where eligible, between delivery and passenger transport. Higher incentives from Uber raise the opportunity cost of remaining exclusively available to a delivery service. At the same time, higher fuel costs reduce earnings after expenses. Delivery platforms must therefore accept weaker availability and service quality, increase compensation, improve utilization, or pass costs to consumers.

For Meituan, the mechanism is particularly relevant while Keeta is expanding its Brazilian network: customer acquisition and merchant onboarding are insufficient if courier availability requires more subsidy than planned. For Prosus, the issue is protecting iFood’s service levels and profitability against several well-funded competitors. This is a cost and execution read-through, not evidence that either company has already lost share.

A critical relationship qualification is that Uber and iFood are distribution partners in Brazil. Their announced integration allows access to iFood delivery through Uber and Uber rides through iFood. That partnership can improve demand and customer acquisition economics, but it does not eliminate competition for a shared labor pool. The commercial benefit and the supply-cost headwind can coexist.

Timing: Q4’s seasonal demand peak is the immediate pressure point. The relevant subsequent disclosures are courier incentives, fulfillment reliability, delivery contribution margins, and overseas investment spending. Over 2027, persistent fuel and labor pressure could delay operating leverage even if order growth remains healthy.

GROCERY AND MEMBERSHIP RETAIL

COSTCO GAINS DISTRIBUTION OPTIONS WITHOUT HAVING TO REPLICATE THE DELIVERY NETWORK (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: Costco Wholesale Corporation (COST: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for convenience, channel diversification, and member engagement. Moderate strategic significance, with a likely smaller near-term consolidated earnings effect.

Call evidence: Uber highlighted nationwide Costco expansion as a selection investment and said additional selection improves conversion and attracts consumers. Grocery & Retail was described as operating at an approximately $15 billion annualized bookings pace, growing 40%.

Transmission mechanism: Costco can increase the convenience and accessibility of its assortment through an established demand and fulfillment platform rather than independently building a comparable last-mile network. The September expansion brought nearly 600 Costco locations onto Uber Eats across 47 states. Costco also expanded its DoorDash relationship, while retaining significant Instacart relationships. Multiple channels reduce dependence on any single intermediary and strengthen Costco’s ability to negotiate service, economics, and customer access.

The non-consensus point is that marketplace competition can benefit the retailer even when the platforms themselves face higher spending. Uber, DoorDash, and Instacart have incentives to make Costco attractive within their respective memberships and shopping experiences. Costco gains additional distribution options while the platforms compete to fund convenience and acquire demand.

The earnings benefit should not be overstated. Existing warehouse or online orders may migrate between channels rather than represent incremental sales. Platform fees, picking costs, pricing arrangements, and customer mix determine retained profit. Uber One participation does not establish incremental Costco membership income, and the call provides no basis for adding a specific number of new Costco members.

Timing: The rollout occurred during September, making Q4 a fuller-period test of adoption. Near-term evidence should come from digital sales, same-day delivery engagement, and member behavior. Longer-term value lies in convenience and distribution flexibility, not simply the gross value of orders routed through another app.

RETAIL MEDIA AND ADVERTISING TECHNOLOGY

INSTACART CAN MONETIZE SOME UBER GROCERY GROWTH EVEN WHEN UBER IS THE CONSUMER DESTINATION (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: Maplebear, Inc., operating as Instacart (CART: United States). DoorDash, Inc. (DASH: United States) would inherit this exposure only if its acquisition closes.

Direction and magnitude: Positive for Instacart’s advertising ecosystem, providing a partial hedge against marketplace competition. Small-to-moderate business significance from this specific relationship; no defensible incremental EPS estimate is disclosed.

Call evidence: Uber reported approximately 40% Grocery & Retail growth and emphasized advertising and merchant-funded promotions as contributors to affordability and demand. The call referred to a combined advertising-and-promotion figure exceeding $10 billion, but did not provide a sufficiently clear period or split to treat that amount as advertising revenue.

Transmission mechanism: Uber’s published advertising partnership gives U.S. CPG advertisers access to Uber Eats sponsored inventory through Instacart’s Carrot Ads technology and Ads Manager. Accordingly, more grocery transactions and product discovery on Uber can expand the inventory and advertiser reach available through Instacart’s advertising ecosystem. Instacart does not have to own every consumer transaction to participate in the associated advertising opportunity.

This is an important offset to a simplistic thesis that every Uber grocery gain is an equivalent Instacart loss. Instacart’s transaction marketplace and advertising technology have different exposure to competition. Its Q3 advertising and other revenue increased 23% to $331 million, compared with 15% GTV growth, demonstrating the broader monetization opportunity, although those results do not isolate Uber’s contribution.

The limits are equally important. The integration covers particular U.S. CPG advertising functions, not all Uber advertising globally. Commercial fee-sharing is undisclosed, and merchant-funded discounts are not interchangeable with advertising revenue. The partnership was announced in 2025, so the Q3 call validates a continuing opportunity rather than establishing a newly awarded contract.

Timing: Near-term evidence is continued advertising growth and clarity on the partnership during the pending DoorDash transaction. Longer-term value depends on Instacart remaining useful as advertising infrastructure even when retailers and consumers use competing storefronts. For CART shares, transaction consideration and closing risk may dominate the immediate benefit of stronger standalone operations.

AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES AND ELECTRIC VEHICLE MANUFACTURERS

LUCID’S COMMERCIAL ROBOTAXI START IS LATER THAN THE EARLIER PUBLIC TARGET (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: Lucid Group, Inc. (LCID: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Negative for near-term commercialization expectations and the speed of operating validation. Moderate narrative significance ahead of earnings; the immediate vehicle-revenue impact cannot be quantified.

Call evidence: Uber’s accompanying written commentary anticipates fully driverless Nuro-Lucid testing in Q4 and a Bay Area commercial launch in Q1 2027. On the call, management similarly placed Nuro’s fully driverless commercial deployment in early 2027.

Transmission mechanism: Lucid’s April 2026 partnership expansion described a San Francisco Bay Area commercial launch later in 2026. Uber’s current schedule therefore confirms a later commercial start than that earlier public target. The economic consequences are delayed operating validation, later accumulation of paid-service experience, and potentially slower progression toward larger deployments.

This matters because Lucid’s robotaxi program is part of a broader operating reset rather than an immaterial experiment. Lucid reported Q3 production of 2,954 vehicles and deliveries of 3,806, while reducing inventory and aligning production with demand. A scalable enterprise channel could eventually improve manufacturing utilization, but commercialization must precede confidence in a large recurring fleet opportunity.

The approximately 35,000-vehicle partnership commitment is multiyear and should not be treated as near-term deliveries. Similarly, Uber’s target of more than 2,000 fully driverless vehicles across all partners by year-end 2027 is not a Lucid allocation. Vehicles may be delivered and recognized as revenue before entering commercial service, so the later service launch does not mechanically establish a Q4 shipment reduction.

Timing: Lucid’s November 9 earnings update is the immediate catalyst for distinguishing production-validation deliveries, billable vehicle sales, software readiness, and commercial deployment. Q1 2027 is the subsequent service milestone. The longer-duration investment issue is conversion of a large strategic commitment into repeatable manufacturing demand and cash generation.

WERIDE HAS A MORE DIRECT PATH FROM UBER’S AUTONOMOUS TARGETS TO COMMERCIAL ACTIVITY (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected company: WeRide Inc. (WRD: China).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for commercialization and demand access. Potentially material to the robotaxi business over time, although Uber’s disclosed fleet targets do not support a specific consolidated revenue or earnings uplift.

Call evidence: Uber stated that it was already operating without drivers with WeRide in international markets and expects approximately half of its more-than-2,000 fully driverless vehicles at year-end 2027 to be outside the U.S. Management emphasized existing demand, local operations, and the ability to launch at high utilization.

Transmission mechanism: WeRide is an operating technology partner, not merely a company with thematic exposure to autonomy. Its disclosed Dubai service allows customers to book fully driverless paid rides through Uber, with Tawasul providing local fleet-management services. This structure combines WeRide’s autonomous system, Uber’s demand aggregation, and a local operating partner.

Access to established demand can reduce the need to build a separate consumer network in each market. Higher utilization can improve fleet economics and support additional deployments, creating demand for WeRide’s technology and vehicles. If third-party fleet financing becomes available on acceptable terms, better utilization evidence can also make expansion more financeable.

The accounting transmission requires discipline. Vehicle owners, fleet operators, Uber, and the technology provider do not necessarily receive the same economic benefit. The call does not disclose WeRide’s share of the approximately 1,000 international vehicles implied by Uber’s 2027 mix, nor the contractual allocation of fares, fees, or capital expenditure. The positive conclusion concerns commercial access and deployment probability, not a guaranteed margin increase or a new purchase order.

Timing: The relevant milestones are operating fully driverless fleet additions through year-end 2026, expansion of permitted service areas, and utilization and revenue disclosures during 2027. The longer-duration advantage is an export commercialization model that does not require WeRide to independently establish a consumer marketplace in every country.

TESLA’S ROBOTAXI ECONOMICS MUST INCLUDE DISTRIBUTION AND FINANCING, NOT JUST REMOVAL OF THE DRIVER (READ-THROUGH 9)

Affected company: Tesla, Inc. (TSLA: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Negative for aggressive assumptions about standalone robotaxi economics. Potentially significant to long-duration valuation narratives, but not a basis for reducing current automotive earnings estimates.

Call evidence: Uber claimed a roughly 30% utilization advantage for its hybrid deployments and contrasted high-20s daily trips on its network with low-teens daily trips in some newer standalone markets, including Tesla deployments. Management also stated that autonomous residual values are not yet established and that Uber would initially hold some vehicles on its balance sheet.

Transmission mechanism: Removing the driver does not eliminate vehicle depreciation, financing, insurance, charging, cleaning, maintenance, downtime, or the cost of acquiring sufficient demand. If a standalone fleet completes fewer paid trips, fixed ownership and operating costs are spread across fewer transactions. A 30% increase in paid trips reduces fixed cost per trip by approximately 23%, assuming unchanged fixed costs. That is economically meaningful even before considering customer-acquisition spending.

The implication for Tesla is that manufacturing scale and autonomy capability must be translated into high utilization and attractive cash returns. A vertically integrated fleet can avoid paying an external distribution fee, but that advantage must exceed the cost of building demand and any resulting utilization disadvantage. Uncertain residual values also complicate assumptions that fleets can be financed cheaply against conventional automotive collateral.

Uber’s comparisons are management claims, not independently controlled benchmarks. Market maturity, operating geography, fares, service restrictions, and vehicle availability differ. Consequently, the call does not prove that Tesla’s fully loaded cost per trip is higher or that its eventual model will fail. It does establish why underwriting a robotaxi solely from vehicle cost and eliminated driver pay is incomplete.

Timing: Near-term catalysts are credible disclosures of paid trips per available vehicle, operating hours, realized fares, empty miles, and recurring support costs. The longer-duration shift is toward valuing autonomous businesses on demonstrable utilization and capital returns rather than technical capability or announced fleet size alone.

text:
Researchers at the University of Southern California have shown that a two-week course of the experimental drug cinaciguat can reverse key aspects of liver aging in rats. 

In older animals the specialized cells that line the liver’s blood vessels lose their microscopic openings, a change known as pseudocapillarization that impairs the organ’s ability to clear circulating waste. 

Daily treatment restored these openings and re-established signaling between the lining cells and the liver’s main working cells, the hepatocytes. 

As a result, blood levels of amyloid-beta 40, a protein fragment that forms plaques in Alzheimer’s disease, fell by half and returned to the concentrations seen in young rats. 

The same regimen also normalized elevated LDL cholesterol. 

The findings suggest that age-related declines in liver filtration may contribute to rising levels of both amyloid-beta and “bad” cholesterol, and that restoring the liver’s clearance capacity could offer a peripheral strategy for addressing these risks. 

The work remains confined to rats and does not yet demonstrate effects on brain plaques or cognitive function.

Source: de Leve et al., Journal of Biological Chemistry, 2026.

text:
SOME PEOPLE ARE FIGHTING BATTLES YOU KNOW NOTHING ABOUT

Not everyone who smiles is happy. Not everyone who is quiet is at peace. And not everyone who seems to have everything together is doing well.

There are people who wake up every morning carrying burdens they never talk about.

Some are lonely in a room full of people.

Some are struggling financially and too embarrassed to admit it.

Some have made mistakes they wish they could undo.

Some are watching their health deteriorate.

Some are grieving someone they loved.

Others are simply exhausted from trying to hold their lives together.

And perhaps the saddest thing is that many of these people have become very good at pretending everything is fine.

We live in a world where people are often judged by what others can see, while their greatest struggles remain invisible.

A person can be difficult because they're hurting.

Someone can withdraw because they've been rejected.

Someone can seem unfriendly because they're afraid of being hurt again.

We don't always know the story behind someone's behavior.

That doesn't excuse wrongdoing. It reminds us that human beings are complicated, and compassion matters.

Jesus understood something about people that we desperately need to learn.

He saw beyond appearances.

He noticed people others overlooked.

He approached those society rejected.

He recognized suffering where others saw inconvenience.

And He offered hope to people who had nearly given up.

Perhaps one of the greatest gifts we can give another human being is the feeling that they are not invisible.

A kind word.

A little patience.

A willingness to listen.

A moment of genuine interest.

Sometimes these small things mean more than we will ever know.

Before you judge someone today, consider the possibility that you know very little about what they're going through.

And if you're the person quietly struggling, remember this:

Your life has value, even when nobody seems to notice. Your story isn't finished, and your present circumstances do not determine your worth.

You matter.

One question worth asking ourselves today:

When was the last time I made someone feel genuinely seen, heard, and valued?

text:
it’s a brand new day. God is with me. 

though i spent years of my life not being a morning person, i somehow managed to change this. grateful for that

i still wake up with my first thoughts of the morning along the lines of “hey, just kill yourself” and it comes from worthlessness, but i shake it off and go on. 

i work today at a job i’ve missed a few shifts for this past week. i took a lot of sick time off this week. everyone has been really understanding, so far. i am grateful 

this past week was very hard, especially coming to terms with how difficult this whole thing with my mom is. 

i think the number one thing i’m afraid of is myself 

it’s my temperament when i am around my mother. i feel like a different person, and it’s someone i don’t like. she brings out the worst in me. it takes everything in me to stay regulated around her. she is the only person in my life that dysregulates me so fast and so easily like this. my entire nervous system changes when i’m around her. it takes time to recover from being around her too long.

a professional hoarding cleanup service i was willing to pay said my mom was “too challenging” to work with and abandoned her by lying to her. yes, too challenging for even strangers who don’t have childhood trauma from her. i do. imagine how challenging it is for me. 

though i only have weekends to help my mom, and only 8 of them or so, this weekend i needed for myself. to recharge. to spend time with friends and reconnect to a sense of self that is rooted in who i really am, not the person i become around my mother. 

tomorrow i am meeting up with the friend who said he’ll offer some physical moving labor, and my roommate who has been supportive to me, plus a couple of other friends of friends, to see You Can See Everything. 

i need this weekend to myself to ground myself in who i am. to be around kind, calm and gentle people is restorative for me. 

last night I reconnected with my Higher Power, my understanding of God

and I know God is supporting me through this, as God has already answered my previous prayer, to get my mom somewhere to live 

it was like finding a needle in a haystack. or a unicorn.  

fully equipped with everything she needs, and then some, like a shower with a built in disability accessible tub that she can sit down in, with water jets. handlebars by the toilet too. it’s an in-law suite, its own private little house, next to the landlord’s house. no stairs to climb. and laundry is inside the unit. parking may be the only challenge, as she’ll have to share the driveway with the landlord. spacious kitchen. semi-affordable rent. in a good part of the city. coincidentally, it’s around the corner from her sister, though they don’t talk. 

my mother is impossible to please, so the fact that she liked it so much and we managed to get it, to me, is indeed a miracle. 

i mean, that was just One Miracle. it was the main miracle i needed. 

I don’t take for granted that God has been answering my prayers. 

I remain grateful and feel blessed, that I have been carried by God this far

now I pray for the strength, courage and patience to do what it takes to get through clearing the hoard and moving her, with as few nervous system activations, or breakdowns, as possible. 

this is one of the hardest things i’ve ever had to do in my life, and i am not willing to abandon my mom just because i can’t handle her and apparently no one else can either. that is simply not an option. 

miracles do happen. i still freak out and catastrophize when my nervous system is activated. 

keep in mind, i have a psychotic illness that can get triggered by stress. it’s why i was on disability for ten years. 

but lately all the “psychotic” symptoms are me believing in a God that wants me to love and take care of myself so He can better support me

and the feeling that my father, who is deceased, is with me through this, somehow. 

thank you all again, for your donations, your prayers and support 🙏🏽

text:
I Agreed to Be His Fake Wife, But Fell in Love for Real ❤️

When billionaire Daniel Williams offered me $50,000 to pretend to be his wife for six months, I thought he was crazy.

"All you have to do is smile, attend a few family gatherings, and convince everyone we're happily married," he explained.

"And what happens when the six months are over?" I asked.

"We go our separate ways. No feelings, no complications."

I laughed.

"Don't worry, Mr. Williams. I'm not interested in falling in love with you."

He smiled confidently.

"Good. Because I'm not interested in falling in love with you either."

Those were the words that started everything.

Daniel needed a wife to secure his inheritance. His grandfather had made it clear that he would only hand over control of the family business if Daniel settled down and proved he could build a stable family.

I needed money desperately. My mother's hospital bills were piling up, and I had nowhere else to turn.

So, I signed the agreement.

Within a week, I moved into his luxurious mansion. We attended parties together, held hands in public, and shared a bedroom whenever his family visited.

But behind closed doors, we were strangers.

Daniel was handsome, wealthy, and terribly arrogant. He rarely smiled, hated being questioned, and believed money could solve every problem.

I couldn't stand him.

Or at least, that's what I kept telling myself.

Things slowly changed.

He started remembering how I liked my coffee. He would wait for me before having dinner, even after returning home late from work. Whenever I fell asleep on the sofa, I would wake up covered with his jacket.

One night, I developed a terrible fever.

I woke up around 3 a.m. and found Daniel sitting beside my bed, holding a damp towel against my forehead.

"You should be sleeping," I whispered.

He looked at me with worried eyes.

"I couldn't sleep knowing you were sick."

For the first time, I saw something beyond the cold billionaire everyone feared.

I saw a man who cared.

And that frightened me.

Because I was beginning to fall in love with my fake husband.

One evening, while preparing dinner, Daniel came up behind me and gently wrapped his arms around my waist.

"Do you know what's strange?" he whispered.

"What?"

"I used to count the days until this arrangement ended. Now I find myself wishing it would never end."

My heart raced.

I turned to face him.

"Daniel, we agreed this was only business."

He stared into my eyes.

"I know. But somewhere along the way, you stopped being part of a business arrangement."

Before I could respond, he kissed me.

And for the first time, I didn't want the contract to end.

But happiness didn't last long.

Three weeks before our fake marriage was supposed to end, I overheard Daniel speaking to his lawyer.

"Make sure the divorce papers are ready. Once the six months are over, I want everything settled."

My heart shattered.

I had forgotten that, to him, this was still temporary.

That night, I packed my bags and left without saying goodbye.

When Daniel returned home, he found only one thing on the dining table: my wedding ring and a short note.

"Thank you for making me feel loved, even if it was never real for you. I hope you find the happiness you deserve."

He called me dozens of times, but I refused to answer.

Two days later, someone knocked on my apartment door.

When I opened it, Daniel stood there, looking exhausted.

"Why did you leave?" he asked.

I tried to hold back my tears.

"Because our six months are almost over, Daniel. I don't want to be the only person who forgets this was fake."

He stepped closer.

"Look at me."

I shook my head.

"Please don't make this harder."

He took my hands.

"The divorce papers were for my grandfather's records. I was planning to tell him the truth and give up the inheritance if that's what it took to keep you."

I stared at him.

"What?"

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small velvet box.

text:
HOLD YOUR CUP UP

Good food for the soul — Jack David

You could never repay God for the gifts He’s given you. And guess what? He doesn’t want you to.

That’s the beauty of His love. There is no debt to settle, no installments to make, and no price of admission. His love is freely given. The greatest return is that we receive it, love Him freely in return, and allow His goodness to shine through us.

Jesus said, “Freely ye have received, freely give.” (Matthew 10:8)

Now that’s a pretty good deal!

He invites us to hold our cups up so He can fill them again. Not out of obligation, but out of joy, gratitude, and love.

I get to have my cup filled every morning. I wake up, I pray, and the Lord fills it. It’s not half full. It’s running over!

“My cup runneth over.” (Psalm 23:5)

We cannot make installments on blessings already given. We can only receive them with grateful hearts and pass that goodness along. There is no repayment expected, only that we live, love, give, and let His light shine through us.

Some mornings I wake with tears in my eyes because I know the joy of His love. There’s no explanation needed. Just truth.

And here’s where it all comes together: that divine DNA. That beautiful reflection of our Creator showing up in the goodness we share, the compassion we extend, the forgiveness we offer, and the love we give freely. When goodness grows in us, His light becomes visible through us.

We are a work in progress, every one of us, being renewed day by day. Scripture reminds us that we are healed through His sacrifice (1 Peter 2:24), and Jesus came that we might have life more abundantly (John 10:10).

I am blessed. Blessed by His love, growing in His goodness, and learning to walk more faithfully in His way. I know I fall short, but I’m getting there. I’m a work in progress, and I love being loved by God. My God. Simple as that.

So fear not. Be not afraid.

This is the day the Lord has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. (Psalm 118:24)

Do your part. Finish what you start. Live to give. Hold your cup up, let it overflow, and leave a little goodness everywhere you go.

After all, the light was never meant to be kept in the cup. It was meant to shine.

Thank You, Father.

— Jack David

text:
I've seen quite a few posts touting Abdul El-Sayed's “h-index,” implying it establishes him as a seasoned academic with exceptional insights into healthcare. I did a deeper dive. Sharing what I found.

tldr: 
1. Academic output and citation impact do not imply scientific rigor/quality. (H-index fallacy)
2. Most of the papers center on health equity with significant inferential challenges and poor methodology.
3. No one reads the actual papers.

For context, the h-index measures academic citation impact. An h-index of 25 means a researcher has published at least 25 papers, each cited at least 25 times. It measures scholarly visibility and productivity—not necessarily scientific rigor, clinical expertise, or the validity of the conclusions.

I knew relatively little about El-Sayed, so I began reviewing his published research, policy papers, and academic commentary.

El-Sayed graduated from medical school, intending to become a neurosurgeon (props) but subsequently earned a DPhil at Oxford, pursuing a career primarily in epidemiology, public health, and health policy rather than clinical practice. His biography reports more than 100 peer-reviewed publications, although bibliographic databases vary considerably in their coverage. Preliminary searches identified 78 publications through Rankless, 53 through ResearchGate, and 34 through EBSCO. A definitive PubMed count remains unverified.

What interested me wasn't the publication count itself, but a recurring pattern in the research.

Much of his work centers on ethnicity, socioeconomic inequality, health equity, and access to care. These are legitimate subjects of scientific inquiry. But several studies move from documenting a population disparity to statistically adjusting for selected variables, then proposing a broader socioeconomic or structural explanation that the research design cannot independently establish.

The distinction between statistical association and demonstrated causation is fundamental.

1. Consider his 2011 University of Michigan neurosurgery study. The investigators examined 918 cranial and spinal surgical cases and reported significantly higher postoperative complication rates among publicly insured and uninsured patients.

But the analysis combined heterogeneous procedures, relied on retrospective single-center data, and remained vulnerable to confounding from disease severity, comorbidities, surgical complexity, and urgency. The uninsured group's adjusted odds ratio was 3.6, with a wide 95% confidence interval of 1.3–10.3.

The authors suggested that limited access to postoperative outpatient care might explain the disparity and could mediate their findings.
(Read that sentence again.) Yet they did not directly establish that mechanism.  Complications occurring before discharge, for example, could not be attributed to inadequate postdischarge follow-up.  They also failed to highlight that every surgical procedure carries a 90-day global period with zero cost to the patient/payer; but still posit a cost basis for an access issue.

2. His study of suicide among Arab Americans presents a similar inferential challenge. The investigators reported lower suicide rates among Arab Americans and suggested that "ethnic density may protect against suicide among Arab-Americans.” (Again, read that out loud and tell me if that raises any red flags).  The paper raises a legitimate epidemiological hypothesis. It does not establish a causal benefit from ethnic concentration, much less self-segregation.

3. El-Sayed's 2015 infant mortality study analyzed 1.43 million Michigan births and concluded that environmental factors likely played a greater role than genetics in racial mortality disparities. But neither genetic contributions nor the proposed environmental mechanisms were directly isolated.

A related 2020 PNAS study by Greenwood et al. associated physician–newborn racial concordance with lower Black newborn mortality. A subsequent 2024 reanalysis found that adjusting for very low birth weight—a major clinical confounder—substantially weakened the association, rendering it statistically insignificant in expanded models.

The studies address different hypotheses, so the reanalysis does not invalidate El-Sayed's findings. But it illustrates the same methodological concern: observed racial disparities and statistically significant associations do not, by themselves, establish the mechanisms responsible.

Compelling explanations still require rigorous causal evidence.

Each of these papers offer legitimate epidemiological findings. Neither establishes the proposed causal mechanism. To their credit, the authors generally describe these explanations as possibilities rather than proven conclusions.

And that's the central issue.

There is a meaningful difference between documenting disparities and scientifically explaining them. Observational associations can generate valuable hypotheses, but regression analysis and statistical significance do not automatically validate the broader narratives built around those findings.

El-Sayed's publication record demonstrates academic activity and citation impact. Whether individual studies support the conclusions drawn from them requires a more demanding assessment of study design, confounding, causal inference, and reproducibility.

An h-index cannot substitute for that scrutiny.

Academic authority should be earned through the strength of the evidence—not inferred from the number of citations or the appeal of an ideological framework.

Most of the people parroting the h-index talking point have never perused, much less read, any of his papers.

Anderson Cooper: “here's the closing events for the michigan senate race. republican mike rogers on the left with a rally in rochester hills. democrat abdul el-sayed on the right with a rally in detroit. not on either stage tonight is michigan democratic congresswoman haley stevens, who surprised her party yesterday by changing her endorsement from el-sayed to his republican challenger mike rogers. i spoke to congresswoman about her decision last night. she had reportedly told fellow michigan democrat debbie dingell that she would not endorse mike rogers and then did here. my question though is what changed from the phone conversation you had with congresswoman debbie dingell and waking up refreshed in the morning? did you talk to anybody? did you have a long night at the soul? were you up all night? what do you have a dream? what happened?”

Haley Stevens: “no look i would just say that you know i had some time to you know think. i wasn't on the phone i think that late, but i know debbie's always working around the clock. it might not have been midnight when when i spoke with her, but i i was there and just you know alone with my thoughts. i was writing things out. and look, this level of anger and the things that we are seeing. look, we all want democrats to win. i'm a really proud democrat. and by the way, abdul's got every other democrat with him.”

Anderson Cooper: “one of those other democrats is michigan's secretary of state jocelyn benson. she's also the democratic candidate running from governor there, and she joins me now. secretary benson, do you think congresswoman stevens' endorsement of mike rogers could matter on the margins, especially if the election is closer than the polls suggest?”

Jocelyn Benson: “well first, thanks for having me. and what i've seen on the ground here in michigan is that there's actually the impact it's had is to actually increase the enthusiasm for dr. al syed. and look, i'm proud to be leading a ticket full of democratic leaders, including dr. al syed, who are all focused on the same thing, lowering costs, raising wages, and ending corruption. and as i traveled through churches yesterday, as all of this the ripples of of this played out, what i heard people actually talking about and reacting to on the ground was one, the lions, because we're all happy that the lions beat the vikings, but secondly, the costs of everything, the cost of gas, the cost of groceries. i mean that is real, and that is on the front of minds of michigan voters in this moment. and then beyond that, enthusiasm actually sort of grew for, and unity really started to build, as people recognize, and i think voters are smart, we recognize the sharp contrast between the slate of democratic candidates who have a plan for driving down costs and defending democracy, and republican candidates on the other side, whether it's mike rogers or john james, who have supported tariffs that are driving up costs in michigan more than any other state, and who together are parroting lies about our elections to try to undermine faith in our democracy. so we know in michigan, one thing is clear. mike rogers and john james will work for trump, not for michigan, and michigan voters deserve better. and that is what i see our party uniting around.”

Sunlen Serfaty: “well anderson, there certainly is a sense within the campaign that this has potential. this defection of haley stevens has the potential to galvanize democrats in advance of election day. and certainly those stunning fundraising numbers reported just yesterday by the lca campaign, 2.4 million dollars in one single day, it really is reflective of that feeling. one voter telling me just a few minutes ago at this campaign rally here that nothing drives people like the sense of betrayal. at this question though, the open question tonight is, will that impact actually how people vote tomorrow? and certainly the campaign is hoping that that anger, that sense of betrayal, will drive democrats to the polls tomorrow. but again, it is still very much an open question.”

David: “well if it will actually have impact on the electoral votes, i think that what they're saying has some validity. you know, he is not that you have validity, that it actually galvanized em. you don't think you give some permission to some people who may have doubts about say it. first of all, i think most people have made their decisions already in this race. and you know, i think the times poll may be a little over optimistic for him, but it does show, and other polls have shown, you know, 93, 94, 95 percent support among democrats. but in terms of turnout, i think it's it's good. it it'll excite people. it's been interesting to watch sort of the regular democrats, you know, active democrats, kind of rally around him as a result of this, because he wasn't their favorite. he wasn't the candidate they supported in the primary. she was. and now there's this rallying going on. so i at the end of the day, i don't think this is gonna make that much of a difference, but i certainly don't think it's gonna hurt him.”

Van Jones: “her decision to do this has consolidated the democratic party behind and around abdul in a way that was inconceivable 48 hours ago. and it comes down to a couple of things. one is if you're she was playing this moral role of challenging abdul to do better against some of the hate that was showing up in this campaign. but if you go from challenging hate in our party, but then you hug and french kiss maga, and you don't say anything about the hate coming from their campaign, all the anti-muslim hate, then you kind of fall between two chairs. so i think she's lost a lot of moral authority. the other thing is, which we haven't talked about enough, she chose to do this in front of a black church. that was an error, because a lot of black people thought, what is this woman doing using our church as a prop for this stunt? and it sent a real wave of anger through the black community. you really, i mean the black churches, you know, is very precious to us, and the idea that somebody would show up and pull this thing off. and so you had had some black people holding back. you have black people now who had been quiet because they maybe didn't like a blow that much going on facebook endorsing. you had a huge wave of unexpected volunteers in the detroit offices, which you have not seen. you saw this massive spike in fundraising. well, it changed the outcome. i don't think it does, but it allows him to close strong. and and that, and i think that was a kind of an unforced error on her part. i think she had been playing a moral leadership role, a useful role, but once you join the other team, you you galvanize the other side.”

Anderson Cooper: “i can't get this french kiss.”

“listen, it's hard to say if this is going to materially impact the race. i mean, the how much attention your interview got, in the discussions around it, in the denunciations by democrats, honestly surprised me. this is a house member who's not running for re-election. but one thing is critical. there's about a hundred thousand jewish voters in michigan. many jewish voters have felt very alienated by abdul el-sayed's campaign, making a play for those voters and creating a permission structure to say you can be with mike rogers and you could still vote down ballot for the rest of candidates as democrats. that makes a difference. i'd remind you, alyssa slot can only won by about 20,000 votes in michigan a cycle ago. so that's where you could maybe see some swaying.”

Anderson Cooper: “scott, i know you interviewed her today on your show.”

Scott: “i did. she came on the radio and i'd never met her before. i've never spoken to her. and you know, i think she was a little bit out of shape about some of the frankly vile commentary that's been lobbed her way. if you look at some of the things that like james carville and george conway and other prominent democrats have said about her, allegations that somehow because she's a woman she doesn't have her own agency, or because you know she made this choice to endorse a republican, she's a lunatic and needs to be locked up in a mental hospital. and other people have even alleged that her fiancee, you know, made her do it. and she came on and she pushed back pretty forcefully against all of that. she also talked about the fact that she's been hearing from a lot of democrats today. she said people who said, thank you so much, this is what's on my mind. you had the courage to go out and do it. and and this is what happens to people on the left when they get out of line in the middle of an election. they come for you. but she had the courage to do that. so she said she's been getting a lot of support from her network. and you know, we'll see how the chips fall on this.”

Anderson Cooper: “as he's chuckling a little hearing you say that. but on the on what i read, the transcript of her comments, you enunciated her position much better than she actually did during your inner son.”

Scott: “i'm a communication provider, as we all know here. just one thing on the on the on the jewish vote. there's no doubt that there will be there will be some who vote against him because of his position on israel. it's also true that the jewish vote is half the size of the arab muslim vote in that state, which is a larger population. that vote may be elevated in the primary. so we'll see how it all nets out.”

Van Jones: “yeah i think david makes a point that we should talk about more. if you look at what happened in the election in israel, bibi netanyahu was very tough on the arab population and they came out in record numbers. they went in from 10 per 10 seats in the knesset to 19, doubled. i think you got a very large arab community that's been watching all this. what has mike rogers offered the people of michigan? what is his job proposal? what is his health care proposal? it's just been a steady diet of anti-muslim rhetoric, but better that lands as anti, not anti-islamist, but anti-muslim. the gop piling on, calling him a jihadist. do you think that all those voters are just gonna sit there and say, well that's fine with us? you see in the south, you see black voters mobilizing, feeling insulted by donald trump. i think you're gonna see an arab turnout. i think if mike rogers had offered something other than just a bunch of anti-muslim hysteria, he would be doing better. i don't think, i don't think abdul's up by 11. he's up by a lot because his hate campaign has fallen flat in michigan.”

text:
Perfect example of siphoning wealth off the people. Signed up for Wal Mart Spark deliveries because I was curious and people said they took care of their people. Paid well. Yeah right! Crazy that the richest companies in this country can’t pay their workers without their workers having to tap into their own assets to work for them.  I got my first offer this morning. 

For anyone that doesn’t understand what it means to be an independent contractor and to work for these little tech delivery companies that are making billions off of us. Here’s an example. The standard business mileage tax write off is $.76/mile. DoorDash, UBER, WalMart and Amazon all pay independent contractors to work for them. I was on strike against Walmart for over a decade. I wouldn’t step foot in a store and I wouldn’t buy anything from there. For one, in Minnesota because it was a high crime area in that suburb, they treated you like a criminal when you walked in and it was because they didn’t treat their employees well. Then recently they lowered the cost of food and I thought they turned over a new leaf, so I figured I would give it a try. As an independent contractor, they do not provide you a company vehicle, gas, insurance that covers accidents while working for them in most cases and the offers either barely cover your business expenses and you have no or little pay. It’s nowhere near minimum wage and they also don’t have to pay out benefits like health insurance. These are the same people who want to automate everything and call it a good thing for America. 

This is the reality of it. The more money they make the greedier they get. Uber is a terrible one. They have to legally give you 100% of your tip so they instead take away your base pay if the customer tips well enough. I would’ve never even believed this was legal. Had I not experienced it for myself. 
1-2% of the American workforce does these jobs over 3 million Americans being scammed of their assets but this is America prospering. Give me a fucking break! These companies are already billion dollar companies and we borrow equity out of our own assets to work for them. These corporations have successfully manipulated it so that customers take all of the losses and now employees also take the losses of their business.  Meanwhile, Uber sends you an offer and says you’re gonna make $22 an hour for this job. It’s lies, deception and the more these jobs are getting popular as America gets burnt out on the political polarity and corporate exploitation. If corporations have an option to hire part-time non benefits labor they have the option to lower or keep employees pay and benefits stagnant while the cost of living rises but wages don’t. 
I can’t remember what it was but something happened like 10 years ago. I think someone tried to force these companies to pay people benefits or something and in retaliation they started just giving everybody part-time work. You don’t have to pay full-time benefits for part-time work. Do you think these people wanna automate everything to make humanity better? Look at how they already treat the part-time work clearly humans are just an inconvenience to their profit margins.  Scary ass world we live in that’s all I can say.  Corporations run the government. The people become the silent majority at elections. Major parties divide, and conquer the country right down the middle. Fake wealth. Crazy times. 

Anyways my first offer from Walmart for rural delivery is 6 stops (customers) 19 miles of driving and the pay- $19.88 estimated time for completion 1 hour 1 minutes. Tell me how that is a job? Well below minimum wage in Texas and not even including  the ten miles to get to the store. 19 miles x $.70/mile = $13.30 $19.88-$13.30= $6.58/hr. Minimum wage here is $7.25! And the $19.88 includes a tip of $4.57 from 6 customers. Without it, the pay is $2.01/hr  What is going to be done about this in Texas @GinaHinojosaTX @jamestalarico?  
Hoping for real change here.

A good description of "spiritual bypassing." Sri Aurobindo also pointed out similar fallacies in certain Eastern spiritual practices, including traditional yogic and Buddhist approaches, especially the tendency to confuse suppression and repression with true transformation and transmutation. 

He offered a more integrated approach through his Integral Yoga. His books "The Synthesis of Yoga" and "Essays on the Gita" explore these fallacies in more depth.

A major aspect of his teaching is that the aim is not to escape the world into Nirvana or a state of samadhi, but to bring down and embody the Divine Consciousness, transforming and spiritualizing the body, mind, life, and ultimately matter itself. 

His approach also challenges the old religious and spiritual idea that life is maya, an illusion to escape from, or that the ultimate aim is simply liberation from samsara. 

You see similar tendencies in contemporary, oversimplified victimhood-inducing conspiracy theories such as "Earth is a prison planet" or "reincarnation is a trap," which reflect certain world-denying religious interpretations that view earthly existence as inherently fallen or sinful, with the ultimate purpose being to escape it all.

I believe Steiner taught something similar about bringing Spirit into earthly existence and confronting darkness and evil rather than escaping into some spiritual la-la land. 

Jung's work also addresses these issues from a more psychological, practical, and grounded perspective, particularly through shadow integration and individuation.

text:
《Texas Lost: Republicans Still Reeling, a Comeback Yet Uncertain》

In the early days of World War II, Germany’s blitzkrieg shook Europe with the speed of its advance. The result of this Texas gubernatorial election delivered a sudden political shock of its own. A military offensive can be planned in advance; a political upheaval can build for years before revealing its full force on election night.

In my view, Democrats may have anticipated a close contest and seen a path to victory. What may have surprised even them was winning so decisively in a state where Republicans had held the governor’s office for more than three decades.

Democrats organized a successful campaign. Republicans must also examine how their own years in power helped create the opening.

Counting the votes takes a night. Reaching the decision to replace those in power can take voters many years.

Republicans need to answer a difficult question: Why did decades of organization, resources, and governing experience fail to give enough Texans a reason to keep supporting you?

The longer a party governs, the more capable it should become at solving problems. But if those years also produce institutional arrogance, evasive answers, and indifference to ordinary people’s difficulties, a supposedly strong political foundation can become a burden that voters eventually decide to remove.

People have no obligation to preserve a party’s governing record. They have no obligation to sacrifice their own well-being to protect its political pride.

My reading of this election is that some Texans had simply waited long enough. They wanted to try someone else and see whether life could improve.

Years of support do not amount to permanent consent. A voter can agree with a party’s principles and still lose patience with its performance. When everyday problems remain unanswered, past loyalty faces a practical question: After all these years of my support, what have you actually made better?

If the answer remains a collection of slogans, voters may use their ballots to end the wait.

Replacing one familiar face with another from the same governing circle may no longer be enough. To disappointed voters, that can look like the same pot, the same soup, served under a different name.

So they replace the pot as well.

Behind that choice is a simple hope: Let us try someone else. Perhaps she can put something better on the table.

Democrats should understand the weight of that opportunity. Voters who removed Republicans from a long-held governorship can also remove Democrats after four years.

From the moment of victory, the governor-elect must prepare to be judged by results. Campaign promises require action. Problems require measurable progress. People seeking help need answers that lead somewhere.

The new administration should explain what it inherited and how it intends to address it. Blaming a predecessor cannot pay a family’s bills or make daily life easier.

Republicans, meanwhile, have no four years to waste.

Borrowing and adapting Tang poet Du Mu’s poem about Xiang Yu:

Victory and defeat are never certain in war;
It takes resolve to bear disgrace and persevere.
Texas still has people of talent—
Who can say a comeback is beyond reach?

A comeback remains possible. But possibility requires work.

If all that remains after defeat is the same question circling in your minds—Why? Why? Why?—then take that question back to your governing record.

Which promises went unfulfilled? Which problems remained unresolved? Which voters kept waiting for a response?

Texas has talent. Can you bring forward people with the ability, responsibility, and willingness to address ordinary people’s needs? Can you offer candidates whom voters can look at and say, “This person deserves a chance”?

Winning back votes requires acknowledging shortcomings in governance, addressing concrete everyday difficulties, and offering proposals that can withstand scrutiny. It also requires candidates whom voters are willing to give a chance.

Four years from now, Democrats must present their governing results, and Republicans must show how they have changed. What matters is whether the people of Texas can see and feel an improvement in their lives.

Four years also leave time to reflect, change, and rebuild trust.

Texas still has people of talent—
A comeback may yet be possible.

《德州失守：共和党惊魂未定，卷土重来未可知》

二战初期，德军的闪电战以迅猛攻势震动欧洲。这次德州州长选举揭晓时，共和党长期经营的政治堡垒，也遭遇了一场骤然显形的冲击。军事上的闪电战可以预先部署，政治上的震动，却往往积累多年，直到开票之夜，才显露出全部力量。

在我看来，民主党或许预见过竞争接近，甚至看见过获胜的可能。真正令他们始料未及的，很可能是在共和党长期占据优势的德州，竟能赢得如此干脆利落。

民主党的竞选抓住了机会，共和党多年的执政表现，也为对手留下了机会。

选票揭晓只需要一个夜晚，选民走到决定换人的那一步，可能已经等了很多年。

共和党真正需要回答的是：为什么一个经营了三十多年的州长席位，最终没能留住足够多的选民？这些年积累的组织、资源、经验，为什么没能变成让人愿意继续支持的理由？

执政时间越长，越应当拿出解决问题的本领。倘若积累下来的是机构的傲慢、办事的推诿，以及对普通人困境的迟钝，那么所谓深厚的执政基础，也可能逐渐变成压在选民心上的沉重负担。

老百姓没有义务替一个政党维护它的执政纪录，更没有义务牺牲自己的生活，为它保住政治颜面。

在我看来，这次投票传递出的一个重要信号，就是一些选民已经不愿意继续等了。他们要换一个人，看看日子能不能好过一些。

长期支持，并不意味着永远支持。一个人可以认同某个政党的理念，同时对这个政党交出的治理成绩失去耐心。当生活中的困难迟迟得不到回应，过去的认同就会受到现实的追问：我支持了你这么多年，你究竟为我的生活解决了什么？

如果答案始终是口号，选民就可能用选票结束这场等待。

继续在同一套执政体系里换一张面孔，未必足以重建信任。在一些失望的选民眼中，那仍然是同一口锅、同一种汤，端上桌时换了一个名字。

所以，他们索性连汤带锅一起换。

这句话背后，是一个再朴素不过的愿望：让我们试试另一个人，看看她能不能端出一锅更好的生活。

民主党得到的这次机会，也因此有着清楚的分量。选民既然能够让长期执政的共和党交出州长席位，同样能够在四年之后，要求民主党交还权力。

新州长从胜选之日起，就必须准备接受这种检验。竞选时说过的话，要落实为行动；答应解决的问题，要拿出进展；面对普通人的困难，要让人找到回应、看到结果。

前任留下了什么问题，应当交代清楚。自己准备怎样解决，更要交代清楚。把责任全部推给前任，无法替选民支付账单，也无法让他们的日子自动好起来。

共和党同样没有四年可以虚度。

借杜牧《题乌江亭》改写四句，送给今天面对败局的德州共和党：

胜败兵家事不期，包羞忍耻是男儿。
德州子弟多才俊，卷土重来未可知。

“未可知”，留下的是重新争取的可能。四年时间，可以用来反省、改变、重建信任，也可能在不甘与困惑中白白流走。

如果败选之后，你们心里只剩下一个反复盘旋的问号——为什么？为什么？为什么？那么就请把这个问号带回自己的执政记录里：

哪些承诺没有兑现？哪些问题迟迟没有解决？哪些选民的期待没有得到回应？

德州不缺人才。共和党需要回答的是：你们能否让有能力、肯担当、愿意回应民生的人走到前面，让选民看见值得重新托付的希望？

赢回选票，需要正视执政中的不足，回应具体的民生困难，提出经得起追问的办法，还要拿出让选民愿意说“这个人值得试一试”的候选人。

四年之后，民主党要交出治理的成绩，共和党也要交出改变的证明。归根到底，要让德州人民看见，自己的日子究竟好在了哪里。

四年，也留给了人们反省、改变和重建信任的时间。
