Polybius - The Histories - Robin Waterfield - Oxford Press - Review - 3 of 3

"... the constitution so framed by Lycurgus preserved independence in Sparta longer than anywhere else in recorded history."

"The best analogy for the Athenian democracy is a ship without a captain."

"And in due course of time, once democracy turns to violating and breaking the law, mob rule arises and completes the series."

The Roman Constitution

Polybius devotes Book 6 of Histories to explaining the Roman Constitution, and how it is superior to all others for the mission he is describing, creating a global empire. This focus on the form and function of government separates him from other ancient historians, where he delves deeply into political science with such impressive and logical arguments that he inspired leaders 2,000 years after he wrote. John Adams and other Founding Fathers in their formation of the Constitution of the United States relied extensively on the concepts of “mixed government” that Polybius so deftly explains in this book.
Polybius never cites Plato or Aristotle on the topics of forms of governments or constitutions, but he certainly uses the same terminology and agrees with their findings. Since Polybius enjoys the benefits of formal Greek education, and both of the two great philosophers taught and wrote two centuries before he wrote The Histories, perhaps these ideas were generally well-known and accepted among the intelligentsia. But compared to Plato’s discussions of these ideas in The Republic and Laws, and Aristotle’s treatment in Politics and Nichomachean Ethics, Polybius provides fuller explanations with expansive detail. He begins Book Six by explaining the basis for these observations on forms of governments, “In the Greek world, there are states that have grown and then experienced utter collapse, over and over again.” He is writing from the perspective of the lessons learned from about 1,000 independent Greek city-states with a known history going back 500-600 years. Following a common practice in antiquity of not citing his sources, in 6.3 he explains the distinctions between forms of governments made clear by quoting the ideas of Plato and Aristotle:

"Most of those who want to educate and instruct us in such matters say that there are three kinds of political system, which they call kingship, aristocracy and democracy. But I think it would be perfectly reasonable to ask these people whether they mean that these are the only constitutions or the best ones. …After all, there can be no doubt that the best form of government to be the one that combines all three of these constitutions…. We have actual experience of such a system in the Spartan constitution, which Lycurgus founded along these lines."

Referring here to the excellence of the Spartan constitution, this is a familiar concept to readers of The Republic where Plato never makes the comparison to his theoretical, ideal form of government, but to those who are familiar with Spartan government, it sounds very familiar. In Aristotle’s studies of 158 constitutions, he explicitly states that the three best were those of Crete, Carthage, and Sparta. Polybius then goes on to introduce another concept familiar from the famous philosophers, the evolution or decay of each form of government to first, a degraded version, and then to one of the other three primary forms – kingship, aristocracy, and democracy. Readers of Plato and Aristotle will find the following passage especially familiar.

"Our position, then, should be that there are six kinds of constitution – the three commonly recognized ones I have just mentioned, and three more which are congenital with them: tyranny, oligarchy, and ochlocracy or mob-rule. … Kingship changes into its congenital vice – that is, into tyranny – and then it is the turn of aristocracy, after the dissolution of tyranny. Aristocracy necessarily degenerates into oligarchy, and when the general populace gets impassioned enough to seek redress for the crimes committed by their leaders, democracy is born. And in due course of time, once democracy turns to violating and breaking the law, mob rule arises and completes the series."

Plato in The Republic, which his most renowned exploration of the theoretical perfect government run by philosopher kings, in Book VIII at 544.b, discusses four forms of constitutions in a way that is similar to Polybius’ analysis here.

"First, there’s the constitution praised by most people, namely, the Cretan or Laconian (Spartan, “honor loving”). The second, which is also second in the praise it receives, is called oligarchy and is filled with a host of evils. The next in order, and antagonistic to it, is democracy. And finally there is genuine tyranny, surpassing all of them, the fourth and last of the diseased cities."

Aristotle’s Nichomachean Ethics at Book VIII.x covers concepts that Polybius may have been referring to.

"There are three kinds of (political) constitution, and an equal number of perversions or corruptions of them. The constitutions are monarchy, aristocracy and thirdly the kind that is based on a property qualification, which it seems natural to call a timocracy, although most people usually called it a polity. Of these the best is monarchy and the worst is timocracy. The perversion of monarchy is tyranny. … The tyrant regards his own interest, but the king regards that of his subjects. … From aristocracy the change is into timocracy… Thus it is a few bad men, instead of the best, who hold power. From timocracy the change is into democracy… The least bad (of the three perversions) is democracy, because it departs little from polity."

In Aristotle’s terms, a polity was a middle-class democracy where the lowest income group had no power. In Aristotle’s Politics at 1265b he criticizes Plato’s Laws by saying “Socrates does not tell us how the rulers differ from the subjects.” Aristotle continues his criticism and then describes the type of government that combines the three natural forms in the Spartan Constitution.

"The whole system of government tends to be neither democracy nor oligarchy, but something in a mean between them, which is usually called a polity, and is composed of the heavy-armed soldiers. … Some, indeed, say that the best constitution is a combination of all existing forms, and they praise the Lacedaimonians because it is made up of oligarchy, monarchy, and democracy, the king forming the monarchy, and the council of elders the oligarchy, while the democratic element is represented by the Ephors; for the Ephors are selected from the people.
Polybius provides deep and colorful detail in explaining exactly how the common weakness of human nature leads to the inevitable degradation of governments within society in 6.7-9.

"In the olden days, once a man had been chosen as king and had gained this position of authority, he retained it for life. … once the kings had made things as secure as they could and ensured more than an adequate supply of food, the fact that there was so much of everything tempted them to begin to indulge their appetites. … This behavior aroused people’s resentment and disgust … so kingship gave way to tyranny … conspiracies began to be formed against the tyrants … among the most noble, high-minded, and courageous men, because they are the ones who find it hardest to bear insolence from those set over them.
For the reasons I have already mentioned, the common people lent their support to these new champions of theirs and the actions against their leaders, and so kingship and tyranny were wholly obliterated, and a new era of aristocracy began.
But then the sons in their turn inherited this position of authority from their fathers. … Before long, however, it was their turn to arouse those same feelings of resentment and disgust … leading to the same result: they met with just as catastrophic an end as the tyrants."

This story of the natural evolution of constitutions that occurs with an impetus all its own continues, always explained by Polybius as the expected outcome of human nature. In each stage of this evolution, the tipping point is when the ruler goes from acting lawfully for the good of the people to acting selfishly and unlawfully for their own greedy benefit. After kingship devolves to tyranny, which is replaced by aristocracy which devolves to oligarchy, Polybius makes the next step seem only logical, natural to human beings everywhere. Because they remember and fear tyranny and oligarchy, the third form of government follows.

The only remaining untried alternative was for them to rely on themselves. So that was the system they resorted to: they changed the constitution from oligarchy to democracy, and assumed administrative duties themselves.
But by the time a new crop of young men had been born and democracy was in its third generation, the principles of freedom and equality were too familiar to seem important, and some people began to want to get ahead of everyone else. It was especially the rich who succumbed to this temptation and longed for power. … Once this inane hunger for glory had made the common people greedy for such largesse and willing to accept it, democracy in its turn was overthrown, and replaced by violence and government by main force.
When they found someone to champion their cause – a man of vision and daring, who had been excluded from political office by his poverty – they instituted government by force: they banded together and set about murdering, banishing, and redistributing land, until they were reduced to a bestial state and once more gained a monarchic master.
This is the cycle of constitutions, the natural way in which systems of government develop, metamorphose, and start all over again."

Polybius describes the best constitution, as devised by the legendary Spartan Lycurgus, the Law Giver. In explaining how the three natural good forms of government contain the elements of their own decay, he uses the analogy “Just as rust is the corruption in iron, woodworm and grubs are the corruption inherent in timbers” to show that even unaffected by outside forces, political systems contain their own destruction. At 6.10, Polybius describes exactly how Lycurgus solved this intractable problem.

"Lycurgus … bundled together all the merits and distinctive characteristics of the best systems of government, in order to prevent any of them growing beyond the point where it would degenerate into its congenital vice. … Kings were prevented from becoming overbearing by fear of the citizen body, who were assigned a fair share of government… common citizens, in their turn, were deterred from disrespecting the kings by fear of the elders, all of whom were bound to cleave constantly to justice, because the criterion for selection for the Council of Elders was virtue. … And the upshot was that the constitution so framed by Lycurgus preserved independence in Sparta longer than anywhere else in recorded history."

Having earlier declared the reason of Lycurgus to be “superhuman”, Polybius explains that the Romans created a constitution that achieved the same result, but in contrast “this was not at all the outcome of reason, but of many struggles and trials.”

"On every occasion, they drew on the knowledge that they had gained from their setbacks to make the best choices, and this enabled them to achieve the same result as Lycurgus, and to make theirs the best system of government in the world today…."

At 6.11, Polybius describes the Roman Constitution in its prime as the ideal, a mixed form of government which was favorably comparable to that devised by Lycurgus in ancient times for Sparta.

"There were three fundamental building blocks of the Roman constitution – that is, all three of the systems I mentioned above. Each of them was used so equitably and appropriately in the ordering and arrangement of everything that even native Romans were hard put to say for sure whether their constitution was aristocratic, democratic or monarchic. That is not surprising … depending on whether one focused attention on the powers of the Senate, the powers of the common people, or the powers of the consuls."

Polybius describes the roles and powers of each of the three parts of the government in the Roman Republic at 6.12-14: kingship, aristocracy and democracy.

"6.12 - While the consuls are resident in Rome – they are responsible for all matters of public concern, since all other officers, except the tribunes of the people, are subordinate to them … They also draw up the agenda of issues requiring the Senate’s prompt attention. … As for preparation for war … the power they have is almost unlimited … on this aspect of the constitution, one might reasonably conclude it was pure monarchy or kingship.
6.13 – The Senate’s most important role is that it controls the treasury … all crimes … fall under the jurisdiction of the Senate … Outside Italy, it is the Senate’s business to send missions to arbitrate disputes, offer advice, make demands, accept submissions and declare war; likewise, when missions arrive in Rome from overseas, it is entirely the Senate’s job.... a visitor to Rome who arrived when the consuls were away would think the Constitution was thoroughly aristocratic.
6.14 – But the people do have a part to play, and a very important one at that, because they control rewards and punishments. There is no other provision within the constitution for these functions, but without them human life itself has no coherence, let alone governments and constitutions. … all this means that it would be plausible to suggest that the people’s role is paramount, and that the constitution is a democracy."

In 6.43, Polybius begins comparing the Roman Constitution to others with short histories of the most notable ancient city-states. Thebes didn’t owe its brief dominance over Greece after its defeat of Sparta at Leuctra in 371 to its constitution, rather he declares that “Thebes’ growth, prime, and collapse coincided exactly with the lives of Epaminondas and Pelopidas, and so we should regard the cause of Theban ascendancy at the time to be these men, not the constitution.”
In this historian’s judgement, Athens was like Thebes in that both of their “constitutions did not follow the normal course of development and did not remain long in their primes.” Polybius states that Athens peaked under Themistocles, the great leader who convinced the people to put their faith in a powerful navy of triremes and led their triumph over Xerxes and the invading Persians at Salamis. Polybius’ disdain for direct democracy is apparent in his description of Athens history.

"The best analogy for the Athenian democracy is a ship without a captain. On such a ship, the crew do their duty outstandingly well as long as fear of the open sea or the threat of a storm induces them to cooperate with one another and obey the helmsman. But when there is no cause for alarm, they start to ignore their superiors and to fall out with one another. … More than once, a display of exemplary virtue from both the people and their leaders has enabled it to survive an appalling crisis, but then is has come to grief for no good reason at all, at a time of untroubled calm."

He then turns to and summarily dismisses the theoretical ideal system described by Plato, even though “it too is highly acclaimed in philosophical circles.” Such a comparison is unreasonable “until it proves it can act in the real world.”
Until then, discussing it and comparing it with Spartan, Roman and Carthaginian systems would be no different than bringing forward a statue for comparison with real, live human beings.
At 6.56, Polybius presents an opinion which is certainly surprising to modern readers. Indeed, it seems more like an irreverent explanation for the invention of religion than something that was the key pillar of Roman society and governance, indeed, vital to the behavior of the citizens.

"But the respect in which, in my opinion, the Roman constitution is most markedly superior is in its view of the gods. It seems to me that superstition, which we criticize in other people, is precisely what gives the Roman state its cohesion. … In a state of enlightened citizens, there would presumably be no need for such a course. But since the common people everywhere are fickle – since they are driven by lawless impulses, blind anger, and violent passion – the only option is to use mysterious terrors and all this elaborate drama to restrain them."

The Histories by Polybius, trans. Robin Waterfield (Oxford University Press, 2010)

text:
An important 2025 publication investigating how Öcalan’s democratic confederalism opposes only one state, the Kurdish one, by socially engineering and removing Kurdish social and political structures that act against assimilation. This is proven using his own writings and notes. In his original Turkish he calls Turkey’s borders legitimate and says the Turkish flag can fly over his grave. He told Kurdish MPs that asking the state for Kurdish education “is a mistake”. He promised that his model removes the “danger” of Kurdish becoming an official language, and eases the assimilation process of Kurds in the countries they live in. He said he built the KCK during talks with Turkish intelligence chief Emre Taner. He also called the Kurdish National Congress the body that would “determine the Misak-ı Milli”, the 1920 pact that claimed Mosul, Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah for Turkey.

It draws on Öcalan’s post-2000 Turkish texts, including the KCK Social Pact, Democratic Confederalism, Problems of Democratization in Turkey, Defending a People and his İmralı notes from 2013 and 2014, and prints the originals in the footnotes. Democratic confederalism is presented as an alternative to the nation-state, yet it leaves all occupying forces that rule Kurdistan untouched and treats them as legitimate.

The translation problem is specific. Democratic Confederalism is under 50 pages, yet its flag statements, “I respect the Turkish flag” and “your flag is mine”, appear only in the Turkish edition. The English version uses the word “assimilation” five times, always critically. The Turkish original uses it once, and there Öcalan accepts the “natural assimilation” of Kurds, describing them as a “sociological phenomenon” and a “richness” for the Turkish nation. Most Western scholarship on Öcalan, including Jongerden, Akkaya, Gunes, Dirik and Graeber, rests on these selective translations. Kamran Matin and Michiel Leezenberg are among the few critical exceptions.

The story that Öcalan converted from Kurdish statehood to post-nationalism under Murray Bookchin’s influence does not hold, because there was no statehood project to give up. In 1977 he said the PKK “did not emerge exclusively for only one nationality”. In 2004 he admitted that “Independent Kurdistan” was a slogan and that the PKK never thought the question of a state through. In a 1988 interview with Mehmet Ali Birand he spoke of coexistence and “internal independence”. At a 1993 press conference in Lebanon with Jalal Talabani he said Kurds and Turks could not separate, comparing them to “a fingernail and the surrounding flesh”, and offered to disarm in return for legal guarantees. In 1996 interviews with Nabil al-Mulham he denied that Western Kurdistan exists, saying “it is correct to say Syrian Kurds”, and proposed federalism inside Turkey, Iran and Iraq on the German, Spanish and Swiss models. The real shift after his capture was from supporting Kurdish federalism to opposing it. He also claims that without his “insight” in prison he “would have been a primitive nationalist aspiring for the nation-state”, which contradicts his own account.

Behind this sits a Kemalist view of Kurds that runs through his writing. In 2004 he wrote that Kurds “were not even aware of the extent of their betrayal” and that “neither human nor animal laws applied to them. They almost played the role of a third kind of being.” He spoke of the “old Kurdish trouble”. He told cadres that Kurds who believe they are free “must first be enslaved, and then these slaves must be freed”. He said his personality and principles “are more like those of a prophet”. In 1992 he told Birand that Kurdish power must stay under a single leadership: “I hold all these strings in my hand.” The PKK’s working language remained Turkish, and in 47 years it has produced no serious plan to revive Kurdish. Meanwhile the war emptied 2,685 Kurdish villages and hamlets by 1996, according to Human Rights Watch. A Van teachers’ union estimate puts the share of Kurds speaking Kurdish at 90% in the 1920s and around 7 to 8% today, with voluntary assimilation peaking during the Turkeyification years under the AKP.

In Öcalan’s own words, democratic confederalism leaves the Turkish state untouched. “The institutions and existing borders of the Republic of Turkey are considered legitimate. Issues such as whether it should be unitary, federal or confederal are not discussed, and it is not even recommended to bring them up.” “Yes to state reform, no to opposition to the state.” A completely stateless democracy is “adventurism”. “I am not saying that Turkey should become confederal. I am saying that it should be a democratic republic without losing its unitary structure.” Kurds should build their confederalism “without touching the borders”. The 2005 KCK Social Pact declares that three legal systems will now apply in Kurdistan: EU law, unitary state law and democratic confederal law. Öcalan describes the KCK as a civil society body that belongs “within the totality of the people or nation of Turkey”. He calls it parallel and complementary to the unitary state, and says its flexible idea of the nation will block “the problem-causing potential of federalist solutions”. He calls the nation-state fascist and compares it to Hitler and Mussolini, yet he declares the Turkish nation-state legitimate by calling it a republic. France, the first modern nation-state, was also a republic. Real multinational states such as Switzerland and Belgium rest on decentralisation and constitutional multilingualism, the very things Öcalan rules out.

On where the KCK came from, the İmralı notes are blunt. “We want to be a fundamental democratic element of this state… I built the KCK on this condition during Emre’s time.” Emre Taner was then head of Turkish intelligence (MİT). Öcalan describes five exhausting years of negotiations with Taner and a 156-page roadmap that was rejected. In his 2009 book he calls for “an intensive dialogue with the state’s security forces” to resolve the KCK’s legal questions. The KCK came out of bargaining with the Turkish state, not out of a Bookchinite change of paradigm.

Then there is the Misak-ı Milli. The last Ottoman parliament adopted it in 1920, and it defined Turkey’s borders as the armistice line of 1918. Mustafa Kemal’s own definition ran from south of İskenderun through the Jarablus bridge between Aleppo and Katma to the Euphrates and down to Deir ez-Zor. It included Mosul, Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah, which means South and West Kurdistan. He wrote to Talat Pasha that “all our provinces where Turkish and Kurdish are spoken will belong to us”. He told parliament that “the line that we will determine with our strength and power will be the border”. Turkey annexed Hatay on the same logic in 1939, and Erdoğan invoked the Pact over Mosul in 2016.

Öcalan presents this pact as a Kurdish-Turkish brotherhood. He writes that its borders were “built on the unity of Kurds and Turks”. He says its break-up after 1925 “is actually the fragmentation of the Kurds” and that “when we mention the Middle East Confederation, it is about reviving this”. He says he does not see it as “an imperial event”. He tells the PKK: “All Kurds will establish a strong alliance with Turkey. The National Pact Commission will discuss this… This alliance has existed since the Hittites.” He describes the KCK as an umbrella for “all Kurds of the Middle East within the framework of Turkey’s national integrity”. He builds a thousand-year history for this alliance, from Manzikert in 1071 to the Treaty of Qasr-e Shirin in 1639, which he calls a betrayal of it. He says he pitched the Mitanni-Hittite alliance to Emre Taner and the Battle of Manzikert to Taner’s successor, Hakan Fidan. He also claims Kemal’s speech of 23 April 1920 described Kurds and Turks respecting each other’s rights. The parliamentary minutes show that Kemal never mentioned Kurds. He spoke of Turks, Circassians and “Islamic elements” and put off all details until “after our existence is saved”.

The plan was put into practice through the Kurdish National Congress. “This Kurdish congress will be the thing that determines the Misak-ı Milli,” Öcalan told a pro-Kurdish delegation. He proposed four conferences. One was in Diyarbakır and open even to Hizbullah and Kemal Burkay. One was in Ankara under the HDP, one in Europe, and one in Erbil, which “should approach it within the framework of the National Pact”, with Kurds from Syria taking part. When Selahattin Demirtaş asked for a message for the Erbil conference, Öcalan told him to explain “the issue of Misak-ı Milli in the right form”. HDP MP Nursel Aydoğan put it plainly: Öcalan “is the main obstacle to the establishment of a Kurdish state”, and every negotiation on İmralı aimed to resolve the Kurdish issue within the framework of the Misak-ı Milli. The whole project fits the AKP’s neo-Ottoman foreign policy.

Öcalan says Jewish lobbies first planned “a proto-Israeli project” in South Kurdistan. Later they “got rid of Saddam” in order to take over the Kurds through Kurdish nationalism. He recasts Sheikh Said’s 1925 revolt as a British-provoked attempt to restore the caliphate, which reverses his earlier view that it was a religious and national uprising against near-genocidal attacks. He calls Iraqi Kurdish self-rule “a bomb” placed at “the very bottom of Turkey’s belly” and the Kurdistan Region “a cheap collaborator state”, likening it to Enkidu. In the Social Pact, self-determination shrinks to villages, neighbourhoods and cities managing their own affairs, and the UN system is dismissed as a failed model built on nation-states.

From 2004 the Kurds stop being a nation in his writing and become a people, and Kurdish becomes “the local language”. By 2011 he questions whether Kurds have even “reached the stage of nationhood”, while Turks remain “the Turkish nation”. He writes that “considering the Kurds as a sociological phenomenon serves the interests of the Turkish nation better” and that “leaving social phenomena to natural assimilation” has been humanity’s basic tendency. His “fraternal unity” comes with a guarantee: “With this approach, there is no danger of Kurdish becoming the official language, followed by a federation.” He dismisses insistence on nation and language as “dogmatic values” and writes that he was “born into a society that has not really progressed beyond Neolithic culture”. He calls this policy Türkiyeleşme (Turkeyification) and presents it as Atatürk’s own inclusive idea of a “nation of Turkey”. In reality Kemal used “Turkish State” and “Republic of Turkey” interchangeably, spoke of the “Turkish nation”, and called Kurdish identity an “incorrect label” left over from despotic times. Turkeyification is voluntary Turkification.

The İmralı notes from 2013 show where this leads. When pro-Kurdish MPs pressed for state-funded Kurdish education, Öcalan replied: “Asking the state is a mistake. This is not the duty of the state but of society. If you cannot teach your mother tongue to your own child, how can you ask the state?” He said there is “a principle of equality in the constitution”, so such education “cannot be demanded”. He said boycotts only inflame things and that the MPs should open model schools in Diyarbakır instead. A Kurdish school did open there in 2013, and the authorities later sealed it. Elsewhere in the notes he says: “I am not even discussing language education.” When the PKK leadership in Qandil demanded that the new constitution name the existence of the Kurdish people, he refused: “Do not conflate national identity with state citizenship.” The only wording he proposed was “our constitution accepts all historical cultures as the richness of Turkey”. He told MPs “we belong to the state” and borrowed the AKP’s Islamic language of a shared millet. He summed it up: “There is a Turkish nation, and that is a reality… We can call it the nation of Turkey.” Elsewhere he says: “We have no objections to the unitary state, to the republic. Turkish will remain the official language, the flag will of course be there.”

This is the constitution he declared legitimate. Article 66 says that everyone bound to the state by citizenship is a Turk. Article 42 says no language other than Turkish may be taught as a mother tongue. The preamble places sovereignty in the Turkish nation alone, and Article 301 of the penal code makes “insulting Turkishness” a crime. It is the system İsmet İnönü summed up as “our task is to Turkify everyone, no matter what the cost”. Iran’s constitution allows regional languages in the media and the teaching of their literature in schools, which is more than Öcalan asks for. His position also falls short of UN standards on language rights. It is a neoliberal position: a self-declared enemy of “capitalist modernity” leaving the survival of Kurdish to the market.

In 2003 he wrote that forced assimilation should end and “voluntariness should be the basis”, because “the necessities of life take care of one’s own language”. He warned that forcing Kurds to count as Turks damages “Turkish purity” and produces “an ugly hybridisation”. In 2004 he described assimilation before the Republic as “peaceful and culturally enriching”. The results can be measured. A 2023 Kurdish Studies Center survey found that only 30% of Kurds in Turkey are proficient in Kurdish, 30% have intermediate skills and 40% do not use it in daily life. More than half the children of fluent parents know little or no Kurdish, and nearly 60% of respondents report discrimination. Öcalan’s prescription leads to language death from the top down. He says that Kurdish can only be encouraged at primary level, and he treated Turkish as the sole official language.

Öcalan opposes a Kurdish state, not the nation-state. His proposal asks Turkey to tolerate the physical existence of Kurds and to replace forced assimilation with voluntary assimilation, and in return he promises that Kurds will not seek federalism or official status for their language. The result is a “civil society of subjects” under colonial sovereignty.

text:
If you lost someone you love, there is something you can do for them today that most Catholics were never taught. It costs an ordinary morning, and Fr. Dan Reehil, an exorcist, says it is why he is not afraid of his own death.

He explained it in a long interview with Shawn Ryan:

"THERE'S SOMETHING WE HAVE CALLED PLENARY INDULGENCES IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH WHERE IF I DO CERTAIN THINGS AND I UNITE THEM TO JESUS SUCH AS GOING TO MASS, RECEIVING COMMUNION IN A STATE OF GRACE, GOING TO CONFESSION EVERY TEN DAYS AND THEN IF I PRAY A ROSARY IN THE CHURCH, I CAN ASK FOR ONE SOUL TO BE BUSTED OUT OF PURGATORY EVERY DAY."

Nothing exotic. Mass. Communion. Regular confession. A rosary in front of the tabernacle. Things an ordinary Catholic can decide to do this week.

Then he grinned about his own math:

"MY THEORY ON THIS IS IF I'M BUSTING ALL THESE OTHER GUYS OUT, GOD'S GOING TO BE MORE LENIENT TO ME AT THE END OF MY LIFE."

And this is how he pictures his own last day:

"I'M GOING TO LOOK AT THIS BIG ARMY OF SAINTS THAT ARE LIKE, HEY, WELCOME. GOOD JOB. WE'VE BEEN PRAYING FOR YOU."

"SO I HAVE A DIFFERENT VIEW OF DEATH THAN MOST."

November is the month the Church gives to the dead. Think of the names you carry. Your mother. Your grandfather. The friend who went far too young. And the souls nobody prays for anymore, because everyone who knew them is gone too.

One of them could be welcomed home because of your ordinary Tuesday.

The Church sets out the exact conditions for a plenary indulgence, and your parish priest can walk you through them in two minutes. Through November 8 she also attaches one, for the souls only, to a visit to a cemetery with a prayer for the dead there. Ask your priest this week, and start today.

Out loud, ten seconds:

"Lord Jesus, I offer You this day for one soul who has no one left to pray for them. Bring them home to You, and remember me when my own hour comes. Amen."

Then go to Mass this week with a name in mind.

👇 One word if you are offering today for one soul: WELCOME.

For the 100th time, gooning will make you poor, r*ped by Satan and gay.

This is not my opinion. 
The science is clear on this. 

Acute activation of the dopamine system by p*rn is followed by reduced firing of dopaminergic neurons.

When exposed to a supernormal visual sexual stimulus, midbrain dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area fire rapidly in high-frequency “phasic” bursts, flooding the nucleus accumbens with dopamine.

To prevent overexcitation and maintain equilibrium, this massive influx of dopamine stimulates the synthesis and release of dynorphin (an endogenous opioid peptide) in the NAcc.

Dynorphin acts as a local inhibitory feedback signal.

It binds to kappa opioid receptors (KOR) on the presynaptic terminals of VTA dopamine neurons, which directly inhibits and depresses further dopaminergic neuron firing.

“So it’s not weird that these dysregulate me and turn me into a rude ahole? I have ADHD”

Maybe not.

Once again, anything that suddenly drops, depletes, or disrupts baseline dopamine will rapidly lower an ADHD individual’s threshold for frustration, directly triggering severe irritability, mood slumps, and emotional volatility

Biochemically speaking, irritability in individuals with ADHD is not a personality flaw.

It is a direct byproduct of your neurotransmitter dysregulation and altered brain connectivity. 

“I thought that ADHD was just about attention/focus”.
No. 

The exact same biochemical pathways that govern focus also manage our “emotional brakes”.

For example, the ADHD brain is characterized by a baseline deficiency or rapid reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine.

But besides focus and alertness, these also act as chemical stabilizers for frustration. 

When dopamine levels are chronically low or fluctuating wildly, the brain’s threshold for frustration drops significantly for example. 

So minor inconveniences, like a sudden interruption, a delayed task, or sensory overload, cause a rapid chemical crash, triggering an immediate, irritable “fight-or-flight” response.

This is why you can be mislabeled as rude, an a-hole etc while your reactions are not targeting the person you have in front you.

“So it’s just about dopamine?”
I wish it was that simple.

In individuals with ADHD, there is an altered structural and functional connectivity between the PFC and the limbic system.

The prefrontal cortex is the executive command center of the brain, responsible for self-control, logical reasoning, and overriding impulsive reactions. 

So without strong, catecholamine-driven signals from the PFC to dampen down an overactive amygdala, emotions surge rapidly and cool down slowly. 

While ADHD is most famously linked to the prefrontal cortex, abnormalities in the limbic system are also heavily linked to core symptoms like emotional dysregulation, impulsivity, and attention deficits.

Think of the limbic system as our survival software.

-The amygdala scans the environment for danger and processes emotional responses.

-The hippocampus helps store long-term memories so the brain can remember past dangers or safe spaces

-The hypothalamus manages basic needs like hunger, thirst, and body temperature.

So it’s crucial for homeostasis overall, reward and threat detection, memory  and learning.

Now in many individuals with ADHD, the amygdala shows structural differences or atypical connectivity with the rest of the brain. 

This can lead to “bottom-up” emotional hijacking, where feelings like frustration, impatience, or boredom are felt with extreme intensity, driving impulsive actions before the prefrontal cortex can step in to modulate them.

The hippocampus is essential for contextual memory. 

In ADHD, alterations in this area can cause struggles with working memory (forgetting what you were doing mid-task) and “time blindness” (difficulty using past experiences to judge how long a future task will take)

The limbic system is a major pathway for dopamine.

In ADHD brains, a deficit in dopamine signaling makes it difficult for the thalamus to filter out irrelevant sensory data, resulting in chronic distractibility, fatigue, or low motivation.

“How to fix?”

There is no simple way to “fix” the limbic system. 

It is not a single broken part that can be repaired.

It is a network of structures whose activity and connectivity can become dysregulated by chronic stress, trauma, sleep deprivation, inflammation, or other factors. 

Recovery and better regulation are possible because these circuits are plastic, but the process is gradual.

There is a long list of things that can help.
For example:

-Exposure-based therapies and CBT help extinguish exaggerated fear responses by repeatedly pairing threat cues with safety in a controlled way. 

This strengthens prefrontal inhibition over the amygdala and builds new extinction memories.

-Regular physical activity is one of the most reliable ways to support hippocampal neurogenesis.

-Optimizing sleep.
Chronic short or fragmented sleep amplifies amygdala reactivity and weakens prefrontal regulation. 

-Trauma-focused therapies (including EMDR and prolonged exposure) are particularly relevant when past trauma has left the amygdala hyper-reactive and the hippocampus less able to contextualize threats.

-Regular meditation is associated with increased prefrontal and anterior cingulate thickness/activity and reduced amygdala reactivity to emotional stimuli.

“Okay so how do i quit though?”

If you are actually interested in outgrowing your bad habits with things such as alcohol, nicotine, dr*gs, gooning, video games or even social media, realize that the reason most people struggle to change and get rid of their bad habits, isn’t that change has to take years.

The reason most people struggle to change and get rid of their bad habits, isn’t that change has to take years.

It’s because they keep targeting the symptoms instead of the underlying patterns.

Your bad habits live as automatic, stimulus-driven neural circuits inside your brain’s basal ganglia.

This means that pure willpower usually fails once stress exhausts your prefrontal cortex.

Most people who want to change already know what they should do.

They know the habits that are quietly wrecking their body, their work, or their relationships.

They’ve read the books, made the resolutions, sometimes even paid for therapy or coaching.

And they still find themselves, night after night, doing the same thing they said they wouldn’t.

It’s not that they lack information.

It’s that most of their decisions are already made before the conscious mind shows up to vote.

The vast majority of human behavior runs on older, faster systems (dopamine prediction maps, stress chemistry, habit circuits in the striatum, emotional signals from the amygdala etc).

These systems were built to repeat whatever reduced discomfort or delivered reward in the past.

They do not care about the person you want to become next year.

They care about what worked yesterday.

You cannot reliably out-willpower a system that has already loaded the action.

By the time you feel the urge and try to “just be disciplined,” the chemical and circuit conditions that favor the old behavior are already active.

Willpower is a late, expensive intervention. It is useful in short bursts. It is a terrible primary strategy for lasting change.

This is why so many honest, intelligent people keep breaking the promises they make to themselves.

They are trying to change the output while leaving the wiring untouched.

If you want to quit a bad habit (or even addiction) and adopt a new, better one, you can not rely on willpower alone.

Let’s take doomscrolling as an example.

How many times have you picked up your phone just to check one thing, only to mindlessly doomscroll twenty minutes later?

In general, how many times have you told yourself, and you meant it, that you were done with a habit that keeps getting between you and the person you’re trying to become?

You had a plan.

You had a reason.

And you did it anyway.

Then comes the part that actually hurts.

The voice in your head says:

“What’s wrong with me? Why can’t I just do what I know I should do?”

Most people answer that question the same way: “I don’t have enough discipline.”

I want to show you why that’s the wrong diagnosis, and why it matters, because if you misdiagnose the problem, you will keep applying the wrong solution.

Your brain isn’t broken.

It’s learning exactly as designed.

Here’s how that learning works.

The first time something rewards you, your brain doesn’t just record the reward.

It records everything around it: the time of day, the room you were in, who you were with, how you felt beforehand, even the sound a notification makes.

Over time, those signals start working on their own.

You don’t need to taste the food to start wanting it when you smell it.

You don’t need to take a drink to feel the urge when you see the bottle.

You don’t need to open the app to feel a tug when your phone lights up.

The wanting arrives before the decision.

By the time you “choose,” your brain has already been leaning for a while.

That’s not a character flaw.

That’s a learning system doing what learning systems do.

For example, there’s this study led by Gillinder Bedi that took 86 adult smokers and asked them to abstain for 7, 14, or 35 days.

Then they exposed them to smoking-related cues and measured how strongly they craved a cigarette.

You’d expect the person who’d gone 35 days to be doing better than the person who’d gone 7.

Further from the habit, weaker craving, right?

On some measures, it was the opposite.

Cue-triggered craving was higher at 35 days than at 7 days.

Withdrawal symptoms had faded.

The learned pull had not.

The researchers called it the incubation of craving.

So removing a habit does not erase what your brain learned about it.

That’s why someone can go weeks, months, even years, and still get hit by a sudden urge when they walk past a familiar place or feel a familiar feeling.

It doesn’t mean they’ve lost their progress.

It means learning leaves lasting traces.

The good news is that the brain’s ability to change runs both ways.

The same learning process that built the habit can build a new one.

Old associations can be weakened.

New responses can be practiced until they become the default.

But it works best when you stop treating willpower as the only tool and start working with how your brain learns.

“So what do I actually do about this?”

Let me start with an image.

Imagine trying to teach someone to swim while they’re drowning.

The lesson might be excellent.

The instructor might be brilliant.

But the person isn’t in a state to learn.

They’re in survival mode.

That’s a surprisingly good picture of what trying to quit on willpower alone can feel like.

Your prefrontal cortex is the part of your brain that plans, weighs consequences, holds long-term goals in mind, and holds back impulses.

It’s the part that says, “Don’t. You’ll regret this.”

It’s also one of the most easily strained parts of your brain.

Research on stress shows that even moderate uncontrollable stress can impair working memory and self-control.

Poor sleep makes it worse.

Strong cravings make it worse.

And in people dealing with addiction, brain imaging studies have reported reduced prefrontal activity during early recovery (how much varies between people and substances, and researchers are still working it out).

Now think about when you actually relapse into a habit. It’s rarely at 10 a.m. on a calm, well-rested day. It’s at 11 p.m. after a stressful week. It’s when you’re tired, lonely, bored, or overwhelmed, with the cue sitting right in front of you.

The moments you need self-control the most are often the moments it’s weakest.

That’s not a moral failure.

It’s biology and circumstances working together against you.

So the answer isn’t more pressure.

The answer is to make the right choice easier before the hard moment arrives.

Here’s what the research supports:

1. Change the environment, not just your intentions.

Every cue you remove is one fewer battle you have to win.

Delete the app. Move the charger out of your bedroom.

Turn off notifications. Use a blocker. Rearrange the places and routines where the habit lives.

Why does this work?

Because cues are what trigger the learned “wanting.”

If your brain has linked 11 p.m. + bed + phone to a reward, then fighting that urge nightly is a losing strategy.

Changing the setup means the urge shows up less often, and when it does, there’s friction between you and the behavior.

You don’t need to be a more disciplined person. You need fewer decisions to win.

2. Plan the response in advance.

Researchers call it an implementation intention, an “if-then” plan.

Not “I’ll try to scroll less,” but: “If I feel the urge to open Instagram, then I will stand up and drink a glass of water.”

This has good evidence behind it because it pre-wires the replacement behavior. You’re not deciding in the heat of the moment, when your prefrontal cortex is struggling.

You decided earlier, when you were calm, and now you’re just executing.

3. Replace, don’t just remove.

Your brain still wants what the habit was giving you.

Maybe it was stress relief. Maybe stimulation. Maybe connection, or a break, or a feeling of control.

If you only remove the habit and leave a hole, your brain will keep pulling toward the old solution.

So you give it a competing, healthier source of the same thing: a walk instead of a scroll, a call instead of a cigarette, something absorbing instead of something numbing.

4. Treat the state underneath.

That’s your health.
If your baseline dopamine levels for example are cooked, you will be WAY more prone to addictions.
https://t.co/eXCNhiGzzm

5. Expect relapse, plan for it but don’t use it as an excuse.

This one matters more than people realize.

When you stop a habit, your brain doesn’t erase the old association.

It builds a new, competing memory: “in this situation, I do something different.”

That new memory is real, but it’s fragile and context-dependent.

So an old trigger can bring back an old urge even after months of progress.

That’s not failure. That’s what the science predicts.

The people who do best are usually the ones who expect a slip and have a plan for it, instead of treating it as proof they’re hopeless.

“I already know all this.”

Maybe you do.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth: knowing why you scroll doesn’t weaken the cue-reward link that makes you reach for the phone.

Insight isn’t enough.

That link only changes through new learning: repeated practice of a different response, in the situations where the old one used to happen.

That’s the hard part. Not understanding. Doing it consistently, for weeks, when you’re tired, stressed, and the cue is right in front of you.

“I’ve tried before and failed.”

That’s exactly what you’d expect if the approach relied on willpower.

Most people who “fail” at changing a habit have really failed at a strategy: one that took a brain under stress and asked it to out-resist its own learning, over and over.

Changing the strategy is different from trying harder.

“Did you just tell me to use neuroplasticity, environmental changes, identity changes and biohacking in order to quit my bad habits?”

Yes.

Now thankfully if you want to know more, the techniques inside this offer practical, science-backed ways to interrupt these loops and rewire your brain.

Inside of this you will discover:

-The little-known experiment that changed what we know about the brain regions responsible for cravings and states like rumination

-Why drug-related cravings can be much stronger than cravings for survival needs like water and food.

-Why a psychiatrist and neuroscientist with years of experience believes literally EVERY addiction can be solved (it’s not just neuroplasticity) and how to use this knowledge to your advantage.

-Why some people form habits more easily than others, and what determines how easy or difficult it is.

-The experiment showing why asking yourself why you relapse into a bad habit or addiction may not be that useful, and what to do instead.

-The little-known reasons people keep doing things even when they know they hurt themselves and the people around them, and how to bring awareness into the picture to stop the behavior.

-The simple 3-step framework for breaking a bad habit (number 3 is what most people overlook, making it difficult to break the habit no matter how hard they try).

-What animal experiments reveal about a brain region heavily involved in repeated alcohol and opioid use.

-Why substance addiction and repeatedly performing bad habits are more similar than you might think, and the little-known yet highly effective way to become addicted to something that doesn’t involve substances but can happen naturally.

-Why some habits feel so hard to form while others come easily, including the little-known term coined by a neuroscientist that explains why some habits are harder to form than others, and a technique for using easier habits to build harder ones.

-How to finally stop relying on willpower, motivation, and discipline alone (and why these alone often don’t work)

-How a normal survival mechanism gets hijacked and can work against you.

-What to actually do the next time you feel a craving instead of relying on discipline alone so you reduce the chances of relapsing

-The little-known experiment that showed decision fatigue might be real (and how it relates to recovery and how easily you give into cravings)

-Why saying “no” to your cravings many times might make you more likely to say “yes” later on (and what to do instead when you feel a craving)

-Why relapsing isn’t necessarily a failure (and how to use it to your advantage instead).

-How to know if you’re actually addicted to something or not

-Why therapy might be useless/not work that well on its own for many people until they do something else that’s essential for recovering from any type of addiction.

-Why fighting with yourself over breaking a bad habit or addiction is not a good idea (and what approach to take instead)

-Why feeling ashamed of something you repeatedly do might only make things worse (and what to tell yourself instead).

-Why you might be addicted to something without even realizing it (and the simple question to ask yourself to see if you actually are)

-Why discipline alone doesn’t work.

-Why you don’t need to rely on motivation.

-How some people broke a bad habit they’d had for years in just 5–15 days.

-Why the reason you do something or relapse often isn’t what you think it is.

-The little-known driver behind repeated alcohol and opioid use.

-Why you probably misunderstand bad habits, addiction, and their relationship with dopamine.

-The habit you engage in daily that contributed to a 5% increase in emergency department visits for children aged 0 to 5.

-The “slot machine” everyone uses and how it affects your brain.

-Why neuroscientists warn that avoiding a negative feeling can be more dangerous than seeking pleasure.

-Why the 21-day habit rule is a myth and where it comes from (and what science actually tells us about how long habits take to form).

-The real reasons you might keep doing something even when it hurts you and the people around you (it’s not just dopamine or trauma).

-What parents should be very careful about even if they’re not addicted to any type of substance (the habit that might put children at risk)

-Why you’re not broken and there’s nothing wrong with you if you’re addicted to any type of behavior or substance (what’s actually going on in your brain when you reinforce a behavior and the mechanism around it)

-The two opposite states that can result in the same behavior (and how they’re related to you forming a new habit)

-What we actually mean when we’re talking about using neuroplasticity to break bad habits and addictions (it’s not as simple as repeatedly doing something)

-What scientists injected into rats in experiments that reduced excessive drinking and opioid use (and what these findings can teach you about why you reinforce such behaviors).

-The little-known stress-signaling neurotransmitter/brain’s main stress-signaling system that scientists have linked to excessive drinking and drug use

-How one of your brain’s essential survival mechanisms gets hijacked every day.

You’re one decision away from feeling healthier and happier than you have in years.

text:
IS NORWAY GENUINELY CONCERNED ABOUT THE PEOPLE OF AMBAZONIA AND CAMEROON, OR IS IT ACTING AS AN AGENT OF NEO-COLONIALISM AND TRANSNATIONAL REPRESSION?

Is the Government of Norway sincerely concerned about the lives and well-being of the people of Ambazonia and Cameroon? Or is the Norwegian Government acting as an agent of neo-colonialism and transnational repression to silence dissenters and political opponents on behalf of the Cameroonian Government?

If the Norwegian Government truly cares about peace and the lives of Africans, the right approach would be to bring the Government of Cameroon and the Ambazonian Government to the negotiating table and offer to serve as a peace mediator between both sides.

The same goes for the Government of Finland and its interference with the declaration of the restoration of Biafra's independence.

Article 1(2) of the United Nations Charter recognises the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples. Article 1(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) expressly states:

"All peoples have the right of self-determination."

Why are these principles celebrated when Europeans invoke them but treated with suspicion when Africans demand the same rights?

Furthermore, just as concerns have been raised by the Organization of Emerging African States (OEAS), the United States of Biafra Mission in Norway reiterates its concern that Norwegian authorities may have shared information extracted from the electronic devices of H.E. Dr. Cho Ayaba with the Cameroonian authorities, just as Finnish authorities may have done with Nigeria.

Did Norway share information from Dr. Cho Ayaba's electronic devices with the Cameroonian authorities? Did Finland do the same with Nigeria in the case of H.E. Simon Ekpa?

If so, what information was shared, with whom, for what purpose, and under which legal authority?

Is such conduct lawful under Norwegian, Finnish, and European law, particularly where the receiving authorities are accused of persecution, torture, war crimes and other grave human rights violations?

Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Article 8 protects private life and correspondence. Sections 93 and 102 of the Norwegian Constitution provide corresponding protections against torture and unjustified interference with privacy.

The Finnish Constitution, particularly Section 10, protects private life and confidential communications. Articles 4, 7, and 8 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights are also relevant where EU law applies.

If these information transfers occurred, we demand an independent examination of their legality and the risks posed to the individuals concerned.

NOW, TO THE PEOPLE OF AMBAZONIA:

Please remember that you alone can tell your story. An ignorant Norwegian who does not understand your history cannot know your story better than you.

Our attention has been drawn to statements attributed to the legal representative of H.E. Dr. Cho Ayaba, referring to the people of Ambazonia as "separatists."

This is deeply troubling.

How can a people fighting against illegal occupation and annexation be casually labelled separatists without properly examining their history, their sovereignty claims, and the circumstances surrounding the 1961 plebiscite?

The people of Ambazonia maintain that they are fighting for the restoration of their sovereignty, not merely seeking separation from a legitimate political arrangement.

Who exactly are you separating from?

You are fighting for your own sovereign homeland, Ambazonia. This is about the history, identity, dignity, and future of the people of Ambazonia.

Even Norway supported the United Nations process concerning the future of British Southern Cameroons. That historical record deserves serious examination rather than being reduced to the convenient label of "separatism."

As far back as 21 April 1961, Norway voted in favour of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 1608 (XV), recognising the distinct political status of British Southern Cameroons and endorsing its right to determine its political future through a UN-supervised plebiscite. Ironically, the Republic of Cameroon itself voted against that resolution.

The question today is whether Norway has adequately considered that historical and legal record when addressing the claims of the people of Ambazonia to self-determination.

Please learn from the mistakes made in the Finland–Nigeria proceedings against H.E. Simon Ekpa.

He was initially sentenced to six years' imprisonment, and the Finnish Court of Appeal subsequently reduced the sentence to four years while upholding the terrorism-related convictions.

We strongly challenge the legal reasoning behind that outcome and maintain that the right of the Biafran people to self-determination, and the lawful self-defence of civilians against extermination, must be properly considered.

This judgment must be challenged, overturned, and quashed in its entirety. The name and reputation of our Prime Minister, H.E. Simon Ekpa, must be fully cleared and vindicated. We categorically reject any attempt to associate him or his legitimate political struggle for Biafran self-determination with terrorism. Our Prime Minister is not a terrorist, and the pursuit of freedom, self-determination, and the lawful defence of our people against persecution and extermination must never be criminalised. We will continue to pursue every available legal avenue until justice is served, his conviction is overturned, and his name is cleared.

If your lawyer does not understand your history, does not accurately present the nature of your struggle, or fails to challenge the prosecution's interpretation of the facts and applicable law, you have every right to question whether that lawyer is properly representing your interests.

And if the lawyer cannot adequately defend your case, seek alternative legal representation. It is that simple.

While we are in the process of securing permission to visit H.E. Dr. Cho Ayaba, we have also written to his lawyer, offering whatever assistance we can provide, including relevant legal research, documentation, and international human rights expertise.

We want to ensure that the historical and legal arguments are properly examined before the Norwegian courts.

WE ALSO CONTINUE TO QUESTION WHETHER NORWAY HAS JURISDICTION OVER THE CAMEROON–AMBAZONIA WAR.

Under Sections 4–6 of the Norwegian Penal Code, the application of Norwegian criminal law to acts committed abroad depends on the applicable jurisdictional requirements.

The Norwegian authorities must explain precisely which acts they allege occurred in Norway, which acts allegedly occurred in Cameroon, and the legal basis upon which Norwegian courts claim jurisdiction over each charge.

The mere fact that an African political leader resides in Europe does not automatically make him criminally responsible for everything that happens during a war in Africa.

Political leadership is not, by itself, proof of individual criminal guilt.

LET ME END WITH SOME FOOD FOR THOUGHT.

Have Ukrainian soldiers committed, or been accused of committing, crimes associated with the Russia–Ukraine war?

YES.

Does that automatically make the current President of Ukraine criminally responsible for every crime committed by individual Ukrainian soldiers?

NO.

Individual criminal responsibility must be established through evidence and the applicable legal principles. Political leadership alone is not enough.

Why should the same principle not apply to the leaders of Ambazonia and Biafra?

Why is the Ukrainian struggle discussed in terms of sovereignty, territorial integrity, and self-defence, while African struggles for self-determination are so often dismissed as separatism and terrorism?

In addition to all the legal jargon, the Norwegian authorities must apply common sense.

Article 14(2) of the ICCPR and Article 6(2) of the ECHR guarantee the presumption of innocence. The European Court of Human Rights has also emphasised the need for relevant and sufficient reasons for prolonged pretrial detention, including in Buzadji v. Republic of Moldova [GC], Application No. 23755/07 (2016).

The Norwegian authorities must answer the questions surrounding Dr. Cho Ayaba's prolonged detention, the evidence against him, and the jurisdiction being asserted.

text:
The character I feel most sorry for in the Harry Potter universe is Neville Longbottom. Unlike Harry, who lost his parents at a young age, Neville had to grow up knowing that both his parents were still alive but could no longer recognise him. Frank and Alice Longbottom were respected Aurors and members of the original Order of the Phoenix before Bellatrix Lestrange and other Death Eaters tortured them into permanent mental incapacity using the Cruciatus Curse. They refused to reveal information about Voldemort, but Neville was left to live with the consequences of their sacrifice.

One of the most heartbreaking moments in Order of the Phoenix happens at St Mungo's Hospital. When Neville's mother, Alice, approaches him and offers him an empty Drooble's Best Blowing Gum wrapper, he quietly accepts it and thanks her. His grandmother tells him to throw it away, but Harry notices Neville secretly putting it in his pocket. That small moment reveals how much he treasures even the smallest gesture from a mother who no longer remembers who he is. The film adaptation does not include this hospital visit, making it one of the important book moments many film-only fans miss.

What makes Neville's story even more sad is how he eventually transforms his pain into courage. He initially struggles with confidence, is constantly underestimated and even doubts his own abilities. However, he becomes an active member of Dumbledore's Army, helps lead the resistance at Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows and ultimately destroys Nagini with the Sword of Gryffindor. He never gets the chance to have the childhood or family life he deserved, but he becomes exactly the kind of brave wizard his parents would have been proud of.

text:
THANOS DIDN’T WANT TO RULE THE UNIVERSE. HE WANTED TO SAVE IT, AND THAT WAS WHAT MADE HIM DANGEROUS

Most people look at Thanos and see a monster who wanted to destroy half of all life in the universe. But if you pay attention to his story, you begin to understand something interesting. Thanos never believed he was the villain. In his own mind, he was the only person brave enough to do what nobody else was willing to do.

His plan started long before he ever got his hands on the Infinity Stones.

Thanos came from Titan, a planet that was slowly dying because its population had grown beyond what its resources could support. He watched his home fall apart and believed he knew the solution. His proposal was simple: randomly eliminate half the population so the remaining half could survive with enough resources.

But his people rejected the idea. They considered him insane and refused to listen.

Eventually, Titan collapsed.

That experience changed Thanos forever. Instead of accepting that his idea had failed, he became convinced that he had been right all along. He believed the universe was heading toward the same disaster, and he decided that no other civilization should suffer the fate of his home planet.

So he began conquering worlds.

Wherever he went, he offered the same solution. Half of the population would die, and the other half would be allowed to live. He believed his actions would create balance, even if the people he saved hated him for it.

But Thanos had one major problem. His army could only conquer so many planets, and his method required enormous resources and time. He needed something much more powerful.

That was where the Infinity Stones came in.

Thanos discovered that six stones existed across the universe, each possessing control over a different aspect of reality.

The Space Stone controlled space. The Mind Stone controlled minds. The Reality Stone could change reality itself. The Power Stone provided unimaginable power. The Time Stone controlled time, while the Soul Stone held power over life and souls.

Together, they could make someone powerful enough to reshape the entire universe.

With all six stones, Thanos wouldn’t need armies to conquer planets anymore. He wouldn’t need to travel from one world to another, killing people one civilization at a time

He could simply snap his fingers

And that was exactly what he planned to do.m

However, getting all six stones wasn’t going to be easy. They were scattered across different parts of the universe, and some of the most powerful beings were protecting them

Thanos first sent Loki to Earth to retrieve the Tesseract, which contained the Space Stone. When Loki failed, Thanos understood that he would have to take matters into his own hands

He attacked the Asgardian ship, defeated the Hulk, killed Loki, and took the Space Stone

From that moment, the Avengers became one of the biggest obstacles standing between him and his mission

But there was something about Thanos that made his plan even darker. He wasn’t simply collecting stones because he wanted power. He genuinely believed the universe would be better after he completed his mission

And he was willing to sacrifice absolutely anything to make it happen

The biggest example was Gamora

She was the daughter he raised, the person he claimed to love, and perhaps the only person he had a genuine emotional connection with. Yet when he discovered that obtaining the Soul Stone required sacrificing someone he loved, he threw her off the cliff

He sacrificed his own daughter for the mission

That moment showed just how far Thanos was willing to go. Even love couldn’t stand in the way of what he believed was his destiny

Eventually, Thanos collected all six Infinity Stones and completed his plan in Wakanda. He snapped his fingers, and half of all life across the universe disappeared

Then he went somewhere quiet, watched the sunset, and smiled

text:
I am already familiar with the Quran and its history, and I choose the other table.

Start here.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

text:
Iran-US/Israel war, 7 November

Iranian side

- Hormuz position: Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said Iran's armed forces control the strait and that it "will remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran's conditions". He said forces are stronger, more experienced and better motivated than at the start of the war in late February, and noted that pre-war traffic was about 130 ships a day carrying about 20% of global oil.

- A senior security official cited by Press TV warned that any new aggression will bring an "immediate, unlimited, and devastating" response, with no geographic, temporal or target limits. States that help the US would become legitimate targets. Akraminia added that American bases and interests across West Asia are within range and that forces will act on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's order.

- The IRGC and Navy say tankers and a tugboat caught fire or hit mines on unauthorised southern and eastern routes after ignoring warnings or disabling navigation systems. They also claim to have seized LUCAS drones and downed an MQ-9, described as the 56th.

- The seven conditions: 
• A full ceasefire on all fronts including Lebanon
• An end to the blockade
• An oil-sanctions waiver 
• Release of frozen assets (about $12 billion in Iranian reporting)
• Cancellation of post-June sanctions
• No new strikes
• Acceptance of the Iran–Oman route.

FM Araghchi's timetable starts a clock when the US accepts. Days 1–5 are for US implementation, day 6 reopens Hormuz, and day 7 resumes talks, including on nuclear issues. A two-day version has been floated.

- Baghaei and Araghchi describe only message exchanges through Qatar, with Oman and Pakistan involved. Gen Rezaei described the US response as inadequate and said there is no return to the earlier status quo. Qalibaf said Iran is ready both to fight and to negotiate.

- Araghchi spoke to 12 counterparts in 48 hours, including Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey and Pakistan, stressing sovereignty, an end to threats and regional security arrangements without outside powers. Rezaei delivered a letter from the Leader to Putin in Moscow, with reports of interest in military equipment, including S-400s.

US and Western Side

- Trump confirmed "minor strikes" on a newly built anti-aircraft installation near Qeshm: "we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." IRNA and Tasnim reported two missile impacts at Suza and Iran claims it downed a US MQ-9. CENTCOM called the situation "relatively calm" and gave no detail.

- UKMTO has logged several incidents since early November, including waterline explosions, unidentified projectiles and, earlier, limpet mines. Reuters counts at least five vessels with incidents since 1 November. Traffic is a fraction of normal.

- Qatari bridge proposal: 
The US would lift the naval blockade and release part of about $8 billion in frozen assets. 
Iran would allow IAEA inspectors at bombed nuclear sites, drawing on a Cairo understanding, without being required to remove its stockpile.
On day two, Iran would reopen the strait on the Oman-negotiated route. 
Nuclear talks would follow, focused on the stockpile. Iran distrusts the inspectors, fearing the data could aid targeting.

-The prime minister says significant progress has been made and the US remains interested after the midterms. He rejects claims that talks have failed, saying they benefit those who want the war prolonged. The emir spoke with Trump about the proposal.

- Trump claims "a lot of progress" and that Iran wants a deal, but also that the US may have to "destroy" the rest of Iran and that people will "know soon enough". He says it is not really a full war. Gulf allies have reportedly been briefed on possible short, intense strikes if diplomacy fails, & up to 03 carriers have been in or heading to the region.

- CENTCOM offered a reward of up to $20 mn for info on Iran's nuclear. 

- Iran granted exemptions to ships from China, India, Iraq & Qatar.

text:
I would like to offer the beginnings of a possible counterpoint to the argument presented below for the necessity of British entry into the FWW. I stress that these are just some tentative thoughts.

It’s far from obvious that - in the counter-factual where Britain did not interfere with the Schlieffen Plan - Germany would have wanted to pick a fight with Britain once the 1914 European quarrel had subsided and the Kaiser had established his nation as the pre-eminent European power. Keeping Britain out of European conflicts had been a long-standing German diplomatic aim, and the two nations had largely different strategic interests. Germany was and always had been a continental power, albeit one with a few scattered overseas colonies, not a seafaring global empire like Britain. 
In a world where London had already declined to support France, Russia and Belgium against Germany, there would have been no clear reason for the Germans to fight Britain, and to do so would have been difficult and risky for them given the enormous power of the Royal Navy (which in this alternative timeline would have been unaffected by the serious losses incurred during the First World War).
It’s true also that in the early twentieth century, there were warm scientific and academic relations between the two countries, and also considerable family connections, especially in the upper and upper-middle classes. Robert Graves writes in Goodbye To All That of idyllic visits to his relations in the Black Forest during the “long Edwardian summer”. Viscount Haldane, the immensely distinguished intellectual and politician who served as Secretary of State for War 1906-12 and Lord Chancellor 1912-15, was a lover of German culture, a fondness which led to his removal from the Cabinet amid febrile accusations of pro-Germany sympathies.
