text:
FOLLOWING THE SMART MONEY: 5 BUYING SIGNALS THAT DESERVE INVESTORS’ ATTENTION

1. JUBILANT INGREVIA: MULTIPLE MUTUAL FUNDS INCREASE EXPOSURE

One of the strongest institutional accumulation signals this week.

• Franklin MF: +0.56 percentage points to 2.38%
• Axis MF: +0.30 pp to 2.11%
• Kotak MF: +0.12 pp to 3.19%
• HDFC MF: +0.05 pp to 2.16%

Combined increase: approximately 1.03 percentage points.
Multiple fund houses increasing exposure makes this worth investigating.
What are they seeing in the company's growth outlook, margins, capacity utilisation and earnings visibility?
Investor watch: Examine segment growth, margin trajectory, return ratios, cash-flow conversion and valuation.

2. JINDAL STAINLESS: REPEAT PROMOTER BUYING

JSL Overseas purchased shares worth approximately ₹77.9 crore at an average price of ₹683.

What makes this interesting is the recurring pattern:

• 12 September: ₹47.5 crore
• 3 October: ₹62 crore
• Current week: ₹77.9 crore

Repeated purchases are more interesting than a one-off transaction.

The key question is whether this reflects sustained promoter confidence in the business outlook.

Investor watch: Stainless steel demand, capacity utilisation, margins, capital expenditure and valuation.

3. CARTRADE TECH: GLOBAL LONG-ONLY INVESTORS ABSORB A LARGE EXIT

MacRitchie Investments sold approximately ₹470 crore worth of shares at ₹2,583.
Identifiable buyers included:

• Capital Group's Smallcap World Fund: ₹369 crore
• Norges Bank: ₹76 crore

Together, these purchases absorbed approximately 95% of the disclosed sale value.

The stock subsequently gained around 4.5% to ₹2,700 in the price data reviewed.

This is an interesting example of a large shareholder exit being absorbed by identifiable global institutional investors.

Investor watch: Used-car penetration, transaction volumes, growth, profitability and valuation.

4. GO FASHION: PROMOTER BUYING + PLEDGE RELEASE

The promoter group purchased approximately ₹24.8 crore worth of shares.
At the same time:

• Franklin MF sold approximately ₹32.7 crore.
• Promoter-related pledge release of approximately ₹41.7 crore was reported.
• The stock gained around 10.1% in the price data reviewed.

The combination of promoter buying and pledge release is worth monitoring.

However, it does not by itself establish a business turnaround.

Investor watch: Further promoter purchases, pledge levels and operating performance.

5. ALIVUS LIFE SCIENCES: SEVEN BUYERS ABSORB NIRMA'S EXIT

Nirma sold approximately ₹390 crore worth of shares.

The disclosed transaction data showed seven buyers absorbing the entire sale.

The stock subsequently gained around 8.1%.
A diversified buyer base can be constructive, but the identity and investment horizon of the buyers matter.

Investor watch: New shareholder profile, earnings growth, margins and valuation.

OTHER INSTITUTIONAL ACCUMULATION SIGNALS

A few more names deserve attention:

• Tata Steel: ICICI Group increased its holding by approximately 1.04 pp to 3.35%.

• AstraZeneca Pharma India: ICICI Group added approximately 0.79 pp to 2.18%.

• Punjab Chemicals: Ares Diversified increased its holding by approximately 1.46 pp to 4.89%.

• Ardee Industries: Ashish Kacholia crossed the 1% holding threshold, with a reported holding of 1.20%.

• Horizon Industrial Parks: Radhakishan Damani held 1.16%; SBI Group held 1.45%.

These are research leads, not automatic buy signals. The reporting period behind each shareholding change needs to be checked.

PROMOTER SELLING: WHO IS MONETISING?

Insider trading disclosures showed:

• Open-market purchases: approximately ₹206 crore
• Open-market sales: approximately ₹959 crore
• Sell-to-buy ratio: approximately 4.7 times by value

However, three names—Sri Lotus Developers, Shreeji Shipping and Dr Reddy's KMP—accounted for approximately 93% of the reported market-sale value.

Some notable transactions:

• Sri Lotus Developers: Promoter Anand Pandit sold approximately ₹573 crore, representing around 4.88% of equity. Promoter holding remained approximately 65%.

• V2 Retail: Promoters sold approximately ₹258 crore, representing around 4.4% of equity, to six private buyers.

• Gallantt Ispat: Promoter Dinesh Agarwal sold approximately ₹250.5 crore through a block deal, plus around ₹20 crore through market transactions.

• Shreeji Shipping Global: Promoters sold approximately 1.84% of equity, worth around ₹257 crore, through market transactions.

Promoter selling is not automatically negative. The important questions are:
How much equity is being sold?
What is the promoter's residual holding?
Who is absorbing the shares?
Is the selling recurring?

The identity of the buyer matters as much as the identity of the seller.

LARGE SHAREHOLDER EXITS: NOT ALL ABSORPTION IS EQUAL

Two transactions illustrate why investors should look beyond headline deal values.

LENSKART
SVF II Lightbulb exited approximately ₹1,846 crore worth of shares.
Disclosed buyers substantially matched the sale value. Kotak MF bought approximately ₹331 crore, while a significant portion was routed through Societe Generale, Goldman Sachs and BNP desks.

The stock gained around 4%.

Good absorption, but the ultimate end-clients behind the investment-bank desks remain partly undisclosed.

GROWW

Peak XV and YC Holdings sold approximately ₹2,457 crore worth of shares.

Goldman Sachs ODI was identified as a buyer of approximately ₹764 crore—around 31% of the sale.

The remaining ₹1,693 crore was not identifiable from the available disclosed buyer information.

This is a substantial exit, but the ultimate ownership of the balance remains unclear.

Key lesson: A transaction routed through an investment bank does not automatically represent long-term institutional buying.

PLEDGES: ONE LARGE DEVELOPMENT TO MONITOR
Knowledge Realty Trust reported pledge creation by four Blackstone sponsor entities.
• Approximately 60.7 crore units pledged.
• Equivalent to around 13.7% of the trust.
• Reported value: approximately ₹6,719 crore at ₹110.60 per unit.

The lender and purpose were not disclosed in the dataset.

Other developments:

• Swan Corp: approximately ₹280 crore pledge creation.
• Ravindra Energy: approximately ₹57.5 crore pledge creation.
• Go Fashion: approximately ₹41.7 crore pledge release.
• ideaForge: approximately ₹25 crore pledge release.
• Responsive Industries: approximately ₹14.5 crore pledge release.

A pledge does not automatically imply financial distress. But large sponsor-level pledges deserve scrutiny, particularly around the financing purpose, collateral terms and potential invocation risk.

STRATEGIC OWNERSHIP CHANGE: GRT JEWELLERS AND TBZ

GRT Jewellers acquired approximately 74.12% of Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri (TBZ) through an off-market transaction.

• Shares acquired: approximately 4.95 crore
• Transaction price: ₹209 per share
• Consideration: approximately ₹1,034 crore

This is a strategic change in ownership, not an ordinary block deal.

Investors should track the applicable open-offer requirements or exemptions, final offer terms, acquisition rationale and the potential for operating synergies.

 OUR WATCHLIST

Based on this week's ownership and transaction signals:

Accumulation signals to investigate

Jubilant Ingrevia – multi-fund accumulation.
Jindal Stainless – repeat promoter buying.
CarTrade Tech – global long-only absorption.
Go Fashion – promoter buying and pledge release.
Alivus Life Sciences – seven buyers absorb a large exit.

Tata Steel – ICICI Group accumulation.

Punjab Chemicals – significant Ares Diversified addition.

TBZ – strategic ownership change.

Developments requiring caution or monitoring

• Groww – large shareholder exits and buyer opacity.
• V2 Retail, Gallantt Ispat, Sri Lotus Developers and Shreeji Shipping – significant promoter selling.
• Syrma SGS – institutional shareholding reductions.
• Knowledge Realty Trust – sizeable sponsor-level pledge.
• Swan Corp and Ravindra Energy – pledge creation.

text:
AI-LINKED STOCKS REBOUNDED SHARPLY ON FRIDAY. BUT THE DIVERGENCE ACROSS TECHNOLOGY IS WHAT CAUGHT MY ATTENTION.
Friday's market action caught my attention, particularly the strength across several different parts of the AI investment cycle.
But this wasn't a uniform technology rally. Some stocks surged by double digits while others suffered equally sharp declines.
FRIDAY'S BIGGEST S&P 500 MOVERS — NOVEMBER 6, 2026
TOP GAINERS
🔹 Coherent $COHR: +13.58%
🔹 Airbnb $ABNB: +11.67%
🔹 AMD $AMD: +11.04%
🔹 Vistra $VST: +10.55%
🔹 AppLovin $APP: +9.86%
TOP LOSERS
🔻 Axon $AXON: −18.18%
🔻 Microchip $MCHP: −10.02%
🔻 Charter $CHTR: −6.19%
🔻 Insulet $PODD: −6.16%
🔻 Dexcom $DXCM: −5.98%
WHAT CAUGHT MY ATTENTION
1. COHERENT $COHR — AI CONNECTIVITY
Coherent gained 13.58%, highlighting the importance of the infrastructure required to connect increasingly complex AI systems.
As AI clusters scale, optical networking becomes critical to moving data efficiently between processors, servers and data centres.
I'm watching whether that demand translates into stronger margins, higher free cash flow and sustainable returns.
2. AMD $AMD — AI COMPUTE
AMD surged 11.04%.
I remain bullish on AMD's long-term opportunity as hyperscalers seek alternatives and complementary suppliers to Nvidia.
But competitive performance, customer adoption and profitable market share matter more than accelerator demand alone.
The key question is how much of that opportunity AMD can capture without sacrificing margins.
3. VISTRA $VST — POWER FOR AI
Vistra advanced 10.55%.
AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of reliable electricity, making power generation an increasingly important part of the investment cycle.
But rising electricity demand doesn't automatically guarantee higher shareholder returns.
What matters is Vistra's ability to convert demand into profitable contracts, cash generation and attractive returns on invested capital.
4. APPLOVIN $APP — AI MONETISATION
AppLovin gained 9.86%, continuing its strong earnings-related momentum.
Unlike companies spending heavily to build AI infrastructure, AppLovin offers exposure to AI-driven advertising optimisation and monetisation.
I'm bullish on the business, but valuation, competition and the sustainability of its margins remain important considerations.
THE SEMICONDUCTOR DIVERGENCE
AMD gained 11.04%, while Microchip $MCHP declined 10.02%.
That contrast illustrates why I don't treat the semiconductor industry as one investment category.
AI accelerators, optical networking, industrial chips and automotive semiconductors face different demand cycles, competitive pressures and margin structures.
Strong AI spending doesn't automatically translate into stronger earnings across the entire industry.
MY TAKE
I see Friday's performance as evidence of selective buying, not confirmation of a lasting sector rotation.
What interests me is that several of the strongest performers represent different stages of the AI economy.
🔹 $AMD — Compute
🔹 $COHR — Optical connectivity
🔹 $VST — Power generation
🔹 $APP — AI-driven monetisation
I'm still bullish on the long-term AI investment cycle.
But I believe the next phase will increasingly distinguish companies benefiting from AI demand from those actually generating attractive financial returns.
Capital → Power → Compute → Connectivity → Utilisation → Revenue → Free Cash Flow → Returns on Capital.
That's the framework I'm watching.
Friday's winners caught my attention. Whether their earnings, cash flow and valuations justify sustained leadership is what matters next.
Market-move figures are based on the November 6, 2026 WOLF Terminal snapshot and have not been independently verified.

text:
Lifetime deals are not automatically bad for business. Undefined promises and weak cost assumptions are the problem.

Compare contribution, not just revenue. In one illustrative subscription model, a customer pays $50 a month for 10 months. With $8 in monthly variable costs and $75 in acquisition and onboarding costs, the estimated contribution is $345:

($50 − $8) × 10 − $75 = $345

That is a comparison point, not a lifetime price. For the lifetime offer, subtract transaction fees, acquisition and onboarding costs, expected future delivery costs and a support reserve from the upfront payment.

Before selling it, ask:
1. What contribution would an ordinary subscription customer generate?
2. What might this lifetime customer cost to serve?
3. Exactly what does the promise include and exclude?
4. What will the upfront money fund?

Test higher usage, longer customer lifetimes and rising costs. A deal that works only under the most optimistic assumptions needs more work.

$COF I don’t make trades on a whim. I research, gather evidence, create a hypothesis, and then test it with my investment. I have a process, and I recommend developing one for yourself. I try to look at the macro, and then find sensitive nodes within that offer volatility. 

$NKE was a recent example. I called bottom on it, and predicted a rise to $40. 💯🎯🔥 It offered a stable dividend alternative for institutional investors exiting a now less stable AI/tech investiture. 

$COF I am now positioning for the downside. Credit defaults were actually down quite a bit YOY, and their last ER and credit numbers looked excellent, except one little fact. This is the red flag 🚩 that stands out.

From the Q3 2026 results (period ended September 30, 2026):

•  Domestic credit card 30+ day performing delinquency rate was 3.74%.

•  Increased up 35 basis points from the prior quarter (Q2 2026 at ~3.39%).

•  Still down about 15 basis points year-over-year. However, the September monthly metrics (released mid-to-late October) also showed the same 3.74% level, higher than the August reading of ~3.57%.

Credit delinquency precedes credit default. This is incredibly important to understand. The uptick in delinquency with concurrent inflationary costs to include high gas/oil/housing expenses/healthcare/food costs (I’m looking at you beef 🐄) means the market is very sensitive to any shift in % changes. $COF maintains the riskiest sub prime credit card and loan profiles of all US banks/institutions. Their chart reflects a very large institutional sell off began about three months ago. This is in line with other banks; however, they are showing evidence of a slowdown in selling. COF does not.

Long story short: A very, very large drop is coming imo.

NFA and JFF as always.

text: I value the autonomy that open-source projects provide. Compared with proprietary products from major tech companies, open-source solutions allow me to deploy, configure, and audit them independently, giving me greater freedom and transparency. For example, I currently run Hermes Agent on my own VPS. It uses an open-source model and has been granted extensive permissions in a production environment, including access to some of my social media accounts. Given the right conditions, it could even maintain an independent virtual network identity—capable of functioning almost like a genuine digital assistant, with the sole limitation of being unable to receive SMS messages. This level of complete personal control is something that closed-source products can rarely offer.

Alibaba ($BABA) surged 12% last week, defying a 5% Nasdaq 100 (NDAQ) drop. The rally stemmed from Apple’s plan to integrate Alibaba’s Qwen AI model in China.

Money moved from US hardware stocks to discounted Chinese tech giants like Alibaba and Tencent. This shift coincided with a 6% jump in the Hang Seng Tech index on Thursday, supported by a central bank swap facility.

Apple’s developer test of Qwen features began in China on Wednesday. While this offers cheap reach for Alibaba’s AI Labs, the unit posted a RMB 13.9 billion adjusted EBITA loss in the June quarter. Apple aims to catch Huawei on features in its holiday quarter.

Chip supply remains tight. Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance ordered about 6 million Nvidia chips but expect only 1% delivery over the next four months. Tencent also launched its new AI model, sharing similar infrastructure challenges.

Alibaba trades at roughly 13x forward earnings, slightly above its five-year average. The company reports its September quarter results on November 19. Analysts expect normalized earnings to double from fiscal 2026 to 2028. Investors are watching for shrinking AI losses before buying more.

Can Saudi Arabia’s burgeoning biotech hub withstand geopolitical pressures?

Saudi Arabia is building the regulatory framework, partnerships infrastructure and IP landscape needed to support a biotech ecosystem, despite regional political instability. Whether it can produce sustainable biotech companies and a resilient manufacturing base for global production remains an open question, but the future looks bright.

Saudi Arabia is making strides to becoming a major biotech and manufacturing player in the regional and global life sciences landscape, but can it fulfill its hopes?

BioSpace heard experts praise recent regulatory reforms, growing international partnerships and a national focus on technology transfer that has bolstered the trajectory of the Saudi science ecosystem. Even geopolitical issues in the Middle East have not overly negatively affected progress.

The next stage of growth will depend on clinical trial and hospital engagement, intellectual property (IP) generation and training experienced biotech leaders.

“Saudi?Arabia?has?the?financial?resources?to?build?a?pharmaceutical?manufacturing?industry,” said Ravi Kiron, managing director at Biopharma Strategy Advisors. Its next challenge is demonstrating that it can build an internationally competitive biotechnology innovation ecosystem.

Progressive regulatory revisions

One of the most significant developments over the past year has been the Saudi Food and Drug Authority’s (SFDA’s) effort to connect accelerated regulatory pathways across the entire drug development lifecycle, said George Syrmalis, CEO at Bioscience Equity Partners.

At the Drug Information Association Singapore Annual Meeting in September, SFDA CEO Hisham Aljadhey spoke on the integration of the Breakthrough Medicine Program, the New Accelerator Program for Drugs in Rare Diseases (NADR) and the Research and Investigational Drugs (RAID) pathway. Notably, the SFDA CEO highlighted a 20-working-day process for rare-disease drug classification under NADR.

Syrmalis explained this allows clearer and more responsive processes to help companies plan their development programs.

More recently, on October 7, the SFDA and the Saudi National Institute of Health announced five initiatives to advance clinical trials. These measures address practical issues that determine whether a company can run a development program efficiently, Syrmralis said, such as contracting, identifying suitable sites, establishing research capabilities and navigating regulatory review.

Additionally, Singapore’s Health Sciences Authority signed an MOU with the SFDA on September 14. It covers regulatory cooperation, information and expertise exchange, and exploration of pathways for conventional and novel products, including biotechnology.

“For companies developing medicines internationally, that cooperation has the potential to make development and registration more efficient,” Syrmalis said.

Combined, these announcements can be seen as evidence of increasing regulatory sophistication, Syrmalis concluded.

Robust partnerships

The transition from ambitious investment announcements to tangible execution, is noteworthy, Kiron said. He highlighted Saudi CDMO Lifera’s MOUs with Pfizer, Sanofi, MSD and others, alongside expanding clinical research activity.

“Saudi Arabia is beginning to demonstrate that its sovereign capital can attract international pharmaceutical expertise and build capabilities, although the ultimate test will be how successfully these partnerships translate into commercially sustainable operations,” he said.

An encouraging sign for the life science ecosystem is having institutions such as the King Abdullah International Medical Research Center (KAIMRC) deepen ties with international groups, especially in infectious disease research, said Stefan Wagener, CEO at Biorisk Management International. The Ministry of Health’s BioLabs accelerator, launched under the Kingdom’s National Biotechnology Strategy in its Vision 2030 initiative, has also helped Saudi founders develop research strategies and commercial plans.

“For me, these are practical examples of investment linked to scientific expertise and entrepreneurship,” Wagener said. What remains to be seen is how planned collaborations become active research programs, training opportunities and possibly centers of excellence, for example, in biorisk management, he added.

Having the Riyadh Global Medical Biotechnology Summit in September, despite the escalated regional tension, brought together many cross-border collaborators, said Abdulrahman Alshaya, KAIMRC’s chairman of collaboration and partnerships. Forty-six agreements were signed.

“That shows the global interest is real,” he said.

Manufacturing capabilities

The role of manufacturing is also important, to give local scientists responsibility for improving the production process and for developing IP, Wagener said. “To me, that is how localization builds lasting innovation capability,” he added.

Manufacturing is an important foundation for the broader innovation ambition, Syrmalis said, with the development of technical skills, quality systems, supply chains and experience in operating within a regulated industry. Biomanufacturing is one of the four pillars in the National Biotechnology Strategy of Vision 2030.

“Manufacturing is an entry point, not the destination,” said Alshaya, noting the Saudi leadership’s focus is on technology transfer. He referenced how South Korea moved from electronics into global biologics through decades of sustained R&D investment; Singapore paired manufacturing with discovery through biomedical sciences research and development hub Biopolis and its Agency for Science, Technology and Research.

Geopolitical turbulence impact

Despite recent geopolitical instability, Alshaya said he continues to see sustained engagement with international partners. “To me, that shows global partners believe the current [geopolitical] circumstances are temporary and that things will return to track, even stronger,” he said.

In addition, he noted that South Korea, Israel and Taiwan built world-leading industries under persistent security pressure.

Saudi Arabia’s ambitions can withstand the turbulence, Syrmalis said, provided the country continues to execute consistently and companies plan realistically for the operating environment. Still, investment decisions may take longer, visits may be postponed and partnerships may require additional safeguards.

“I remain positive about the opportunity, while recognizing that the pace of progress will depend on both execution and the security environment,’” he said.

Practical continuity and resilience are of ultimate concern in biorisk management, Wagener said. For example, a biotech needs to know whether temperature-sensitive materials can reach its laboratories during transport disruptions. Saudi Arabia’s efforts to reroute trade during recent disruptions offer a concrete example of meaningful resilience, he added. That preparedness should be reflected in research institutions and companies as well.

Success considerations and obstacles

“In five years, I would like to see Saudi-founded biotech companies reaching major M&A or IPO stage, multinational firms running real R&D and tech transfer programs here, regulators and investors moving at the same speed and a trained Saudi biotech workforce leading facilities and research,” Alshaya said.

In that timeframe, Syrmalis said biotech success would mean companies progressing through meaningful clinical milestones, hospitals participating effectively in international trials and Saudi research producing IP that attracts serious commercial interest.

The biggest challenge is building and sustaining the expertise required, such as having an experienced, local team remain through product development, regulatory review and commercial scale-up, Wagener said.

Building experienced management teams, generating and protecting commercially valuable IP and establishing the entrepreneurial culture needed to convert promising science into successful businesses are further concerns, Kiron noted.

Regardless, all experts expressed optimism for Saudi Arabia’s biotech future.

“My genuine belief is that this sector is growing - slowly but steadily - and will continue to expand even more,” Alshaya said. “My message to partners is to be part of the journey and take it one step at a time.”

【猫笔刀晚报｜两件意外：国家队没进场，A股却扛住了】

11月6日亚太市场普遍承压，猫笔刀当晚这篇点出了两件“没想到”的事。

第一，全天看不到“国家队”进场的痕迹，六大宽基ETF成交都明显缩量——行情这么凶险，却放手让市场自己走。第二，在没有护盘资金的情况下，A股靠前几天聚拢的存量资金居然撑住了：收盘仍是跌，但个股跌幅中位数约 -1.84%，在东亚一圈里算跌得最少的。同日日本约 -6%、韩国约 -6.5%、台湾约 -4.5%，基本都是被前一晚美股大跌拖累。

美股这边流传的“鬼故事”，是民主党中期选举大胜后要对AI科技行业动手、推一系列限制法案。作者不太信：科技七巨头里除了特斯拉，另外六家都是民主党的大金主，很难想象会对自家大客户下狠手。他认为这轮下跌的本质是美股已经连涨四年、涨得太久太多，任何风吹草动都会被放大。例子是英特尔：业绩指引低于预期约10%，股价直接跌约30%，因为此前一年已涨了约700%，预期早已打满。

他回看纳斯达克100 ETF月线：上一次像样的调整在2022年，最大回撤约35%，持续约一年。“美股不是不会跌，他们只是跌完了以后填坑能力很强。”这次纳指罕见连续两个月收长阴线，有中期见顶迹象，目前最大回撤约15%，按历史经验未必跌够，有没有“下半场”还要看。作者也分享了他的经验性看法：回撤越深，长期胜率越高（10%、20%、30%三档依次更有利）。

回到A股，为什么国家队全天旁观？他按可能性从高到低给了三个猜测：一是担心美股继续下跌，不愿在全球普跌中硬接，战线后撤；二是认为当天波动尚可接受，不必强行干预；三是授权资金可能有限，需要斟酌节奏。他注意到一个细节：午间光模块龙头集体发公告称基本面良好，明显是在安抚市场。10月23日也用过同样的做法，当时午后板块应声大涨；这次却只涨了不到1%就被打回。作者的评语是：“靠喇叭护盘，可一不可再。”

文章后半段换了话题：为什么中国互联网上缺乏“原谅机制”，公众人物犯错就社死封杀？作者的推论是，网民拒绝原谅，是因为原谅对他们没好处。反例是运动员——各种丑闻并不少，但因为还能为国争光、带来（哪怕只是情绪上的）收益，公众往往默许他们继续比赛。所以关键不在于网民会不会原谅，而在于原谅你和惩罚你，哪个对他们更“划算”。

【我们的看法】
外部冲击下A股在无明显护盘时跌幅相对可控，算是一个积极信号；但“喊话”效果递减也提醒我们，政策托底的边际作用在下降。对QDII投资者来说，纳指15%左右的回撤需要放在长周期里看，历史上的深度调整往往持续较久，节奏和仓位管理比猜底更重要。

—

English summary:
On Nov 6, Asian markets sold off after a sharp overnight drop on Wall Street: Japan about -6%, Korea about -6.5%, Taiwan about -4.5%. Mao Bidao (猫笔刀) highlights two surprises in China's A-share market. First, there was no visible sign of the "national team" (state-backed funds) stepping in—trading in the six major broad-based ETFs shrank noticeably. Second, the market held up anyway: the median stock fell about 1.84%, the smallest decline in the region.

He is skeptical of the narrative that a Democratic midterm sweep will crush AI/Big Tech, noting six of the "Magnificent 7" (all except Tesla) are major Democratic donors. In his view, the real driver is that US stocks have rallied for four straight years and expectations are stretched—e.g., Intel fell ~30% on a ~10% guidance miss after a ~700% one-year run. The Nasdaq-100 has posted two consecutive large monthly declines, a possible medium-term top signal; the current max drawdown is ~15%, versus ~35% in 2022.

He offers three possible reasons Beijing stayed on the sidelines (fear of further US losses, tolerable volatility, limited funding) and notes that verbal reassurance from optical-module leaders worked far less well than on Oct 23. The second half of the essay argues that online "cancel culture" in China depends on whether forgiving someone benefits the public—hence athletes are often forgiven.

Not investment advice.

text:
Jensen Huang said he overcame shyness to join X for his direct leadership communication online, because AI was too important to stay quiet about. But he has still said nothing there about the extraordinary questions now surrounding his own dealings with a woman US intelligence suspects of working for Beijing. So far, the NVIDIA corporate social accounts are also silent. 

But when The New York Times reported on Alice Huang, NVIDIA spokesperson John Rizzo said: "Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job." Huang himself told Bloomberg that their dealings were "completely normal and not unusual."

Do you read a denial here? I don't...

Now The Financial Times reports that a US intelligence memo alleged a romantic relationship. NVIDIA now declines to comment. But its spokesperson had already offered a reassuring account of the CEO’s interactions on the company’s behalf. Did the CEO give him the full story before he spoke? Who approved that reassurance? Was NVIDIA's spokesperson speaking with full knowledge of the facts, or was he put in the position of defending an incomplete account? 

Having lived and worked and done business in China for years (including leaving Beijing in a hurry having locked horns with CCP operatives), I know firsthand how relentlessly the PRC party-state system pursues access and influence overseas. 

Chinese commercial interests are also well known to be pursuing "go global" strategies through Singapore and Southeast Asia (to reduce the appearance of being Mainland-based and Mainland-controlled). Alice Huang – no relation to Jensen and also known as Huang Le – is a Chinese businesswoman and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based datacentre company. Megaspeed and its affiliated companies purchased billions of dollars' worth of NVIDIA AI hardware, including some of its most advanced, export-restricted processors.

The geopolitical stakes here in the AI race extend well beyond Jensen Huang’s private life: he lobbied for advanced AI chip sales to China, while US investigators have examined whether NVIDIA chips supplied to his friend's company were then diverted there.

Three US House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Huang on November 18. NVIDIA’s shareholders and the public deserve a credible explanation from him, in his own voice.

This will be the acid test of leadership accountability and responsibility from a CEO under credible attack owing to the most concerning of claims. 

Huang found his public voice when he wanted to influence Washington's AI policy, the real measure of his leadership communication acumen is now, when Washington wants answers from him in the glare of a public spotlight.

text:
The story keeps getting crazier. To recap everything that has been reported so far: 

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. What is a POSSIBLE good explanation for why Megaspeed is still receiving chips? Why is there not a license requirement for AI chip shipments to all of Southeast Asia? This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.

After US President Donald Trump announced in June 2025 that Iran’s nuclear program had been destroyed, Washington is now offering a reward of nearly $20 million in exchange for “information” about Iran’s nuclear program, sparking a wave of mockery and questions on social media. How can Washington be seeking information about something it had already claimed to have destroyed?

In an irony described on social media as “disastrous” and “embarrassing,” the US Central Command (CENTCOM), through the State Department’s Rewards for Justice program, announced a reward of up to $20 million, along with "possible relocation” or resettlement in a safe location, in exchange for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, scientists associated with it, and their movements.

Some viewed the reward as nothing more than an attempt to recruit informants from within Iran’s scientific community and put pressure on those working in the field.

The reward comes despite US President Donald Trump’s announcement in June 2025 that American strikes had “successfully obliterated” Iran’s nuclear facilities, describing the operation as a “historic military success.” This has once again raised questions about the extent of the actual damage Washington inflicted on Iran’s nuclear program and the extent of the intelligence Washington had on it.

At the time, the White House had published a statement titled: “Iran’s Nuclear Facilities Have Been Obliterated, and Suggestions Otherwise Are Fake News.”

The contrast between the US claim that Iran’s nuclear program had been destroyed and the offer of millions of dollars for new information about it has turned the American proposal into a subject of mockery, casting doubt on the narrative previously presented by President Trump regarding the outcome of strikes against Iran.

Sarcastic comments quickly spread on X, including: “I thought they destroyed it like four times already?”; “They’re offering $20 million for information about a nuclear site that Trump already destroyed”; while another user commented: “Fake news. Trump said he destroyed Iran’s nuclear program back in 2025. Are you suggesting Donald Trump is a liar?”

Criticism also targeted Trump and his administration, with some expressing their opposition to the war and questioning its justifications through comments such as: “So you have started a war to ‘dismantle’ a nuclear program you know nothing about?! Because it doesn’t exist, you child-killing terrorists…” Another user wrote: “Nothing screams defeat louder than this,” while one commenter sarcastically remarked: “NEW: The United States, 8 months into the disastrous Iran War, has one clear message: ‘DEAR GOD SOMEONE HELP US!!!!’”

Democrats today celebrate the tsunami that has destroyed the Republicans. They should know that there are two types of tsunamis. 

The waves of a distant tsunami arise far away and give people on the shore enough warning to prepare themselves. A local tsunami occurs close to shore, arrives with little or no warning, and hits with an enormous wave.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐭 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐬𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢. 

𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐚 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐬𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢, 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐒𝐨𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐬, 𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬' 𝐰𝐚𝐲. 

𝐁𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐙𝐨𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐦𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐢 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐘𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐂𝐢𝐭𝐲, 𝐊𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐞 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞, 𝐍𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐲𝐚 𝐑𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐋𝐨𝐬 𝐀𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐬, 𝐉𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐬𝐞 𝐋𝐞𝐰𝐢𝐬 𝐆𝐞𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐨𝐧, 𝐃.𝐂., 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐑𝐡𝐨𝐝𝐞 𝐈𝐬𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐧 𝐮𝐧𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲.

𝐈 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐲 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐨𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐮𝐩 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐨𝐫 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐌𝐀𝐆𝐀 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐭𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐟.

text:
When the Kent Homelessness Coalition joined Community Solutions' Built for Zero initiative in 2020, the community began strengthening how local organizations coordinate their efforts to reduce homelessness.

Six years later, that work is earning recognition. At our recent Built for Zero Learning Session in Seattle, Washington, Kent County was celebrated for four significant accomplishments:

🏆 Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble: Recognizing collaboration across business, healthcare, philanthropy and homeless service providers.

📉 Measurable reductions: Kent County is one of 32 Built for Zero communities recognized for achieving a reduction in chronic homelessness.

📊 Reliable data: The community maintained 12 consecutive months of quality data tracking people experiencing homelessness by name, with the fastest reporting among 25 communities.

🤝 Expanding its approach: Kent County is one of 16 communities to achieve quality data for a new population through its youth by-name list.

As Kent County looks toward its 2027 goals, this recognition offers both a moment to celebrate and a foundation for continued progress.

Congratulations to the Kent Homelessness Coalition, Grand Rapids Chamber and all the local partners helping make homelessness rare and brief.

text:
Chapter Three - Section 2

Saturday morning arrived bright and clear.

Haneul Cove had been preparing for its anniversary for weeks, but by eight o’clock the resort had begun visibly transforming.

Gardeners worked along the stone paths, trimming the edges of planting beds and checking arrangements of seasonal flowers.

Technicians adjusted the lighting beneath the trees and along the broad terrace overlooking the ocean.

A temporary stage had been erected near the ballroom’s glass doors, positioned so guests moving between the indoor reception and the garden could enjoy the view.

The grounds themselves were already beautiful.

The preparations didn’t attempt to disguise that beauty.

Warm lights had been placed among the low trees, carefully aimed so the dark volcanic stone walls would catch their glow after sunset. Small arrangements of white and blue flowers stood beside the paths, their colors echoing the sea beyond.

Along the main terrace, tables had been arranged beneath discreet overhead lighting. Each was dressed in pale linen, with simple centerpieces and enough space between them for guests to converse comfortably.

Inside the ballroom, staff were polishing glassware, checking place settings, and adjusting the arrangement of tables.

The room was elegant without being extravagant.

Large windows faced the ocean. Pale walls, dark wood, and restrained decorative lighting gave the space a warmth that didn’t depend on chandeliers or gold trim.

A small jazz ensemble was setting up near one end of the room.

The kitchen staff were already working.

The evening menu reflected the property’s identity. Korean dishes prepared with exceptional ingredients would be served alongside international selections, allowing guests to choose familiar favorites or enjoy something less expected.

There would be seafood from Jeju’s waters, grilled meats, seasonal vegetables, beautifully prepared rice and noodle dishes, and a selection of desserts.

The catering director had spent weeks refining the menu.

Ji-hoon had approved it after two tastings.

He’d also insisted that several dishes remain recognizably Korean rather than being transformed into elaborate presentations that looked impressive but tasted like very little.

The resort was celebrating five years in Jeju.

He wanted the food to reflect where they were.

At nine-thirty, Ji-hoon walked through the ballroom with his operations manager.

He checked the seating arrangements, the lighting, the musicians’ schedule, and the timing of the evening’s presentations.

There were still things to be done.

There always were.

But everything appeared to be proceeding according to plan.

He stopped near the windows and looked toward the gardens.

Five years.

He remembered the opening week, when half the staff had been terrified and the other half had pretended not to be.

He remembered the first major wedding, the first international conference, and the winter storm that had forced them to move an entire outdoor event inside with less than two hours’ notice.

He remembered guests who had returned every year.

And employees who had started as trainees and were now department managers.

He was proud of the place.

He’d worked too hard not to be.

His operations manager asked whether anything else required attention.

Ji-hoon shook his head.

“No. Everything looks excellent.”

The manager smiled.

“Thank you, sir.”

“Please thank the staff. They’ve done a wonderful job.”

He looked toward the terrace again.

Then checked his watch.

He had another appointment to attend.

Luna arrived at the concierge’s private fitting room at ten-thirty.

She’d expected a collection of formal dresses, perhaps several elegant options selected from a local boutique.

Instead, she found a beautifully appointed room with full-length mirrors, a seating area, a dressing space, and three gowns displayed on individual stands.

A woman in a tailored gray suit greeted her warmly.

“Miss Luna. Good morning. I’m Seo Yuna. I’ll be assisting you today.”

Luna smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Your cousin asked us to make certain you were completely comfortable with the arrangements.”

Luna glanced at the dresses.

“He seems to have been very busy.”

Yuna smiled.

“Mr. Kang takes the event very seriously.”

“Yes. He does.”

The first gown was black, elegant, and relatively simple.

The second was a soft champagne color with delicate embroidery.

The third stood near the window.

Luna looked at it.

Then looked again.

The gown was deep midnight blue, dark enough to appear almost black in shadow. Its fabric had a subtle sheen that caught the morning light without sparkling.

The neckline curved softly across the shoulders, leaving them exposed while remaining beautifully balanced with the fitted bodice.

Fine illusion mesh rose from the neckline, carrying delicate lacework that seemed to rest directly against the skin. The pattern was intricate but restrained, revealing little while giving the dress a softness that the structured waist and flowing skirt might otherwise have lacked.

Below the waist, the fabric fell in a clean line to the floor, with enough movement to follow her steps naturally.

It was feminine, elegant, and unmistakably expensive.

Luna approached it.

“This one.”

Yuna smiled.

“Your cousin thought you might like it.”

Luna looked toward her.

“He selected it?”

“He asked us to find something exceptional. We showed him several possibilities, and he suggested that this style would suit you.”

Luna touched the fabric lightly.

“He remembered.”

“Miss?”

Luna smiled.

“Nothing.”

Several years earlier, she’d attended a family wedding wearing a dress she’d bought herself.

Ji-hoon had told her that dark blue suited her.

Apparently, he’d remembered.

Yuna invited her to try the gown.

A few minutes later, Luna stood before the full-length mirror.

The fit was remarkably close, requiring only minor adjustments.

The bodice followed her slender figure without being restrictive. The neckline was open enough to flatter her shoulders, while the illusion lace softened the transition between fabric and skin.

The skirt moved beautifully when she walked.

She turned slightly.

The midnight-blue fabric caught the light.

For a moment, she simply looked.

She’d worn attractive clothes before.

At the Diamond Penthouse, appearance was part of the job.

But those clothes served a purpose dictated largely by other people.

This was different.

The gown wasn’t designed to encourage someone to buy another bottle of whiskey or remain at a table for another hour.

It was simply beautiful.

And it had been selected for her.

Yuna approached with a small jewelry case.

“Mr. Kang also arranged these.”

Inside lay a pair of delicate diamond-and-sapphire earrings and a matching bracelet.

Luna stared at them.

“These are real?”

Yuna smiled.

“Yes. They are on loan for the evening.”

Luna looked up.

“My cousin is insane.”

Yuna laughed.

“He wanted you to have something special.”

Luna examined the earrings.

The sapphires were small enough to remain elegant, their dark blue color complementing the gown. The diamonds caught the light without overwhelming them.

She picked up one earring.

“He’s going too far.”

“Would you like to try them?”

Luna hesitated.

Then smiled.

“Yes.”

Yuna helped her put them on.

The effect was extraordinary.

Luna lifted her hair away from her shoulders.

Her silver-white streak fell naturally along the right side of her forehead.

Yuna looked at the mirror.

“May I make a suggestion?”

“Of course.”

“Your hair. I think we should leave the white section visible.”

Luna looked at her reflection.

“Really?”

“It’s beautiful. With the dark dress, it will be quite striking.”

Luna studied herself.

Most of her life, people had noticed the white streak before they noticed anything else.

Sometimes they’d been curious.

Sometimes rude.

Occasionally, someone had made the kind of remark that lingered long after the conversation ended.

She’d learned to ignore most of it.

But here, in this room, the woman helping her dress was treating it as something worth emphasizing.

Luna smiled.

“Yes. Let’s leave it visible.”

Yuna nodded.

“I think that will be perfect.”

When the fitting was finished, Luna changed back into her jeans and T-shirt.

She looked once more at the gown.

Then at the jewelry case.

“Please thank my cousin.”

“Of course.”

Luna smiled.

“And perhaps tell him he’s completely unreasonable.”

Yuna laughed.

“I’ll try to phrase that diplomatically.”

Luna smiled.

“Good. I understand diplomacy.”

Michael spent much of Saturday morning walking.

He’d declined the resort’s offer of a guided excursion, explaining that he was perfectly capable of wandering around and getting lost by himself.

He carried a camera and wore the same old jeans he’d worn to lunch.

The coast was extraordinary.

The volcanic rock formed irregular shapes along the shoreline, dark against the blue water. Waves broke against the stone, throwing white spray into the sunlight.

Farther inland, low hills rose behind fields divided by stone walls.

Michael took photographs of the coast, the resort gardens, and the mountain visible in the distance.

He stopped at a small overlook and watched the waves for several minutes.

He’d been to beautiful places around the world.

Sometimes work allowed him to see them.

Sometimes it didn’t.

This was one of the better trips.

At noon he returned to the resort and found a message from the concierge confirming that a tuxedo had been arranged.

He was expected at a fitting at one-thirty.

Michael looked at the message.

Then laughed.

“Apparently I’m going to the prom.”

He spent the next hour answering a few emails, checking his Monday flight arrangements, and calling home to confirm that everything was as he’d left it.

His return flight remained scheduled for Monday.

He’d be back in Washington the following day, accounting for the time difference.

He checked the itinerary.

Then closed it.

There was no reason to think about that now.

At one-thirty he arrived for the fitting.

The tuxedo was black, traditional, and beautifully tailored.

The white shirt fit properly. The jacket sat comfortably across his shoulders, and the trousers required only a small adjustment.

The tailor checked the length of the sleeves and made a note.

Michael examined himself in the mirror.

“Well, look at that. Almost respectable.”

The tailor smiled politely.

Michael wasn’t sure whether the man understood the joke.

He decided it didn’t matter.

The tuxedo would be delivered to his suite that afternoon.

He thanked the staff and returned upstairs.

At four o’clock, Luna was still writing.

She’d made considerable progress.

The story had grown from a collection of ideas into something approaching an outline.

She’d begun to understand what the characters wanted, although she wasn’t entirely sure what would happen to them.

The woman wanted to write her own stories.

The man wanted to stop moving long enough to understand why he kept moving.

That seemed promising.

Luna read the last scene she’d written.

She changed two lines of dialogue.

Then she checked the time.

Four-oh-three.

She was expected downstairs for hair and makeup at five.

The gala began at seven.

She closed the laptop.

For a moment she sat quietly, looking at the reflection of the ocean in the window.

Michael would be there tonight.

She wondered what he looked like in a tuxedo.

She’d seen him in a suit at the Diamond Penthouse.

He’d looked very handsome.

He’d also looked handsome in jeans and that ridiculous Iron Maiden shirt.

She smiled.

Perhaps the clothes weren’t particularly important.

Still, she was looking forward to seeing him.

She stood and went to shower.

By six-thirty, Haneul Cove had been transformed.

The sun was descending toward the western horizon, leaving a warm glow across the resort grounds.

The garden paths were illuminated by low lights that traced their edges without overpowering the evening.

The volcanic stone walls glowed softly beneath carefully placed fixtures.

Along the terrace, discreet lighting revealed the tables, flowers, and glassware, while beyond them the ocean remained a darkening expanse of blue.

Inside, the ballroom was ready.

The tables were set with polished silverware, fine porcelain, and crystal glasses. White and blue flowers stood in arrangements that were elegant without obstructing conversation.

The jazz ensemble had begun playing softly.

Servers moved through the room, checking final details.

In the kitchens, chefs were preparing the first courses.

Everything appeared effortless.

It wasn’t.

Dozens of people had spent weeks making it look that way.

Ji-hoon stood near the ballroom entrance, speaking with the events director.

He was wearing a black tuxedo himself.

His expression was calm.

A few minor changes had been requested by late-arriving guests. One investor wanted a different table. Another had brought an unexpected companion.

The staff had handled both without difficulty.

Ji-hoon listened to the final report.

Then nodded.

“Very good.”

The events director smiled.

“Everything is ready.”

Ji-hoon looked toward the entrance.

“Then let’s welcome our guests.”

Michael finished tying his bow tie at six-forty-five.

He stood before the mirror in his suite, adjusted the jacket, and examined the result.

The tuxedo fit well.

Very well.

He’d worn formal clothes often enough to know the difference.

He slipped his phone into an inside pocket and checked his watch.

He was early.

Good.

He’d arranged to meet Luna near the ballroom entrance at seven.

He considered calling her.

Then decided against it.

She’d probably be busy getting ready.

He walked out onto the terrace.

The grounds below were glowing with lights.

Guests had begun arriving.

He could hear faint music drifting up from the ballroom.

For a moment, he watched the people moving across the garden paths.

Men in tuxedos and dark suits.

Women in elegant evening gowns.

Small groups gathered near the terrace.

He’d attended similar events in Tokyo, London, Singapore, Dubai, and half a dozen other places.

They were usually predictable.

Tonight, for some reason, he was looking forward to it.

He checked his watch again.

Six-fifty-one.

He smiled.

“Get a grip, Michael.”

He went downstairs.

Luna stood before the mirror in her room while Yuna made a final adjustment to the fall of her hair.

The silver-white streak curved naturally along the right side of her forehead, disappearing into the black hair swept softly behind one ear.

The rest fell in loose, carefully arranged waves over her shoulders.

Her makeup was elegant and understated.

Her eyes were gently defined, her lips a soft natural color.

Nothing heavy.

Nothing theatrical.

The gown fit beautifully.

The midnight-blue fabric followed her waist before falling to the floor in a graceful line. The off-the-shoulder neckline framed her shoulders, while the delicate illusion lace gave the upper bodice a softness that became more apparent as the light moved across it.

The borrowed earrings caught the light when she turned her head.

The matching bracelet rested lightly against her wrist.

Yuna stepped back.

“There.”

Luna looked at herself.

For a moment she didn’t speak.

Then she smiled.

“It’s beautiful.”

Yuna returned the smile.

“You look wonderful.”

Luna touched the bracelet.

“My cousin really did too much.”

“Perhaps,” Yuna said. “But I think he will be very pleased.”

Luna laughed softly.

“Yes. He probably will.”

She thanked Yuna and collected a small evening bag.

Then she took one final look in the mirror.

She looked like herself.

Not a different person.

Just a version of herself she’d rarely had a reason to present.

She smiled.

Then she left for the ballroom.

text:
Insurance companies have no choice and cannot decide whom they want to cover: Everyone who wants to enroll with them, the insurance company must enroll. And enrollment is mandatory for everyone. So no longer uninsured rushing to the ER for primary care services that they never pay for and those that are insured (and their employers, if someone is employed) have to pay for with higher service costs, higher premiums, and higher deductibles. 
And, with a SINGLE basic plan, EVERYONE knows exactly what the coverage is, regardless of where one lives and what service provider one uses.
Insurance companies make money with voluntary supplemental insurance for which they can set the price and services covered such as private rooms, non-traditional/alternative medicine, Telemed, etc. Insurance companies that offer supplemental insurance offerings that people want AND provide excellent customer service will succeed and be profitable.
Look at Switzerland to see how it works: 
With a population of ~9 million, individuals can choose from more than 30 insurance companies that need to compete based on service quality and voluntary supplemental offerings. In Dallas-Fort Worth (similar population size): Less than 10 insurance companies can be picked at https://t.co/iGDFhMNOTJ and they offer highly confusing plans with massive premiums and deductibles with providers dropping in and out every year; some insurance companies have such limited provider access, that they are not a realistic choice at all. And one major insurance company that has a massive provider network (Baylor Scott White) decided to no longer provide coverage in 2027, leaving a major gap. So, whoever relied on Baylor Scott White providers now struggles to find new providers that may not offer the same quality of service. A healthcare hellscape in a major metro in the United States...

text:
In 2008, Elon Musk was extremely short on cash. Both of his companies were on the verge of bankruptcy. He didn't even own a house in his name and had to borrow money from friends just to pay rent.

As he was desperately trying to raise funds, his girlfriend Talulah Riley's parents offered to remortgage their house to raise some cash for him. Musk firmly refused. He didn't want her parents to take on such a massive risk and lose their home.

That autumn, Musk's two companies were barely hanging on. SpaceX's rockets had exploded three times in a row, and Tesla had only $9 million left in its bank account—barely enough to make payroll. He was also going through a divorce with his then-wife, Justine. The house had already gone to her, and under California law, he had to cover the legal fees for both sides, and borrow that money too.

Musk was under so much stress that he suffered from night terrors, screaming in his sleep and even vomiting. Through all of this, Talulah was by his side. He had just met her in London that July.

Seeing Musk pushed to the edge, Talulah was heartbroken. Worried he was going to break down, she called her parents for help. When she told them what was happening, her parents offered to mortgage their house to help him out.

But Musk refused to take it. If he couldn't repay the money, the bank could take her parents' house. He couldn't do something like that. He told Talulah, "Your parents shouldn't lose their house just because I put everything on the line."

In September 2008, after three consecutive failures, SpaceX's Falcon 1 finally reached orbit on its fourth attempt, which gave NASA the confidence to bet on them. By December, NASA awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract to resupply the International Space Station, effectively saving the company. Almost simultaneously, at 6:00 PM on Christmas Eve, Tesla secured $40 million in funding. Both companies had narrowly escaped bankruptcy.

A year and a half later, in June 2010, Tesla went public on the NASDAQ. When Musk rang the opening bell, Talulah was still standing by his side. Three months after that, they got married in an old church in Scotland.

text:
Tata Chemicals Ltd Concall Summary (Q2 FY27, 7 November 2026) #TATACHEM

🟡 Management Guidance: 
Management expects global soda ash prices to remain range-bound in the near term because of persistent oversupply, elevated Chinese exports and subdued industrial demand. Any sustained pricing recovery will depend on supply rationalisation and stronger demand. India continues to show relatively healthy demand, supported by solar glass capacity additions and infrastructure activity. In the US, Tata Chemicals will focus on North and South America and markets that generate positive netbacks rather than pursuing unremunerative Southeast Asian exports. The Searles Valley customer contracts acquired through bankruptcy proceedings cover approximately 5 lakh tonnes over two years, after which contract renewals will be required. Management expects UK salt and bicarbonate profitability to recover as energy and logistics costs moderate, but did not provide a specific timeline. The standalone business continues to focus on operational efficiency, while the broader strategy is to increase the contribution of non-cyclical specialty and value-added products. Annual CapEx is approximately ₹1,000 crore for FY27, with a similar amount indicated for the following year.

🟢 Green Alert: Standalone Q2 revenue increased 8% YoY to ₹1,300 crore, while EBITDA grew 22% to ₹292 crore. Standalone H1 revenue increased 9% to ₹2,584 crore and EBITDA rose 29% to ₹656 crore. India's business performed relatively well, supported by higher volumes in salt, FOS and silica. The US business secured customer contracts representing approximately 5 lakh tonnes through the Searles Valley Minerals bankruptcy proceedings. These contracts provide geographical advantages by allowing Tata Chemicals to serve customers in California and Mexico through more efficient overland logistics instead of relying entirely on exports. Management also highlighted the long-term potential of bicarbonate, salt and prebiotics, supported by demand from food, feed, pharmaceutical and wellness applications. India remains a relatively stronger soda ash market compared with several global regions. The company is also working towards improving its balance sheet through the sale of selected listed group-company investments, with approximately ₹796 crore of proceeds used towards debt reduction in the US and UK.

🔴 Red Alert: Consolidated Q2 EBITDA declined to ₹381 crore from ₹537 crore in the previous year, while the company reported a loss after tax of ₹50 crore compared with a profit in Q2 FY26. Consolidated H1 EBITDA declined to ₹936 crore from ₹1,186 crore, and profit after tax before exceptional items and non-controlling interests fell sharply to ₹10 crore from ₹535 crore. The main pressure is coming from lower soda ash realisations in overseas subsidiaries, higher UK natural gas and energy costs, increased freight and logistics expenses, and the suspension of Kenya operations. Global soda ash remains structurally oversupplied, particularly due to Chinese capacity additions and elevated producer inventories. Chinese soda ash inventories reached approximately 1.89 million tonnes by the end of September. Indian domestic prices also softened following improved import availability and increased domestic supply. Kenya remains a significant uncertainty. Operations are suspended following a notice from the Ministry of Mining, and management is pursuing administrative and legal remedies. Although management believes its lease rights extend until 2053, there is no confirmed restart timeline. Rallis India also faced pressure from delayed sowing, uneven rainfall, input cost inflation and unfavourable operating conditions. Consolidated net debt, excluding leases, stood at ₹6,127 crore.

🔵 Blue Alert: Tata Chemicals is repositioning its portfolio towards higher-value and relatively non-cyclical businesses under its LIFE framework. Living Essentials includes salt, bicarbonate and FOS, while the company is also developing opportunities in prebiotics, supported by growing interest in gut health and wellness. In the US, the Searles Valley customer contracts strengthen its geographical presence in California and Mexico and could improve logistics economics and customer relationships. The company is deliberately reducing exposure to Southeast Asian soda ash exports because of poor netbacks, while focusing on North and South America and other profitable markets. Management also highlighted potential demand growth from solar glass, lithium-related applications, food and pharmaceuticals. In Kenya, the company had planned to double capacity, add a bicarbonate unit and explore a container-glass partnership before operations were suspended. The company is pursuing its legal rights through the Kenyan courts and has also highlighted protection under the UK-Kenya bilateral investment treaty. The sale of selected group-company investments is part of a broader strategy to monetise assets and reduce debt.

🧠 Deep Insight: Tata Chemicals is facing a difficult combination of a global soda ash downturn and operational problems in overseas subsidiaries. The difference between standalone and consolidated performance is particularly important. Standalone EBITDA grew 22%, but consolidated EBITDA declined because overseas operations, especially the UK and US, are facing lower realisations and higher operating costs. This shows that the problem is not uniform across the business. India remains relatively resilient, while international operations are under pressure. The most important near-term issue is global soda ash pricing. Chinese oversupply is preventing meaningful price recovery, and even demand growth in India may not be sufficient to offset excess international supply. The company is responding by exiting unremunerative export markets and focusing on customers that offer better post-logistics contribution. The Searles Valley contracts are strategically useful because they improve customer proximity and reduce dependence on expensive shipping, but they are secured for only two years and renewals are not guaranteed. Kenya is another major uncertainty. Management is confident about its legal position, but investors should not assume a quick resolution or restart of operations. The ₹6,127 crore net debt position also makes cash generation and capital discipline important. Investors should monitor global soda ash prices, Chinese supply rationalisation, UK energy costs, Kenya's legal proceedings, US contract profitability, Rallis' recovery and debt reduction. The central investment question is whether Tata Chemicals can protect cash flows through the soda ash downturn while improving the profitability and resilience of its international operations.

text:
At 7,Steven Stayner took a ride from a stranger a few blocks from his house. At 14,he walked into a police station holding the hand of a 5-year-old boy who had been taken the same way. At 24,he died in a motorcycle crash. Ten years later,his older brother Cary became one of the most notorious killers in California.

Merced,California,December 1972. A man stopped Steven on his way home from school and asked if his mother might want to donate something to a church. Steven said she probably would. The man offered him a ride. Steven said no,his house was just a few blocks away. The man kept asking. Steven got in.

The car drove right past his street.

The man was Kenneth Parnell. He told Steven his parents had agreed to let him stay the night. Then another night. Then he said a court had given him custody. He changed Steven's name to Dennis. Within a week,Steven was calling him Dad.

For seven years,Steven lived as Parnell's son. Then Parnell brought home a new boy,5-year-old Timmy White. Steven waited for a night when Parnell was at work,took Timmy's hand,and hitchhiked to the police.

In the video below,Steven is 14,two weeks after his escape,sitting next to his parents on morning TV. He's polite and quiet,and he answers like a kid giving a book report. When he's asked how he felt when they told him he now belonged to that man,he says he doesn't really remember. His mother says she never once lost hope. His father admits he did. I kept watching Steven's face during that part.

Parnell served about five years. In 1999,Steven's brother Cary murdered four women near Yosemite and was sentenced to death.

Today in Merced there's a statue of a teenage boy holding a little boy's hand.

How does one family raise a son who saved a child and a son who killed four women? Did what happened to Steven break his brother too,or is there no connection at all?

text:
Deep in the West Virginia hills, at the end of a dirt road, lives a family the internet calls "America's most inbred." The Whittakers. In 2020, a YouTube documentary made them famous around the world.

In September 2025, the state came and took three of them away.

The story reportedly began more than 100 years ago with identical twin brothers, Henry and John Whittaker. Their children married each other. Then their grandchildren did. Two double cousins, John and Gracie, had 15 children together.

Many of those children were born with severe disabilities. None of them has a public diagnosis.

Ray and Timmy can't talk. They communicate with faint grunts. Lorene can't speak at all. Several of them have eyes that point in different directions.

When photographer Mark Laita first drove up in 2004, the family barked at his crew. One man screamed and ran away every time someone looked him in the eye. His pants fell to his ankles. He kicked a garbage can. Then he did it again. And again. Laita called it "the craziest thing I have ever seen."

The neighbors didn't want him there. They protect the Whittakers from outsiders. Laita had to come back with a police escort.

He won the family over with one offer. He would take photos of a relative who had died, to put in the coffin.

In 2020 he finally filmed them. His GoFundMe raised $55,000. Then the strangers came. YouTubers drove down that dirt road to film them for views.

In 2023, Laita took them to the West Virginia State Fair. A family that screamed at strangers walked straight into a crowd of thousands. They played carnival games. They rode the Ferris wheel. They laughed.

Two years later, almost to the day, it was over.

In September 2025, West Virginia adult protective services removed Ray (72), his sister Lorene (79) and her son Timmy (46).

Betty (73) and Larry (69) were left behind. Nobody told them where their family went. They haven't heard from them since.

For 100 years nobody outside those hills knew the Whittakers existed. The internet found them in one day.

Did it save them or destroy them?

Rev War Tales
Dunmore’s Declaration
7 November 1775, aboard the ship William, off Norfolk, Virginia. Lord Dunmore declared martial law and offered freedom to enslaved people and indentured servants of rebels who would fight for the king. John Murray, Earl of Dunmore, dated the proclamation 7 November 1775. Armed Virginians were forming an army and had fired on his tenders. Civil law, he said, could not restore order. He placed the colony under martial law and required all capable men to take the royal standard or be treated as traitors. Then came the clause that changed the war in Virginia. Indentured servants and enslaved Blacks belonging to rebels, able and willing to bear arms, were declared free if they joined his troops. Hundreds came. Patriots called it a bid to raise a slave revolt. It did not save the colony. It drove planters toward independence and gave the Ethiopian Regiment its recruits. Dunmore would lose the land. The offer outlasted his government.

text:
Washington called Lord Dunmore “that Arch Traitor to the Rights of Humanity” and demanded he be crushed with the full force of the colony before his ranks could swell “like a snow Ball,” explicitly warning that the real danger was the slaves who would join once the British looked formidable. The patriots’ response was immediate and uncompromising: they intensified slave patrols, threatened death for anyone who fled to the British, and treated the proclamation as deliberate incitement of domestic insurrection designed to destroy the social and economic order of Virginia. Far from a humanitarian gesture, Dunmore’s offer was a wartime expedient limited to able-bodied men owned by rebels who would bear arms; it left women, children, and the aged in bondage, applied only against patriots (not loyalists), and was issued by a man who himself held slaves. The colonists saw it for what it was—an attempt to weaponize their own labor force against them—and it accelerated, rather than caused, the break with Britain.

Jefferson recorded that reality in the Declaration of Independence, listing as a final grievance that the king “has excited domestic insurrections amongst us.” Mount Vernon’s post inverts this history by centering the seventeen people who left the estate, celebrating Harry Washington’s service in the Ethiopian Regiment, and framing the episode primarily as a British promise of freedom that the Americans then frustrated. That selective emphasis—portraying the British as liberators and the patriots as the obstacle—tracks the 1619 Project’s central thesis that protecting slavery from British abolitionism was a driving motive for independence, despite the decree’s narrow military purpose, the continuation of slavery throughout the British Empire, and the far broader list of political and constitutional grievances that actually produced the Revolution.

text:
🇺🇦 Russian Overnight Strikes Damage Kyiv’s Power And Heating Systems

Russian missiles and drones struck energy infrastructure around Kyiv overnight, damaging electricity and heating systems as temperatures approached freezing, Ukrainian officials said Saturday.

At least two people were killed and around a dozen wounded across Ukraine. Homes and businesses were also damaged. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said several ballistic missiles struck the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River.

Ukraine’s energy ministry reported serious damage to facilities outside Kyiv, including systems carrying electricity from two nuclear plants to the capital and central regions. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said substations in five other regions were hit.

Ukraine’s air force reported 36 ballistic missiles, with four intercepted, and said defenses downed 149 of 172 drones. Those interception figures are Ukrainian military assessments.

Russia’s defense ministry described the operation as a strike against military-industrial targets and energy and transport infrastructure.

The attacks came before planned negotiations in Abu Dhabi. Their consequence, however, is civilian hardship: disruptions to electricity, water and heat as winter approaches.

Damage to transmission infrastructure can threaten services without a direct strike on a generating plant. That makes repair capacity and protection of the wider power network central to civilian resilience. Diplomatic preparations offer little immediate relief to households confronting outages and damaged homes.

text:
YOU CAN'T INSULT PHILLY, ASSHOLE

By The Bulletproof Poet

The greatest thing about Philadelphia
is you can't fucking insult us.

Call us rude?
Thanks, dickhead. We practice.

Call us ugly?
Have you seen the Schuylkill?
Even the river looks ready
to fight a PPA employee.

Call us violent?
Aw, somebody's flirting!

In Philly, an insult
is either a compliment
or an invitation to fight,
which is ALSO a compliment.

We booed Santa Claus.
We threw snowballs.
We cheered a guy eating horse shit
after the Eagles won the Super Bowl.

You think your little insult
is gonna hurt our feelings?

We got Kensington, Frankford,
South Philly, Fishtown,
and Northeast Philly,
where every argument starts with
"Yo, listen, dickhead!"

We got SEPTA,
where the schedule is a suggestion
and the El provides free lessons
in existential despair.

We got Wawa,
which is practically a religion,
and cheesesteak arguments
that could restart the Civil War.

Pat's or Geno's?
Fuck your tourist trap debate.
Ask somebody who actually lives here.

We got Rocky,
a fictional boxer with a statue,
while Joe Frazier had to wait decades
for proper recognition.

We got the Liberty Bell,
cracked and unapologetic.
Even our monuments
tell authority to fuck off.

We got the Mummers,
the Italian Market,
Reading Terminal,
and the Boulevard,
where crossing the street
requires divine intervention.

We say "wooder,"
eat hoagies,
drink Arctic Splash,
and pronounce "jawn"
like it's a constitutional amendment.

New York talks shit?
Cute.

Boston talks shit?
Adorable.

Dallas talks shit?
FUCK DALLAS!
That's not an insult.
That's civic responsibility.

We love our neighbors,
help shovel their sidewalks,
then call them assholes
for stealing our parking spot.

We don't need your approval.
Hell, we don't approve
of each other.

So bring your insults,
your fancy vocabulary,
your suburban superiority.

We'll call you a jabroni,
offer you a beer,
and ask if you wanna take it outside.

Because in Philadelphia,
FUCK YOU
might mean WELCOME HOME.

And if we really hate you?

We won't insult you.

We'll just say,
"Have a nice day."
