text:
Chapter Three - Section 3

Michael was standing near the entrance when she arrived.

He was speaking with a member of the resort staff, who was explaining where the evening’s reception would begin.

Michael nodded politely.

Then he noticed Luna approaching.

The staff member continued speaking for another few seconds before realizing Michael was no longer listening.

Michael turned fully toward her.

For a moment, he simply looked.

Luna smiled.

“Hello, Michael.”

He took a moment.

“Well.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Well?”

Michael smiled.

“That’s a very nice dress.”

Luna looked down at the gown.

“Thank you.”

He shook his head slightly.

“No, that’s not quite right.”

She looked amused.

“Not right?”

“You look beautiful, Luna.”

Her smile changed.

It became a little softer.

“Thank you, Michael.”

He glanced toward the earrings.

“Your cousin?”

“Yes.”

“The man has excellent taste.”

“He does.”

She looked him over.

“And you look very handsome.”

Michael glanced down at his tuxedo.

“Cleaned up okay?”

“Very well.”

“Not bad for a guy wearing Iron Maiden yesterday.”

Luna smiled.

“I liked Iron Maiden.”

“Now there’s a sentence I never expected to hear.”

She laughed.

Then she looked toward the ballroom.

“Shall we?”

Michael offered his arm.

Luna took it.

“Lead the way,” he said.

She smiled.

And did.

The anniversary gala was already filling with guests.

The reception began in the ballroom and extended onto the garden terrace, where the ocean was visible beyond the softly illuminated grounds.

A small jazz ensemble played near the windows.

Their music was pleasant rather than intrusive, providing a gentle background to the conversations.

Servers circulated with champagne, sparkling water, and small appetizers.

The guests represented a broad cross-section of the people connected to Haneul Cove.

There were investors who owned substantial interests in the resort, directors from the company responsible for its development, senior executives from hospitality and transportation companies, and a handful of extraordinarily wealthy individuals whose investments extended far beyond Jeju.

There were also department managers, long-serving employees, and professional staff whose work had shaped the property’s first five years.

Some wore exceptionally expensive clothes.

Others wore the best formal outfits they owned.

The atmosphere was celebratory without being extravagant for its own sake.

People greeted colleagues they hadn’t seen in months, congratulated staff members, and discussed the resort’s growth.

Photographs from the property’s opening year were displayed along one wall, showing unfinished landscaping, early construction, and the first guests arriving.

Another display highlighted the resort’s employees, several of whom had been there since the beginning.

Michael noticed it.

“Nice touch.”

Luna followed his gaze.

“The photographs?”

“Yeah. They included the people who actually run the place.”

She smiled.

“My cousin wanted that.”

“Smart man.”

They entered the main reception.

Immediately, several guests turned toward Michael.

He was easy to notice.

At six feet tall, with blond hair, blue eyes, and a well-fitted black tuxedo, he stood out among the predominantly Korean crowd.

Luna, even in her heels, was several inches shorter.

Standing beside him in her midnight-blue gown, with the silver-white streak visible against her dark hair, she drew attention of her own.

At first, most of that attention came because she was accompanying him.

An important foreign guest.

A distinguished aerospace engineer.

Someone the airline had apparently gone to considerable trouble to accommodate.

People naturally assumed the woman beside him must be someone significant.

Luna understood that immediately.

She’d spent years observing how people responded to status.

She knew that an expensive dress, a prestigious introduction, and proximity to someone influential could change the way a room regarded a person.

She also knew that those impressions could disappear quickly if someone failed to justify them.

She wasn’t concerned.

She’d come to enjoy the evening.

And she knew how to talk to people.

Ji-hoon approached them near the entrance.

For a moment, he stopped.

He looked at Luna.

His professional expression gave way to something warmer.

“Luna.”

She smiled.

“Hello, oppa.”

He looked at her dress, then her face.

“You look wonderful.”

She glanced toward the gown.

“You didn’t have to do all this.”

“I know.”

She looked at him.

He smiled.

“I’m glad you like it.”

Luna’s expression softened.

“Thank you.”

Ji-hoon nodded.

Then he turned toward Michael.

“Mr. Michael. Welcome. You look very distinguished.”

Michael smiled.

“Your concierge is a miracle worker.”

Ji-hoon laughed.

“I’m glad everything was satisfactory.”

“More than satisfactory.”

A small group of guests approached.

Ji-hoon greeted them warmly in Korean.

Then he turned toward Michael and Luna.

“May I introduce Mr. Michael, an American aerospace engineer whose work has been instrumental in advancing the satellite navigation and tracking systems used by one of Korea’s leading airlines.”

The guests bowed and exchanged greetings.

Michael returned the courtesy.

Ji-hoon continued.

“And this is Luna, my cousin. She’s a professional writer and translator, currently working on Mr. Michael’s biography and assisting him during his visit.”

Luna translated the introductions into Korean, adjusting the phrasing slightly to suit the guests.

The response was immediate and polite.

One of the directors smiled broadly and said something complimentary.

Luna thanked him.

Michael leaned slightly toward her.

“Did he make me sound important?”

“Very.”

“Did he mention the forty-two shares of SpaceX?”

“No, Michael.”

“Probably wise.”

Luna suppressed a smile.

Ji-hoon introduced them to several more guests before excusing himself to greet a newly arriving investor.

Michael watched him go.

Then he looked toward Luna.

“Well, that was impressive.”

“What?”

“Your cousin. He makes me sound like I invented airplanes.”

Luna smiled.

“He is proud to have you here.”

“Apparently.”

She glanced toward a group approaching from the other side of the room.

“Michael.”

“Yes?”

“These gentlemen are members of the resort’s investment board.”

“Okay.”

“They are very formal.”

Michael considered that.

“How formal?”

“Perhaps let me do most of the talking.”

He smiled.

“Your ship, Captain.”

Luna looked at him.

“Ship?”

“Never mind. Lead the way.”

She did.

The first conversation went remarkably well.

At least, Michael thought it did.

One of the directors asked him what he thought of Korea.

Michael smiled.

“Love the place. Great people, strange food, things I can’t pronounce to save my life, and K-pop, which I’m pretty sure I’ll never understand.”

Luna listened without changing expression.

Then she turned toward the director and spoke in Korean.

Her answer was longer than Michael’s.

Considerably longer.

The director listened attentively, nodded, and smiled.

He replied enthusiastically.

The two men beside him nodded as well.

One raised his glass.

Michael returned the gesture.

Then he leaned toward Luna.

“That went over better than I expected.”

“Yes.”

“What’d you tell him?”

“That you admire Korea for the kindness of its people, its internationally respected cuisine, and the extraordinary diversity of its cultural traditions.”

Michael turned slowly toward her.

“I said all that?”

“More or less.”

He looked toward the director, who was still smiling.

“Well, hell. I sound positively distinguished.”

Luna lifted her champagne glass.

“You are welcome.”

Michael laughed quietly.

“Okay. I see how this is going to work.”

“Good.”

She smiled.

“Then please let me continue.”

He raised his glass slightly.

“Absolutely.”

The next guest asked about Michael’s engineering work.

Michael began explaining the satellite tracking system.

He was halfway through a description of the relationship between navigation data and communications latency when he noticed Luna looking at him.

Not disapprovingly.

Just looking.

He stopped.

“What?”

She smiled pleasantly toward the guest, then offered a concise explanation in Korean.

The man nodded with evident appreciation.

Michael leaned closer.

“Too much?”

“A little.”

“He asked.”

“Yes. But he does not need to understand the entire airplane.”

Michael considered that.

“Fair point.”

Luna smiled.

They moved on.

As the reception continued, Michael began to recognize just how much Luna was doing.

She wasn’t merely translating sentences.

She was managing conversations.

When a guest asked a formal question, she helped Michael understand what kind of answer was expected.

When someone offered an elaborate compliment, she translated the essential meaning without forcing him to respond to every word.

When Michael made one of his dry observations, she decided whether it would survive translation.

Often it didn’t.

He began watching her more carefully.

She spoke Korean with a confidence and ease he hadn’t seen at the Diamond Penthouse, where most of her conversations had been in English.

She recognized distinctions in status and seniority that he barely noticed.

She knew when to bow slightly, when to accept a compliment, and when to redirect a conversation toward the guest rather than allowing Michael to become its permanent subject.

And she did it without appearing to work particularly hard.

At one point, a senior executive complimented Michael on the successful completion of the airline project.

Michael thanked him.

The man then asked a question in Korean.

Luna translated.

“He wants to know whether you intend to continue working with Korean companies.”

Michael nodded.

“Sure. If they keep paying me.”

Luna gave him a brief look.

Michael paused.

Then smiled.

“Right. Perhaps not that.”

She turned toward the executive and answered in Korean.

The man smiled warmly.

Michael leaned closer.

“What’d we say?”

“That you have enjoyed working with Korean professionals and would welcome future opportunities to collaborate.”

“That’s probably better.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her.

“You’re enjoying this, aren’t you?”

She smiled.

“A little.”

Michael laughed.

He didn’t mind.

In fact, he was beginning to enjoy it himself.

He’d spent much of his professional life in situations where people expected him to know what he was doing.

Here, for once, he didn’t.

And Luna did.

That was perfectly fine with him.

The guests were beginning to notice Luna for reasons beyond her association with Michael.

A woman in an elegant green gown approached them while Michael was speaking with an airline director.

She greeted Luna in Korean and mentioned a television drama.

Luna’s expression brightened.

“Yes. I worked on that production.”

The woman looked delighted.

She’d watched the series twice, she explained, and had especially enjoyed the scenes involving the younger sister.

Luna smiled.

Those were among the scenes she’d helped write.

The woman asked whether Luna had worked closely with the lead actress.

Luna explained that her contribution had been to the script rather than the performance, although she’d met members of the cast during production.

The woman listened with obvious interest.

A second woman joined them.

She recognized the title immediately.

The conversation became animated.

They asked about how television scripts were developed, whether actors frequently changed dialogue, and how much influence individual writers had over the final production.

Luna answered openly.

She didn’t exaggerate her role.

She described the collaborative process, the senior writers, the directors, and the sometimes frustrating experience of watching a scene change after it left her desk.

The women laughed at several of her observations.

One asked whether she was working on anything new.

“Several things,” Luna replied. “And perhaps something of my own.”

The woman looked interested.

“Your own drama?”

“Perhaps. It’s still very early.”

“How exciting.”

Michael had finished his conversation and was standing nearby.

He understood almost nothing of the exchange.

But he could see that Luna was enjoying herself.

Her posture had changed slightly.

She was speaking more freely, gesturing occasionally, smiling as she explained something.

The women listened closely.

Michael took a sip of champagne.

He was beginning to suspect that his biographer was considerably more interesting than her subject.

When the conversation ended, the women thanked Luna warmly.

One asked whether they might speak again sometime.

Luna agreed politely.

They exchanged contact information.

Then the women moved away.

Michael looked toward Luna.

“Friends of yours?”

“No. They know a television show I worked on.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“That’s pretty cool.”

She smiled.

“They liked it.”

“Well, there you go.”

Luna looked pleased.

Michael noticed.

He didn’t make a joke.

He simply smiled at her.

Across the room, one of the women was already telling another guest that she’d met a writer from one of her favorite dramas.

By the time she finished, Luna’s contribution to the production had grown considerably.

She’d met one of the principal writers, she explained, a very talented young woman who was now working on a biography of an important American engineer.

Her listener looked impressed.

The woman smiled.

It was an excellent story to take home from an anniversary party.

Luna knew nothing about it.

Dinner was served shortly after eight.

Guests moved into the ballroom, where the tables had been arranged to encourage conversation without crowding.

Ji-hoon had been careful about the seating.

The wealthiest investors were present, naturally, but they hadn’t been isolated together in a private corner.

Senior managers sat among directors and business partners. Long-serving department heads had places near people who’d supported the resort from its earliest days.

The arrangement reflected Ji-hoon’s belief that the anniversary belonged to everyone who’d helped build the property.

Michael and Luna were seated at a table overlooking the garden terrace.

Their companions included two airline executives, a hospitality investor and his wife, and a senior manager who’d been with Haneul Cove since before its opening.

The conversation moved easily between Korean and English.

Mostly Korean.

Michael soon discovered that his role consisted largely of smiling, answering occasional questions, and trusting Luna.

He was becoming very good at the last part.

The first course arrived.

It was a beautifully presented seafood dish accompanied by several small Korean preparations.

Michael examined the plate.

Then looked at Luna.

She caught his expression.

“Don’t worry,” she whispered.

“I wasn’t.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Much.”

He smiled.

“Okay. A little.”

The meal was excellent.

The catering team had balanced unfamiliar ingredients with presentations that made the food approachable without sacrificing its character.

Later came grilled meats, seasonal vegetables, rice dishes, and an elegant selection of traditional and modern Korean accompaniments.

Michael recognized one of the dishes.

He leaned toward Luna.

“That’s japchae, isn’t it?”

She looked pleasantly surprised.

“Yes.”

“See? I’m learning.”

She smiled.

“You are.”

A director across the table noticed the exchange and asked Michael whether he’d enjoyed Korean cuisine during his visit.

Michael nodded.

“Very much. Especially the japchae. And the galbi we had yesterday.”

Luna translated.

The director looked impressed.

He asked another question.

Michael glanced toward Luna.

She translated again.

“He wants to know how you learned the dishes.”

Michael smiled.

“Excellent teacher.”

Luna looked at him.

He gave her a tiny wink.

She smiled and translated his answer.

The director laughed warmly.

He complimented Luna on introducing their guest to Korean food.

Michael nodded.

“She gets all the credit.”

Luna looked at him.

“All?”

“Well, I did eat it.”

She laughed softly.

The director appeared delighted.

He had no idea what had been said.

Luna translated something appropriate.

Michael decided not to ask.

text:
Today's Satsang on Youtube (A Must Watch) @Gurudev spoke about these mantras and their significance in our life

I checked every mantra against the Rig Veda text of what was said and here is the fuller explanation.

What is Panchamrit Abhishekam?

Panchamrit means five nectars. In abhishekam, the deity is bathed with five sacred substances, one after another, each with its own mantra: milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar. Afterwards the same mixture is shared as prasad. Outwardly it is bathing the idol. Inwardly it is a prayer that our own life takes on the quality of each nectar. Each of the five stands for something: milk for purity, curd for prosperity, honey for unity and sweet speech, ghee for strength and knowledge, sugar for bliss.

The note you shared says Gurudev spoke about these mantras on 7 Nov 2026. It gives them in this order: honey, milk, curd, ghee, sugar. I have kept that order, and cleaned the mantras against the Rig Veda text.

1) Honey, Madhu, from the Madhu Suktam, Rig Veda 1.90.6-8

मधु वाता ऋतायते मधु क्षरन्ति सिन्धवः ।
माध्वीर्नः सन्त्वोषधीः ॥
मधु नक्तमुतोषसो मधुमत् पार्थिवं रजः ।
मधु द्यौरस्तु नः पिता ॥
मधुमान्नो वनस्पतिर्मधुमाँ अस्तु सूर्यः ।
माध्वीर्गावो भवन्तु नः ॥

In simple words: May the winds blow sweetly, may the rivers pour sweet waters, may the herbs be sweet and nourishing for us. May the night be sweet and the dawns sweet, may the dust of the earth be sweet, may heaven above, like a father, look on us sweetly. May the trees be sweet, may the sun give gentle warmth and sweetness, may the cows, our speech and our senses, pour sweetness for us.

This is the heart of the whole abhishekam. It does not ask for sweetness from one place only. It asks that wind, water, plants, night, morning, earth, sky, trees, sun and speech, everything around us and within us, become sweet. Honey here is not only the substance poured. It is the prayer that our words and our life become sweet.

2. Milk, from Rig Veda 1.91.16, a prayer to Soma

आ प्यायस्व समेतु ते विश्वतः सोम वृष्ण्यम् ।
भवा वाजस्य सङ्गथे ॥

Aapyayasva sametu te vishvatah soma vrishniyam, bhava vajasya sangathe.

Meaning: O Soma, grow and gather your strength from all sides, and be with us in the gaining of food, strength and prosperity.

Soma here is the divine life energy, the nectar within. Milk stands for purity and calm, and the mantra asks that our inner strength swell and gather, the way milk nourishes and cools. So the milk bath is a prayer for a pure heart and for strength that comes from every side.

3. Curd, Dahi, from Rig Veda 4.39.6, to Dadhikravan

दधिक्राव्णो अकारिषं जिष्णोरश्वस्य वाजिनः ।
सुरभि नो मुखा करात् प्र ण आयूँषि तारिषत् ॥

Dadhikravno akarisham jishnor ashvasya vajinah, surabhi no mukha karat pra na ayumshi tarishat.

Meaning: I have sung the praise of Dadhikravan, the strong conquering horse. May he make our mouths fragrant, and may he lengthen the days of our life.

Dadhikravan is the divine swift horse, a symbol of victorious energy. Curd stands for prosperity and steadiness. The prayer is very practical: let our speech be fragrant, that is, pure and pleasant, and let our life be long and healthy. This same mantra is also used in daily Sandhyavandanam as a prayer for purifying speech, which shows how central sweet speech is in this whole set of mantras.

4. Ghee, from the Yajurveda, the pavitra mantra

शुक्रमसि ज्योतिरसि तेजोऽसि देवो वः सवितोत्पुनात्वच्छिद्रेण पवित्रेण वसोः सूर्यस्य रश्मिभिः ।

Shukramasi jyotirasi tejo asi, devo vah savitotpunatv achhidrena pavitrena vasoh suryasya rashmibhih. Then the deity's name is spoken, and snanapayami, I bathe you.

Meaning: O Divine Consciousness, you are absolute purity, you are the flame of knowledge, you are spiritual energy itself. Just as the Sun purifies the whole universe with his flawless rays, may that same divine power purify my body, mind and intellect today. I offer this pure ghee as a symbol of my devotion.

Ghee stands for strength, victory and knowledge. It is the most refined form of milk, made through fire, so it also stands for how the gross becomes subtle. This mantra is a prayer for inner purification, and it is the only one of the five that directly asks for the cleansing of body, mind and intellect.

5. Sugar, Sharkara, from Rig Veda 9.85.6, to Soma Pavamana

स्वादुः पवस्व दिव्याय जन्मने स्वादुरिन्द्राय सुहवीतु नाम्ने ।
स्वादुर्मित्राय वरुणाय वायवे बृहस्पतये मधुमाँ अदाभ्यः ॥

Svaduh pavasva divyaya janmane, svadur indraya suhavitu namne, svadur mitraya varunaya vayave brihaspataye madhumam adabhyah.

Meaning: Flow sweetly, O Soma, for the divine birth within us. Flow sweetly for Indra, who is called with devotion. Flow sweetly for Mitra, Varuna, Vayu and Brihaspati, you who are full of honey-like sweetness and cannot be harmed.

Soma Pavamana means Soma the purifier, the nectar being purified as it flows. Sugar stands for bliss and happiness. So the last bath is a prayer that sweetness flows through us and delights all the divine powers, friendship, cosmic law, breath and wisdom, and that the divine nature within us wakes up.

The thread that joins all five

Three of the five mantras are really one prayer said in different ways: let everything be sweet. The Madhu Suktam asks sweetness from the whole world. The curd mantra asks for a fragrant mouth, sweet speech. The sugar mantra asks the nectar to flow sweetly within. Around that, milk asks for purity and gathered strength, and ghee asks for purification of body, mind and intellect. So the abhishekam is a full prayer for a life that is pure, prosperous, strong, sweet in speech and full of bliss, and Gurudev's point in speaking about these mantras is that the ritual is not only about bathing the idol, it is about bathing our own inner being in these five qualities.

text:
Barry Sanders’ dad refused to shake his college coach’s hand.

Barry Files #10 · Part 1

So Barry did something he had never done before.

In the video below, Barry reveals the day he went against his father…

Barry grew up in Wichita, Kansas, one of 11 kids. His dad William was a roofer, and the toughest critic Barry ever had.

In his senior year of high school, Barry got only two college offers. Tulsa and Oklahoma State.

His dad wanted Tulsa, because Barry could start there right away.

At Oklahoma State, he would have to sit behind an All-American running back named Thurman Thomas.

Barry picked Oklahoma State anyway.

The morning the coach came to their house to sign him, his dad wouldn’t shake the man’s hand. He said his son was making a mistake and walked out.

And there was one more problem. William Sanders was a lifelong Oklahoma fan. Oklahoma State is their biggest rival.

His son had just picked the other side.

Barry was 17. It was the first time he had ever said no to his father.

Was his dad right?

First Nations is an important philosophy to be studied and reflected upon in these times....

The Creator and the Animals

Long ago, the Creator gathered all the animals together. He wished to give humanity a profound gift: the understanding that human beings possess the power to shape their own reality.

But the Creator wanted this knowledge hidden until humanity developed the wisdom to understand it.

He asked the animals where such a precious gift should be concealed.

The Eagle stepped forward and offered to carry the knowledge all the way to the moon, where no human could reach it.

The Creator refused, explaining that humanity would eventually travel to the moon.

The Salmon offered to carry the gift into the deepest depths of the ocean.

Again, the Creator refused. Humanity would eventually explore even the ocean's deepest places.

The Buffalo proposed burying the knowledge beneath the vast Great Plains, deep within the earth itself.

But the Creator knew that human beings would eventually dig into the earth and discover it.

Finally, Grandmother Mole came forward.

Although Mole's physical eyes could scarcely see, she possessed a different kind of vision: the wisdom to see beyond outward appearances.

She offered a remarkably simple suggestion:

“Put it inside them.”

The Creator recognized the wisdom of her suggestion and placed the precious knowledge within humanity itself.

text:
Happy Diwali Lance, hope you’re well!

Some thoughts:

The differential regulatory treatment of non-medical wellness devices is already the norm in numerous countries.

Qualifying non-medical wellness devices are not subject to the same regulatory requirements as medical devices under CDSCO in India, MHRA in the UK, or FDA in the US. The precise classification depends on the device’s intended use, claims and applicable regulatory framework.

If that same device claimed to diagnose or clinically monitor a medical condition, such as atrial fibrillation, hypertension or sleep apnoea, those functions could bring it within medical-device regulation. Importantly, regulatory requirements can apply to specific medical functions within a consumer wellness device without necessarily extending to its other non-medical features.

For example, WHOOP MG and Apple Watch Series 11 offer ECG features that can identify signs of atrial fibrillation. Those specific functions are regulated as medical devices. Meanwhile, Apple offers a Health Age estimate based on Apple Watch data as a wellness feature, rather than a diagnostic medical claim.

If Temple claimed to detect or predict an impending TIA, that would similarly constitute a medical claim requiring an appropriate regulatory pathway.

Personally, I don’t think we need paternalistic protections that prevent healthy consumers from buying novel, low-risk wellness technology. People should be free to decide what devices they want to buy. Patients who need devices for clinical purposes can seek advice from their doctors, and some medical devices may even require a prescription.

The knowledge asymmetry has arguably never been smaller. AI is empowering people with access to health information like never before. Public commentary and criticism on social media are also useful for consumers.

The flip side of more stringent regulation for non-medical wellness devices is less freedom of choice for consumers. If there’s a meaningful risk of medical harm, regulators have a responsibility to intervene.

I think we should distinguish between premarket medical-device regulation and postmarket consumer protection. Informed adults should be free to purchase novel, low-risk wellness products without manufacturers having to satisfy medical-device-level premarket evidence requirements. Shouldn’t we require evidence that such additional regulatory burdens would meaningfully improve safety without disproportionately restricting consumer choice or innovation? Where the principal risk is financial loss from misleading product claims, consumer protection laws provide an alternative regulatory mechanism for holding manufacturers accountable.

text:
🚨 $RKLB: ROCKET LAB REPORTS Q3 EARNINGS ON MONDAY. 

HERE'S A RECAP OF WHAT PETER BECK AND HIS TEAM HAVE BEEN DOING.

Rocket Lab reports earnings on November 9 and I wanted to go through some of the developments we've seen during Q3 and since the quarter ended.

There's been a lot happening at  beyond Electron launches. Government contracts, satellite manufacturing, the Iridium acquisition, Neutron customers and new spacecraft technology.

1. $397M U.S. SPACE FORCE CONTRACT: AUGUST 4

Rocket Lab secured a contract worth up to $397M to develop, launch and operate Flatellite spacecraft for the Space Force's Space Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program.

This is one of my favorite developments because Rocket Lab isn't simply providing a launch vehicle. It's taking responsibility for the satellites, their launch on Neutron and their operation in orbit.

It's a much bigger role in the defense supply chain.

2. $266M MISSILE DEFENSE CONTRACT — JULY 27

The Space Force awarded Rocket Lab a contract worth up to $266M for 12 suborbital launches, with options for six more.

These missions support missile defense testing and will primarily use the company's expanding launch infrastructure in Alaska.

It creates another source of launch demand outside traditional commercial satellite deployment.

3. 20 ADDITIONAL ELECTRON LAUNCHES FOR SYNSPECTIVE — SEPTEMBER 30

This was Rocket Lab's largest commercial Electron launch agreement to date.

Synspective signed for another 20 dedicated missions, bringing its total contracted Electron missions with Rocket Lab to 47.

Think about that customer relationship. Instead of booking one launch, evaluating another provider and repeating the process, Synspective continues expanding with Rocket Lab as its constellation grows.

4. THE IRIDIUM ACQUISITION MOVED CLOSER TO COMPLETION — SEPTEMBER

Rocket Lab completed a $1.944B at-the-market equity offering, issuing approximately 29.3M shares to help finance its proposed acquisition of Iridium.

It also arranged for Iridium's existing $1.775B term loan facility to remain in place after the transaction and terminated its $3.6B bridge financing commitment.

Yes, the equity raise created dilution. But the financing significantly reduces uncertainty around funding the acquisition.

The transaction still requires regulatory approvals and is expected to close in 2027.

If completed, Rocket Lab would move much further into owning and operating satellite communications services rather than just manufacturing and launching hardware.

5. EIGHT ROCKET LAB BUILT SATELLITE PLATFORMS REACHED ORBIT — AUGUST 16

Eight satellite platforms built by Rocket Lab for MDA Space successfully reached orbit to support Globalstar's constellation.

These are part of a $143M agreement covering 17 satellite platforms.

All eight established contact and were reported to be functioning normally.

This demonstrates something investors sometimes overlook. Rocket Lab is already a meaningful spacecraft manufacturer, even when another company is the prime contractor.

6. KEPLER BOOKED A DEDICATED NEUTRON LAUNCH — AUGUST 10

Kepler Communications selected Neutron to launch multiple satellites supporting optical connectivity, orbital computing and hosted payloads.

The mission is scheduled no earlier than 2028.

And this is worth watching because Rocket Lab is securing commercial launch commitments before Neutron enters service.

The demand is there. The engineering challenge is delivering the rocket.

7. ROCKET LAB ENTERED THE SPACE FORCE'S SPACE DATA NETWORK PROGRAM — AUGUST 18

Rocket Lab joined the Space Force's Space Data Network Consortium and received two delivery orders totaling $12M.

The work involves demonstrating interoperability for secure optical communications in space.

It may look small compared with the $397M contract, but it's another entry point into military communications infrastructure.

8. ROCKET LAB RELEASED ITS IMM APEX SOLAR CELL — SEPTEMBER 8

The new solar cell offers 31.5% beginning-of-life conversion efficiency and 40% lower mass.

It also eliminates the germanium substrate used in conventional multi junction solar cells.

I like this one because it shows how Rocket Lab is building a business around components that other spacecraft manufacturers need, not just the rockets carrying those spacecraft.

9. ELECTRON CONTINUED DELIVERING — THROUGH SEPTEMBER 30

Rocket Lab completed its 97th Electron flight in September, representing its 18th launch of 2026.

Then, after the quarter ended, it completed its 98th and 99th missions in October and November.

Launch reliability and repeatability are what make the commercial launch business viable.

Customers want their satellites delivered when promised.

10. NASA GDC TRAILBLAZER AWARD — OCTOBER 28

A federal contract record shows approximately $28.9M obligated to Rocket Lab for integration and flight of NASA's Geospace Dynamics Constellation Trailblazer payload.

The listed contract ceiling is approximately $36.8M, including options.

Another reminder that NASA remains an important customer across Rocket Lab's expanding launch portfolio.

11. NEUTRON'S FIRST FLIGHT MOVED TO 2027 — OCTOBER 14

We also need to discuss what didn't go according to plan.

Rocket Lab officially moved Neutron's first launch target from 2026 to 2027 following development and manufacturing challenges.

This is important because Neutron is central to several future contracts, including the Space Force Flatellite program.

The delay creates execution risk and I want management to provide a clearer timeline for qualification testing, development spending and the first flight.

There's no point ignoring this just because the company is winning contracts elsewhere.

NOW, WHAT WE SHOULD BE WATCHING ON MONDAY?

Rocket Lab previously guided for Q3 revenue of $250M–$265M, compared with the $234M it reported in Q2.

I'll be looking at revenue, gross margins, backlog, cash consumption, updated Neutron spending and how the company plans to integrate Iridium if the acquisition closes.

A few years ago, Rocket Lab was mostly discussed as a small rocket company competing for satellite launches.

Today, we're talking about a company manufacturing satellites, producing spacecraft components, developing medium lift rockets, securing hundreds of millions in defense contracts and potentially acquiring an established satellite communications operator.

It's a very different business. The important question is whether Rocket Lab can execute all these programs without allowing development costs, dilution and acquisition risks to overwhelm the economics.

The most imp part of Monday's earnings won't be just how many rockets Rocket Lab launched. It'll be how much progress the company has made toward becoming a fully integrated space infrastructure business.

Let's see what Peter Beck has to say.

Many reasons but a mix of ignorance and-or, party loyalty, above all else?
Why do American Jews vote for antisemites like El-Sayed?
By Jonathan S. Tobin
It doesn’t take a degree in political science or a job as a talking head on a cable news network to understand the 2026 midterm elections. As is usually the case, the results were a referendum on the incumbent administration. Though the reasons for it can be disputed, there is no denying that the blue wave that swept the Democratic Party into control of both houses of Congress was a rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and the Republicans.
But there is one aspect of the voting that remains a puzzle for some. How is it that so many Jews in Michigan, indeed a reported majority of early voters according to one survey, voted for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed?

National midterms exit polling suggested that 68% of those who identify as Jews voted for Democrats. That’s not all that much different from the surveys of the 2024 election. Two years ago, an AP/Fox News poll showed that 66% of Jews backed Democrats, while one conducted by the liberal Jewish Electoral Institute put the number at 71%.

Some observers believed that Jewish support for El-Sayed would be far lower than those numbers. Given his record of open antisemitism, that seemed a reasonable assumption. How could a candidate gain any appreciable Jewish support when he rationalized a terrorist attack on a synagogue and Jewish preschool in West Bloomfield, Mich., opposed Israel’s existence, had credible ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and waged a campaign that hinged on demonizing the pro-Israel AIPAC lobby and driving Jews from the public square, while employing tropes of Jew-hatred that resembled The Protocols of the Elders of Zion?

A majority of Jewish votes went to El-Sayed

The evidence appears to be that the percentage of Jews who voted for him wasn’t all that much lower than those who favored the average Democrat. While one should always take exit polls with a grain of salt, one survey of those who voted early in Michigan showed that a large majority of those who identify as Jewish—57%—voted for El-Sayed.

If that result is even remotely accurate how can that be explained? And what does that say about the state of American Jewry in 2026, especially considering that it took place amid a global surge of antisemitism that began with the Hamas-led, Palestinian Arab terror attacks on Israeli communities on Oct. 7, 2023?

El-Sayed was just one of many Democrats who benefited from the general dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, and he is just one of many opponents of Israel that will be part of the large freshman class of Democrats in the House and Senate in the next Congress.

The list includes such notable additions as Darializa Avila Chevalier, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who led a pro-Hamas demonstration in New York City’s Times Square on Oct. 8, 2023 and will soon represent Northern Manhattan in the House of Representatives.

Other DSA members who oppose the existence of the Jewish state, who will be joining the already expanded left-wing congressional “Squad,” include Claire Valdez, also of New York City, Philadelphia’s Chris Rabb, Denver’s Melat Kiros and Los Angeles’s Angela Gonzales-Torres.

And that’s not even noting the many others, whose anti-Israel stances, including those who repeat the blood libel that Israel committed “genocide” in the Gaza Strip, make them indistinguishable from DSA members.

It’s not about Netanyahu

Many Democrats claim to still support Israel. But the list of those who are willing to emphatically refute the antisemitic lies about the Gaza war or the conflict with the Palestinians in general that have been normalized in public discourse, are now few and far between.

Few oppose restrictions or bans on military aid to Israel in wartime or sanctions against Jews in Judea and Samaria, who have been demonized by the false narrative of “settler violence.” Indeed, once you get past Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Reps. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.) and Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), there aren’t many Democrats in Congress who fit that description.

Moreover, the notion that the Democratic Party’s turn against Israel can be explained by being alienated by the policies and statements of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is a myth.

Pro-Israel Jewish Democrats claim that Netanyahu has destroyed Democratic support for the Jewish state by favoring Republicans, especially Trump. But this is false. In the last two decades, it is the Democrats who have turned on Israel, not just Netanyahu, by embracing appeasement of Iran and clinging to the two-state solution and “land for peace” formulas that most Israelis rightly understand as merely a recipe for more Oct. 7-style terror atrocities, not an end to the conflict.

If anyone still doubts that, they need to read the exchange on X between Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid and Brad Lander, the Democrat who was just elected to Congress from New York City.

Lander, a former city comptroller, won his seat by defeating Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), a man with impeccable liberal and anti-Trump credentials and a critic of Netanyahu, who wouldn’t disavow support for Israel, in a Democratic primary.

Lander is Jewish and claims to not oppose Israel’s existence, but he accused it of “genocide” during the campaign and demanded that Goldman do the same. Lander responded with scorn to Lapid’s expectation that a change in power in Jerusalem and more outreach from Israeli leaders like him, who are eager to be friends with the Democrats, would change things. He made it clear that Democrats like him, who are allied with the antisemitic New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and even others who are not that extreme, aren’t interested in mainstream Israeli opinion, even when it comes from liberals who want to be his allies.

Lander, who campaigned for Mamdani after losing to him in the mayoral primary, wants Israel to show “respect for international law and human rights.” While that comment is rooted in lies about both international law and Israaeli conduct, we know what it means. At a minimum, he’s demanding withdrawal from Judea, Samaria and Jerusalem and the creation of a Palestinian state, likely run by Hamas, that would pose a deadly threat to Israel’s existence. That’s something that not even the left-leaning “anyone but Bibi” coalition that seeks to replace Netanyahu couldn’t possibly accept.

This perspective, which is where many of those Americans—who, like Lander, style themselves “liberal Zionists” as opposed to the anti-Zionists of the DSA—is a partial reason why Jews continue to vote for Democrats.

Yet even that doesn’t fully explain why nearly three in five Michigan Jews may have voted for a person like El-Sayed, who is far more hostile to Jewish national existence than Lander. Indeed, not without reason, the Republican Jewish Coalition called El-Sayed the most antisemitic Senate candidate in America.

Politics flow from demography

In order to fully understand why the majority of Jews remain among the most loyal supporters of the Democrats, one needs to comprehend the cultural shift among Americans in general when it comes to politics. It is now axiomatic that in this hyper-partisan era, in which most Americans are thoroughly secular, politics now plays the role in their lives that was once played by religion.

That is even more the case for the overwhelming majority of Jews, who are non-Orthodox and politically liberal.

For this dominant sector of U.S. Jewish demography, liberal political stands—a list of beliefs that can shift with changing political fashions on the left—and devotion to the Democrats is their religion. Indeed, the positions taken by the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism, the policy arm of the largest U.S. Jewish denomination, are more or less those of most Democrats on a host of issues, many of which are not specifically Jewish in scope.

There has been a lot of talk about some movement toward the Republicans among Jews in recent years. Many Jewish liberals have been deeply shocked by the reaction to Oct. 7 from the American political left, especially as they saw their children targeted by pro-Hamas mobs on campuses. But it is yet to be proved that a significant percentage have drawn conclusions from this and are ready to change how they vote.

There was some reason to believe that in states like Florida, Jews were more likely to vote for candidates from a GOP that had become a lockstep supporter of the Jewish state. Trump’s efforts to combat antisemitism on college campuses also gave them a reason to switch sides. And some prominent Jews, like retired Harvard University legal scholar and longtime liberal advocate Alan Dershowitz, have done so.

But as the 2024 and 2026 elections showed, Jewish loyalty to the Democrats has continued even as they have largely transitioned into being the country’s anti-Israel party, Those who agree with Dershowitz appear to be the exceptions that prove the rule.

Part of the explanation comes not so much from ideology as it does from demography. As surveys conducted by the Pew Research Center have shown, the fastest growing sector of the American Jewish population is characterized by demographers as “Jews of no religion.”

That doesn’t just mean that they don’t practice Judaism. It encompasses a broad shift away from traditional ideas about what it means to be Jewish with devotion to religious faith, Jewish law and tradition and, above all, a sense of Jewish peoplehood being discarded. That has led to significant numbers of those who may identify as Jewish in some way but have no real connection to organized Jewish life, including synagogues, community centers and organizations that represent and serve Jews.

This is a function of the assimilation and intermarriage rates in the vicinity of 70% for non-Orthodox Jews, not critiques of Israeli policies or Netanyahu.

Giving a pass to Jew-hatred

It also means that many of them have increasingly fewer ties to the half of the world’s Jewish population that lives in Israel. That doesn’t just mean that they have a poor understanding or none at all about why Israeli Jews think as they do. They have little idea why Israelis are prepared to fight to defend their homes and families against Palestinian foes, whose national existence is inextricably linked to a century-old genocidal war on Zionism, for which the atrocities of Oct. 7 was just the trailer.

But they also don’t seem to understand that devotion to the land of Israel is central to Jewish identity, as Jews have understood it for the past 3,000 years. Many liberal Jews have rejected the widely-accepted International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism, because they want one that allows opposition to Israel’s existence, and not just criticism of it. without being accused of hating Jews.

Once you grasp that, it’s easier to comprehend why a not-inconsiderable number of Jews are willing to believe that someone like El-Sayed, who is in favor of the destruction of the Jewish state—something that would inevitably require the genocide of half of the Jews currently alive—but claims to love Jews, isn’t an antisemite or a threat to them.

The stances of “liberal Zionists” like the cynical Lander are likely the product of his knowing that liberal Democrats have been largely indoctrinated in the toxic doctrines of critical race theory, intersectionality and settler-colonialism and, therefore, falsely define Israel and the Jews as “white oppressors.”

That is why Democrats like him are becoming difficult to distinguish from open DSA opponents of Israel, or even antisemites like El-Sayed. Even those who merely think Israel should be more amenable to territorial withdrawals have little sympathy for the majority of Jewish Israelis who are religious or nationalist. Such American Jews haven’t paid attention to the way Palestinians have consistently rejected peace offers, because the only solution they desire is one in which Israel no longer exists.

Defining Jewish identity

For those whose Jewish identity is still firmly rooted in Jewish tradition, a vote for someone like El-Sayed is hard to justify even if they are loyal Democrats.

Perhaps few would, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, think that adding another member to the Democratic Senate caucus is more important than Israel’s survival or that of the Jewish people. But in the current political atmosphere, it is likely that some of them might have done so simply because they hate Trump and the Republicans more than they love Israel.

It is arguable that those with such a negligible sense of their identity as Jews are unlikely to maintain themselves as a separate community or one with any coherence. Indeed, that may already be the case, as the number of those Jews of no religion continues to multiply. Part of the problem with surveys that measure Jewish opinion or votes is that a growing number of those who say they are Jewish have few actual ties to Jewish life.

If one were to only count those Jews who have such connections or beliefs, the statistics about their voting habits and their beliefs might be very different from those that show that the Jewish population is as liberal and loyal to the Democrats as they ever were.

Even if that is true, it is still a measure of the ignorance and the lack of identification with the ongoing struggle for Jewish survival in an age of growing antisemitism that so many Jews vote for the likes of El-Sayed, Chevalier, Mamdani and even Lander. It is a sign of a community that has lost its way.

With so much of the mainstream liberal media—upon which most Jews depend for information about the Middle East and the battle against antisemitism— mainstreaming misinformation and blood libels about Israel, it’s not that surprising that they aren’t questioning knee-jerk support for Jew-hating Democrats.

But it must motivate those who understand just how wrongheaded such stances are to redouble their efforts to promote Jewish education and connection to the Jewish state as well as in telling the truth about the war against Israel.

The only way to combat the Jewish illiteracy that leads so many to vote for antisemites out of partisan loyalty is to spread the truth about Jewish life and Israel.

"this week in 1980"

I had just 2 or 3 weeks before moved to Florida.  I was 21.  I hated my job (grocery store cashier).  So, on the spur of the moment - which is easier at 21 than at almost any other age - I loaded up the '75 Nova and drove 1000 miles south with nothing waiting for me there.  But I did have a plan.

I stopped at Cocoa, Florida.  Not sight seeing.  Rather, job seeking.  Didn't find anything there.  Pointed the car north and was in Daytona Beach next day.  Newspapers on strike.  No wanted ads to search.  Back on the road north.  Next stop, St. Augustine.

The "plan" was to keep looking for work at every stop, working my way north.  If I didn't find anything by Charleston, SC, then I'd come home humbled and go back to the grocery store job.

At St. Augustine, I was offered full-time work at the Fountain of Youth.  I took it.  Eventually, I came home.  Partly homesickness.  Partly that Florida really wasn't "me."  Wasn't the paradise I imagined.

That was - to this day - the Gamble of My Life.

Remembered fondly.

text:
A term I explain to almost every buyer at some point: the appraisal gap.

Here's what it means. You offer $300,000 on a house. The bank sends an appraiser, and they value the home at $290,000. The bank will only lend based on that lower number — so now there's a $10,000 gap between what you agreed to pay and what the bank will finance.

In a competitive market, buyers sometimes agree upfront to cover a certain amount of that gap in cash if it happens, to make their offer more attractive to a seller. It's not required, and it's not right for every buyer — but understanding it before you're in a bidding situation means you're not caught off guard.

If you're buying in Southern Indiana or Kentuckiana this year, ask your agent to walk through exactly how this would work for your budget before you write an offer.

text:
Long Post alert.  This is in regards to Lane Myers and Tucson prosecutor. . I am just giving my opinion on what I think is possible. 

I'm going to tell y'all a story, and by the time I'm finished, you'll understand why I believe Lane Myers may have just pulled one of the smartest moves I've ever seen.

First, part of this story is factual. The rest is my personal theory, based on conversations I've had and little things said to me over the years.

George Torres was my landlord when I lived in Downey, California. He was also the millionaire owner of Numero Uno Markets, a chain of Mexican grocery stores throughout California.

Starting back in the late 1980s, law enforcement seemed to have it out for this man. Downey PD, L.A. County Sheriff's Department, you name it. They would arrest him once, twice, sometimes three times a month. He'd sit in jail for days, only to be released because they didn't have enough evidence to move forward.

This went on for decades. At one point, I believe they arrested him four times in a single month. He tried filing lawsuits and fighting back, but nothing worked.

Some believed he was being targeted because he was an immigrant who came here, built a successful business, and dominated the Hispanic grocery market. I don't know why they were after him. I wasn't around when it started.

Then came the federal case.

George Torres was convicted of serious felonies, including RICO, conspiracy to commit murder, solicitation of murder, tax fraud, and numerous other charges. If I remember correctly, there were around 59 felony counts altogether.

He was looking at spending the rest of his life in prison.

A FEDERAL JURY found him guilty.

But then the prosecution's key witness admitted his testimony was a lie. And according to what I understood, it wasn't just a lie. It was a PLANNED lie.

His convictions were overturned.

Now, some people believe Torres paid off federal officials to get out of prison. I'm not saying that kind of corruption doesn't happen, but wouldn't that normally be something you tried BEFORE a conviction?

Go dig into the actual court proceedings instead of just reading what the newspapers wanted everybody to know. Look at what happened after the conviction and the actual outcome.

Because that's where my theory begins.

I knew Mr. Torres personally. He was my landlord. We'd sit outside at the property in Downey, around the patio and pool area, and just talk.

He wasn't some stuck-up millionaire. He was actually a pretty normal, laid-back guy. Everybody was equal to him unless you pissed him off.

And trust me, pissing George Torres off was not a good idea. It could be hazardous to your health.

Luckily, he liked me.

Now, based on conversations we had over the years, I came to believe something.

I think George Torres got tired of being fucked with.

I think he realized law enforcement wasn't going to leave him alone, no matter what he did.

And I think he figured out a way to beat them at their own game.

Here's how I imagine it happened.

What if Torres found some young L.A. County thug and offered him enough money to testify against him, knowing that testimony would later be exposed as false?

Torres was a very intelligent man. He knew pleading guilty would make it extremely difficult to undo his conviction. But if a jury convicted him based on fabricated testimony, that could give him grounds to have the conviction overturned.

And I think he knew that.

What if he let them believe they'd finally won, knowing the whole thing would eventually fall apart?

And what if the person who testified was financially taken care of afterward?

I can't prove that. I'm not saying it happened.

But when I look at where that same witness reportedly ended up in life, living in a multimillion-dollar home with enough financial security to take care of generations of his family, it makes me wonder.

Let's be real. Hypothetically, if somebody offered you ten million dollars to risk 5 years in jail for perjury, how many of y'all would do it?  5 years is the max you can get. And with such a scandal the focus would not be on prosecuting perjury and it was not. 

Shit, some of you would be offering your fingerprints before the man finished talking.

And that brings me to Lane Myers.

Because I think Lane may have done the same exact thing.

Look at everything this man has been through in Tucson.

From what I understand, his problems started because he BOOED at a city council meeting.

Who the fuck gets arrested for booing at a public meeting?

Then came years of legal problems, allegations of stalking, probation, and eventually prison.

I think the people going after Lane looked at him like he was some dorky guy with no intelligence. Somebody they could push around until he finally gave up.

But I think they underestimated him.

Then came those emails allegedly sent to the prosecutor's wife, who was also a university law professor.

And I'm sorry, but telling somebody their husband needs to follow the law doesn't automatically make something a criminal threat.

Yet those emails became central to the allegations that Lane violated his probation.

He sat in county jail for months. Eventually, he ended up in Arizona state prison.

And let me tell y'all something. Arizona prisons are not somewhere you want to be.

So here's what I think happened.

I think Lane knew he hadn't sent those emails. I think he knew the system was stacked against him, and no matter how hard he fought, he wasn't going to win by continuing to play their game.

So what if he decided to let them win first?

What if he accepted going to prison because he knew there was evidence out there that could eventually blow the entire case apart?

He had friends on the outside. He had people who could continue looking into things while he was locked up.

And then comes the bombshell.

Information surfaces suggesting the IP address connected to those emails may have originated with the prosecutor himself.

Now, I don't know who uncovered that information or what evidence led them there. And an IP address alone doesn't prove who physically sent an email.

But somebody had to go looking. That information didn't just magically appear.

And if it turns out those emails were fabricated or sent by somebody connected to the prosecution, imagine what that means.

The very evidence used to send Lane to prison could become the evidence that exposes misconduct by the people prosecuting him.

Who the fuck wins then?

Think about it.

You spend years going after this man. You arrest him, prosecute him, put him on probation, and eventually send him to prison.

And then potentially the entire thing blows up in your face.

Now Lane could become the victim of serious constitutional violations, with the possibility of civil litigation and substantial damages.

We're talking potentially millions of dollars if the evidence supports those claims.

Of course, there could be things we don't know. Evidence could come out that changes everything, and Lane could end up back in prison. I'm not claiming to know how this will end.

But if it turns out the way many of us believe it might, the people who spent years trying to beat this man may have handed him the biggest victory of his life.

And that's why I keep thinking about my old landlord, George Torres.

Two completely different men. Two completely different cases.

But possibly the same strategy.

Sometimes the only way to beat somebody is to let them think they've already won.

I think Lane got tired, just like I believe Torres got tired.

And I think Lane may have realized that the only way to expose what was happening was to let the system overplay its hand.

If he deliberately allowed himself to go to prison knowing the evidence would eventually come out, that's not stupidity.

That's intelligence. That's patience. That's cunning.

And that's one hell of a way to tell the Pima County Prosecutor's Office to go fuck itself.

Again, this is my opinion. I can't prove either man planned any of it.

But after the conversations I personally had with George Torres, and everything I've watched happen with Lane Myers, I can't help seeing the similarities.

And if I'm right?

Hell, maybe Lane Myers shouldn't be booing at city council meetings.

Maybe he ought to be running for city council.

A Canadian business with at least $1 million in annual revenue may qualify for BDC's LIFT digital transformation and AI financing.

That stream offers loans from $25,000 to $2 million for eligible projects involving digital systems, data, AI or cybersecurity. A BDC Advisory Services Digital Plan is required. Profitability, credit history and the proposed investment also matter.

The productivity and equipment stream has different rules: at least $5 million in revenue, eligible sectors, and loans from $350,000 to $5 million. Don't use that higher loan limit when planning an application to the digital/AI stream.

Start with the business problem you need to solve, the implementation costs and how you'll measure the result. Then ask BDC which stream fits.

This is repayable financing with advisory support, not a grant. Check BDC's current requirements before building it into your budget.

text:
The MAGA Coalition Disintegrates. 
MAGA 'Coalition' never existed.
The Tea Party 'Coalition' never existed.

'Movements' have to be institutionalized.  Otherwise they fade away. @elonmusk passed up the chance to institutionalize MAGA into another political party and the Republican Party simply split.

The Republican Party barely exists. The Democrat Party is about to undergo a nasty cultural civil war. What does it mean to say you are a Republican, Democrat, Liberal or Conservative? 

Things could hardly have been worse for Trump’s Republicans on Tuesday—but they may be in 2028.

‘The president always loses, for whatever reason, the midterms,” President Trump said a few weeks ago. What makes 2026 remarkable is the size and scope of GOP losses—and the political left turn those losses portend.

Democrats had their best midterm since 1974, when public furor at the Watergate scandal, President Nixon’s resignation and President Ford’s controversial pardon of Nixon moved Congress decisively to the left. The Democrats are projected to win the 2026 national House vote by 13 points. One estimate has them winning 258 seats, their largest majority since 2008.

At this writing, Democrats have picked up seven Senate seats. They may pick up additional seats in Alaska and—this isn’t a misprint—Mississippi. Democrats flipped at least five governorships, in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. At least 12 state legislative chambers flipped from red to blue.

Democrats overcame structural barriers that might have limited their reach, beginning with the political terrain. Republicans believed they could hold ground in states that voted for Mr. Trump by double digits several times. They were wrong. Democrats won every Senate election that the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rated a tossup, from Maine, which Kamala Harris carried by 7 points, to Kansas, which Mr. Trump won by 16 points. Kansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Republicans redrew state congressional maps last year to protect their House majority. The gerrymandering backfired. Republican votes were spread too thin, and not even the most sophisticated gerrymander can withstand an electoral tsunami. 

Democrats feared that a Supreme Court decision striking down racial gerrymanders would reduce black political participation and voting power. Instead, black representation at both the state and federal levels is set to rise. Black statewide candidates won many contests, including the Georgia governorship and probably that Mississippi Senate seat.

The Republican National Committee and outside groups had built up a significant cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts. The money had little effect. Democratic candidates outraised Republicans, and Democrats outspent Republicans overall for the second straight election, according to https://t.co/E87AfTF95r. Two of the Democrats’ favorite bogeymen—the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision and Elon Musk—couldn’t stop the party’s advance.

That’s because the GOP was overwhelmed by a wave of revulsion to Mr. Trump and his policies. The most telling midterm statistic is presidential job approval. Exit polls had Trump’s approval rating at 38%. The 76% of voters who said they are “dissatisfied or angry” at the way things are going in the country voted overwhelmingly for Democrats. So did the 75% of voters who said the economy is “not so good or poor.” Voters said Mr. Trump has the wrong priorities, puts his personal interest above the public interest, and made economic conditions worse. Economic growth and full employment mattered less than inflation and the corresponding decline in real wages.

Mr. Trump was elected in 2024 on the promise of reducing inflation, closing the border, bringing change to Washington and achieving peace through strength. Though he has made strides toward all these goals, especially curbing illegal immigration, he hasn’t crossed the finish line and often trips over his own feet.

Voters probably know more about Mr. Trump’s renovations to the White House and Reflecting Pool than about the tax cuts, savings accounts and welfare and education reforms in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. They certainly have learned through experience that while inflation rates may fall, prices generally don’t. Inflation eats up wage gains—and presidential support.

Failing to address voter concerns meaningfully causes political coalitions to disappear. Mr. Trump won white voters by 15 points two years ago; on Tuesday, Republicans split them evenly with Democrats. Mr. Trump lost Latino voters by 5 points in 2024; Republicans lost them by 27 points in 2026.

The same shift happened with other key blocs: Mr. Trump lost independents by 3 points; Republicans in 2026 by 14. Mr. Trump lost 18- to 29-year-olds by 11 points; Republicans this year by 47. Mr. Trump won suburban voters by 4 points; his party lost them Tuesday by 18. The entire country—every region, every demographic—felt the blues.

How large a role the Iran war played in this debacle is unclear. Vice President JD Vance said in a fiery social-media post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.” Mr. Trump told reporters that while the war “drove gasoline up a little bit short term,” he stands by his decision to attack because “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

No one mentioned that the Iran war has been on pause, alternating between inconclusive negotiations and occasional punitive strikes, since Mr. Trump announced a ceasefire in April. Nor has the president or any prominent member of his administration devoted significant time to making the case for the intervention. Though 63% of voters said Operation Epic Fury was the wrong decision, only 34% said it was “crucial” to their vote. By contrast, 49% said the cost of living and 55% said government corruption was crucial.

To be sure, the Iranian regime’s closing of the Strait of Hormuz and threat to Gulf energy infrastructure has contributed to the cost of living. But tariffs have too. When asked if Mr. Trump’s tariff policies have helped or hurt the economy, 66% said they hurt. A slightly smaller majority—58%—said the administration’s immigration enforcement has gone too far.

An unresolved foreign intervention, protectionism, excessive use of force in deportation efforts and the stench of corruption all contributed to the Republican rout. No single variable could have been changed to make things right. But that won’t stop various GOP factions from blaming their intraparty antagonists for failure at the polls.

Mr. Trump began the finger-pointing on election night when he told the Journal that some Republican candidates “could have been better” and “had a lot of flaws.” He neglected to mention that his hand-selected candidates in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas went down in double-digit defeats. Nor did he name another of his picks, Darline Graham of South Carolina, who lost by 4 points. Mr. Vance followed up by assigning responsibility for the defeat to Iran hawks and supporters of the U.S.-Israel alliance—his boss presumably excepted.

The infighting will continue throughout the 2028 presidential campaign. As retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik pointed out, Mr. Trump is a singular historical figure whose winning coalitions can’t be replicated. His victories were tied less to principles than to personal charisma. Republicans will spend the coming years arguing over their post-Trump identity: What new face do they wish to present to the electorate? Which agenda will persuade swing voters and also lead to a flourishing economy and society? How best to combat the axis of aggressors—China, Russia, Iran and North Korea—dead-set on bringing America to heel?

While Mr. Vance may be the GOP front-runner, he won’t be the only Republican offering answers to such questions. The election results make it more likely that he will have multiple challengers for the presidential nomination, possibly including fellow members of Mr. Trump’s cabinet. Arguments over economic growth, foreign intervention, abortion, welfare and the nature of American citizenship will define conservatism and the Republican program. Looming above will be Mr. Trump, who is never reluctant to offer his opinions, and whose executive orders and foreign policy will shape the environment in ways no one can predict.

Still, you don’t need a betting market to know that American politics is tacking left. Progressive causes and proposals have been center stage for the past year—anti-ICE protests, demands for healthcare subsidies, calls for moratoriums on data-center construction and artificial-intelligence development, denunciations of Israel and its American supporters. Socialist and progressive stars such as New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Ro Khanna drive the discourse.

Offshoots of Mr. Trump’s coalition have joined forces with the left to call for ending aid to Israel and withdrawing from the Middle East. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed ran ads featuring Tucker Carlson’s endorsement. Mr. Vance said last December that he appreciated Mr. Mamdani, Mr. Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders. He didn’t say anything about Sen. John Fetterman, the pro-Israel Democrat who appeared in a video at the GOP’s midterm convention in September.

The socialist “Squad” of congressmen aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America is set to double in size. The much larger House Progressive Caucus—currently some 100 members—will grow even more. The line between socialism and progressivism is blurry: Rep. Ilhan Omar is a founding member of the Squad and deputy chairman of the Progressive Caucus. The Squad and Progressives will push Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer to the left on tech, immigration and Israel, no matter how much the party elite would prefer to emphasize affordability and investigations ahead of 2028.

As Mr. Trump pointed out, the president’s party regularly suffers losses in the sixth year of his term. The fallout spreads beyond that presidency. The 2006 midterm election was a preview of Democratic gains in 2008 and Barack Obama’s attempts to put America on a “New Foundation” from 2009-11. The Democrats’ loss of the Senate in 2014 was a taste of Mr. Trump’s first victory and unified GOP control of government from 2017 to 2019.

Thus conservatives who believe in the Constitution, limited government, the rule of law and the Declaration of Independence’s principles of liberty and equality confront a dire prospect: Nov. 3 may foreshadow a period of progressive governance in both parties that would leave Americans poorer, weaker and less free. It may turn out that the most prescient words of this election were uttered last month in New York City when Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told donors, “Because if you can win, if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere. Anywhere.”

We are about to find out if she’s right.

Mr. Continetti is a columnist for WSJ Opinion’s Free Expression.

text:
🧬 A Thiel-Backed Startup Is Selling Embryo Selection by IQ. The Ad Regulator Has Already Asked It to Rethink the Claims

Nucleus Genomics, a New York company founded in 2021 by Kian Sadeghi — a Thiel Fellow — and backed by investors including Peter Thiel, Founders Fund, Balaji Srinivasan and Alexis Ohanian's Seven Seven Six, is plastering New York with advertising for its IVF+ service under the slogan "Have your best baby." The poster at the Broadway–Lafayette subway station shows a newborn held in adult hands with the line "IQ is 50% genetic."

What is on offer: after IVF, parents can compare embryos using polygenic scores — risks for conditions such as breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's and schizophrenia, plus height, eye and hair colour, male-pattern baldness and IQ. On 2 September 2026 the company released Nucleus Vitruvian, models for height, body-mass index and intelligence; the catalogue carries 35 polygenic models in total. No DNA is edited, and CRISPR plays no part: the choice is among embryos that already exist.

Where "14.3 IQ points" comes from — and why it is not a gain. In Nucleus's own whitepaper the figure is the spread between the highest and lowest predictions across ten hypothetical embryos, not a promised increase for the child finally chosen. The company's calculator is worded the same way: the expected difference between the lowest- and highest-scoring embryo in a set of two to ten. The accuracy of the intelligence model is about 19% of variance explained within families (43% for height, 18% for BMI), built on a joint analysis of roughly seven million variants.

The regulator responded. On 11 September 2026 the National Advertising Division of BBB National Programs, acting on a monitoring inquiry, recommended that Nucleus modify or discontinue claims that the service can accurately compare embryos' disease risks, identify which embryo will grow up tallest or smartest, and determine eye and hair colour. The NAD's reasoning: models may show an average benefit from selection, but that does not establish how accurately the service ranks a group of five embryos, nor validate the specific numbers in the advertising. Nucleus will appeal.

The professional body is blunter. In its 2026 ethics opinion, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine calls polygenic embryo screening "a nascent and unproven technology that is not recommended for clinical use and should not be offered as a clinical service at this time," with a place only in research under IRB oversight. There is also a line easy to skim past: selection for traits such as height, intelligence and eye colour is not considered reproductive medicine at all — the opinion explicitly places it outside its own scope.

There are substantive reasons for doubt beyond the ethics. Polygenic models are trained mostly on people of Western European ancestry, and by the ASRM's own assessment polygenic scoring accounts for only 5–10% of clinical variation; the rest is environment, diet, education and lifestyle. Pleiotropy compounds it: selecting for one trait drags others along. In a widely cited analysis, selection on educational attainment came with a higher risk of bipolar disorder.

Criticism of the company is not marginal. In Scientific American, bioethicist Arthur Caplan and geneticist James Tabery argued that Nucleus's products do not do what the company claims, comparing its founder to Theranos's Elizabeth Holmes; Cambridge geneticist Ruxandra Teslo called it a "non-rigorous company," and Harvard Medical School's Sasha Gusev has said the technology is not clinically actionable. The company counters that its scores are probabilistic risks, not guarantees.

The short version: the market is already selling a child chosen by predicted traits, while the scientific and regulatory consensus says it is too early. Between those two realities sit the parents paying for a certainty the technology does not yet have.

text:
i just turned 21.

ever since i started building a startup, my life has changed in ways i could never have imagined.

this past year, i've spent more time working than probably any other year of my life. there were days when i was so exhausted that i wanted to disappear from everything for a while. times when i questioned myself, when things felt painfully difficult, and when i genuinely had no idea how we were going to make it work.

but we always chose to keep going.

wanted to take a moment to reflect on everything that's happened this past year:

> launched a completely new version of @hyperknow_ai  on X, somehow went viral with 1.3M views, and made it to Global Tech Trending
> grew Hyperknow from 10k to 100k+ users. still feels surreal that so many people are loving something we built.
> watched 3 competitors attempted to copy our product. was pretty frustrated at first, but seeing people flood their comment sections with "isn't this Hyperknow?" honestly meant a lot. guess we’ve outcompeted the copycats :)
> opened our first office in Beijing, then doubled its size as the team grew
> hired our first full-time member, and grew from just me and my cofounder doing literally everything, to an incredible 10-person team with a working system
> packed up our first office, said goodbye to Beijing and my family. cried at the airport, and leave for New York to start another chapter
> questioned at least 10 times whether being a girl was why I wasn't being taken as seriously as i hoped. tried hard to earn the same respect, but didn’t succeed. eventually learned to make peace with it, and choose not to let it define me
> received an offer from angel investor, but after a lot of hesitation, eventually decided to turn it down
> went to SF Tech Week for the first time and finally met so many incredible people in person
> brought Hyperknow to 7 universities across the US, and became a guest speaker at Harvard China Forum
> returned to Columbia after a year on-leave. walked back into classes with a completely different mindset, and somehow managed to balance school and building a startup
> had countless arguments with @yi1inz , my work and life partner. learned a lot about each other, fought, made up, and slowly figured out how to actually make things work, both in life and in building a company together.
> kept working with some of the smartest, most passionate, and brilliantly idealistic people i've met, toward our shared dream of changing how the world learns.

a year ago, i was still just a student feeling lost about the future, unsure of how to carve out a path of my own.

along the way, i was forced to confront something i've struggled with for most of my life: the instinct to run away when things get difficult. and perhaps for the first time, i started learning how to face them.

i couldn't have done any of this without the support of my family, friends, and @yi1inz.

it's a little bittersweet to see how fast time flies, but more than anything, i'm excited to embrace whatever comes next. :)

text:
Microsoft sent 25 pages of legal threats to a teenager over MikeRoweSoft․com.

They offered him $10 for it, even though he was 17 years old and his legal birth name was Mike Rowe.

He put their threats online, crashed his server with 250,000 visitors in 12 hours, and auctioned Microsoft's legal papers on eBay.

This is the story of Mike Rowe and how a teenager backed a tech giant into a PR nightmare.

August 5, 2003

- Mike Rowe, 17 years old, starts an after school web design business in Victoria, Canada
- adds "Soft" to the end of his own birth name
- registers MikeRoweSoft․com for $10

November 19, 2003

- Microsoft's lawyers email Mike demanding he hand over the domain for sounding like Microsoft
- when Mike asks for compensation to rebuild his site, they offer him $10
- annoyed at the $10 insult, the teenager counters with $10,000

January 14, 2004

- a FedEx Priority Overnight package lands at Mike's house
- inside is an inch thick WIPO book and 25 pages of cease and desist threats accusing a high schooler of cybersquatting

January 15 to 19, 2004

- Mike posts the fight on his website and goes to the press
- 250,000 page views hit MikeRoweSoft․com in 12 hours and crash his server
- strangers donate over $6,000 to his defense fund and a lawyer steps up for free
- trademark experts point out Microsoft could actually lose in court because Mike is using his real birth name

Late January to March 2004

- trapped in global backlash, Microsoft admits it took the matter too seriously and folds into a settlement
- Mike trades the domain for paid expenses, certification training, an Xbox, and a paid family trip to Redmond headquarters
- he donates most of his $6,000 defense fund to a hospice for terminally ill children
