text:
Incindent Files(Dark) #024 Unplanned

THE DARK FILES

INCIDENT FILE #024: THE KINDNESS OF STRANGERS

PROLOGUE TO INCIDENT FILE #025: THE TWENTY-FIFTH PERFORMANCE

Classification: Unplanned Encounter
Location: North Texas
Subject: Natalie
Final Disposition: Undisclosed
Plausible Definitely: Undisclosed 

---

11:43 P.M. | FRIDAY NIGHT

There's something almost biblical about a Texas thunderstorm.
The sky opens up, the heavens start throwing furniture, and every idiot with a driver's license suddenly forgets how to operate a motor vehicle.
I've always enjoyed a good storm.
Not because I'm particularly fond of getting wet. At six-foot-five, I present a fairly substantial target for lightning, and I'd rather not discover whether my pacemaker comes with a manufacturer's warranty against acts of God.
No, I enjoy storms because they remind people of something they spend most of their lives trying to forget.
They're not in control.
Not really.
Money won't stop the rain. A fancy automobile won't negotiate with a flooded highway. And a thousand-dollar cellphone becomes an expensive flashlight when there's no signal.
Nature has a wonderful way of reminding humanity that its technological achievements mean precisely dick when the weather decides otherwise.

My name is Duff.
Fifty-six years old. Retired Marine. Owner of a successful private security company. Respected businessman. Occasional philanthropist. Full-time smartass.
I've been called a lot of things.
Dependable.
Professional.
Generous.
Intimidating.
A pain in the ass.
All accurate, depending on who's doing the talking.
People generally like me.
That's not arrogance. It's an observation.
I remember birthdays. I tip generously. I hold doors open for strangers. I've helped elderly neighbors carry groceries, paid restaurant bills for families who looked like they needed a break, and spent more money than I care to admit feeding a small army of raccoons.
I'm also very good at my profession.
People hire me because they're frightened of something.
Sometimes it's a stalker.
Sometimes it's a disgruntled employee.
Sometimes it's a threat against their family.
Whatever the problem, they come to me looking for reassurance.
And I provide it.
Funny, 
business security.
You're essentially selling people the belief that the world is less dangerous because you're standing beside them.
I suppose that makes me something of a salesman.
A very successful one.
But that's not what this particular file is about.
This file concerns a woman named Natalie.
And a rather unfortunate coincidence.

My truck was rolling along a narrow stretch of North Texas highway, its headlights struggling to carve a path through the rain.
A 1987 Ford F-150.
Two-tone tan and brown.
A little weathered around the edges, but then again, so am I.
The old girl had carried me through more adventures than I could count, and she'd never once complained about the company.
Unlike some people.
Snickers was curled up beside me.
My little Yorkie had claimed the passenger seat years ago and treated the truck as his personal kingdom.
He'd been sleeping until a particularly enthusiastic thunderclap rattled the windows.
His head popped up.
He stared at the windshield.
Then at me.
"Don't look at me, buddy. I didn't order this shit."
He sneezed.
"Exactly. I'd like to speak to management myself."
I scratched behind his ears.
He settled down again.
There's something reassuring about a dog.
Dogs don't care about your bank account, your reputation, or whether the world thinks you're a saint.
They care about whether you love them.
And whether you remembered to bring snacks.
Snickers was particularly passionate about the second issue.
I glanced at the dashboard clock.

11:43 P.M.

"Come on, little man. Let's get home before this weather turns us into a couple of drowned rats."
And that's when I saw the hazard lights.
Two amber flashes.
A pause.
Two more.
Barely visible through the rain.
A small white sedan sat crooked on the shoulder, one tire buried in mud.
Beside it stood a woman holding a jacket over her head.
She waved both arms when my headlights reached her.
I sighed.
"Oh, for fuck's sake."
Snickers lifted his head.
"Yeah, I see her."
I slowed.
The sensible thing would've been to keep driving.
I was tired.
My back hurt.
My coffee had gone cold.
And I had absolutely no desire to stand in a thunderstorm diagnosing somebody else's automotive catastrophe.
But there she was.
Alone.
Soaked.
Apparently having a truly miserable evening.
"Well, Snick, looks like we're doing a little community service."
I pulled over.
The woman hurried toward my window.
I rolled it down.
Rain immediately blew into my face.
"Evening!"
"Oh my God! Thank you for stopping!"
"Don't thank me yet. I might be here to discuss your vehicle's extended warranty."
She laughed.
A genuine laugh.
I liked that.
People who can laugh while standing in the middle of a thunderstorm generally have something going for them.
"Is your car dead?" I asked.
"Completely! It started making this horrible noise, and then everything just shut off!"
"Sounds like my accountant."
"What?"
"Nothing. You got a phone?"
"Yeah, but I can't get any signal!"
"Of course not. Technology works beautifully until somebody actually needs it."
Thunder cracked overhead.
She flinched.
I glanced at Snickers.
He was standing on the seat, his little tail wagging.
"Well, the boss seems to approve."
She leaned closer.
"Oh my goodness! Is that a Yorkie?"
"That's Snickers. He's in charge of personnel."
She laughed again.
"He's adorable!"
"Don't tell him that. His ego's already unbearable."
She reached through the window and scratched his head.
The little traitor practically melted.
"Really, Snick? Thirty seconds and you've already forgotten who buys the groceries?"
She smiled.
"I'm sorry. I'm just so relieved somebody stopped."
"Where you headed?"
"Fort Worth."
"Well, you're heading in the right general direction. Unfortunately, your car appears to have resigned without giving notice."
She looked back at the sedan.
"Do you think it's fixable?"
"Most things are. Question is whether they're worth fixing."
She sighed.
"I honestly don't know what to do."
I looked at the empty road.
Then at her.
"Tell you what. I've got a warm truck, a working heater, and enough fuel to get us somewhere with a phone signal. I can give you a ride."
She hesitated.
I couldn't blame her.
Getting into a stranger's truck after midnight isn't exactly something they recommend in driver's education.
"Look," I said, "I'm not offended if you'd rather wait. Matter of fact, that's probably what I'd tell my own family to do."
She studied me.
The gray flattop.
The black-framed glasses.
The long, neatly groomed goatee.
The black button-down shirt.
Then her eyes moved to the company identification clipped to my pocket.
"You're security?"
"Private security. I own the company."
"Seriously?"
"Unfortunately. Employees, paperwork, taxes. Whole miserable operation."
She laughed.
"Well, that actually makes me feel better."
"That's generally what people pay me for."
She looked at Snickers again.
He wagged his tail.
"Besides," I added, "I'm pretty sure the dog would report me if I did anything inappropriate."
That settled it.
She opened the passenger door.
Snickers moved toward the middle of the bench seat, apparently delighted to have company.
"Oh my God, it's warm in here!"
"Texas hospitality. We provide heat, sarcasm, and complimentary dog hair."
She climbed in and closed the door.
I handed her a clean towel from behind the seat.
"Here. Dry yourself off."
"Thank you so much."
"You're welcome."
She rubbed her hair.
Snickers placed his chin on her thigh.
"He's so sweet."
"Don't let him fool you. He's a hardened criminal. Stole half my dinner last Tuesday."
She scratched his ears.
"What's your name?"
"Duff."
"Duff?"
"Yep."
"That's unusual."
"My sister couldn't pronounce Jeff when we were kids. Duff stuck."
"That's actually kind of cute."
"Careful. I've got a reputation to maintain."
She smiled.
"I'm Natalie."
"Nice to meet you, Natalie."
I put the truck into gear.
And we pulled away.

12:02 A.M. | THE LONG WAY HOME

For the first few miles, everything was perfectly ordinary.
Natalie was twenty-eight.
Worked in an insurance office.
Recently moved to Fort Worth.
Had spent the evening visiting a friend.
Her boyfriend was out of town.
Her parents lived in Oklahoma.
She didn't know the back roads.
She talked a lot.
Nervous people often do.
I listened.
Asked questions.
Made jokes.
Snickers accepted an absolutely unreasonable amount of affection.
Eventually, Natalie relaxed enough to lean back against the seat.
"You're really nice, you know that?"
I glanced at her.
"Don't spread that around. It'll ruin my business."
"No, seriously. Most people would've just driven past."
"Most people have better things to do."
"Well, I'm glad you stopped."
I nodded.
"So am I."
There was a pause.
Then she asked, "Were you in the military?"
"What gave it away?"
"The haircut. And the way you talk."
"Twenty years in the Marines."
"Wow."
"That's usually what people say before asking whether I've killed anybody."
She went quiet.
I looked over.
Then laughed.
"Relax, Natalie. That's a joke."
"Oh!"
She laughed nervously.
"Sorry."
"Don't be. It's a terrible joke."
She shook her head.
"You're awful."
"Frequently."
The rain intensified.
The windshield wipers struggled against the water.
Natalie leaned forward.
"Can you even see?"
"Enough."
"That's reassuring."
"I could lie and tell you visibility's excellent."
"Please don't."
"All right. Visibility's shit."
She laughed.
And I found myself enjoying the conversation.
That's something people have difficulty understanding.
I can enjoy someone's company.
I can appreciate their humor.
I can genuinely like them.
None of those things necessarily changes what happens next.
Human beings are remarkably good at keeping contradictory ideas in separate compartments.
I simply have more compartments than most.
We reached an intersection.
The road toward Fort Worth continued straight.
I turned right.
Natalie looked up.
"Wait. Isn't Fort Worth that way?"
"Usually."
"Usually?"
"Flooding ahead. This road reconnects farther down."
She glanced at her phone.
Still no signal.
"Oh. Okay."
I drove on.
Snickers settled against my leg.
The radio played quietly.
An old country song.
Something about heartbreak and whiskey.
I turned it down.
"Tell me something, Natalie."
"Sure."
"Do you believe people are basically good?"
She thought about it.
"Yeah. I think so."
"Really?"
"I mean, obviously there are bad people. But I think most people are good."
"Interesting."
"What about you?"
I considered the question.
"Depends on the day."
She smiled.
"That's a pretty cynical answer."
"Occupational hazard."
"Because of security work?"
"Among other things."
She looked out at the rain.
"I guess you've probably seen some pretty awful stuff."
"More than I'd recommend."
"Does it change you?"
I glanced at her.
"Everything changes you."
She nodded thoughtfully.
"I guess that's true."
We drove another mile.
Then another.
The road narrowed.
Fields stretched into darkness on either side.
Natalie checked her phone again.
"Still nothing."
"Signal gets spotty out here."
"How much farther?"
"Not far."
She looked toward the dashboard.
Then at the empty road.
"Are you sure this is the right way?"
I smiled.
"Would I lie to you?"
She laughed.
"Well, I don't really know you."
"No," I said.
"You don't."

12:19 A.M. | TWENTY-FOUR

I should probably explain something.
Natalie wasn't planned.
There was no elaborate scheme.
No months of preparation.
No carefully selected target.
I'd been driving home with my dog.
That was it.
Twenty-three people had already disappeared from my life into places I rarely allowed myself to revisit.
Twenty three names.
Twenty three sets of people who would never receive the answers they wanted.
And somehow, through all of it, I had maintained a perfectly respectable existence.
My company was successful.
My employees were happy.
My clients trusted me with their families, their homes, and their livelihoods.
I attended charity functions.
I donated money.
I shook hands with people who appeared on television.
I was the fellow who could be counted on.
And that evening, I'd genuinely intended to go home.
That's what made Natalie different.
She was an interruption.
A detour.
A chance encounter.
I hadn't been looking for number twenty-four.
Number twenty-four had been standing in the rain.
Beside me, Natalie shifted.
"Duff?"
"Yeah?"
"Could you stop for a minute?"
"Something wrong?"
"I just... I don't feel very comfortable."
I glanced at her.
"About what?"
"This road. It's really dark."
"Most country roads are."
"I know, but..."
She stopped.
I waited.
"I think I'd rather call somebody."
"All right."
"Could you take me back to the main highway?"
I looked ahead.
The headlights illuminated a stretch of wet pavement.
Beyond that, darkness.
"Sure."
She exhaled.
"Thank you."
I continued driving.
After a few seconds, she spoke again.
"Duff?"
"Yes?"
"You passed a place where you could turn around."
"I know."
"Then why didn't you?"
I said nothing.
She looked toward the window.
Then toward the door.
Snickers lifted his head.
"Hey, Natalie?"
Her voice had changed.
"Yeah?"
"Can I ask you a question?"
She swallowed.
"Okay."
"What's the difference between a good man and a bad man?"
She stared at me.
"What?"
"Simple question."
"I don't know."
"Sure you do."
She looked toward the windshield.
"A good man helps people."
I nodded.
"And a bad man?"
"Hurts them."
"Fair enough."
I slowed the truck.
Natalie gripped her phone.
"Please take me back."
I looked at her.
"Here's the problem with your definition."
"What?"
"Sometimes the same man does both."
I pulled onto the shoulder.
The engine idled.
Rain hammered the roof.
Natalie stared at me.
"Unlock the door."
I didn't answer.
"Duff."
Snickers stood and looked between us.
"Unlock the fucking door."
I sighed.
"You're going to upset the dog."
"I DON'T CARE ABOUT THE DOG!"
Snickers flinched.
That irritated me.
Not the shouting.
The fact that she'd frightened him.
"Now, that was unnecessary."
"LET ME OUT!"
I reached toward the dashboard.
She pressed herself against the passenger door.
"What are you doing?"
I opened the glove compartment.
Her breathing became quick and shallow."
Please..."
I took out a roll of gray duct tape.
She stared at it.
Then at me.
Then back at the tape.
For a moment, neither of us spoke.
The rain filled the silence.
Finally, she whispered:
"No."
I looked at the roll.
Then at her.
"Funny thing about trust, Natalie."
She shook her head.
"No. No, no, no..."
"People think it's something you earn."
I pulled the loose end of the tape free.
Rrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrip.
Natalie screamed.
"NO! PLEASE! SOMEBODY HELP ME!"
Snickers barked.
Thunder cracked overhead.
And then, for a moment, everything seemed to stop.
I looked at Natalie.
She was trembling.
Her eyes were filled with tears.
And I felt something approaching regret.
Not remorse.
Not guilt.
Just the quiet disappointment of a man whose evening had taken an unfortunate turn.
"Natalie," I said softly, "there's something I want you to understand."
She stared at me.
"I wasn't looking for you tonight. Hell, I wasn't looking for anybody. I was just trying to get home, get Snickers fed, and put my feet up."
She shook her head.
"Please..."
"Then I saw your hazard lights."
Rain drummed against the roof.
"And the funny thing is, I really did stop because I wanted to help."
Her breathing quickened.
"You seem like a nice girl. You've got a good sense of humor, and Snickers certainly took a liking to you."
I glanced at the little dog.
He was watching us.
"That's what makes this whole thing so unfortunate."
Natalie began crying.
"You didn't do anything wrong. You weren't supposed to be part of my evening."
I paused.
"But sometimes two people cross paths who really, really shouldn't have."
She whispered something.
I couldn't make it out.
I leaned closer.
"And tonight, Natalie..."
Thunder rolled across the fields.
"I'm afraid you crossed paths with me."
The windshield wipers continued their steady rhythm.
Thump.
Squeak.
Thump.
Squeak.
Then the recording ended.

6:38 A.M. | SATURDAY MORNING

By morning, the rain had stopped.
The sky was pale blue.
Birds were singing.
The world had apparently decided that nothing particularly interesting had happened overnight.
I pulled into my driveway just as the first sunlight reached the roof of the house.
Snickers was asleep on the passenger seat.
I switched off the engine.
For a moment, I simply sat there.
My shoulders ached.
My back was killing me.
I was hungry.
And I had an appointment at ten with a client who wanted to discuss upgrading the security system at his lake house.
Ordinary responsibilities.
Ordinary life.
I looked at Snickers.
"Well, little man."
He opened one eye.
"That was an eventful evening."
He yawned.
"I Couldn't agree more."
I carried him inside.
Fed him breakfast.
Made coffee.
Took a shower.
Put on a clean black shirt.
Then I stood in front of the bathroom mirror and trimmed a stray hair from my goatee.
My reflection looked tired.
A little older than yesterday.
Otherwise, perfectly normal.
I smiled.
The man in the mirror smiled back.

At 9:17, my phone rang.

A client.
I answered cheerfully.
"Morning! Duff speaking."
A familiar voice greeted me.
"Hey, brother. Sorry to bother you on a Saturday."
"No bother at all. What's going on?"
"We've got a situation."
I poured another cup of coffee.
"Well, that's what you pay me for."
He laughed.
"Yeah, I guess it is."
We discussed his concerns.
I listened.
I offered advice.
I scheduled a meeting.
Before hanging up, he said something that almost made me laugh.
"Man, I don't know what we'd do without you."
I looked toward the living room.

LSnickers was curled up on the couch.
Sunlight streamed through the window.
Everything was peaceful.
"Well," I said, "hopefully you'll never have to find out."
We said goodbye.
I set the phone down
Then opened my laptop.
There were emails waiting.
Invoices.
Employee schedules.
A reminder about renewing an insurance policy.
And one message from a prospective client.
The subject line read:

PRIVATE SECURITY CONSULTATION | VIVIENNE VEX

I opened it.

A representative for the international recording artist was seeking a discreet, experienced security professional for an upcoming series of private appearances in Texas.
The message emphasized confidentiality.
Professionalism.
Reliability.
And absolute trust.
I read it twice.
Then leaned back in my chair.
Vivienne Vex.
Even I knew that name.
Platinum-blonde hair.
Outrageous costumes.
A voice that could fill an arena.
Millions of devoted fans.
One of the most recognizable women on the planet.
I glanced at Snickers.
"Well, buddy."
He raised his head.
"Looks like we're moving up in the world."
I began typing my reply.
Professional.
Courteous.
Reassuring.
Exactly what they'd expect from the owner of a respected security company.
And when I finished, I added my customary closing.
Your safety is my priority.
I read that sentence.
Then laughed.
Not loudly.
Just enough to wake the dog.
Snickers looked at me.
"What?" I asked him.
He tilted his head.
I scratched his ears.
"Nothing, buddy."

I clicked Send.

Outside, the last puddles from the previous night's storm were drying in the morning sun.
Somewhere, a family would soon begin wondering why Natalie hadn't come home.

But here, in my kitchen, the coffee was hot, the dog was happy, and business was looking exceptionally good.
Twenty-four.
I closed the laptop.
And smiled

END OF INCIDENT FILE #024

PROLOGUE COMPLETE

CONTINUED IN THE DARK FILES: INCIDENT FILE #025,

text:
To the Youth of Nigeria:
Has it ever occurred to you why many of the long-entrenched politicians go to such lengths to cling to power? Their primary aim is to remain in control indefinitely so that young people continue to live in subservience, dependent on their patronage and constantly seeking their favour. Even when they eventually step aside, they carefully position their children to inherit influence and authority. In this way, the next generation is expected to serve both father and son.

Consider the current situation surrounding President Tinubu and his family. There is a clear pattern of consolidating power within a single lineage, turning public office into something resembling a family enterprise. Lagos offers a telling example: one family member has long occupied a senatorial seat, another holds a prominent traditional market leadership position, and a younger relative appears to be preparing for higher executive office. The risk is that what has happened in Lagos is replicated at the national level.
Have we paused to consider what a liberated Nigeria would look like? In a system free from these self-serving political dynasties, no young person would feel compelled to offer automatic deference or run errands for those in power. This is not merely about the present; it is about the future of today’s youth and the generations that will follow.
It is the poor who suffer most under the current arrangement. The system is structured to keep large numbers of people in a state of dependence, ensuring they remain at the mercy of those who control resources and opportunities. Contrast this with a well-functioning democracy such as the United Kingdom: a citizen can walk through Trafalgar Square and pass the Prime Minister without any expectation of greeting, deference, or service. That is possible because institutions work, the economy offers genuine opportunity, and people have confidence in their own futures. In Nigeria today, that sense of a secure future has been severely undermined.

The 2027 elections are not a trivial matter. They represent a decisive opportunity to choose a different path one that prioritises competence, accountability, and genuine national progress over the preservation of political families. The stakes are the future of this country and of every young Nigerian who refuses to accept perpetual subservience as the price of survival.

text:
THE DUTY OF PARENTS
J C Ryle 1816 - 1900

Continued...

PART 16-17 of 17

16. TRAIN THEM REMEMBERING CONTINUALLY THE PROMISES OF SCRIPTURE

I name this also shortly, in order to guard you against discouragement.

You have a plain promise on your side, "Train up your child in the way he should go, and when he is old he shall not depart from it" (Prov. xxii. 6). Think what it is to have a promise like this. Promises were the only lamp of hope which cheered the hearts of the patriarchs before the Bible was written. Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph,óall lived on a few promises, and prospered in their souls. Promises are the cordials which in every age have supported and strengthened the believer. He that has got a plain text upon his side need never be cast down. Fathers and mothers, when your hearts are failing, and ready to halt, look at the word of this text, and take comfort.

Think who it is that promises. It is not the word of a man, who may lie or repent; it is the word of the King of kings, who never changes. Has He said a thing, and shall He not do it? Or has He spoken, and shall He not make it good? Neither is anything too hard for Him to perform. The things that are impossible with men are possible with God. Reader, if we get not the benefit of the promise we are dwelling upon, the fault is not in Him, but in ourselves.

Think, too, what the promise contains, before you refuse to take comfort from it. It speaks of a certain time when good training shall especially bear fruit,ó"when a child is old." Surely there is comfort in this. You may not see with your own eyes the result of careful training, but you know not what blessed fruits may not spring from it, long after you are dead and gone. It is not God's way to give everything at once. "Afterwards' is the time when He often chooses to work, both in the things of nature and in the things of grace. "Afterward" is the season when affliction bears the peaceable fruit of righteousness (Heb. xii. 1 1). "Afterward" was the time when the son who refused to work in his father's vineyard repented and went (Matt. xxi. 29). And "afterward" is the time to which parents must look forward if they see not success at once,óyou must sow in hope and plant in hope.

Cast your bread upon the waters," says the Spirit, "for you shall find it after many days" (Eccles. xi. 1). Many children, I doubt not, shall rise up in the day of judgment, and bless their parents for good training, who never gave any signs of having profited by it during their parents' lives. Go forward then in faith, and be sure that your labor shall not be altogether thrown away. Three times did Elijah stretch himself upon the widow's child before it revived. Take example from him, and persevere.

17. TRAIN THEM, LASTLY, WITH CONTINUAL PRAYER FOR A BLESSING ON ALL YOU DO

Without the blessing of the Lord, your best endeavors will do no good. He has the hearts of all men in His hands, and except He touch the hearts of your children by His Spirit, you will weary yourself to no purpose. Water, therefore, the seed you sow on their minds with unceasing prayer. The Lord is far more willing to hear than we to pray; far more ready to give blessings than we to ask them ;óbut He loves to be entreated for them. And I set this matter of prayer before you, as the top-stone and seal of all you do. I suspect the child of many prayers is seldom cast away.

Look upon your children as Jacob did on his; he tells Esau they are "the children which God has graciously given your servant" (Gen. xxxiii. 5). Look on them as Joseph did on his; he told his father, "They are the sons whom God has given me" (Gen. xlviii. 9). Count them with the Psalmist to be "an heritage and reward from the Lord" (Ps. cxxvii. 3). And then ask the Lord, with a holy boldness, to be gracious and merciful to His own gifts. Mark how Abraham intercedes for Ishmael, because he loved him, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you" (Gen. xvii. 18). See how Manoah speaks to the angel about Samson, "How shall we order the child, and how shall we do unto him?" (Judg. xiii. 12). Observe how tenderly Job cared for his children's souls, "He offered burned-offerings according to the number of them all, for he said, It may be my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually" (Job i. 5). Parents, if you love your children, go and do likewise. You cannot name their names before the mercy-seat too often.

And now, reader, in conclusion, let me once more press upon you the necessity and importance of using every single means in your power, if you would train children for heaven.

I know well that God is a sovereign God, and does all things according to the counsel of His own will. I know that Rehoboam was the son of Solomon, and Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, and that you do not always see godly parents having a godly seed. But I know also that God is a God who works by means, and sure am I, if you make light of such means as I have mentioned, your children are not likely to turn out well.

Fathers and mothers, you may take your children to be baptized, and have them enrolled in the ranks of Christ's Church; you may get godly sponsors to answer for them, and help you by their prayers; you may send them to the best of schools, and give them Bibles and Prayer Books, and fill them with head knowledge but if all this time there is no regular training at home, I tell you plainly, I fear it will go hard in the end with your children's souls. Home is the place where habits are formed; home is the place where the foundations of character are laid; home gives the bias to our tastes, and likings, and opinions. See then, I pray you, that there be careful training at home. Happy indeed is the man who can say, as Bolton did upon his dying bed, to his children, "I do believe not one of you will dare to meet me before the tribunal of Christ in an unregenerate state."

Fathers and mothers, I charge you solemnly before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, take every pains to train your children in the way they should go. I charge you not merely for the sake of your children's souls; I charge you for the sake of your own future comfort and peace. Truly it is your interest so to do. Truly your own happiness in great measure depends on it. Children have ever been the bow from which the sharpest arrows have pierced man's heart. Children have mixed the bitterest cups that man has ever had to drink. Children have caused the saddest tears that man has ever had to shed. Adam could tell you so; Jacob could tell you so; David could tell you so. There are no sorrows on earth like those which children have brought upon their parents. Oh! take heed, lest your own neglect should lay up misery for you in your old age. Take heed, lest you weep under the ill treatment of a thankless child, in the days when your eye is dim, and your natural force abated.

If ever you wish your children to be the restorers of your life, and the nourishers of your old age, if you would have them blessings and not curses joys and not sorrows Judahs and not Reubens Ruths and not Orpahs, if you would not, like Noah, be ashamed of their deeds, and, like Rebekah, be made weary of your life by them: if this be your wish, remember my advice betimes, train them while young in the right way.

And as for me, I will conclude by putting up my prayer to God for all who read this paper, that you may all be taught of God to feel the value of your own souls. This is one reason why baptism is too often a mere form, and Christian training despised and disregarded. Too often parents feel not for themselves, and so they feel not for their children. They do not realize the tremendous difference between a state of nature and a state of grace, and therefore they are content to let them alone.

Now the Lord teach you all that sin is that abominable thing which God hates. Then, I know you will mourn over the sins of your children, and strive to pluck them out as brands from the fire.

The Lord teach you all how precious Christ is, and what a mighty and complete work He has done for our salvation. Then, I feel confident you will use every means to bring your children to Jesus, that they may live through Him.

The Lord teach you all your need of the Holy Spirit, to renew, sanctify, and quicken your souls. Then, I feel sure you will urge your children to pray for Him without ceasing, and never rest until He has come down into their hearts with power, and made them new creatures.

The Lord grant this, and then I have a good hope that you will indeed train up your children well, train well for this life, and train well for the life to come; train well for earth, and train well for heaven; train them for God, for Christ, and for eternity.

Someone please correct me if I'm wrong, (only learned of it recently), but if true, it could help many more with compromising schedules make First Saturdays difficult.

The short version:  Our Sunday Mass Communion meets the First Saturday requirements.

I'm pretty sure this is true, IF, we are in a state of grace.  As long as we receive communion within 24 hours of First Saturday (and who wouldn't unless they are not going to Sunday mass)?  This has always been the most difficult part.  I know the first time I made mine, it was really hard to make the 5 consecutive Saturday masses, especially when travelling.  I would often be in places that didn't even offer a Saturday mass other than the evening mass for Sunday. 

In addition, the other necessary requirements are:

Pray five decades of the Rosary (one complete Rosary of five mysteries).

Spend 15 additional minutes meditating on the mysteries of the Rosary, keeping Our Lady company. This meditation is separate from simply reciting the Rosary.

Offer these acts in reparation to the Immaculate Heart of Mary.

I'm fairly sure it's the 5 Eucharists rec'd on the five consecutive First Saturday's that make this difficult for many.  The other thing which I came to learn (again, anyone please correct me if I'm wrong), is that as beneficial as a mass is at any time, the only requirement for First Saturdays is to receive the Eucharist. Of couse, if we are fulling our Sunday obligation, and I'm correct that our Sunday Eucharist fulfills the FS, that's a non-issue.

I just made the choice to (of course go to the Saturday masses when possible), but for sure be in union with all of the other requirements regardless.  Prayer is never wasted and I have to tell you, those deep rosary meditations on 20 different mysteries are powerful.

text:
Rivers State: When the People Become Spectators in Their Own Political Captivity

Letters from Stockholm — The Kio Solution

By Kio Amachree, President, Worldview International

The Stadium Was Full. Who Paid, and What Was Being Celebrated?

I watched Saturday's spectacle in Port Harcourt with sadness, anger and disbelief. Not because President Bola Ahmed Tinubu visited Rivers State. A president is entitled to visit any state in the federation. What troubled me was what the occasion revealed about the relationship between political power, public suffering and the readiness of ordinary citizens to applaud those who govern them.

At the Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium, Nyesom Wike welcomed the President before a vast crowd. Wike had predicted 70,000 people, far beyond the stadium's capacity of roughly 38,000. The organisers mobilised supporters, arranged transport, decorated the venue and staged what was plainly intended as a demonstration of political strength.

One question occurred to me before the first speech had ended.

How much did this cost, who paid for it, and whose interests did it serve?

**Who Paid for the Celebration?**

There were campaign buses, banners, security arrangements, decorations, political delegations and the considerable logistics required to assemble a crowd of that size. Reports described more than 80 buses deployed for the mobilisation alone.

I have seen no verified public accounting of the total expenditure, and nothing that establishes whether Wike financed the event personally. But the absence of figures makes transparency more important, not less.

Who supplied the money? Was it entirely private political funding? Were public resources, vehicles or personnel involved? How much was spent transporting, feeding and accommodating supporters? And will the organisers publish an independently verifiable account?

These are legitimate questions in any democracy. They are urgent ones in a country where millions cannot afford a bag of rice.

**The President Who Suspended Rivers Democracy**

The symbolism of this visit is particularly troubling.

On 18 March 2025, President Tinubu declared a state of emergency in Rivers State. He suspended Governor Siminalayi Fubara, his deputy and the elected members of the House of Assembly for six months, and installed an administrator appointed from Abuja.

The Nigerian Bar Association challenged the constitutional basis of those suspensions, arguing that emergency powers do not authorise a president to displace elected state institutions. Tinubu defended the intervention as necessary to end a political and security crisis, and the National Assembly approved it.

I have never accepted that a president may suspend an elected state government because its political quarrels have become inconvenient to Abuja. The Constitution is not a document to be obeyed when convenient and set aside when expedient.

Yet here we are, barely fourteen months after constitutional government was restored, watching the same President celebrated in the very state whose elected institutions he suspended.

Where is the political memory? Where is the demand for constitutional accountability? Where is the insistence that the votes of Rivers people must never again become bargaining chips in a contest between powerful men?

A full stadium cannot answer those questions. It can only drown them out for an afternoon.

**Wike and the Politics of Permanent Control**

Nyesom Wike is no longer Governor of Rivers State. He is Minister of the Federal Capital Territory. Yet his grip on the state's political machinery remains one of the most striking features of Nigerian politics today.

He speaks with confidence about the political future of Rivers. He assembles coalitions, coordinates the President's campaign in the state and presents himself as the man who can deliver Rivers to Tinubu.

But Rivers State is not a private estate. Its citizens are not the property of a former governor, a serving minister or any political organisation.

Political influence is legitimate. Political organisation is legitimate. Supporting a president is legitimate. What deserves scrutiny is a concentration of influence that allows one man to appear indispensable to every decision affecting an entire state, years after leaving its governorship.

No individual should confuse temporary political dominance with permanent ownership of a people's future. And no democracy can flourish when public institutions are subordinate to personal political arrangements.

**The Suffering Outside the Stadium**

While the political elite celebrated in Port Harcourt, ordinary Nigerians continued to live through one of the hardest economic periods in the country's history.

Fuel prices have risen dramatically. Food prices have broken household budgets. Healthcare remains out of reach for many, and insecurity continues to stalk communities across the federation.

Reuters reported petrol at roughly ₦1,400 to ₦1,500 per litre in September, while noting that the government's reforms have improved some public-finance indicators and rebuilt foreign reserves. Those improvements are real, and I do not dismiss them. But macroeconomic statistics cannot substitute for the lived experience of families deciding which meal to skip.

What, then, should a presidential visit to Rivers State represent? An opportunity to explain how the reforms will reach ordinary households? An account of federal investment in the state's hospitals, schools, roads and security? Or simply another occasion for politicians to congratulate one another before a cheering audience?

A campaign rally is not a substitute for governance.

**Kaduna and Port Harcourt: Two Competing Pictures**

The contrast with Kaduna deserves careful examination.

After Tinubu's October rally there, the opposition African Democratic Congress alleged that attendance was poor and that some supporters had been paid to attend. Other observers, including journalists on the ground, described crowded sections of the stadium. The claim that nobody came to Kaduna is therefore not established. What is established is that the size and authenticity of political crowds have become matters of fierce public dispute.

Port Harcourt now raises the same question. Does a large gathering demonstrate popular approval, or does it demonstrate the organisational capacity of powerful political networks?

A person may attend a rally out of conviction, party loyalty, curiosity, obligation to an employer or the hope of some material benefit. Without evidence, it would be wrong to assume that everyone was paid or coerced. It would be equally wrong to treat every person inside the stadium as an unquestioning endorsement of every decision the President has made.

**The American Files and the Question of Accountability**

There is another matter that should not disappear beneath the music, the applause and the campaign speeches.

In the United States, litigation continues over FBI and Drug Enforcement Administration records from investigations in the early 1990s in which Tinubu's name appeared. On 30 October 2026, Judge Beryl Howell of the District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that the agencies had not adequately justified several categories of withheld information, and required further explanation if they wished to keep those records closed. Tinubu's lawyers have defended the privacy protections and opposed further disclosure.

I must be precise about what this means. The proceedings concern public access to historical investigative records. They do not establish that Tinubu committed any offence, and the court did not order the immediate release of every disputed document.

Nevertheless, Nigerians are entitled to ask why questions about their President's historical dealings with American law enforcement remain unresolved in the public domain, three years into his tenure.

The presidency carries an exceptional duty of transparency. That duty is hard to reconcile with a political culture in which supporters are expected to applaud first and ask questions later, if at all.

**The Ancestors Who Built Rivers State**

Perhaps what troubles me most is the historical dimension of what I witnessed.

Rivers State was not created for the convenience of contemporary politicians. It emerged from decades of struggle, negotiation and determination by communities that wanted recognition, security and control over their own affairs.

Men such as my father, Chief Godfrey Kio-Jaja Amachree, belonged to a generation that understood the importance of building institutions that would outlive their founders. They knew that public office was temporary and that the institutions of government had to endure.

My father gave his professional resources, his business interests and his personal influence to the early development of Rivers State. He believed in a state whose different peoples could share in its prosperity rather than serve as instruments in the ambitions of powerful individuals.

I sometimes wonder what those founding figures would make of the struggles consuming Rivers today. I imagine their disappointment at seeing so much political energy spent on questions of loyalty and control while the state's enormous economic potential goes unrealised.

Rivers has oil, gas, ports, maritime infrastructure, fertile land, an educated population and a strategic position in the Niger Delta. These should be the foundation of a remarkably prosperous society. Yet the argument that dominates its politics is about who controls the governor, who controls the legislature, who controls the party machinery and who can deliver the largest crowd to a visiting president.

That is a profound narrowing of political ambition.

**The Danger of Political Surrender**

I refuse to believe that the people of Rivers State have collectively surrendered their dignity or their capacity for independent judgment.

Those who filled the stadium on Saturday cannot be taken as representative of the whole state. There are Rivers men and women who support Tinubu sincerely, others who oppose him, and many whose immediate concerns are jobs, healthcare, schooling and survival rather than party politics. All of them deserve to be heard.

But I worry about a political culture in which access to power matters so much that constitutional principles become negotiable. When citizens come to regard political patrons, rather than the institutions established by law, as the source of their rights, democracy becomes dangerously dependent on individuals.

The question is not whether Wike can fill a stadium. It is whether the institutions of Rivers State can function independently of him, of Tinubu and of every other political figure.

The question is not whether people can sing and dance for a President. It is whether that President can be held to the same constitutional scrutiny as every other public official.

And the question is not whether Saturday's rally succeeded as a political event. It is whether the people who attended will see any meaningful improvement in their lives.

**No Position Is Permanent**

History offers a consistent reminder: political influence changes hands.

Governors become former governors. Presidents leave office. Ministers surrender their portfolios. Alliances dissolve, and men who once seemed indispensable discover that public life has moved on without them. That is not a threat. It is the ordinary rhythm of constitutional democracy.

No politician should mistake the applause of a crowd for a guarantee of permanent authority. And no citizen should have to surrender independent judgment in exchange for access to the political establishment.

Rivers State deserves institutions stronger than any individual, a political culture capable of tolerating disagreement, and a government whose achievements can be measured by something other than attendance at a campaign rally.

I hope the organisers of Saturday's gathering will publish the cost of the event and identify its sources of finance. That would be a modest but meaningful act of accountability. I hope, too, that the constitutional controversy of the 2025 emergency rule will not be forgotten merely because the actors involved have reached new accommodations.

The greatest tribute Rivers State can pay its founders is not a statue, a street name or another elaborate political ceremony. It is the preservation of the democratic institutions they made possible.

A stadium may be filled for an afternoon. The constitutional rights of a people must endure for generations.

When the music stops, the banners come down and the presidential convoy leaves Port Harcourt, the people of Rivers State will still be there. Their schools will still need teachers. Their hospitals will still need medicines. Their young people will still need jobs. Their communities will still need security.

That is where the true measure of political leadership begins.

*Letters from Stockholm — The Kio Solution*
*Kio Amachree | President, Worldview International*

Amahara: One of the Most Innovative Writers in the Manga Industry! 🔥🔥🔥

I believe Amahara is one of the most innovative writers in the manga industry. What makes him so fascinating as a writer is his willingness to break away from conventional storytelling traditions and explore subjects that many other manga authors would hesitate to tackle. I think this aspect of his writing is particularly evident in two of his works: Interspecies Reviewers and The Idaten Deities Know Only Peace.

Interspecies Reviewers: A Refreshingly Unconventional Premise.

Interspecies Reviewers has one of the most unusual premises in manga. The story follows a group of male friends who visit various succubus brothels, experience the services offered by different women, and subsequently publish reviews based on their experiences. What makes this premise so refreshing is the way it incorporates sexuality into the story in a manner that is incredibly rare in manga.

There are two main reasons why I particularly enjoy this series.

First, the protagonists actually engage in sexual intercourse, and sexuality itself is an important part of the story. Rather than simply being implied or vaguely alluded to, it is incorporated into the very foundation of the series.

This might seem like an obvious observation, but it is surprisingly uncommon in manga. Even in series that explore romance and sexual relationships, actual intimacy is often postponed until the very end of the story or conveniently skipped over with a fade to black.

That's precisely why I thought Studio Passione's adaptation was particularly impressive. Rather than shying away from sexual content or leaving everything to the viewer's imagination, they weren't afraid to depict sexual encounters in considerable detail.

Personally, I believe that kissing, intimacy, and sex are perfectly natural aspects of human relationships and human nature. That's why I wish more manga and anime would incorporate these elements into their storytelling.

That is precisely why I find it so refreshing that a writer like Amahara doesn't simply include sexuality in his work but makes it a fundamental part of the premise itself.

The second reason I enjoy Interspecies Reviewers is how believable the protagonists feel, particularly when they exchange their opinions and reviews.

Their discussions reflect how real people might talk among friends when discussing women's attractiveness and their own sexual preferences. Even among men, people don't necessarily agree on what makes a woman attractive. Some might prefer large breasts, others might place greater importance on body shape, while others might prioritize facial features. These differences in personal preferences are represented particularly well throughout the series.

What I especially appreciate is how differently the characters can rate the same succubus. One reviewer might give a woman an exceptionally high score, while another might give her a considerably lower rating. This makes the characters feel more realistic because attraction is subjective. What one person considers beautiful and appealing might be completely unappealing to someone else.

What's even more interesting is how Amahara takes this concept further by making the protagonists members of different races and species. Their biological differences, cultural backgrounds, and perspectives on beauty make their disagreements even more interesting.

For example, in the first chapter, Stunk, a human, finds an elf woman named Elma attractive. She possesses many of the physical characteristics that would conventionally appeal to human men, including a youthful appearance, large breasts, and an attractive face. Zel, however, has a completely different perspective.

As a half-elf, Zel has a different understanding of aging and beauty. Elves have considerably longer lifespans than humans, meaning their perceptions of age and attractiveness aren't necessarily the same as those of humans. Consequently, Zel finds it strange that Stunk would consider a woman of Elma's age attractive.

What's even funnier is that, in the same sequence, an extraordinarily old elf woman appears, looking as though she is practically on her deathbed. Zel proceeds to kiss her, much to Stunk's disgust.

What's amusing about this interaction is how completely opposite their standards of beauty are. Something one character finds attractive is completely unacceptable to another. I find this exchange hilarious, and I think it cleverly exaggerates something that happens in real life. Beauty standards and personal preferences vary considerably between individuals and cultures, and Amahara uses the differences between species to explore this idea in an entertaining way.

Another interesting example is Crim, the angel who possesses both male and female sexual characteristics. Because of his unique anatomy, combined with his curiosity and desire to explore different experiences, he chooses a hyena succubus who has a feminine appearance but male reproductive characteristics.

This might understandably be unappealing to some of the other reviewers, particularly those who are exclusively attracted to women. However, Crim approaches the experience from his own perspective. I think his decision reflects his individuality, curiosity, and self-confidence.

I found this entire sequence hilarious. It's another example of Amahara taking a subject that would rarely be explored in conventional manga and turning it into an entertaining interaction between characters.

There are also biological differences that determine whether certain characters are physically compatible with particular succubi. A good example is Tiaplate, a fire succubus whose body radiates extreme heat. However, because Crim is an angel with a natural resistance to fire, he is completely unaffected by her body temperature. As a result, he is the only member of the group who can comfortably spend the night with her.

I find it interesting how these kinds of details allow the characters' individual biological characteristics to directly influence their experiences.

I also appreciate the sheer variety of succubus women in the series. There are humans, elves, demons, fairies, and many other species, each possessing different physical characteristics, personalities, and forms of appeal. Amahara clearly enjoys experimenting with different character designs, and I think that creativity is one of the reasons the series remains so entertaining.

Aloe: One of the Most Memorable Character Designs!

My personal favorite succubus is Aloe. Her character design is absolutely incredible, and she stands out to me because of the many different elements that come together to create her appearance and personality.

Visually, she has a voluptuous body, a large bust, and a distinctive sense of fashion. Her ear piercings, tattoos, clothing, and overall appearance give her a very recognizable design. She's undeniably sexy, but what makes her particularly appealing is how her femininity is combined with an air of experience and confidence.

Her personality is another major reason why I like her so much. Aloe is easygoing and laid-back, but she's also remarkably bold when discussing sexual matters. Her vulgar and unapologetic way of talking about intercourse is particularly amusing. This sort of bluntness is something more commonly associated with male characters in conventional manga. Combined with her relaxed personality, it gives her a distinctive charm.

Another detail I find fascinating is her smoking habit. Aloe smokes a slender pipe known as a kiseru. This accessory evokes the image of the courtesans who worked in Japan's Edo-period pleasure districts. I find this particularly interesting because it reinforces her identity as an experienced madam.

What I particularly appreciate is the contrast between her different characteristics.

On one hand, she's quite vulgar and unreserved when discussing sex. She sits with her legs open and shows very little concern for conventional modesty. Some people might find this behavior off-putting, but personally, I find her personality charming.

On the other hand, she retains a distinctly feminine and alluring appearance. Her voluptuous body, large bust, high-heeled boots, revealing clothing, and the way she handles her kiseru all contribute to her visual appeal.

The combination of her sexy character design, distinctive fashion sense, and the confidence of an experienced courtesan gives her an identity that is difficult to confuse with anyone else.

To me, Aloe represents an interesting combination of sensuality, femininity, professional experience, and confidence. Considering her personality and experience, her position as a madam makes perfect sense.

Whenever I think about the succubus characters in Interspecies Reviewers, Aloe is easily one of the first characters who comes to mind. I can also understand why she became such a popular character in Japan. Her design is distinctive, her personality is entertaining, and she has a presence that makes her memorable.

I also think Yōko Hikasa was an excellent choice for her voice actress. Given her experience voicing mature and seductive female characters, she was particularly well-suited for the role of Aloe.

The Idaten Deities Know Only Peace: Another Example of Amahara's Unconventional Storytelling.

Amahara's other major work, The Idaten Deities Know Only Peace (Heion Sedai no Idaten-tachi), demonstrates many of the same qualities that make Interspecies Reviewers so interesting.

Once again, sexuality isn't treated as something that needs to be pushed into the background. Instead, it plays an important role in the story and directly influences the characters' motivations and decisions.

One example is Miku and her female allies attempting to become pregnant in order to expand the demon army. It's an unusual plot development, but it demonstrates how Amahara incorporates sexuality into the actual mechanics of his fictional world rather than treating it as something that exists purely for fanservice.

Another example involves Piscalat and Cory, who become willing to betray the demon army because of their physical attraction to Ysley and Paula, respectively. I also appreciate the artwork accompanying some of these intimate scenes. The illustrations are genuinely impressive, and I find it refreshing that these moments receive proper attention instead of being conveniently skipped over.

What I particularly appreciate about Miku is that, despite having a sexy character design and an extremely horny personality, she's also highly intelligent.

Her intelligence and strategic thinking play an essential role in the demons' eventual success.

This is another aspect of Amahara's writing that I find refreshing. Too often, manga authors create female characters with attractive appearances and sexy personalities but fail to develop them much beyond those qualities. Miku, however, is genuinely intelligent and capable of devising strategies that have significant consequences for the story.

Her intelligence makes her considerably more interesting because she's not simply there to look attractive. She's an important character whose decisions and strategic abilities directly influence the direction of the story.

I also appreciate that Amahara allows the demons to win.

In many conventional stories, the protagonists are expected to emerge victorious because that's the traditional formula audiences have become accustomed to. However, Amahara is willing to subvert those expectations by allowing the antagonistic side to achieve victory.

I find this particularly interesting because it demonstrates that he isn't afraid to challenge conventional storytelling traditions. Rather than automatically following the familiar formula of good triumphing over evil, he's willing to explore alternative outcomes.

Conclusion: A Writer Who Isn't Afraid to Break Conventions.

Ultimately, what makes Amahara such an interesting and innovative writer is his willingness to incorporate sexuality into his stories in ways that most manga authors simply wouldn't attempt.

In Interspecies Reviewers, sexuality is the foundation of the entire premise. The protagonists visit succubus brothels, experience different types of women, and compare their experiences through their reviews.

In The Idaten Deities Know Only Peace, sexuality becomes an important plot element that influences character motivations, political decisions, and even the expansion of an army.

What I appreciate most is that Amahara doesn't seem interested in following conventional storytelling formulas simply because they're familiar. He's willing to experiment with unusual premises, explore subjects that other writers might avoid, and create characters whose motivations and personalities aren't always predictable.

His willingness to make sexuality a genuine part of his fictional worlds, rather than something that exists exclusively for fanservice, is one of the things that makes his writing stand out to me.

I genuinely can't wait to see what Amahara comes up with next. If he continues working on Interspecies Reviewers, I particularly hope Aloe receives even more screen time. She's easily one of my favorite characters in the series, and I would love to see more of her personality, her interactions with the other characters, and her experiences as a madam.

Amahara is a writer who clearly isn't afraid to do things differently, and that's precisely why I find his work so enjoyable. 👍

A celebratory event dedicated to Azerbaijan’s Victory Day was held in The Hague, the Kingdom of the Netherlands. As part of the event, a concert featuring Azerbaijani folk and traditional music was organized at the Paleiskerk Church.

The event was jointly organized by the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan to the Kingdom of the Netherlands, the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and the Fund for Support to Azerbaijani Diaspora.

The ceremony was attended by representatives of Dutch state institutions, the diplomatic corps accredited in the country, political, public, business, cultural, and academic circles, and the media, as well as members of the Azerbaijani community.

In his opening remarks, Anar Ajamov, Ambassador of Azerbaijan to the Kingdom of the Netherlands, emphasized that the celebration of Victory Day, State Flag Day, and Constitution Day, all of which fall around the same time, serves as a testament to the strength of Azerbaijan’s statehood traditions, as well as its national unity and solidarity. He noted that this historic Victory was achieved thanks to the resolute leadership of President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev, the heroism of the Azerbaijani Army, and the unity of the Azerbaijani people. The Ambassador also highlighted the historical significance of the restoration of Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, as well as the role such events play in promoting the country’s national and cultural heritage on the international stage.

The event continued with an artistic programme. The concert featured works by both Azerbaijani and Dutch composers, performed by faculty members of the Department of Instrumental Mugham at the Azerbaijan National Conservatory: Honored Artist and kamancha player Toghrul Asadullayev and tar player Rustam Muslimov. They were joined by Honored Artist Nargiz Aliyeva, a member of the Gara Garayev Azerbaijan State Chamber Orchestra, and Ravan Gajayev, a soloist with the Jahangir Jahangirov Choir.

The performers presented a selection of folk songs, mugham pieces, and compositions reflecting the richness and diversity of Azerbaijani musical culture, including “Küçələrə su səpmişəm,” “Şuşanın dağları,” “Mənim Azərbaycanım,” “Tellərini yan dara, qız,” “Qarabağ,” “Vətən yaxşıdır,” and “Yaşa, Azərbaycan!”

The concert offered guests an opportunity to gain a deeper appreciation of the unique spirit of Azerbaijani music and its rich national and cultural heritage. The performances were received with great interest by the audience.

THE FALL OF A GENERAL: RETIRED LIEUTENANT GENERAL PETER ELWELU FACES UPDF GENERAL COURT MARTIAL OVER ALLEGATIONS OF SUBVERSIVE ACTIVITIES AND PLANS TO DESTABILISE THE TESO REGION.

By Keefa Nuwahereza.

Retired Lieutenant General Peter Elwelu, the former Deputy Chief of Defence Forces of the Uganda People’s Defence Forces, stands at the centre of one of the most dramatic military and political confrontations in contemporary Uganda. On the evening of 2 November 2026, security forces took him into custody in Soroti City in the Teso sub-region of eastern Uganda. The Uganda People’s Defence Forces subsequently confirmed that he would face prosecution before the UPDF General Court Martial over alleged subversive activities, including plans to destabilise Teso, following the reported recovery of firearms, military fatigues, and vehicles linked to him. The announcement, issued by Acting Director of Defence Public Information Colonel Chris Magezi, emphasised that no one is above the law and that Elwelu would be held fully accountable for his actions without special presidential guarantees of personal safety. This development marks a sharp reversal for a man who rose through the ranks of the UPDF over nearly four decades, commanded high-profile operations, served as a senior presidential adviser, and retired only in August 2025.

The events that precipitated Elwelu’s detention began in late October 2026. On 27 October, Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the son of President Yoweri Museveni, used his X account to accuse the retired general of treasonous conduct. Muhoozi declared that Elwelu had been stripped of his ranks and demoted to Private, ordered him to surrender, and claimed that more than twenty former soldiers previously associated with him had been arrested and were cooperating with investigators. He further alleged that weapons and ammunition had been recovered from one of Elwelu’s residences in Teso and issued an ultimatum: Elwelu had hours to give himself up before being declared a rebel. Subsequent posts by Muhoozi referred to the recovery of additional arms, the arrest of Elwelu’s driver, and the seizure of a vehicle. Political commentator Andrew Mwenda amplified the accusations, alleging that Elwelu had plotted to assassinate Muhoozi in order to seize power, though these claims remain unverified. Elwelu’s family rejected the allegations of rebellion, with his wife Patricia Apolot stating that he was innocent and could not contemplate such actions. Relatives described him as having gone into hiding out of fear for his life following the public statements.

Security operations intensified in Teso. On 2 November, forces recovered fifteen firearms, military fatigues, and two pickup trucks allegedly linked to Elwelu. Colonel Magezi described him as a “renegade” officer who had been on the run over involvement in subversive activities aimed at destabilising Teso. Accounts of how Elwelu entered custody varied. Initial military statements framed the event as an arrest following a manhunt. Sources close to the family and some reports indicated that he contacted security personnel and handed himself over at his office in Soroti’s Senior Quarters after calling to alert them of his presence. The UPDF later clarified that while the surrender was peaceful, it occurred because security forces had closed in and left him with no viable alternative. He was transferred to Makindye Military Barracks in Kampala, where senior officers are sometimes held pending proceedings. Senior Presidential Advisor Charles Elasu stated that Elwelu was safe, had been provided with accommodation, and was allowed certain personal arrangements, though the precise conditions of detention have not been independently verified in full detail.

On 5 November, the UPDF issued a formal statement confirming that Elwelu would appear before the General Court Martial. Magezi explicitly rejected media reports that President Museveni had negotiated Elwelu’s surrender or offered assurances of personal safety. “At no point did the President and the Commander-in-Chief, General Yoweri Kaguta Museveni, offer Elwelu ‘assurances for his personal safety,’” the statement read. The military insisted that the President has full confidence in the security forces to maintain order and that Elwelu would answer for his alleged actions under military law. No specific charges or court date have been publicly announced. Legal observers have noted that the demotion announced on social media by Muhoozi lacks formal confirmation through the procedures required under the UPDF Act, as amended in 2025. The Act provides that a commissioned officer cannot be reduced below substantive rank except through a sentence issued by a competent military court and confirmed by the High Command. The prosecution of a retired officer also raises jurisdictional questions, although the 2025 amendments to the UPDF Act addressed aspects of military justice concerning veterans and reservists. In January 2025, Uganda’s Supreme Court had ruled against the broad prosecution of civilians before military courts, finding certain aspects unconstitutional; the subsequent parliamentary amendments sought to clarify procedures.

The Uganda Law Society responded promptly. On 3 November, ULS President Isaac Ssemakadde issued a statement committing the society to upholding due process and constitutional rights in Elwelu’s case. The society cited Article 23 of the Constitution, which requires that an arrested person be held in a place authorised by law, informed immediately of the reasons for arrest and the right to a lawyer of choice, brought before a court within forty-eight hours, and afforded reasonable access to next-of-kin, legal counsel, and a personal doctor. ULS condemned trial by media, including public pronouncements that presume guilt or strip ranks outside established legal processes. It demanded transparency on the legal basis for detention, probable cause, place of detention, and access to counsel and family. The society explicitly warned against a repetition of patterns observed in other high-profile cases involving interference with legal teams and opaque processes. It invited Elwelu’s next-of-kin, lawyer, and personal doctor to its offices for coordinated engagement. These interventions underscore the tension between the military’s insistence on accountability and broader concerns about constitutional safeguards in cases involving senior figures.

To understand the full weight of the present confrontation, one must examine Elwelu’s long military career. Born on 12 June 1966 in Aloet Village in what is now Kalaki District in the Teso sub-region, Elwelu joined the National Resistance Army in 1987 after completing secondary education. He trained at the Tanzania Military Academy in Monduli and later served at installations including Kabamba and the Cadet Officer School at Jinja. His early deployments included participation in UPDF operations in what was then Zaire, contributing to the overthrow of Mobutu Sese Seko alongside Rwandan forces. He later served in northern Uganda against the Lord’s Resistance Army of Joseph Kony, during which he was reportedly wounded. In 2007, he commanded Uganda’s first contingent deployed to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia, an assignment that enhanced his reputation within the force. He subsequently commanded the UPDF 3rd Division based at Moroto and, from June 2013, the 2nd Division at Mbarara. In January 2017, he was appointed Commander of Land Forces, the third-highest position in the UPDF hierarchy. On 24 June 2021, he became Deputy Chief of Defence Forces, serving until March 2024. He later held the position of Senior Presidential Adviser on Teso and Karamoja Affairs before retiring in August 2025.

The episode that defined Elwelu’s public profile more than any other was the military operation in Kasese on 26 and 27 November 2016. As commander of the 2nd Division, then-Brigadier Elwelu directed forces that assaulted the palace of Omusinga Charles Wesley Mumbere, the traditional ruler of the Rwenzururu Kingdom, and related administrative offices. The operation followed years of tension between the central government and the kingdom over security arrangements, the role of volunteer royal guards, and the creation of a separate cultural institution for the Bamba people in Bundibugyo. Clashes had already occurred earlier in 2016. On 26 November, security forces moved against kingdom offices in Kasese town, resulting in deaths among royal guards and civilians, as well as the killing of police officers in related violence. The following day, forces stormed the palace compound. Mumbere was arrested, along with scores of others, including children. Human Rights Watch documented at least 153 deaths across the two days, including children, and reported that many of those detained were severely beaten. Official casualty figures varied and were inconsistent. Elwelu publicly defended the operation, stating that the palace had become a legitimate military target serving as a command post and that the people inside were armed fighters. President Museveni later told Al Jazeera that Elwelu had done his duty. No independent investigation with full accountability has been conducted by Ugandan authorities. In May 2024, the United States imposed travel sanctions on Elwelu, citing extrajudicial killings committed by UPDF members under his command. Human Rights Watch welcomed the sanctions and renewed calls for an independent inquiry, noting that prosecutors had dropped charges against 218 people apprehended during the raid in 2023 without subsequent accountability for the deaths.

The Kasese events remain a source of deep controversy. Supporters of the operation argued that royal guards had engaged in armed attacks on police and that the military response was necessary to restore order. Critics, including human rights organisations, contended that the scale of lethal force was disproportionate, that civilians and children were among the dead, and that the absence of transparent investigation undermined the rule of law. Elwelu’s subsequent promotions indicated that the government viewed the operation as successful. His later public comments continued to justify the use of force. The sanctions, however, marked an international judgement that the command responsibility for the deaths warranted restrictions. This history now intersects with the 2026 allegations. While the current charges concern alleged activities in Teso rather than Kasese, the earlier episode shapes perceptions of Elwelu’s record of decisive and lethal military action, as well as questions of accountability within the UPDF.

Teso itself provides additional context. The sub-region has a complex history of cattle raiding, rebellion in the 1980s, and subsequent integration into the national military and political structures. Elwelu’s origins in Aloet Village and his later advisory role on Teso and Karamoja affairs placed him in a position of regional influence. Accusations that he sought to destabilise the area therefore carry particular resonance. Muhoozi’s statements framed the alleged activities as a direct threat to national stability, while local reactions have included both support for accountability and expressions of concern about the manner of the public accusations and detention. The recovery of weapons has been presented by the military as evidence of preparations for unrest, though the precise nature, ownership, and intended use of the firearms have not been detailed in open court or independent forensic reporting.

The broader political and institutional setting is significant. General Muhoozi Kainerugaba’s role as Chief of Defence Forces has been accompanied by frequent public commentary on social media. His October 2026 posts on Elwelu continued a pattern of direct engagement with military and political matters. Relations between the two officers had deteriorated earlier; in December 2024, Muhoozi had criticised Elwelu publicly. The present confrontation raises questions about command authority, the boundaries between formal military processes and public statements, and the position of retired officers. The UPDF’s insistence that Elwelu will face the General Court Martial without special deals affirms a principle of equal accountability. At the same time, the Uganda Law Society’s intervention highlights the necessity of constitutional protections, timely judicial review, and access to counsel. The Supreme Court’s 2025 ruling on military courts and the subsequent legislative amendments form part of the legal framework against which any proceedings will be assessed.

Elwelu has not made extensive public comment on the latest allegations. Family statements have maintained his innocence and described the accusations as an attempt to damage his reputation. The military has characterised the case as one of subversion and weapons stockpiling. Until formal charges are laid and evidence is tested before the General Court Martial, the allegations remain unproven. The process will determine whether the recovered items and any other evidence support the claims of intent to destabilise Teso or whether alternative explanations exist. Proceedings will also test the application of military justice to a retired senior officer and the durability of due-process guarantees in a high-profile case.

The story of Peter Elwelu encompasses decades of military service, a defining and contested operation in Kasese that produced substantial loss of life and international sanctions, a period of senior command and advisory responsibility, and a rapid descent into arrest and prospective court martial. The UPDF has stated clearly that he will be held accountable for his actions. Constitutional advocates have demanded that any accountability occur within the bounds of law, with transparency and respect for rights. The outcome of the General Court Martial proceedings, whenever they commence, will clarify the legal merits of the present allegations and contribute to ongoing debates about military discipline, command responsibility, and the rule of law in Uganda. As of early November 2026, Elwelu remains in secure custody, investigations continue, and the formal arraignment has not yet been scheduled. The case continues to attract attention both within Uganda and internationally, reflecting the intersection of personal military trajectories, institutional authority, and constitutional principle.

text:
On November 4, Toronto gave a remarkable Canadian a new place in its memory.

The bronze statue unveiled at Scrivener Square honours William “Billy” Barker, the First World War flying ace whose journey began in rural Manitoba and led to extraordinary acts of courage above Europe.

Born near Dauphin in 1894, Barker began his wartime service in the Army before transferring to the Royal Flying Corps. He became one of Canada’s most accomplished fighter pilots, credited with 50 aerial victories.

His defining battle came on October 27, 1918, just fifteen days before the Armistice. Flying alone over France, he encountered successive formations of German aircraft. Wounded repeatedly, he brought down four enemy planes and managed to reach Allied lines, where he crash-landed. He survived. His actions earned him the Victoria Cross.

When he died in a flying accident in 1930, aged just 35, more than 50,000 people watched his funeral procession in Toronto.

Now, as Remembrance Day approaches, his statue offers another reason to pause on a Toronto street and remember the person behind the medals.

Remember his name. Tell his story.

Pictured with the statue are Barker’s grandson, Ian Mackenzie, and sculptor Armando Barbon.

#BillyBarker #CanadianHistory #Toronto #LestWeForget

In 2002, 21-year-old Michelle Knight was abducted in Cleveland, Ohio. She would spend nearly 11 years inside her captor’s house. Early in her captivity, he told her she would stay chained to a pole until he could trust her.

Her captor was Ariel Castro, a school bus driver who later kidnapped Amanda Berry and Gina DeJesus. He held all three women in his house on Seymour Avenue, subjecting them to repeated rape, beatings and confinement.

Knight had been trying to reach an appointment about custody of her young son when Castro offered her a ride. He brought her to his house with the promise of a puppy for the boy.

She was his first captive. For months, she was alone with him.

In this interview, Dr. Phil asks what Castro meant by trust.

“Until I submitted to him.”

Knight explains that this meant obeying him and doing nothing he considered wrong, including trying to escape. Asked how she tried to make him less suspicious, she describes changing the things she said to him.

“You’re not bad. You’re just a little abnormal.”

She told him that everybody did something wrong, that there were places where he could get help, and that he could stop. These were words she chose while trying to survive the man controlling whether she could move, eat or leave the room.

On May 6, 2013, Berry’s cries for help brought a neighbor to the house. Police found Knight and DeJesus inside.

Castro pleaded guilty to 937 criminal counts. On August 1, 2013, he was sentenced to life without parole plus 1,000 years.
